systems.name: A/C or heat pump — cooling
systems.ok_note: Charge, airflow and pressures read normal. Check the thermostat or controller settings, duct leaks or closed registers, the indoor heat load, and whether the unit is simply undersized for the space.

systems.name: Heat pump — heating mode
systems.ok_note: The refrigerant side reads normal for heating. Check the thermostat staging (aux heat lockout), duct losses, and whether the outdoor temperature is below the unit's balance point.

systems.name: Walk-in cooler or freezer
systems.ok_note: The refrigeration circuit reads normal. Check door use and gaskets, warm product loaded recently, the controller setpoint and probe, and the defrost schedule.

systems.name: Reach-in, prep table or display case
systems.ok_note: The sealed system reads normal. Check door use and gaskets, loading (blocked air paths), the controller setpoint and probe placement, and the room temperature around the condenser.

systems.name: Ice machine
systems.ok_note: The refrigeration side reads normal. Check water supply and filters, water temperature, scale, the ice thickness setting, and the room temperature.

systems.name: Boiler & oil burner
systems.ok_note: The burner and boiler read normal. Check the call for heat and the distribution side (pumps, zone valves, air in the loop), and whether the load exceeds the boiler's rating.

systems.name: Oil-fired warm-air furnace
systems.ok_note: The burner and furnace read normal. Check the call for heat, the filter and ducts, and the blower.

systems.name: Hot-water & glycol loop
systems.ok_note: The loop reads normal. Check the heat source (boiler or heat recovery) and the controls calling the zone, and compare the load with what the terminal units can deliver.

systems.name: Steam heat & condensate
systems.ok_note: The steam side reads normal. Check the boiler's pressure control and water level, and the zone controls.

systems.name: Unit heater, fan coil or baseboard
systems.ok_note: The unit itself reads normal — hot water or steam reaches it, the valve opens, the coil heats evenly and the fan moves air (or the elements draw full current). Compare the unit's rating with the room's heat loss (doors, infiltration, a cold snap, an exhaust fan), check the thermostat setpoint and schedule, and if several units are short, work the loop or boiler in the Hydronic or Steam system.

systems.name: Air handler & ventilation
systems.ok_note: The air handler reads normal. Check the control sequence and setpoints, the zone loads, and the plant that feeds its coils.

context.ask: How is the fan driven?
context.hint: Belt and sheaves, or the wheel on the motor shaft (direct drive / plenum fan).

context.ask: Is there a VFD (variable-frequency drive) on the fan?
context.hint: A drive with a keypad and a frequency readout. Otherwise a starter or contactor runs the motor.

context.ask: What kind of unit is it — does it mix return air with outdoor air, take 100 % outdoor air, or recover heat from the exhaust?
context.hint: A makeup-air unit (MAU) has no return damper and no mixing box. An HRV or ERV passes outdoor air and exhaust air through a core or wheel without mixing them. The shares are rough, for units where this is not answered.

context.ask: Does it have an economizer (outdoor and return dampers that modulate for free cooling)?
context.hint: Modulating outdoor and return dampers that open up for free cooling. A fixed minimum-position damper on its own answers No.

context.ask: What heats the air?
context.hint: Glycol loops — check the fill records or test a sample; ethylene and propylene glycol freeze differently.

context.ask: What cools the air?
What fuel does it burn?
context.hint: No. 2 heating oil and No. 2 diesel wax up in the cold (around +10 to +20 °F). Kerosene, No. 1, JP-8, AN8 and arctic diesel stay fluid to about −40 °F, but below that, in outdoor tanks and lines, they can cloud too — check the lot's cloud point.

options.label: Kerosene, No. 1, JP-8 / AN8, arctic diesel

context.ask: How is the fuel unit piped?
context.hint: One-pipe has no return line (return port plugged, bypass plug out). Two-pipe has a return line and the bypass plug in. A two-stage pump has two gear sets.

context.ask: How does the primary control prove the flame?
context.hint: A CAD cell is the little photocell under the ignition transformer, looking down the air tube. A stack relay is a box clamped on the smoke pipe with a bimetal helix inside (older installations).

options.label: Stack relay / stack switch on the smoke pipe

context.ask: Hot-water or steam boiler?
context.hint: Steam boilers have a gauge glass and a pressuretrol; hot-water boilers have an aquastat, an expansion tank and a pressure/temperature gauge.

context.ask: What fluid is in the hydronic loop?
context.hint: Glycol loops use inhibited propylene glycol (PG) or ethylene glycol (EG) for freeze protection. Not sure? Leave it on Don't know and the glycol checks stay in play.

context.ask: What type of system is it?
context.hint: A conventional ducted split or packaged unit, a variable-speed (inverter) ducted system, or a ductless mini-split / multi-zone. Inverter boards and electronic expansion valves come with the last two. Flare joints, wall heads, condensate pumps and branch boxes come only with the ductless one. Strip heat, defrost boards and O/B thermostats belong to the ducted ones.

context.ask: Which mode energizes the reversing-valve coil?
context.hint: Meter the coil leads in cooling and in heating, or read the wiring diagram. Most US ducted splits energize it in cooling (thermostat terminal O). B-type units, and many ductless heads, energize it in heating. Go by the diagram or the meter, never by the brand name.

context.ask: What tells the equipment to run?
context.hint: A room thermostat (a mechanical one has a dial and a heat anticipator; a digital one has a screen and runs on batteries or a C wire), a building automation (DDC) controller, or only the unit's own control (a box controller or a set-point dial on the unit).

context.ask: Is it a heat pump (with a reversing valve) or cooling only?
context.hint: A heat pump has a 4-way reversing valve in the outdoor unit and an O or B wire at the thermostat.

context.ask: Which refrigerant?
context.hint: On the nameplate or the compressor sticker.

context.ask: What meters the refrigerant into the evaporator?
context.hint: A TXV has a sensing bulb strapped to the suction line. A piston sits in a brass fitting at the coil inlet. A cap tube is a long thin tube, usually in reach-ins.

context.ask: Is there a receiver tank with a sight glass?
context.hint: Common on walk-ins and commercial units; rare on home A/C, heat pumps and cap-tube reach-ins.

context.ask: What temperature does it run at?
Where are you reading the suction line temperature?
context.hint: Superheat targets differ. At the evaporator outlet (next to the TXV bulb) it should be small; at the condensing unit it is larger.

context.ask: How does the condenser reject heat?
How efficient is the outdoor unit?
context.hint: Sets the expected gap between condensing temperature and outdoor air.

context.ask: Does it have cold-weather head pressure control?
context.hint: A flooding valve (headmaster) near the receiver, fan-cycling switches, or a variable-speed condenser fan. Outdoor condensers in cold places almost always do.

context.ask: How does the evaporator defrost?
Is the compressor single-phase or three-phase?
context.hint: Nameplate. One run capacitor and two power leads is single-phase; three line leads (T1 T2 T3) and no capacitor is three-phase.

context.ask: What heats the unit?
context.hint: Hot water, glycol and steam come in pipes through a valve. Electric heaters have a power cord or conduit, a nameplate in kW, and no pipes.

context.ask: What kind of terminal unit is it?
context.hint: A unit heater hangs high with a propeller or blower. A cabinet unit heater sits in an entry or stairwell. A fan coil has a filter and a fan behind a room cabinet or above the ceiling; 2-pipe ones heat or cool on one coil, 4-pipe ones have separate heating and cooling coils. Baseboard, convectors and radiators have no fan.

options.label: Unit heater (propeller or blower, hung high)
Cabinet unit heater (entry, stairwell, wall or ceiling cabinet)
Fan coil, 2-pipe (one coil, heats or cools)
Baseboard, fin-tube, convector or radiator (no fan)

features.name: Fan
features.ask: Is the fan running?
features.how: Listen at the motor and watch the shaft or belt from outside the guard, or look through an inspection window or the inlet screen. A motor that runs with the wheel still means the belt (belt drive) or the wheel or coupling (direct drive). To look inside — stop the fan, lock out and tag it at the disconnect (on a VFD also wait out the bus-discharge time and verify zero), let the wheel stop, then open the door.
features.caution: Never open an access door or guard with the fan running — suction can pin the door shut, pressure can throw it open, and a spinning wheel takes a hand or a sleeve. "Power off" is not enough; lock out and tag, and wait for the wheel to stop.

states.motor_only: Motor runs but the wheel isn't turning
states.trips: Starts then trips, or hums and won't start

features.name: Motor starter
features.ask: What is the motor starter doing (with a run command present)?
features.how: Look at the contactor and the overload relay's trip flag, then meter line voltage in and out across each pole.
features.caution: Live voltage — qualified person only, with a properly rated meter and PPE, and the panel door closed where possible. Otherwise lock out and use continuity.

states.ok: Pulled in, full voltage out on every pole
states.burnt: Pulled in but a pole or fuse is open — voltage lost across it

features.name: VFD
features.ask: What does the VFD show?
features.how: Read the keypad or display with the drive door closed. Note any fault text, and whether it shows Hand/Local or Auto and a run command.
features.caution: Keep the drive door closed. To open a drive or touch its terminals, lock out, wait the maker's discharge time (several minutes) and verify zero volts on the DC bus — the capacitors stay charged after power is cut.

states.not_enabled: Powered up but stopped — no run command, in local/Hand, or stop/enable open

features.name: VFD fault type
features.ask: What kind of fault is the VFD showing?
features.how: Read the fault description, not just the code — every maker names them differently. Note what it was doing when it tripped (starting, slowing, running steady, hot afternoon).
features.caution: Don't keep resetting a drive that tripped on overcurrent or a ground fault — find the cause first. Opening the drive means lockout, the maker's discharge wait and a zero-volt check on the DC bus.

states.none: No fault shown
states.line: Undervoltage, phase loss or DC-bus overvoltage

features.name: VFD speed vs command
features.ask: Does the VFD's output frequency match what the controller is asking for?
features.how: Compare the drive's Hz readout with the speed reference the drive is actually receiving — read it on the keypad. A BAS percent does not always map 0–100 % onto 0–60 Hz, because most drives scale the reference between a minimum and a maximum frequency.
features.caution: Read the keypad with the drive door closed. Opening the drive means lockout, the maker's discharge wait and a zero-volt check on the DC bus.

states.low: Running below the command (by more than about 5 Hz)
states.fixed: Ignores the command — sits at one speed

features.name: Fan rotation
features.ask: Is the wheel turning the right way (arrow on the housing)?
features.how: With every door shut and latched and the guards on, watch the wheel through the inlet screen or an inspection window. Make sure nobody is in the unit, bump the starter (or jog the drive at low speed) once, and compare the direction with the arrow cast into the housing. A centrifugal wheel running backward still blows air — just much less of it.
features.caution: Never reach in or open a door to check rotation. Doors latched, guards on, and nobody inside the unit before you bump the starter or jog the drive.

features.name: Belt
features.ask: What condition is the belt in?
features.how: Lock out. Press the belt midway between the sheaves — about 1/64 in. of deflection per inch of span is right. Look for glazing (shiny sides), cracks, frayed cords, and dust under the drive.
features.caution: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the belt guard — a fan can start on a schedule.

states.ok: Tensioned, in good shape
states.worn: Cracked, frayed, or worn down into the groove

features.name: Sheaves and alignment
features.ask: Are the sheaves tight, aligned, and the right size / pitch setting?
features.how: Lock out first. Straightedge across both sheave faces for alignment. Try to rock each sheave on its shaft (key and set screws). On a variable-pitch motor sheave, count the turns open and compare with the record or the balancing report.
features.caution: Lock out before touching a sheave or opening the belt guard. Take RPM with a photo-tach on reflective tape fitted while locked out, never by reaching at a running shaft.

states.ok: Tight, aligned, as set
states.misaligned: Misaligned, or loose on its shaft
states.wrong: Pitch or size changed — fan speed no longer what the design calls for

features.name: Fan motor amps vs FLA
features.ask: What does the fan motor draw compared with its nameplate FLA, allowing for the speed it is running at?
features.how: Clamp the highest leg with the fan steady. Compare at full speed with the boxes open, or enter the drive's Hz — a fan the controller has slowed is supposed to read low (on a drive the draw falls roughly with the square of the speed). A motor that runs light with the wheel still points to the belt or the coupling.
features.caution: Live circuit — qualified person only, with a properly rated clamp and PPE. Don't open the panel or the drive to get at the leads if you can read them another way.

states.low: Low — under half of what this speed should draw (under 50 % of FLA at full speed)
states.normal: Normal
states.high: High — over FLA

features.name: Bearings
features.ask: How are the fan and motor bearings — spin, noise, heat?
features.how: Running (guards on, from outside) — listen on the stationary housing with a mechanic's stethoscope and read each housing with an IR thermometer. Compare with the bearing at the other end of the machine, and suspect one that runs much hotter than its twin, is over the maker's limit, or keeps climbing between visits. Then stop, lock out, and spin the wheel by hand — it should coast smoothly and silently.
features.caution: Never put a hand on the bearing or shaft of a running machine. Read it with an IR thermometer from outside the guards, and lock out before you spin anything by hand.

states.ok: Smooth, quiet, cool

features.name: Noise or vibration
features.ask: What does it sound or feel like?

states.normal: No unusual noise or vibration
states.squeal: Squeal or chirp, worst at start
states.vibration: Shaking — vibration you can feel in the housing or duct

features.name: Fan wheel
features.ask: What does the fan wheel look like — clean, loaded with dirt, or damaged?
features.how: Stop the fan, lock out and tag it, let the wheel stop, then open the fan section. Look at the blades for caked dirt (it comes off in flakes), cracks, bent blades, and a wheel that has walked on its shaft or lost a balance weight.
features.caution: Block the wheel before reaching into the housing — a wheel can turn from airflow or stack effect even with the motor locked out.

states.damaged: Damaged, bent, cracked, or loose on the shaft

features.name: Fan motor test
features.ask: What do the motor windings read (each lead to lead, each to ground; thermal protector)?
features.how: Lock out and disconnect the leads. Three-phase windings should read equal and low lead-to-lead; any lead to ground should be megohms. A single-phase motor whose protector has opened reads open until it cools. On a VFD, lock out, wait out the bus-discharge time and verify zero, then disconnect the motor leads at the drive's output terminals (T1/T2/T3) before any megger test — never megger through the drive.
features.caution: Verify dead at the motor leads before you touch them — a drive output can be live with the keypad showing stopped. Megger the motor and cable only with the leads off the drive.

states.ok: Windings balanced, open to ground
states.overheated: Hot — thermal protector open, reads normal after it cools

features.name: Three-phase supply
features.ask: Are all three phases present and balanced at the motor or drive terminals?
features.how: Meter each pair (L1–L2, L2–L3, L1–L3) with the unit trying to run. One pair far below the others, or a motor that growls and won't come up to speed, means a lost leg.
features.caution: Live voltage — qualified person only, with a properly rated meter and PPE, and the panel door closed where possible. At a drive's terminals, wait out the bus-discharge time before opening anything.

states.ok: All three present and within a few percent
states.phase_loss: One leg missing or far off

features.name: Safeties in the fan start circuit
features.ask: Is a safety or interlock in the fan start circuit open (other than the freezestat)?
features.how: Follow the start circuit through each device and meter across it — the open one shows voltage across its terminals. Typical devices are the duct smoke detector, high-static and low-static switches, the outdoor/isolation damper end switch, and a dirty-filter or door switch (the firestat and the freezestat sit in the same circuit, but the freezestat has its own check).
features.caution: Live voltage — qualified person only, with a properly rated meter and PPE, and the door closed where possible; otherwise lock out and use continuity. Never jumper a device in the start circuit to get the fan running.

states.other: Another interlock open (filter, door, remote stop, fire alarm relay)

features.name: Freezestat / low limit
features.ask: Has the freezestat (low-temperature limit) tripped?
features.how: Most are manual reset — a button on the stat. Note whether the reset held, or it trips again within minutes. After a freeze trip, inspect the coil for bulged bends and split tubes before restoring flow or restarting the pump; if any are found, isolate the coil and follow the frozen-coil cause. A stat that won't reset has an element still below setpoint — the coil is cold. Don't hold the button or jumper it.
features.caution: A freezestat trip is the unit protecting its coil. Never jumper, tape or hold the stat to keep the fan running; reset it only once the coil is warm and you know why it tripped.

states.ok: Freezestat not tripped
states.tripped: Found tripped — reset it and it stayed reset
states.retrips: Trips again after reset, or won't reset (element still cold)

features.name: Freezestat setpoint and element
features.ask: Check the freezestat itself — setpoint, element routing and condition?
features.how: Compare its setpoint (usually 35–38 °F — the drawing's figure rules) with the coldest spot you can measure where the element runs. Follow the capillary — one long element zig-zagged across the leaving-air face of the first water (preheat) coil, about 1 ft of element per ft² of face (follow the maker's sheet), without touching the casing or hanging in the outdoor-air stream. It trips on its coldest section, not on an average. A stat in the mixed-air plenum ahead of a preheat coil sits under setpoint every cold day by design and will trip on all of them, so move it. Check the element for kinks and continuity.
features.caution: Don't lower the setpoint, add a delay or jumper the stat to stop a trip — that hides a real cold spot and leaves the coil unprotected.

states.ok: Setpoint reasonable, element intact and routed across the leaving face of the coil
states.set_high: Set above its design value, or the element sits ahead of the preheat coil, on cold metal or in the outdoor stream
states.element_bad: Element kinked, broken, lost its charge, or too short — a bulb or short capillary where a long capillary covering the whole face belongs

features.name: Filters
features.ask: What do the filters look like?
features.caution: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the filter section — a running fan pins the door shut or slams it, and pulls at loose clothing.

states.ok: Clean enough, seated, dry
states.loaded: Loaded with dirt — pressure drop at or past the filters' final rating
states.bypass: Missing, collapsed, or gaps around them — air bypassing

features.name: Fan static vs design
features.ask: What is the fan's own static pressure rise (discharge minus inlet, across the fan — not the duct static the BAS shows) compared with design?
features.how: Manometer across the fan — inlet side (after filters and coils on a draw-through) to discharge — through the test ports or fittings. High static with low air means a restriction somewhere; low static with low air means the fan isn't producing. Compare with design at full speed with the boxes open, or enter the drive's Hz — a fan the controller has slowed is supposed to read low (about design times the square of the speed ratio). On a VAV system holding a duct-static setpoint it falls less than that, so treat the corrected figure as a floor. A moderate upstream restriction (filters, coil, intake) moves the fan's static rise by only 5–20 % — find it from the ΔP across that item. Static 25 % or more over design with low airflow means a big restriction or a closed damper. A fan handling −40 °F air should read about 1.26 times its design static.
features.caution: Use the test ports or fittings. Never open a door on a running fan to place a manometer hose.

states.low: Low — under 70 % of design for this speed, fan not producing
states.normal: Normal — 70 to 125 % of design for this speed
states.high: High — over 125 % of design for this speed, working against a restriction

features.name: Dampers in the air path
features.ask: Are the dampers in the supply and return path open — fire/smoke dampers, isolation dampers, balancing dampers, VAV boxes?
features.how: Check fire/smoke damper indicators and access doors, isolation damper blades, and whether the VAV boxes are all driven to minimum (a VAV system can starve the fan when every box closes).
features.caution: A duct access door sees the same suction or pressure as the unit's doors. Stop the fan and lock out before opening one, and never reach into a duct to reset a fire damper.

states.closed: One or more closed or dropped

features.name: Coil face (air side)
features.ask: What does the air-entering face of the coil look like?
features.caution: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the coil section.

states.dirty: Matted with dirt, lint or dust
states.snow: Snow, frost or ice packed in the fins

features.name: Outdoor intake
features.ask: Is the outdoor intake clear — hood, louver, bird screen, snow fence?
features.caution: In high wind or blowing snow don't work at the intake alone. Stay clear of the louver face while the fan runs (it pulls hard), and mind your footing on drifts and ice.

states.blocked: Blocked — snow, ice, debris, or a clogged screen

features.name: Coil damage (frozen)
features.ask: Are any coil tubes, headers or return bends split or bulged, or wet with water or glycol?
features.how: Stop the fan and lock out, then open the coil section and look at the headers and return bends — a frozen coil bulges the bends and splits tubes near the headers. Wet fins or glycol on the floor of the section tell the same story.
features.caution: Lock out the fan first so the coil isn't fed cold air while it's open, and never open the section on a running fan. A thawing coil can dump its loop, and glycol on the floor is slippery.

states.yes: Split or bulged tubes — coil frozen

features.name: Supply air vs setpoint
features.ask: How does the supply (discharge) air temperature compare with its setpoint?
features.how: Reference thermometer in the supply duct, a few feet past the fan, against the controller's setpoint. Within about 3 °F is holding.

states.low: Supply air more than 3 °F colder than setpoint
states.ok: Supply air within 3 °F of setpoint
states.high: Supply air more than 3 °F warmer than setpoint

features.name: Mixed air vs return and outdoor
features.ask: Does the mixed-air temperature sit between the return and outdoor temperatures?
features.how: Mixed air can only be a blend of return and outdoor air, so it must land between them. Traverse the mixed-air plenum with a long probe through the test ports — a single spot can be in a cold or warm stream.
features.caution: Probe from outside through the test ports. Don't open a mixing-box door with the fan running.

states.outside: Outside the pair — colder than both or warmer than both (by more than 3 °F)

features.name: Outdoor-air fraction vs expected
features.ask: What outdoor-air fraction is the unit actually taking compared with what it should be taking?
features.how: Fraction = (mixed − return) ÷ (outdoor − return), using return and outdoor temperatures at least 10 °F apart (the wider the spread, the better the reading). Compare with the design minimum fraction when the damper is at minimum, about 100 % when it is commanded full open, and about 0 % when it is closed. A part-open blade position is not an air fraction.
features.caution: Probe from outside through the test ports. Don't open a mixing-box door with the fan running.

states.low: Much less outdoor air than expected (short by more than about 10–30 points; the allowance grows as the return–outdoor spread shrinks)
states.ok: About as expected
states.high: Much more outdoor air than expected (over by more than about 10–30 points)

high: 100 percent outside air when it shouldnt

features.name: Outdoor-air damper vs command
features.ask: Does the outdoor-air damper actually move with its command, and does it seal when it is closed?
features.how: Stop and lock out the fan before you open the mixing-box door — never open it with the fan running. Drive the damper from the BAS or the actuator's manual override and watch the blades through the intake louver or the door, and the actuator shaft. Note where it sits when it won't move, and with it commanded closed look for daylight or a draft along the blade edges and jambs.
features.caution: Never open the mixing-box door with the fan running. Spring-return actuators and damper blades store energy — keep fingers out of the linkage.

states.open_stuck: Sits open — won't close on command
states.closed_stuck: Sits closed — won't open on command
states.lagging: Partly follows — blades lag or stop short of the actuator
states.leaks: Shuts on command but leaks — daylight or a draft at the blade edges, frost on the seals

leaks: outside air leaking in when off

features.name: Damper stroke test
features.ask: With the fan locked out and the damper supported, unhook the linkage — do the blades move freely by hand, and does the actuator stroke on command with a signal at its terminals?
features.how: Lock out the fan first. Meter the control signal (0–10 V, 4–20 mA or 24 V floating) at the actuator while the BAS commands it, then support the damper, unhook the linkage, stroke the actuator and swing the blades by hand.
features.caution: A spring-return actuator and the damper blades store energy. Support the damper before you unhook the linkage, and keep fingers out of the linkage when releasing an override.

states.ok: Blades free, actuator strokes, signal present
states.blades_bound: Blades bound — frozen, iced, jammed, bent or seized pivots
states.actuator_dead: Signal present but the actuator doesn't stroke
states.no_signal: No control signal (or no power) at the actuator
states.linkage: Actuator strokes, blades don't follow — linkage or crank arm slipped

linkage: set screw slipped on damper shaft

features.name: Return-air damper
features.ask: Does the return-air damper move with its command?
features.caution: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the mixing-box door — never open it with the fan running.

states.stuck_closed: Stuck closed — unit pulls nearly all outdoor air
states.stuck_open: Stuck open — short on outdoor air

features.name: Economizer mode vs outdoor conditions
features.ask: Is the economizer in the right mode for the outdoor conditions?
features.how: Outdoor air below (supply setpoint − fan heat) should mean dampers open for free cooling with no mechanical cooling. Between that and the changeover (outdoor cooler than return, or under the dry-bulb or enthalpy high limit) the dampers stay at 100 % and mechanical cooling trims — that is correct, not a fault. Above the changeover the unit should be at minimum outdoor air with mechanical cooling. The faults are dampers past minimum with outdoor air above the changeover; minimum outdoor air with mechanical cooling while outdoor air is below it; and dampers past minimum while heating (unless CO₂ demand ventilation is calling for it).

states.ok: Right mode for the conditions
states.econ_when_hot: Dampers open for free cooling while outdoor air is above the changeover
states.mech_when_cool: Mechanical cooling at minimum outdoor air while outdoor air is below the changeover
states.heating_with_econ: Heating while the dampers are open past minimum (and no demand-ventilation call)

econ_when_hot: free cooling with hot outside air
mech_when_cool: compressor running when its cold out

features.name: Heating and cooling at once
features.ask: Are the heating and cooling both active at the same time (both valves open, or heat and DX together)?

yes: heating and cooling at the same time

features.name: Hunting / mode cycling
features.ask: Does the supply temperature or a valve swing back and forth (hunting), or does the unit flip modes several times an hour?

features.name: Sensor check against a reference
features.ask: Compare the BAS temperature readings with a reference thermometer — which one is off?
features.how: Hold a known-good thermometer at each sensor (supply, mixed, outdoor, return) and compare with the BAS value. More than about 1–1.5 °F off a reference you trust, stuck flat, or reading an impossible value means the sensor. For duct static, compare the transducer's reading with a manometer on the same tap.
features.caution: Reach sensors from outside or through the test ports. Don't open a door on a running fan to hold a thermometer at a sensor.

states.all_agree: All agree with the reference (within about 1–1.5 °F)
states.mat_off: Mixed-air sensor off (or in a stratified stream)
states.oat_off: Outdoor-air sensor off (in the sun, on a warm wall, in an exhaust plume, or iced)
states.static_off: Duct-static reading disagrees with a manometer at the same tap

mat_off: mixed air sensor in cold spot

features.name: Air rise across the heating coil
features.ask: How much does the air warm across the heating coil, compared with what the valve (or stage) command should give?
features.how: Thermometer before and after the coil. With the valve commanded wide open, expect the design rise; with it commanded closed, expect none.
features.caution: Probe through test holes or ports. Don't open a coil or mixing-box door with the fan running.

states.none: No rise with heat commanded (under 3 °F)
states.low: Well under what the command should give (less than half)
states.normal: Rise matches the command

none: no delta t across heating coil

features.name: Air drop across the cooling coil
features.ask: How much does the air cool across the cooling coil, compared with what the command should give?
features.caution: Probe through test holes or ports. Don't open a coil or mixing-box door with the fan running.

states.none: No drop with cooling commanded (under 3 °F)
states.low: Well under what the command should give (less than half)
states.normal: Drop matches the command

none: no delta t across cooling coil
unwanted: cooling coil sweating with no call

features.name: Heat supply at the coil
features.ask: Is hot water, glycol or steam actually arriving at the coil (supply pipe hot)?
features.how: Strap a thermometer on the supply pipe at the coil, upstream of the valve, or read it with an IR thermometer. Don't put a hand on hot-water, glycol or steam piping. A steam coil's supply should read at or above about 212 °F.
features.caution: Hot piping — read it with a thermometer, never with a bare hand. Steam, hot water and glycol scald, and glycol loops run hot and under pressure.

states.warm: Lukewarm — 80 to 110 °F, plant running low or loop barely circulating
states.cold: Cold — under 80 °F, nothing coming from the plant

features.name: Water/glycol ΔT across the coil
features.ask: How does the return pipe compare with the supply pipe at the coil?
features.how: Read both pipes at the coil with a contact or IR thermometer, never with a bare hand. Supply hot and return barely cooler means plenty of flow and little load; return far colder than supply means flow is starved; both the same with no air heating means no heat is being taken. Only meaningful with the valve at least 20 % open and the fan running.
features.caution: Hot piping — read it with a thermometer, never with a bare hand.

states.normal: Return 10–40 °F cooler than supply (close to the coil's design ΔT)
states.high: Return far colder than supply (over about 40 °F, or well over the design ΔT) — flow starved
states.none: Return as hot as supply (under 3 °F apart) — no heat being taken

features.name: Heating valve vs command
features.ask: What is the heating valve commanded to do, and what is it actually doing?
features.how: Read the command on the BAS (or the signal), then look at the stem and position indicator and read the pipe temperature after the valve with a thermometer. Don't put a hand on the piping.
features.caution: Hot piping — read it with a thermometer, never with a bare hand.

states.saturated: Commanded 100 % open and setpoint still not met
states.not_moving: Commanded open but it isn't moving
states.leaking: Commanded closed but hot water still passes — pipe after the valve hot

saturated: valve fully open and still cold

features.name: Valve actuator test
features.ask: With the valve commanded open — is there a signal at the actuator, does the actuator stroke, and does the stem move freely with the actuator off?
features.how: Meter the control signal at the actuator (0–10 V, 4–20 mA, or 24 V floating/spring return). Run the manual override or power the actuator directly and watch the stem. To work the stem by hand, lock out the actuator power first and then pull the actuator.
features.caution: Lock out the actuator power before pulling an actuator — a spring-return valve can swing fully open, and the stem packing can weep hot water or glycol.

states.ok: Signal present, actuator strokes, stem free
states.no_signal: No control signal or power at the actuator
states.stem_stuck: Actuator strokes but the stem is seized or the valve is jammed

features.name: Chilled water at the coil
features.ask: Is chilled water arriving cold at the coil (supply pipe cold and sweating)?

states.warm: Warm — nothing cold coming from the plant

features.name: Chilled-water valve vs command
features.ask: What is the chilled-water valve commanded to do, and what is it actually doing?

states.saturated: Commanded 100 % open and setpoint still not met
states.not_moving: Commanded open but it isn't moving
states.leaking: Commanded closed but chilled water still passes — pipe after the valve cold

features.name: Strainer at the coil
features.ask: Is the strainer ahead of the coil (or the coil itself) plugged?
features.how: Isolate, relieve the pressure, drain the strainer body and pull the screen. Scale, rust and sludge pack the screen first; a strainer with blow-down valves can be checked by the pressure drop across it. A steam coil's strainer holds live steam and condensate — isolate and relieve first.
features.caution: Isolate both sides and relieve pressure before opening a strainer — hot water, glycol and steam scald.

features.name: Air in the coil
features.ask: Open the coil's air vent slowly, with a hose to a bucket — what comes out first?
features.how: Vent at the top of the coil or return header. Open the vent slowly with a hose run to a bucket, and wear a face shield on a hot loop. Air hissing out before solid water means an air pocket.
features.caution: A hot loop is under pressure — open the vent slowly, hose to a bucket, face shield on.

states.water: Solid water or glycol right away

air: air in the loop at the coil

features.name: Glycol strength vs the air it sees
features.ask: Is the glycol strong enough for the coldest air the coil sees (or is it plain water)?
features.how: Refractometer on a sample from the coil's vent or drain — open it slowly, hose to a bucket, face shield on, since a hot loop is under pressure — read against the right scale (ethylene or propylene). The freeze point should be at least 9 °F (5 °C) below the coldest air that can reach the coil; glycol makers typically ask for several degrees of margin under the lowest expected temperature. Use the design low or the coldest night on record, whichever is colder — −40 °F at McMurdo is a floor, not a ceiling. A loop with no glycol in it at all is plain water.
features.caution: A hot loop is under pressure — open the vent or drain slowly, hose to a bucket, face shield on.

states.adequate: Freeze point at least 9 °F (5 °C) under the coldest air the coil sees
states.weak: Too weak — freeze point within 9 °F of the coldest air, or above it
states.none: No glycol at all — plain water in the loop

features.name: Stratification at the coil
features.ask: Traverse the mixed-air plenum or the coil face with a thermometer — is there a cold layer or stream (more than about 10 °F spread)?
features.caution: Probe from outside through the test ports. Don't open a mixing-box or coil door with the fan running.

states.stratified: Stratified — a cold stream or layer

features.name: Space temperature / air quality
features.ask: How is the space it serves?

states.ok: Space comfortable
states.stuffy: Space stuffy or stale — poor ventilation

features.name: Building / space pressure
features.ask: How is the space pressure — neutral, negative (pulling in) or positive (pushing out)?
features.how: Crack an exterior door and feel the air; a tissue at the gap or a smoke pencil tells the direction. A manometer across the envelope settles it (±0.02 in. w.c. is about neutral).
features.caution: In a strongly negative or positive building a door can slam or pull the handle out of your hand — hold it with both hands and keep fingers clear of the frame.

states.negative: Negative — air pulls in at doors and cracks
states.positive: Positive — air pushes out, doors blow open

features.name: Exhaust vs makeup air
features.ask: Are the exhaust fans serving this space running, and is the makeup/supply air running with them?

states.balanced: Both running (or both off) as scheduled
states.exh_only: Exhaust running with the makeup/supply unit off or throttled
states.makeup_only: Supply/makeup running with the exhaust fan off

features.name: Cold outdoor air
features.ask: Is the outdoor air below about 35 °F?

features.name: Electric heat stages
features.ask: With a call for heat, are the electric heat stages energizing (amps on each stage)?
features.how: Clamp each stage's leads with the stage commanded on. Check the airflow switch or sail switch proves first — electric heat is locked out without airflow.
features.caution: Live heater leads — qualified person only, with a properly rated clamp and PPE. Never jumper the airflow (sail) switch or a high limit to force heat or to test.

states.all_on: Every stage draws amps when commanded

features.name: BAS fan status vs the fan
features.ask: Does the BAS fan status (run proof) agree with what the fan is actually doing?
features.how: Compare the BAS status point and any fan-failure alarm with the wheel and the motor amps. A run-status point is usually a current switch on a motor lead or a differential-pressure switch across the fan; if it says off while the wheel turns and the motor draws normal amps, the proof device is wrong, not the fan.
features.caution: Live circuit — qualified person only, with a properly rated clamp and PPE. Look at the wheel from outside; never open a door on a running fan.

states.agrees: Status matches what the fan is doing
states.says_off: BAS says the fan is off or failed, but the wheel is turning
states.says_on: BAS says the fan is running, but the wheel is stopped

features.name: Fan motor capacitor
features.ask: On a single-phase fan motor, what does the run or start capacitor test as?
features.how: Lock out, then discharge the capacitor through a resistor before touching it. Meter µF with the leads off — it should be within the tolerance printed on the label (commonly about ±6 %). A bulged, leaking or burnt can fails regardless of its reading. Skip this check on a three-phase motor.
features.caution: A capacitor holds a charge after the power is off. Lock out, then discharge it through a resistor before you touch it.

states.ok: In range, or this motor has no capacitor

features.name: Condensate drain, trap and pan
features.ask: Is the condensate drain flowing — pan, trap and line clear?
features.how: With the fan stopped and locked out, look at the pan and the drain, pour a little water in and watch it go. On a draw-through unit the trap's inlet leg has to be at least the unit's negative static (in. w.c.) plus 1 in., and primed — a trap that is too shallow gets sucked dry and the pan overflows. Look for ice in a drain line that runs through cold space.
features.caution: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the coil section to look at the pan.

states.free: Draining freely — pan clear, trap primed, line open
states.blocked: Plugged, trap seal lost or too shallow, pan overflowing, or the line frozen

features.name: Steam coil condensate
features.ask: Is the steam coil draining its condensate — trap cycling, return line warm, coil hot top to bottom?
features.how: With the coil running, read the bottom of the coil and the trap outlet with an IR thermometer, and listen for hammering or gurgling. A cold bottom with a hot supply, or a banging coil, means condensate is backing up. Check the vacuum breaker on a modulating steam valve.
features.caution: Steam and condensate scald. Isolate and relieve before opening a trap, strainer or union, and read pipes with a thermometer, never a bare hand.

states.draining: Draining — trap cycling, coil hot top to bottom
states.backed_up: Backed up — bottom of the coil cold, banging or gurgling, trap or return blocked

features.name: Recovery core condition
features.ask: What does the heat-recovery core (or wheel) and its filters look like — clean, dirty or plugged, frosted or iced?
features.how: Look at the air passages on both faces of the core and at the filters ahead of it. Frost and ice build on the exhaust side where warm, wet air meets the cold core; lint, dust or grease plugs the passages. Note whether the supply airflow dropped off as the core iced.
features.caution: Stop both fans, lock out and tag, and let any wheel stop before opening the core section. Don't chip or pry at ice with tools — plates and fins cut and crush easily.

states.clean: Clean — passages open, filters in good shape
states.dirty: Dirty or plugged — loaded filters, or dust, lint or grease in the core
states.frosted: Frosted or iced — frost or ice built up on the core

features.name: HRV/ERV defrost cycle
features.ask: How is the defrost cycle behaving?
features.how: Watch one full cycle if you can. Defrost methods vary (supply fan off with the exhaust running, a recirculation damper, or an electric preheater), but the unit should start one when the core frosts, run it for a few minutes, and return to normal. Note whether it ever starts, and whether it ever finishes.
features.caution: Watch from outside, through the inspection window. Dampers and fans change state on their own during defrost — don't open the core section while the unit is running.

states.ok: Defrosts when it should and returns to normal
states.stuck: Stuck in defrost — recirculating or throttled for long periods
states.never: Never goes into defrost, even with ice on the core

stuck: hrv in defrost all the time

features.name: Recovery wheel
features.ask: On a wheel-type unit, is the recovery wheel turning?
features.how: Watch the wheel through the inspection window, or check the wheel motor's rotation indicator or sensor on the controller. A healthy wheel turns slowly and steadily; stopped, jerky or slow points at the drive. A plate core has no wheel — skip this check.
features.caution: Never reach in to feel or turn a wheel. Stop the unit and lock out first, and keep hands clear of the rim and the drive belt.

states.stopped: Stopped — drive motor silent, or running with the wheel still (belt off or slipping)

features.name: HRV/ERV bypass or recirculation damper
features.ask: Does the core's bypass (or recirculation) damper go where it is commanded?
features.how: Compare the damper position with the unit's command. In cold weather it should stay closed except during defrost, and in mild weather it opens to skip the core. Look for an iced edge or a slipped linkage.
features.caution: Stop the unit and lock out before opening a door or reaching at the damper — actuators and springs store energy.

states.open_stuck: Stuck open or leaking — supply air passes around the core
states.closed_stuck: Stuck closed or iced shut — won't open for defrost or free cooling

features.name: HRV/ERV supply vs exhaust airflow
features.ask: How do the supply and exhaust airflows through the core compare?
features.how: Measure both ducts (flow hood, traverse, or the unit's balancing ports and a manometer per the maker's data). They should be close to equal; a ratio far from 1 to 1 starves the core of effectiveness and swings the building pressure. Note which side is low — low supply pulls the building negative, low exhaust pushes it positive.
features.caution: Measure through the test ports or from outside. Don't open a core or filter door with the fans running.

states.unbalanced: Well out of balance — supply and exhaust differ by a lot (supply low, or exhaust low)

features.name: Recovery effectiveness
features.ask: How much of the temperature difference is the core recovering?
features.how: With the unit running steady in cold weather, read outdoor air, supply air leaving the core and exhaust air entering the core at the same moment, and enter them in the readings. Effectiveness = (supply leaving the core − outdoor) ÷ (exhaust entering the core − outdoor). Compare with the maker's rating; this check only flags a clearly poor core.
features.caution: Probe through the test ports or from outside. Don't open a core or filter door with the fans running.

states.low: Low — under about 50 %, well below the rated figure
states.normal: In the normal range

features.name: Lockout
features.ask: Is the primary control locking out (red light, reset button)?
features.how: Reset ONCE and watch one start, and keep count of the resets. A lockout that comes back has just pumped oil for the full safety time, so find what is stopping the flame before you reset again — no restart until the cause is known (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).
features.caution: Reset once only, and keep count. Every failed try sprays oil for the full safety time. Before any further reset, look into the chamber with the burner off — liquid oil, or a glowing or smoldering floor, means no relight until the oil is removed, the chamber has cooled and the vapor has cleared.

states.once: Locked out once or now and then — ran again after one reset
states.repeats: Locks out again on every try or within minutes

once: locks out once in a while

features.name: Burner on a call
features.ask: Watch one start — what does the burner do on a call for heat?
features.how: Turn the thermostat up or jumper T–T at the primary control and watch through the inspection port. Watch one start, not several. With a CO complaint, do not cycle the burner until the flue and vent are proven clear.
features.caution: One start only. If it fails to light and locks out, do not keep resetting — look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause first. Stand to the side of the inspection port, and with a CO complaint keep the burner off until the flue and vent are proven clear.

states.normal: Lights within a few seconds and runs steady
states.nothing: Nothing happens on a call — the burner motor never runs
states.no_flame: Motor runs but no flame — then locks out
states.flame_lost: Lights, then the flame drops out or it locks out later
states.delayed: Lights late — a puff, bang or rumble at light-off

flame_lost: runs a minute then locks out

features.name: Flame appearance
features.ask: With the burner running, what does the flame look like through the inspection port?
features.how: Wait a minute after light-off. A good gun-burner flame is bright yellow-orange with a defined shape, steady, and clear of the chamber walls.
features.caution: Look from the side, not straight into the port, and keep the port closed except to look. After a puff, bang or misfire, shut the burner off and check the chamber for liquid oil before you try another start.

states.normal: Bright yellow-orange, steady, clear of the chamber walls
states.stringy: Sparky, stringy or one-sided — streaks of raw oil
states.impinging: Hits the chamber wall or floor — bright spot, carbon on the brick

impinging: flame too big for the chamber

features.name: After-drip
features.ask: When the burner shuts off, does the flame hang on, smoke, rumble or drip oil (after-drip)?

states.yes: After-drip — flame hangs on, smokes or drips at shutdown

features.name: Oil smell
features.ask: Is there a fuel-oil or kerosene smell around the unit or in the building?

features.name: Soot or smoke outside the appliance
features.ask: Is soot or smoke getting out of the appliance — on the jacket, at the draft regulator, in the room?

states.yes: Soot or smoke outside the appliance

features.name: Fuel pump noise
features.ask: Is the fuel pump noisy — whine, growl or chatter?

features.name: Oil leak
features.ask: Is oil leaking anywhere — pump shaft, filter, fittings, nozzle line, under the burner?
features.caution: Oil on a hot burner housing or in the chamber is a fire hazard. Close the oil supply valve at the tank and kill burner power before you touch anything.

features.name: CO in the building
features.ask: Has a CO alarm gone off or has CO been measured in the building or the supply air?
features.caution: If CO is confirmed, ventilate and shut the burner off before you troubleshoot. Do not cycle the burner until the flue and vent are proven clear.

states.yes: CO alarm or CO measured in the building

features.name: Burner motor
features.ask: With voltage at the motor, what does the burner motor do — and does the shaft turn freely by hand?
features.how: Power off to spin it. Try the motor shaft or fan wheel by hand with the coupling on, then with it off; a seized pump binds the shaft only while coupled.
features.caution: Power off and locked out before you turn the shaft, coupling or fan wheel by hand.

states.hums_bound: Hums or trips its overload — shaft hard to turn (seized pump or motor bearings)
states.hums_free: Hums or trips — shaft turns freely (start winding, capacitor or overload)
states.silent: Voltage present, silent — open winding or open thermal protector

features.name: Voltage to the burner motor
features.ask: Does the primary control put line voltage out to the burner motor on a call?
features.how: Meter the motor leads (orange/black on most primaries to white) with the thermostat calling and the control reset.

missing: no power to the burner motor

features.name: Line voltage into the primary control
features.ask: Is there line voltage into the primary control (through the limit and safety string)?
features.how: Meter the primary's hot-in (black) to white. Missing here with power at the service switch means a limit, LWCO or other safety is open — check each one.

states.missing: Missing — a limit or safety ahead of it is open

missing: no voltage to the primary control

features.name: Call at the primary (T–T)
features.ask: Is the call for heat reaching the primary control — T–T closed, or the burner starts when you jumper T–T?
features.how: Jumper T to T at the primary for a few seconds only, then take the jumper off. If the burner starts, the thermostat, zone relay, end switch or interlock upstream is the problem; if not, the primary or its power is.
features.caution: On a boiler, confirm the circulator is running before you jumper T–T — a zone valve or flow interlock may be open to keep the boiler from firing with no flow. Jumper for a few seconds, watch one start, and take the jumper off; if it fails to light, do not keep resetting.

states.no: No call at T–T (runs when T–T is jumpered)

features.name: Polarity at the burner
features.ask: Is hot/neutral polarity correct at the primary control (hot on black, neutral on white, ground good)?
features.how: Meter black to ground (should read line voltage) and white to ground (should read near zero). Modern primaries are polarity-sensitive and misbehave or lock out when reversed.

states.ok: Correct

features.name: Ignition spark
features.ask: Does the ignition transformer / igniter throw a strong arc across the electrode tips?
features.how: Take the oil away first — oil supply valve closed at the tank, the oil solenoid unplugged if there is one, and, if the primary allows it, the motor leads lifted so the pump does not turn. Oil still in the pump and line can reach the nozzle in the first seconds, so wipe the drawer assembly dry. Then, with the assembly out, start the burner for a moment only and watch the gap. Use an igniter tester or the burner maker's method on solid-state igniters — don't arc them by hand.
features.caution: Oil off before the igniter is live — supply valve closed, solenoid unplugged, and the pump not turning if you can lift the motor leads. An arc beside a spraying nozzle is a fire. There are 10,000 V or more at the electrodes, so keep hands clear, and never arc a solid-state igniter by hand.

states.none: No arc

features.name: Electrodes
features.ask: How do the electrodes look — gap and position to the burner's spec card, porcelain intact, tips clean?
features.how: Typical settings are a 1/8–5/32 in. gap with the tips just ahead of and above the nozzle, out of the spray. Look for cracked or carbon-tracked porcelain, burnt tips, carbon bridging, loose clamps.

states.ok: Set to spec, porcelain clean and intact
states.off_spec: Gap or position off spec, tips worn back
states.damaged: Cracked or carbon-tracked porcelain, carboned or bridged tips

features.name: Nozzle
features.ask: What does the nozzle look like, and does it match the rating plate (gph at rated pressure, angle, pattern)?
features.how: Pull it with a nozzle wrench. Check the stamping against the appliance plate and the burner's spec. Replace, don't clean in the field; never put a metal needle in the orifice (TM 5-642 ¶3-13b).

states.ok: Clean, correct size, angle and pattern
states.plugged: Plugged or dirty — carbon or sludge on the face, strainer loaded
states.worn: Worn or eroded orifice, bad spray pattern
states.wrong: Wrong size, angle or pattern for the appliance

features.name: Motor-to-pump coupling
features.ask: Is the coupling between the motor and the fuel pump intact and driving the pump?

states.ok: Intact, drives the pump

features.name: Combustion chamber
features.ask: How does the combustion chamber / refractory look through the port?
features.how: Burner off first. Look for liquid oil on the floor, carbon, cracks or a collapsed liner, and for a floor that is glowing or smoldering.
features.caution: Burner off and the chamber cool before the port or door is opened; stand to the side. Liquid oil, or a glowing or smoldering floor, means no relight — remove the oil, let it cool and let the vapor clear first.

states.ok: Sound and clean

carbon_oil: puddle of oil in the chamber

features.name: Fuel supply at the tank
features.ask: Is there fuel in the tank and is the supply valve (and fusible-link fire valve) open?
features.how: Stick the tank or check the gauge against a stick — gauges stick. The spring-loaded fire valve above the burner closes when its fusible link lets go; look for a tripped lever.
features.caution: A tripped fire valve means its fusible link let go — look for fire or a heat source at the burner before you reset it, and don't reset it with oil leaking.

states.ok: Fuel present, valves open
states.empty: Tank empty or below the pickup
states.valve_closed: Supply valve or fire valve closed

features.name: Tank vent
features.ask: Is the tank vent open — does air move at the vent cap, and does the pump vacuum fall when the vent is cleared?
features.how: Look at the vent cap for rime, ice, snow or a screen packed with frost. A vent whistle that has gone silent, or air rushing in when you crack the fill cap, means the vent is plugged and the tank is pulling a vacuum.
features.caution: No flame, torch or heat gun at a tank vent — there is fuel vapor there. Thaw a frozen vent with warm water or warm rags.

states.blocked: Blocked — frost, ice, snow or a pinched vent line

blocked: air rushes in at the fill cap

features.name: Fuel filter / strainer
features.ask: What's in the fuel filter and the pump strainer?
features.caution: Oil supply valve closed before a filter or strainer is opened. Catch the oil and wipe up every spill before the burner runs again.

states.clogged: Clogged with sludge, rust or dirt
states.waxed_iced: Coated with wax, slush or ice

features.name: Fuel sample
features.ask: What does a fuel sample from the filter bowl or tank bottom look like?
features.how: Drain a little into a clear jar and let it settle. Water sits on the bottom as a clear layer or shows as ice crystals; waxed fuel is cloudy or jelled; bad fuel is dark with sediment or stringy growth.

features.name: Pump pressure
features.ask: What does a gauge on the pump's pressure port read with the burner running?
features.how: Gauge in the gauge port or nozzle port. Most pumps are set at 100 psi; many newer burners run 140–150 — check the burner's spec. The needle should be steady, and drop sharply to a held cutoff pressure at shutdown. Pressure that comes up to spec on a start and holds at cutoff also proves oil is leaving the pump.
features.caution: Fit the gauge with the burner off and the oil supply valve closed, and check it for leaks before the burner runs. Oil leaves a loose gauge or bleed port at pump pressure (100 psi or more) and can go through skin. Read the needle at the start; if it will not light, shut down — no repeated tries.

states.normal: At spec (within about 10 psi) and steady
states.low: Low — more than about 10 psi below spec
states.high: High — more than about 10 psi above spec

features.name: Pump vacuum
features.ask: What does a vacuum gauge on the pump inlet read with the burner running?
features.how: Expect roughly 1 in. Hg per foot of lift plus 1 per 10 ft of horizontal run. How much a pump may pull depends on its piping — about 6 in. Hg on a one-pipe system (above that, air comes out of the oil), about 10 on a two-pipe single-stage pump, about 15 on a two-stage; the pump's data sheet rules. Over its limit is a restriction (filter, valve, kinked or frozen line, iced tank vent, thick or gelled fuel), and so is a reading well above what the lift explains. Near zero with real lift means air is getting in. On shutdown the needle should hold — a steady fall is a suction-side air leak.
features.caution: With the tank above the burner, close the oil supply valve before the vacuum-gauge plug comes out, or oil runs out of the port. Wipe up before the burner runs.

states.normal: Normal for the lift, holds on shutdown
states.high: High — over the pump's limit (about 6 in. Hg one-pipe, 10 two-pipe single-stage, 15 two-stage) or well above what the lift explains
states.low_zero: Near zero with real lift, or won't hold on shutdown

low_zero: vacuum drops when it shuts off

features.name: Oil reaching the nozzle
features.ask: With ignition off and the motor running, does oil leave the pump and get as far as the nozzle line?
features.how: Prove delivery at the pump first, with ignition off (lift the igniter or transformer lead) so nothing can light. Put the gauge with its bleeder in the pump's gauge port, run a hose from the bleeder into a container, put on safety glasses, open the bleeder, and run the motor for a few seconds. A solid, air-free stream means oil is leaving the pump. Shut the burner off at the service switch before you close the bleeder — closing it with the motor running pressures the pump up and sprays the nozzle with the igniter off. Pressure that comes up to spec on a normal start and holds at cutoff (see the pump pressure check) proves the same thing, and an oil valve that clicks open on a powered coil lets the oil through to the nozzle line. Only if the nozzle line itself is still in doubt, make sure ignition is off, take the line off at the nozzle end so any oil valve is tested too, clamp the open end into a container so it cannot whip, and run the motor once for a few seconds. A solid stream means the pump and supply are fine and the fault is at the nozzle or ignition. Never run the burner with the drawer assembly out or the nozzle line open to the room — the nozzle sprays at pump pressure and the igniter is a spark in the middle of it.
features.caution: Ignition OFF before the motor runs — lift the igniter or transformer lead. Safety glasses on, a container under any open line or port, hands clear; oil leaves at pump pressure (100 psi or more) and can go through skin. Burner off before you close the bleeder. Never run the burner with the drawer assembly out or the nozzle line open to the room.

states.no: No oil, or only a dribble

features.name: Oil solenoid / delay valve
features.ask: Does the oil valve get voltage and open on a start (click), and does it hold tight at shutdown?
features.how: Meter the coil on a start. The delay valve opens a few seconds after the motor (TM 5-642 ¶3-14b says at least 4 s) and must shut instantly when the motor stops.
features.caution: This needs a start — one try only. If it will not light and the primary locks out, stop, look into the chamber for liquid oil, and find the cause before any further reset.

states.ok: Powered, opens and closes clean
states.no_power: No voltage to the coil on a start
states.stuck: Powered but doesn't open (dead coil, stuck plunger)

no_power: no voltage to the oil valve

features.name: Pump bypass plug vs piping
features.ask: Does the pump's bypass plug match the piping — plug IN for two-pipe, OUT for one-pipe?
features.how: Pull the return-port plug on the pump and look for the small bypass plug inside. A plug on a one-pipe system dead-heads the pump and blows the shaft seal; no plug on a two-pipe system means it never primes properly.
features.caution: Burner off and the oil supply valve closed first; catch the oil that runs out of the return port.

states.ok: Matches the piping

features.name: Outdoor temperature
features.ask: How cold is it outside?

features.name: Fuel line / filter exposed to the cold
features.ask: Does the fuel line, filter or tank sit outside or in an unheated space?

states.yes: Outdoor or unheated tank, line or filter

features.name: Warming test
features.ask: Does gently warming the exposed line or filter (warm rags, warm water, moving it indoors) restore flow?
features.how: Warm the suspect section, then watch pump vacuum or oil flow.
features.caution: No open flame or torch on a fuel line, filter or tank. Use warm water, warm rags or heat trace; a heat gun only on a dry metal line with no fuel leaking and the burner locked out.

states.restores: Flow comes back as it warms

restores: warmed the line and it ran
runs when the sun hits the tank

features.name: CAD cell resistance
features.ask: What does the CAD cell read — with the flame on, and dark?
features.how: Pull the cell leads off the primary (F–F) and ohm them. Flame on, most controls want under 1,600 Ω (the burner maker's limit rules); dark, well over 20 kΩ. A cell that reads low in the dark sees light or is shorted and the control will refuse to start or lock out.
features.caution: Reading it with the flame on means lifting a lead off the primary, which makes the primary shut the burner down — usually a lockout you caused. Reset once, and only with a dry chamber. Burner off and power locked out for the dark reading.

states.good: Under ~1,600 Ω with flame, high dark
states.high: Over ~1,600 Ω with the flame on — flame not seen
states.low_dark: Low with no flame — cell sees light or is shorted

low_dark: cad cell low in the dark
cell reads low with no flame
good: cad cell reads low with flame

features.name: Stack relay
features.ask: Does the stack relay's helix move freely and do its contacts switch cleanly when the stack heats?
features.how: Pull the relay out of the smoke pipe. Soot binds the bimetal helix so the hot contacts never make or never break; worn contacts drop the burner.
features.caution: Burner off and the smoke pipe cool before the relay comes out, and reseal the hole before any restart — an open hole upsets the draft and can spill flue gas into the room. After a stack-control lockout let its safety element cool before you reset, and never hold the relay in (TM 5-642 ¶3-11b(7), ¶7-9h).

states.ok: Helix free, contacts clean
states.faulty: Helix sooted or stuck, contacts worn or dirty

features.name: Net stack temperature
features.ask: What is the net stack temperature (flue minus room), after 10 minutes of running?
features.caution: The smoke pipe, the probe and the test hole are hot (400–600 °F). Gloves on, hose and cable clear of the pipe and the draft regulator, and plug the test hole when you are done — an open hole upsets the draft and can spill flue gas into the room.

states.normal: Normal (about 275–600 °F net)
states.high: High (over 600 °F net)
states.low: Low (under 275 °F net)

features.name: Flue O2 / excess air
features.ask: What is the flue O2 (or CO2) with the burner running steady?
features.caution: The smoke pipe, the probe and the test hole are hot (400–600 °F). Gloves on, hose and cable clear of the pipe and the draft regulator, and plug the test hole when you are done — an open hole upsets the draft and can spill flue gas into the room.

states.normal: Normal (about 3–8 % O2, about 9.5–13 % CO2 on light oil)
states.low: Low O2 (under 3 %) — too little air
states.high: High O2 (over 8 %) — too much air or a flue leak

features.name: Flue CO (air-free)
features.ask: What is the flue CO, corrected to air-free?
features.how: Correcting to air-free needs the flue O2 from the same sample, so read both together.
features.caution: The smoke pipe, the probe and the test hole are hot (400–600 °F). Gloves on, hose and cable clear of the pipe and the draft regulator, and plug the test hole when you are done — an open hole upsets the draft and can spill flue gas into the room.

states.normal: Under 100 ppm air-free
states.high: 100–400 ppm air-free

features.name: Smoke spot number
features.ask: What is the smoke spot number (0–9 scale)?
features.caution: The smoke pipe, the pump probe and the test hole are hot (400–600 °F). Gloves on, and plug the test hole when you are done — an open hole upsets the draft and can spill flue gas into the room.

states.normal: 0–1 (trace)

features.name: Over-fire draft
features.ask: What is the draft over the fire (through the inspection port) with the burner running warm?
features.how: Type draft as a NEGATIVE number — a gauge that says "draft 0.04" is −0.04 here, and a plus sign means pressure. A flame-retention burner usually wants about −0.02 in. w.c.; TM 5-642 wants the firebox just below atmospheric once warm so nothing pushes out, and says starting conditions need about 0.03–0.06 (¶3-13f), so judge against the burner's own spec.
features.caution: Reading through the inspection port — stand to the side. If the chamber is under pressure, hot gas and soot come out of the port. Close it again when you are done.

states.normal: Draft of about 0.01 to 0.04 in. w.c. (reads −0.01 to −0.04)
states.none_positive: No draft — reads zero or positive (pressure over the fire)
states.excessive: Strong draft — more than 0.05 in. w.c. (reads below −0.05)

features.name: Breech draft
features.ask: What is the draft in the smoke pipe between the appliance and the barometric regulator?
features.how: Type draft as a NEGATIVE number — a gauge that says "draft 0.04" is −0.04 here, and a plus sign means pressure. TM 5-642 quotes the draft unsigned, 0.02–0.04 in. w.c. to start (¶3-11b(1)); running practice is 0.04 to 0.06 (−0.04 to −0.06). Weak draft means a cold, blocked, leaky or undersized chimney; a very strong draft means the regulator isn't regulating.
features.caution: The smoke pipe and the test hole are hot. Gloves on, and plug the test hole when you are done — an open hole upsets the draft and can spill flue gas into the room.

states.normal: Draft of about 0.03 to 0.07 in. w.c. (reads −0.03 to −0.07)
states.weak: Weak — less than 0.025 in. w.c. of draft (reads −0.02 or closer to zero), no draft, or reversing
states.excessive: Strong — more than 0.08 in. w.c. (reads below −0.08)

features.name: Flue and chimney
features.ask: Is the smoke pipe, breeching and chimney clear, dry and intact?
features.how: Open the smoke-pipe cleanout and the chimney base; look up the flue and at the cap. Snow, frost and ice at the cap, soot and scale at the base, a fallen liner, a nest.
features.caution: Burner off and locked out before a cleanout or the chimney base is opened — a running burner can push flue gas out of it. Test for CO before you put your head near it.

states.restricted: Restricted — soot, debris, collapsed liner, snow or ice at the cap
states.wet: Wet or corroded — moisture, rust streaks, white deposits

features.name: Combustion air to the room
features.ask: Is combustion air getting into the boiler room — intakes open and clear, louvers open, room not pulled negative by exhaust fans?

states.ok: Open and clear
states.restricted: Restricted — intake drifted shut, louvers closed, tight room, exhaust fans pulling it negative

features.name: Soot in the heat exchanger
features.ask: How much soot is in the flue passages / heat exchanger?
features.how: Open a cleanout or the flue collector. A light dusting is normal between cleanings; piles, flakes and narrowed passages are not.
features.caution: Burner off, locked out and cool before a cleanout is opened. Wear eye and dust protection.

states.heavy: Heavy — passages narrowed, soot falling out

features.name: Spill / blocked-vent switch
features.ask: Is a spill or blocked-vent switch tripped (manual reset button at the draft regulator or flue collar)?
features.caution: A tripped spill or rollout switch is a safety. Find out why it tripped before you reset it, reset it once only, and never jumper or bypass it.

states.ok: Not tripped (or none fitted)

features.name: High limit
features.ask: Is the high limit (aquastat, pressuretrol or furnace limit) open with a call — and is the boiler or plenum actually hot?
features.how: Meter across the limit contacts with a call present, and read the boiler temperature / steam pressure / plenum temperature against the dial setting. Line voltage across the open contacts means the limit is open.
features.caution: Never jumper a limit, pressuretrol or low-water cutoff to test it or to get heat — meter across the open contacts instead.

states.open_overheat: Open and the boiler/plenum really is at or past the setting
states.open_early: Open while not hot — mis-set, failed, or the sensor is out of its well
states.closed_hot: Still closed though the boiler/plenum is past its setting

features.name: Operating control setting
features.ask: Are the aquastat / pressuretrol / fan-limit settings right for the system (setpoint and differential)?
features.how: Typical hot-water high limit 180–200 °F with a 10–20 °F differential; steam pressuretrol cut-in ½–1 psi with a 1–2 psi differential; furnace limit about 175–200 °F.

states.ok: Reasonable
states.too_low: Set too low or differential too tight
states.too_high: Set too high — dial or cut-out turned up well past design

features.name: Low-water cutoff
features.ask: Is the low-water cutoff open or closed — and is the water really low?
features.how: Meter across the LWCO contacts; then check the gauge glass (steam) or confirm the boiler is full (hot water). Open with the water low is the cutoff doing its job. Open with water visible at the right level means a dirty probe, a sludged float chamber or a bad control. Closed with the water below the cutoff level and the burner still firing means the cutoff has failed (stuck, bridged, jumpered or not fitted) — shut the burner off first.
features.caution: Never jumper the cutoff, to test it or to get heat. If the water is low or out of sight, shut the burner off first and do not feed water into a hot boiler (TM 5-642 ¶4-78).

states.ok: Closed, and the water is at the normal level (steam) or the boiler is full (hot water)
states.open_low: Open and the water IS low
states.open_fooled: Open but the level is fine — probe, float chamber or control
states.stuck_closed: Closed and the burner is firing, but the water is below the cutoff level (cutoff failed, jumpered or not fitted)

open_fooled: lwco holding off burner with water in the glass
stuck_closed: burner kept firing with low water

features.name: Water level in the gauge glass
features.ask: Where is the water in the gauge glass, and is it steady?
features.how: Blow down the glass first so you're not reading a stale column. Compare with the boiler's marked normal water line. If the glass is empty or you cannot find the water, shut the burner off first and do not feed water to a hot boiler (TM 5-642 ¶4-78).
features.caution: Open the glass drain slowly, face turned away, with the drain piped to a safe place — it is hot water and steam. If the water is out of sight, burner off first.

states.normal: At the normal line, steady
states.low: Low or out of sight at the bottom
states.high: High — flooded, near or above the top
states.bouncing: Bouncing or surging an inch or more

high: water out the top of the glass

features.name: Boiler water condition
features.ask: What does the boiler water look like — drain some from the gauge-glass cock or the LWCO blowdown?
features.caution: It is hot water and steam. Open the cock or blowdown slowly, stand to the side, and run it to a drain. Watch the glass while you do it and shut the valve if the level drops toward the low-water mark.

states.dirty: Dirty, oily film, foam or sediment

features.name: Steam pressure
features.ask: What does the steam gauge do while the burner runs?
features.how: Open the test cock to prove the gauge isn't lying (TM 5-642 ¶4-79). A heating boiler should build to the pressuretrol cut-out (a few psi at most) and cycle on it; the safety valve is 15 psi.
features.caution: The test cock vents steam. Open it slowly with your hand and face clear of the outlet.

states.normal: Builds to the pressuretrol setting and cycles
states.none: Never builds pressure while firing steadily
states.high: Above the pressuretrol setting — approaching the safety valve

features.name: Boiler pressure (hot water)
features.ask: What does the boiler's pressure gauge read?
features.how: A residential system fills to about 12 psi cold and runs 15–22 psi hot with a 30 psi relief valve; larger systems differ — compare with the relief valve rating and the fill setting. Pressure that climbs toward the relief setting as the water heats points at the expansion tank; pressure that creeps up cold points at the fill valve or a leaking coil.

states.normal: Normal for the system
states.high: High — within a few psi of the relief valve or above
states.low: Low or zero

high: pressure too high on the boiler

features.name: Pressure with the fill valve shut
features.ask: With the make-up water valve closed and the burner off, does boiler pressure still creep up over an hour?

states.yes: Still climbs — domestic water is getting in

yes: pressure climbs with the fill valve off

features.name: Expansion tank
features.ask: With the boiler cool and the tank valved off from the system, what do you find at the expansion tank — tap test and air valve?
features.how: Isolate the tank and drain its water side before you gauge the air side. A bladder tank should ring hollow on the air end and dull toward the water end. Press the air valve briefly — air is good; water means a ruptured bladder or a waterlogged tank. The air precharge should be about the cold fill pressure (roughly 12 psi) with the system side off the tank.
features.caution: Isolate the tank and drain its water side before you gauge the air side. Press the air valve briefly with your face clear — on a ruptured bladder it spits system water at boiler temperature. Never open a tank valve on a hot, pressurized system.

states.ok: Hollow on top, air at the valve, precharge holds
states.waterlogged: Solid all over, water at the air valve, or no precharge

waterlogged: water out of the air valve
no air in the expansion tank

features.name: Fill (make-up) valve
features.ask: Cold boiler, burner off — does the pressure creep up with the fill valve open and hold steady once you close the shutoff ahead of it?
features.how: Close the shutoff ahead of the fill valve and bleed the pressure back to the cold fill pressure (about 12 psi). If it then holds steady, the fill valve was passing (or set high); if it keeps climbing with the shutoff closed, look at the tankless coil instead.

states.ok: Holds steady, fill valve shuts off tight
states.passing: Creeps up with the fill valve open, steady with the shutoff closed

features.name: Relief / safety valve
features.ask: Is the relief or safety valve weeping or popping?
features.caution: Stay out of line with the discharge pipe — it can throw boiling water or steam. Do not lift the lever by hand unless the pressure is 80 to 85 percent of the popping point (TM 5-642 ¶4-41c), and never tighten the spring to stop a leak.

states.ok: Dry

features.name: Kettling
features.ask: Does the boiler rumble, percolate or bang like a kettle while the burner runs?

states.yes: Kettling — rumbles, percolates or bangs while firing

features.name: Domestic hot water from the coil
features.ask: Is the tankless coil giving hot water while the boiler is hot?

states.ok: Plenty of hot water
states.weak: Little or no domestic hot water with the boiler hot

weak: no hot water at the tap
no hot water from the boiler

features.name: Furnace blower
features.ask: What is the blower doing once the furnace is hot?

states.ok: Runs when hot, good airflow
states.weak: Runs but weak airflow (slow, dirty wheel, slipping belt, backwards)
states.off: Doesn't run when the plenum is hot
states.constant: Runs all the time, even cold

weak: not much air from the vents

features.name: Voltage to the blower motor
features.ask: With the plenum hot, is there voltage at the blower motor leads?

states.missing: Missing — the fan control isn't switching

missing: no power to the blower motor

features.name: Furnace air filter
