features.ask: Is the furnace air filter dirty, collapsed or missing?

states.dirty: Dirty, clogged, collapsed or sucked into the blower

features.name: Ducts and registers
features.ask: Are supply registers and dampers open and the ducts intact?

states.ok: Open and intact
states.restricted: Closed registers or dampers, crushed or undersized duct, blocked return

features.name: Supply plenum temperature
features.ask: How hot is the supply plenum with the burner running and the blower on?
features.how: TM 5-642 ¶6-40g — outlet air shouldn't stay over 160 °F; the usual cause when it does is airflow. Shield the probe from the heat exchanger's radiant heat or it reads high and sends you after airflow that is fine. Supply minus return temperature against the nameplate rise is the better test when the return air is cold.

states.normal: Normal (about 120–160 °F)
states.high: High (over 160 °F) — starved airflow or overfired
states.low: Low (under 110 °F) — underfired, blower on too early, or blower never stops

features.name: Heat exchanger integrity
features.ask: Any sign the heat exchanger is cracked — flame changes when the blower starts, CO or O2 shift in the supply air, visible crack?
features.how: Watch the flame as the blower starts (a crack lets blower air disturb it); sample the supply air with the analyzer for CO or an O2 drop; inspect with a light and mirror or a camera.
features.caution: If the analyzer finds CO in the supply air, shut the furnace down at once and ventilate. Stand to the side of the inspection port, and keep the probe and hose clear of the hot heat exchanger.

states.ok: No sign
states.cracked: Cracked — flame disturbed by the blower, CO in the supply air, or a visible crack

cracked: flame changes when the blower comes on
flame jumps when the fan starts
flame rolls out when the blower starts

features.name: {Output}
features.ask: How much {output} is it giving?

states.none: No {output} at all
states.normal: {Output} is normal

features.name: Completely dead
features.ask: Is the unit completely dead — nothing runs, no lights, no display, no sound?

features.name: Short cycling
features.ask: Does it start and stop every few minutes (short cycling)?

states.yes: Short cycling — starts and stops every few minutes

features.name: Runs nonstop
features.ask: Does it run nonstop without ever reaching setpoint?

features.name: Water leaking
features.ask: Is water leaking, dripping or puddling from the unit?

states.yes: Water leaking or on the floor
states.no: No water where it shouldn't be

features.name: Burning smell
features.ask: Is there a burning, hot-electrical or scorched smell?

features.name: Comes and goes
features.ask: Does the problem come and go, working fine at other times?

features.name: Recently worked on
features.ask: Was it serviced, repaired, charged, moved or modified recently?

features.name: Started after a power event
features.ask: Did it start after a power outage, generator switch-over or storm?

states.yes: Started after a power outage or switch-over
states.no: Not tied to a power event

features.name: Line voltage at the unit
features.ask: Is there line voltage at the unit's disconnect or power terminals?
features.how: Meter across the line terminals (L1–L2, or L–N on 120 V) at the unit, not just at the panel. On a three-phase unit meter L1–L2, L2–L3 and L1–L3 — a dead leg shows as two low pairs, while one pair alone can read full voltage.

features.name: Breaker / fuses
features.ask: Check the breaker and fuses feeding the unit — what do you find?

states.ok: On and intact
states.tripped: Tripped, off, or a fuse blown

features.name: Control voltage (24 V)
features.ask: Is there 24 V control power at the transformer secondary or control board?
features.how: Meter R to C (or the transformer secondary). Expect about 24–28 V AC.

features.name: Call for {output}
features.ask: Is the thermostat or controller actually calling for {output}?
features.how: Check the setpoint, mode and schedule, then meter the call terminal (Y for cooling, W for heat) to C at the unit, or watch the controller's output light.

features.name: Supply voltage under load
features.ask: What is the supply voltage at the unit with it running?

states.low: Low (more than 10 % under; under 187 V on a 208/230 unit)
states.normal: Within ±10 % (187–253 V on a 208/230 unit)
states.high: High (more than 10 % over; over 253 V on a 208/230 unit)

features.name: Low-voltage fuse
features.ask: Is the low-voltage fuse (the 3 or 5 A fuse on the board or in the transformer secondary) intact?
features.how: Look at the blade fuse on the control board, or the inline fuse in the transformer secondary. With power on, 24 V measured across the fuse means it is open. A fuse that holds until a call comes on, then blows, points at the circuit that call energizes. Many boilers and zone panels have no 24 V fuse.
features.caution: Line voltage sits beside the 24 V terminals. Keep the probes on the 24 V side; a probe bridging R to C blows the fuse.

states.reblows: A new fuse blows again (often as soon as a call comes on)

features.name: Control transformer
features.ask: Does the control transformer have line voltage on its primary and 24–28 V on its secondary?
features.how: Meter the two primary leads (120, 208/240 or 277 V), then the secondary at the transformer (R to C), before the fuse. An unloaded secondary reads about 24–28 V.
features.caution: The primary is line voltage. Use a CAT III meter with insulated probes and keep hands off the terminals; it is safe to touch only after lockout and a dead test.

states.ok: Line voltage in, 24–28 V out
states.no_secondary: Line voltage in, no 24 V out
states.no_primary: No line voltage reaching the primary

no_secondary: no 24 volts out of the transformer
transformer has power in but nothing out
no_primary: no voltage on the transformer primary

features.name: 24 V level with the call on
features.ask: With the call on and the loads pulled in, what does R to C read at the transformer?
features.how: Meter R to C at the transformer or board while the contactor or relays are pulled in. Healthy is about 22–28 V. A reading that sags several volts when the call comes on means the transformer is near its limit.
features.caution: Line voltage sits beside the 24 V terminals. Keep the probes on the 24 V side; a probe bridging R to C blows the fuse.

states.low: Low — under 22 V, or drops several volts when the call comes on
states.high: High — over 28 V

low: voltage drops when the contactor pulls in

features.name: Transformer primary tap
features.ask: Is the transformer's primary connected on the tap that matches the line voltage it is fed?
features.how: Many control transformers have several primary leads (120, 208, 240, 277 or 480 V), with the unused ones capped. Compare the lead in use with the voltage you metered on the primary. A 240 V tap on a 208 V supply runs the secondary low; a 208 V tap on 240 V runs it high.
features.caution: Lock out and dead-test before moving a tap; the leads carry line voltage.

features.name: Phasing between two transformers
features.ask: If two transformers feed the same control wiring, do they read in phase?
features.how: With the two C terminals tied together, meter R of one transformer to R of the other. Near 0 V means in phase. About 48 V means out of phase. Common on a furnace with a heat pump, zoning panels, and boilers with several zone controls.
features.caution: Line voltage sits beside the 24 V terminals. Keep the probes on the 24 V side; a probe bridging R to C blows the fuse.

states.single: Only one transformer in the circuit
states.in_phase: Two transformers, in phase (near 0 V between the R terminals)
states.out_of_phase: Two transformers, out of phase (about 48 V between the R terminals)

features.name: Where the 24 V short is
features.ask: With power off, lift the field wires one at a time and ohm the call terminals to C — what clears the short?
features.how: Power off and fuse out. Ohm R to C and each call terminal (Y, W, G, O/B) to C with the thermostat off the wall. Near 0 Ω is the short. Lift one wire at a time (thermostat cable, outdoor cable, each coil) until the reading clears. A coil that reads under about 2 Ω is shorted.

states.no_short: No short found — every circuit reads normal to C
states.cable: Clears with a cable lifted (thermostat or outdoor run)
states.coil: Clears with one coil lifted — that coil reads near 0 Ω

cable: low voltage wire shorted to the cabinet

features.name: Blower-door safety switch
features.ask: Is the blower-door safety switch closed with the door seated?
features.how: Seat the door and check the switch plunger is pushed in. On most furnaces and air handlers the switch breaks line voltage to the transformer, so the whole control goes dead with the door off.
features.caution: With the door off and the switch held in, the cabinet is live and the blower can start. Hold it in only to watch, hands clear of the blower and terminals. Never tape or pin it, and put the door back before you leave.

states.open: Open — door not seated, or the switch failed

features.name: 24 V lost along the control path
features.ask: With the call on, is the voltage across the coil within 2 V of R to C at the transformer?
features.how: Meter R to C at the transformer, then across the coil it should pull in. Then step along the path (R at the thermostat, Y at the unit, each splice) to find the joint that loses the volts.
features.caution: Line voltage sits beside the 24 V terminals. Keep the probes on the 24 V side; a probe bridging R to C blows the fuse.

states.none: Within 2 V
states.drop: More than 2 V lower at the coil

drop: voltage drop on the thermostat wire
low voltage at the contactor coil
bad splice on the low voltage

features.name: Contactor or relay sound
features.ask: What does the contactor or relay sound like when it is called?

states.quiet: Pulls in clean and quiet (a faint hum is normal)
states.buzz: Loud steady buzz while pulled in

chatter: contactor pulls in and drops out

features.name: Jumper across a safety or control
features.ask: Is there a jumper, a bypass wire or a pinned switch across any safety or control (other than a factory jumper or the one between the two R terminals)?
features.how: Look at every safety and terminal block, and in the thermostat sub-base, for a jumper wire, a wire nut joining two safety leads, or a switch taped or pinned shut. A factory jumper shown on the wiring diagram, or the jumper between the thermostat's two R terminals (Rh and Rc), is normal.

states.none: None found

features.name: The open safety switch, tested at normal conditions
features.ask: With pressure, level or temperature in the normal range, does the open safety switch read closed?
features.how: Read the gauges, the pan or the temperature first, so you know the switch has no reason to be open. Then power off, lift one lead and ohm the switch. Closed reads near 0 Ω.

open: pressure switch open at normal pressure

features.name: Why the rollout or spill switch tripped
features.ask: After checking the draft, the flue and chimney, the heat-exchanger passages, the combustion air and the light-off, did you find why it tripped?
features.how: A rollout or spill switch opens because flame or flue gas left its path. Check the draft over the fire and at the breech, the flue and chimney (including ice or frost at the cap), soot in the passages, the combustion-air opening, and watch a light-off for a delayed or puffing start.
features.caution: Don't reset it until you have looked. Reset once only, never jumper it, and test for CO in the room and at the flue.

states.none_found: Nothing found after the full inspection

none_found: nothing wrong with the draft or flue
draft and flue fine but switch tripped

features.name: Condensate safety (float) switch
features.ask: Is the condensate float or safety switch open — and is there water in its pan?
features.how: Find the float switch on the drain pan, the secondary pan or the drain line. Meter across it with the call on (24 V across it means open), then look at the water level.
features.caution: Line voltage sits beside the 24 V terminals. Keep the probes on the 24 V side; a probe bridging R to C blows the fuse.

states.open_wet: Open with water standing — it tripped for a reason

open_wet: pan full of water and float tripped
open_dry: float switch open with a dry pan
float switch open but pan dry

features.name: Unit control board status
features.ask: What does the unit control board's status light or code show?
features.how: Read the light or code on the outdoor unit's control board and look it up on the panel label or in the maker's service manual. Codes differ by maker.

states.normal: Normal (no fault)
states.fault: Another fault code (look it up in the maker's manual)

lockout: needs a power reset to run

features.name: Unit or zone board output on a call
features.ask: With 24 V and a call at the unit's (or zone panel's) control board, does the board send out its output?
features.how: Meter the board's 24 V input and the call terminal (Y, W or the zone call) to C, then its output (to the contactor, blower relay, zone valve or pump relay). Wait out any start delay, and check its status light.
features.caution: Line voltage sits beside the 24 V terminals. Keep the probes on the 24 V side; a probe bridging R to C blows the fuse.

states.ok: Output on with the call
states.none: 24 V and the call in, nothing out

none: board has 24 volts but no output

features.name: Relay that switches the load
features.ask: With the call on, is the relay (or small contactor) that switches the burner, blower or pump pulled in?
features.how: Look or listen for the armature, and meter 24 V across its coil. Then turn the call off and check that it drops out.
features.caution: Line voltage sits beside the 24 V terminals. Keep the probes on the 24 V side; a probe bridging R to C blows the fuse.

states.pulled_in: Pulled in on the call, drops out after
states.not_pulling: Not pulled in on the call
states.stuck_in: Stays pulled in with no call

features.name: Relay coil resistance
features.ask: Power off, one lead lifted — what does the relay or contactor coil read?
features.how: Power off and one lead lifted (ohming a live coil gives a false reading and can damage the meter). A 24 V coil reads from about 5 Ω on a larger contactor to a few hundred ohms on a small relay; compare with a known-good one. Open (OL) or under about 2 Ω is a failed coil.

states.normal: In range (not open, not near 0 Ω)

features.name: Voltage across the closed relay contacts
features.ask: With the relay pulled in and the load running, what voltage reads across the closed contacts?
features.how: Meter from the line side to the load side of each closed contact while the load runs. Good contacts read under about 1 V. More than that means pitted or burnt contacts.
features.caution: Line voltage on the contacts. Meter with insulated probes only; never touch the contacts or bridge them with a probe tip.

states.ok: Under about 1 V
states.drop: Several volts or more across a closed contact

features.name: 24 V left on the coil with the call off
features.ask: With the thermostat satisfied or turned off, is 24 V still on the contactor or relay coil?
features.how: Turn the thermostat to off (or let it satisfy) and meter across the coil. Any 24 V there means the call is still being sent; none means the contactor or relay itself is stuck.
features.caution: Line voltage sits beside the 24 V terminals. Keep the probes on the 24 V side; a probe bridging R to C blows the fuse.

states.none: No voltage on the coil

present: 24 volts on y with the thermostat off
still 24 volts on the contactor with the thermostat off
voltage on the coil with no call

features.name: When it starts after a call
features.ask: After a call comes on (or power comes back), does it start right away, after a few minutes, or not at all?
features.how: Turn the call on and time it. Many units hold the compressor off 3–5 minutes after it last stopped or after power returns, and a BAS may stagger restarts after an outage.

states.delayed: Waits a few minutes, then starts and runs normally

never: waited and it never came on

features.name: Delay timer in and out
features.ask: With the call on, is 24 V going into the delay timer (time-delay relay) and coming out after the delay?
features.how: Meter the timer's input and output terminals to C. Wait out the delay (up to 10 minutes) before you judge the output.
features.caution: Line voltage sits beside the 24 V terminals. Keep the probes on the 24 V side; a probe bridging R to C blows the fuse.

states.passes: 24 V in, 24 V out after the delay
states.in_no_out: 24 V in, nothing out after 10 minutes

features.name: Thermostat mode, setpoint and schedule
features.ask: Are the thermostat's mode, setpoint, fan setting, schedule and hold set right for the call?

states.ok: Set right

wrong: set to heat instead of cool
set to cool instead of heat

features.name: Thermostat installer setup
features.ask: Is the thermostat's installer setup right for the equipment (system type, stages, fan control in heat)?
features.how: Open the installer menu and compare it with the equipment. Check system type (conventional, heat pump, boiler), the number of stages, auxiliary heat, and who runs the fan in heat. A wrong system type is common after a thermostat swap.

states.ok: Matches the equipment

wrong: thermostat set for heat pump on a furnace
thermostat set for gas on an oil furnace

features.name: Call voltage at the thermostat and at the unit
features.ask: With a call set, is 24 V on the call terminal (Y or W) at the thermostat, and does it arrive at the unit?
features.how: Meter the call terminal to C at the thermostat sub-base (24 V means the thermostat is calling), then the same terminal to C at the equipment's terminal board. Use C at each end, not a ground.
features.caution: At the unit, line voltage sits beside the terminal board; keep the probes on the 24 V terminals. If the thermostat has no R and C terminals, or is wired to 120, 208, 240 or 277 V, treat it as line voltage until you have proved otherwise. Lock out, and don't meter or jumper it as a 24 V circuit.

states.reaches_unit: 24 V at the thermostat and at the unit
states.lost_between: 24 V at the thermostat, none at the unit
states.not_sent: No call leaving the thermostat (R live, nothing on the call terminal)

not_sent: no 24 volts out of the thermostat
no y out of the thermostat
no w out of the thermostat
lost_between: 24 volts at the thermostat but not at the unit
y at the thermostat but nothing at the condenser
w at the thermostat not at the boiler
thermostat calling but no signal at the furnace
reaches_unit: 24 volts on y at the unit and the thermostat

features.name: Jumper test at the equipment
features.ask: At the equipment's terminal board, does it start when you jumper R to the call terminal?
features.how: At the unit (not the thermostat), jumper R to Y for cooling or R to W for heat and watch it start, then take the jumper off. A compressor may hold off 3–5 minutes; if it ran in the last 5 minutes, wait out the delay before you call it a no-start.
features.caution: Jumper R to one call terminal only, never to C (a dead short), and leave every safety in the circuit. If the thermostat has no R and C terminals, or is wired to 120, 208, 240 or 277 V, treat it as line voltage until you have proved otherwise. Lock out, and don't jumper it as a 24 V circuit.

starts: jumper r to y and it runs
jumpered r and w and it fired
starts with r and y jumped
no_start: jumper r to y nothing happens

features.name: Thermostat display
features.ask: What does the thermostat's display show?

states.normal: Thermostat display normal
states.reboots: Thermostat display flickers or restarts (often when the unit starts)

reboots: display flickers when the unit starts
thermostat goes blank when the unit starts

features.name: Thermostat batteries
features.ask: Do the thermostat's batteries test good?
features.how: Meter each cell under load, or swap in fresh ones. Under about 1.2 V a cell is low. A stat with no batteries fitted counts as good.

states.ok: Good, or none fitted
states.low: Low or dead

features.name: C wire at the thermostat
features.ask: Is a C (common) wire connected at the thermostat, if the thermostat needs one?
features.how: Pull the thermostat off and look for a wire on C, then confirm it is landed on C at the equipment too. 24 V from R to C at the sub-base proves it.

states.connected: Connected (or the thermostat doesn't need one)
states.missing: Needed, but not connected — the thermostat steals power

missing: wifi thermostat without a c wire

features.name: Thermostat wiring vs the terminals
features.ask: Do the wires land on the same letters at the thermostat and at the equipment (and is the jumper between the two R terminals right)?
features.how: Trace each conductor color from the thermostat to the equipment terminal board. Check the jumper between the two R terminals, Rh and Rc (in with one transformer, out with two), and that C is not on R.

features.name: Thermostat changed recently
features.ask: Was the thermostat replaced, moved or rewired recently?

states.yes: Thermostat replaced, moved or rewired recently

features.name: Heat anticipator or cycle rate
features.ask: Is the heat anticipator (mechanical thermostat) or the cycle-rate setting (digital) right for the equipment?
features.how: Mechanical thermostat — set the anticipator to the current the W circuit draws. With the thermostat off the wall, wrap the W wire 10 turns through the clamp, put a heat call on (jumper R to W at the sub-base), read the amps once the burner or valve is on, divide by 10, then take the jumper off. Digital thermostat — check the cycles-per-hour setting in the installer menu against the equipment type.
features.caution: You are jumpering R to W, so the heat will fire. Keep the probes and clamp on the 24 V wiring only. If the thermostat has no R and C terminals, or is wired to 120, 208, 240 or 277 V, treat it as line voltage — lock out and don't jumper it.

states.ok: Set right
states.too_fast: Set for too many cycles (short cycles)
states.too_slow: Set for too few cycles (long cycles, big swings)

too_slow: long cycles with big temperature swings

features.name: Mechanical thermostat level and contacts
features.ask: Is the mechanical thermostat mounted level, with its contacts and bimetal clean?
features.how: Pull the cover. A mercury-bulb thermostat must sit level (use the marks on the base); a few degrees off level shifts the switching point. Look for dust or lint on the coil and contacts.

states.ok: Level and clean
states.off: Off level, or dirty contacts or bimetal

features.name: Thermostat or sensor location
features.ask: Does the thermostat or sensor sit where it reads the space (not in sun, a supply-air stream, a door draft or on a cold wall)?
features.how: Look at what the sensor sees. Sun, a lamp or TV, a supply register, an outside wall, a kitchen, or a draft from the wall cavity through the wire hole all fool it. In a walk-in or reach-in, a probe in the evaporator discharge or by the door does the same.

poor: draft from the wall behind the thermostat

features.name: Control's temperature vs a reference
features.ask: Does the thermostat's or controller's reading agree with a reference thermometer held at its sensor?
features.how: Hold a calibrated thermometer next to the sensor for a few minutes, out of your breath and hand heat, and compare it with the reading the control shows. Within 2 °F agrees.

states.off: Off by more than 2 °F (high or low)

off: thermostat reads warmer than the room
thermostat says it is warmer than it is
thermostat reads colder than the room

features.name: Sensor resistance vs its curve
features.ask: If it is a 10 kΩ NTC sensor, does its resistance (one lead lifted) match the chart at the temperature it sits in?
features.how: Power the controller off, then lift one sensor lead at the controller, so the input's own voltage is off the sensor, and ohm the sensor (this also tests the wire run). Read the temperature at the sensor with a thermometer. A 10 kΩ Type II sensor reads about 336 kΩ at −40 °F, 85 kΩ at 0 °F, 32.6 kΩ at 32 °F, 12.5 kΩ at 68 °F, 10.0 kΩ at 77 °F and 5.8 kΩ at 100 °F. A Type III reads lower in the cold (240 kΩ at −40 °F, 29.5 kΩ at 32 °F). Enter both numbers and the app checks them against both tables. In the cold the two curves sit far apart, so "on a curve" is loose there; if you know the sensor's type, compare with that column only. Other sensor types (1 kΩ platinum, 20 kΩ and others) go to the maker's chart.
features.caution: On an inverter unit the board holds 300–400 V DC after power-off. Wait the maker's time and confirm under 10 V DC before you unplug a sensor.

states.ok: On a 10 kΩ curve (within ±10 %)

features.name: Mode it runs in on a cooling call
features.ask: On a cooling call, is the heat pump actually cooling, or running in heat?
features.how: Feel the big vapor line at the indoor unit. In cooling it is cold and sweating; in heat it is hot, and the supply air is warm.

states.heating: Heating on a cooling call (hot supply air, hot vapor line)

heating: heat pump heating instead of cooling
hot air on a cooling call
runs in heat when set to cool

features.name: Thermostat O/B setting
features.ask: Does the thermostat's O/B (reversing-valve) setting match the valve?
features.how: Go by the wiring diagram or a meter on the valve coil, not by the brand. A valve energized in cooling needs O; a valve energized in heating needs B.

states.ok: Matches the valve
states.reversed: Set the wrong way for the valve

reversed: thermostat set to b on an o valve
thermostat set to o on a b valve
reversing valve setting wrong on the thermostat

features.name: Reversing-valve coil voltage in cooling
features.ask: On a cooling call, is the reversing-valve coil getting 24 V if the valve needs it in cooling (and none if it doesn't)?
features.how: Meter at the two coil leads with the cooling call on. An O-type valve needs 24 V in cooling; a B-type valve needs none.
features.caution: Line voltage sits beside the 24 V terminals. Keep the probes on the 24 V side; a probe bridging R to C blows the fuse.

states.wrong: Wrong — none on an O valve, or 24 V on a B valve

wrong: no 24 volts on the o wire in cooling
reversing valve not getting voltage in cooling
no voltage at the reversing valve in cooling

features.name: Point mode at the BAS
features.ask: At the BAS, is the point (start/stop, valve, setpoint) in auto, or held by an operator override or hand?
features.how: Open the point on the BAS workstation (the front end) or a local display and read its mode. An operator override at any level above the program (the BAS calls these levels priorities), or a hand-off-auto switch in hand, takes the equipment out of the program's control.

states.auto: In auto — the program has it

override: forced on at the front end
forced off at the front end

features.name: Controller occupancy mode vs the building
features.ask: Does the controller's occupancy mode (occupied or unoccupied) match what the building is doing now?
features.how: Read the system's actual occupancy point and the schedule behind it, including holidays and exceptions, and compare with the controller clock and the real time and date.

states.occ_when_empty: Occupied while the building is empty

features.name: Occupancy sensor or override button
features.ask: Does the occupancy sensor (or the after-hours override button) change state when it should?
features.how: Walk in and out of the sensor's view, or press the override button, and watch the occupancy input at the BAS. Look for a sensor blocked by furniture or one that sees a hallway.

states.ok: Changes state as it should
states.faulted: Stuck reading occupied, or never sees anyone

features.name: Controller status on the network
features.ask: Is the controller online at the BAS workstation, with its program and clock intact?
features.how: Look for the controller at the workstation (online, last update time), then at the controller itself (status lights, time and date, program version or a default program).

states.ok: Online, program and clock intact
states.offline: Offline — the workstation shows old values or no communication
states.reset: Lost its program or clock (default program, time reset)

offline: stale values on the front end

features.name: BAS command vs what the equipment does
features.ask: Does the equipment do what the BAS commands (start, stop, valve position), and does its feedback agree?
features.how: Compare the command point with the equipment itself and with any feedback point (run status, valve or damper position). Look at the equipment, not only at the screen.

states.agree: Equipment and feedback follow the command

mismatch: bas says on but nothing runs
bas shows open but the valve is shut
bas says it is running but it is off

features.name: Control signal from the BAS output
features.ask: While it is commanded, is the control signal present at the controller's output terminal and at the device?
features.how: Meter the output at the controller terminals (24 VAC for on/off, 0–10 V or 4–20 mA for a modulating output), then at the device end of the wire, including any relay between them that switches the load.
features.caution: Some outputs switch line voltage through a separate relay; meter its load side with insulated probes only. Read 4–20 mA only in series, on the meter's mA jack and range, never across the terminals, and move the lead back to V before the next reading. A solid-state output with nothing connected can show a false voltage; meter it with the load connected. Opening a 4–20 mA loop to put the meter in series makes the device see 0 mA, and a valve or damper may drive to its fail position, so know what it will do first.

states.present: Present at the controller and at the device
states.lost_in_field: Leaves the controller, doesn't reach the device (or its relay doesn't pass it on)

none_at_controller: output relay bad on the controller
no signal out of the controller
lost_in_field: no signal at the actuator but there is at the controller

features.name: Indoor air temperature rise (heating)
features.ask: How much does the air warm up across the indoor unit (supply minus return)?
features.how:
Measure return air entering the indoor unit and supply air leaving the plenum (or the wall head's louver),
with the auxiliary electric heat strips off unless you are testing the strips. Take the reading 10 or more
minutes into the run, never during a defrost cycle, and on a ductless head not during the
cold-air-prevention delay after start-up. A ducted heat pump typically delivers about 15–30 °F, less in
deep cold. Ductless heads at low or medium fan speed run hotter, so a rise of 35–55 °F is normal there.

states.low: Low (under 12 °F, or blowing cold air)
states.normal: Normal (12–38 °F ducted, up to about 55 °F ductless)
states.high: High (over 38 °F ducted, over 55 °F ductless — scorching supply air)

features.name: 4-way valve suction-path rise
features.ask: How much warmer is the valve's center tube (to the compressor) than the tube arriving from the active evaporator coil?
features.how:
After 5–10 minutes of running, clamp pipe probes about 6 in. from the 4-way reversing valve on the cold
vapor tube arriving from the active evaporator (in heating, the outdoor-coil connection) and on the
center tube of the valve, which goes to the compressor. More than 3 °F of pickup on the compressor side
means hot discharge gas is leaking across the slide inside the valve. This is a pipe-temperature check,
so it works on a unit with no true suction port. In heating the big vapor service port is discharge, so
never put the low hose on it.

states.normal: 3 °F or less (tight seal)
states.high: More than 3 °F warmer on the compressor side (internal bypass)

high: suction temperature rise across reversing valve
high delta t on reversing valve

features.name: Actual operating mode on heat call
features.ask: When calling for heat, is the unit actually heating the indoor coil or running backwards in cooling?
features.how:
Feel the large vapor line at the indoor unit and check the air leaving the outdoor unit: in heating mode
the big line going indoors is hot discharge gas and the outdoor unit blows cold air. If the indoor coil
gets cold and sweats while the outdoor unit blows warm air, it is stuck in cooling. On a wall head the same
story shows as cool supply air with the outdoor fan blowing warm air.

states.heating: Heating the indoor coil (even if weak)
states.cooling_in_heat: Running in cooling on a heat call (cold indoor coil, warm outdoor air)

cooling_in_heat: running in cooling on heat call
blowing cold air in heat mode
heats in cool and cools in heat
outdoor unit blowing warm in heat

features.name: 24 V at reversing-valve solenoid
features.ask: Is 24 V on the reversing-valve coil leads when the mode called needs the coil energized, and off when it should not be?
features.how:
Meter right at the two wires going to the solenoid coil, with the unit on the call you are testing. A valve
that is energized in cooling (thermostat O) should read 24 V on a cooling call and 0 V on a heat call. A
valve energized in heating (B) is the opposite. If you do not know which kind it is, read the wiring
diagram or meter the leads on both calls, then judge the call that is giving trouble. Read it against what
the valve needs, not against a fixed expectation.

states.as_required: Right for the mode called (24 V when the valve should be energized, 0 V when it should not)
states.absent_when_needed: No 24 V when the mode called needs the coil energized
states.present_when_off: 24 V on the coil when the mode called needs it de-energized

absent_when_needed: no voltage at reversing valve coil
no 24 volts on the reversing valve coil
reversing valve coil has no voltage
present_when_off: voltage on o wire in heat call
reversing valve energized when it should be off

features.name: Line voltage at the ductless 4-way valve coil
features.ask: On the heat call, is the 4-way valve coil getting its voltage from the outdoor board in the mode that should energize it?
features.how:
Many ductless 4-way coils are line voltage, switched by a relay on the outdoor board, not 24 V, and the
head has no O or B terminal. Check the coil's marking and the maker's wiring diagram first, since the
voltage and the mode that energizes the coil depend on the model. With power on and the call made, meter
at the board's coil connector (or the coil's own plug) and compare with what the diagram calls for in the
mode you are testing.
features.caution: Live line voltage at the outdoor board. Use a CAT III meter and insulated probes, work one-handed, and stay clear of the inverter section, whose DC bus stays charged after the breaker is off.

states.as_required: Voltage on the coil in the mode that energizes it, none when it should be off
states.absent_when_needed: No voltage at the coil connector in the mode that should energize it

absent_when_needed: no power to reversing valve coil on mini split
board relay not switching 4 way valve
no line voltage at reversing valve

features.name: Reversing-valve solenoid coil resistance & magnetism
features.ask: How does the reversing-valve solenoid coil test (resistance, and magnetic pull if it is a 24 V coil)?
features.how:
With power off and locked out, disconnect the coil leads and ohm the coil, then compare with the figure on
the coil or in the maker's data. A 24 V coil reads tens of ohms; a line-voltage coil, as on many ductless
units, reads far higher, so the 24 V figure is the wrong yardstick there. On a 24 V coil you can also apply
24 V and check that it pulls a steel screwdriver tip at the center stem. Skip the pull test on a
line-voltage coil (24 V does nothing to it), and never put line voltage on a 24 V coil.

states.ok: Resistance matches the coil's marking or the maker's data, and a 24 V coil pulls a screwdriver
states.open: Open (∞ Ω), burned, or a 24 V coil with no magnetic pull when energized

features.name: Reversing-valve mechanical shift test
features.ask: Does the reversing valve hiss and shift when its coil is switched with the compressor running?
features.how:
First make sure the valve has what it needs to move: a correct charge and a real pressure difference across
it, which means the compressor must be pumping. A valve will not shift without that, whatever the coil does.
Then, with the compressor running, energize and de-energize the coil (a ducted valve from the thermostat call;
a ductless one by changing mode at the head) and gently tap the valve body with a rubber mallet, never a steel
hammer. A healthy valve shifts with an audible whoosh.

states.no_shift: Coil is energized and clicks, but the valve slide never shifts (mechanically stuck)

features.name: Thermostat O/B polarity setting
features.ask: Is the thermostat's O/B reversing-valve terminal configured to match the valve (energize in cooling, O, or in heating, B)?
features.how:
Open the thermostat installer setup menu and look at the reversing-valve setting. It must match the valve:
O when the valve coil is energized in cooling, B when it is energized in heating. Confirm which one the
valve is from the wiring diagram, or by metering the coil leads in both modes. Do not go by the brand name.

states.ok: Configured to match the valve (O or B)
states.reversed: Configured backwards (O on a B valve, or B on an O valve)

reversed: thermostat set to o instead of b
set to b instead of o

features.name: Outdoor coil ice buildup
features.ask: What does the outdoor coil look like in heating mode?

states.none: Clear (or light uniform frost between defrost cycles)
states.partial_or_band: Ice band along the bottom pan or unmelted patches after defrost
states.encased: Encased in a solid block of ice

partial_or_band: ice at bottom of outdoor coil

features.name: Defrost coil sensor / termination thermostat
features.ask: How does the outdoor defrost coil sensor or snap-disc thermostat test (and the outdoor ambient sensor, if the board has one)?
features.how:
A snap-disc defrost thermostat clipped to the outdoor liquid/distributor tube should be closed (0 Ω)
below ~30 °F and open above ~55–70 °F. An NTC defrost thermistor should match its resistance-vs-temp
table when checked against actual tube temperature. A demand-defrost board also reads an outdoor
ambient sensor and compares coil to ambient, so check that sensor the same way. A drifted ambient sensor
causes both missed and nuisance defrost.

states.ok: Matches coil temperature (closed when icy, opens when warm)
states.open_or_drifted: Stays open or reads warm on a freezing coil
states.stuck_closed_or_loose: Stuck closed on a hot clear coil, or unclipped/hanging loose

features.name: Forced defrost test at board
features.ask: With the coil verified iced or below 30 °F, what happens when you jump the defrost board's TEST / speed-up pins with the unit running in heat?
features.how:
Do this only with the coil verified iced or below about 30 °F. With the compressor running in heating
mode, short the TEST pins on the outdoor defrost board. If nothing starts and you suspect the sensor, also
jumper the DFT/sensor terminals. Take the sensor jumper off as soon as defrost starts: leaving it in
forces the full time-out. On a warm coil the sensor does not call for defrost, so even a healthy board
only enters defrost with the sensor jumpered, and the result proves nothing about the sensor.
features.caution: Never force defrost on a warm, running system. It spikes the head pressure. Check the coil is iced or below 30 °F first.

states.normal: Enters defrost normally with the sensor connected
states.no_response: Nothing happens even with the coil sensor jumped (board dead)
states.starts_when_sensor_jumped: Only enters defrost once you jumper the coil sensor (coil verified iced or below 30 °F)

no_response: wont go into defrost on test pins

features.name: Defrost cycle behavior
features.ask: What does the outdoor unit actually do when it should be defrosting?

states.normal_defrost: Shifts to cooling, stops outdoor fan, melts coil, and terminates cleanly
states.fan_stops_no_hot_gas: Outdoor fan stops and W2 calls, but the 4-way valve never moves to the cooling position that sends hot gas to the outdoor coil
states.fan_runs_in_defrost: Shifts into defrost, but outdoor fan keeps running at full speed
states.runs_too_long: Stays in defrost on a steaming clear coil until 10-minute timer or high-pressure trip
states.nuisance_dry_coil: Goes into defrost repeatedly in cold dry weather with no frost on the coil

fan_stops_no_hot_gas: reversing valve doesnt shift in defrost
fan stops but ice doesnt melt
fan_runs_in_defrost: fan relay welded on defrost board
runs_too_long: trips high pressure at end of defrost
nuisance_dry_coil: defrosts every 30 minutes with no ice

features.name: Outdoor basepan drainage & pan heater
features.ask: Is meltwater draining freely from the outdoor basepan, or is a solid shelf of ice building up in the bottom pan?

states.clear: Basepan drain holes open and draining
states.solid_bottom: Drain holes plugged with ice/leaves or basepan heater failed — solid ice shelf in pan

solid_bottom: fan blade hitting ice in pan

features.name: Cold blow from vents during defrost
features.ask: Does the unit blow cold air from the supply vents for several minutes whenever it goes into defrost?
features.how:
Count this only when the air handler has electric strip heat wired to the defrost output (W2). With no
strips, or strips that are not wired to the defrost board, cool air during a short defrost is normal and
is not a fault.

states.no: Supply air stays warm or tempered during defrost
states.yes: Blows cold air into the space during every defrost cycle

features.name: Thermostat heat-pump mode and lockout settings
features.ask: Is the thermostat in Emergency Heat, or set so the compressor is locked out at today's outdoor temperature?
features.how:
Look for EM HEAT / E-HEAT on the thermostat display, then check the installer menu: compressor lockout
(the lowest outdoor temperature the compressor may run at), the aux-heat lockout (highest outdoor
temperature the strips may run at) and the stage delays. With Emergency Heat on, or a compressor lockout
above today's outdoor temperature, the compressor stays off and the strips do all the work.

states.ok: Heat-pump heat is enabled at this outdoor temperature
states.em_heat: Emergency Heat selected (compressor off, strips only)
states.comp_lockout: Compressor lockout set above today's outdoor temperature

features.name: Aux / defrost heat call (W / W2) at air handler
features.ask: Is 24 V AC reaching the indoor air handler's W / W2 terminal when auxiliary or defrost heat is called?
features.how:
This only means something while a W / W2 call is active: during defrost, second-stage heat or Emergency
Heat. Meter W1/W2 to C at the air handler control strip then. If 24 V is absent, either the outdoor defrost
board's W out wire is open or disconnected, or an outdoor ambient lockout is holding the call off. Both
read 0 V at the air handler, so to tell them apart meter upstream (at the board's W out terminal or the
thermostat) while the call is active.

states.present_at_air_handler: 24 V present at air handler W / W2 terminal
states.missing_at_air_handler: Outdoor board or thermostat calls, but W/W2 wire is open or disconnected to air handler
states.blocked_by_lockout: Held off by an outdoor lockout thermostat or balance-point setting set too low

missing_at_air_handler: no 24v on w2 at air handler
blocked_by_lockout: balance point lockout set too low

features.name: Electric heat strip current
features.ask: What current do the electric auxiliary heat strips draw when called?
features.how:
Clamp ONE conductor (L1 or L2) of each heater circuit, never both together: a clamp around both
conductors of one circuit reads about 0 A because the fields cancel. Call full heat (Emergency Heat) so
every stage is on, and give it time, because during the first 30–90 seconds the sequencers have not all
closed. A 5 kW bank at 240 V draws about 20.8 A and 10 kW draws about 41.7 A. Current falls with voltage,
so the same 5 kW bank draws about 18 A on a 208 V supply. Also check that current drops to 0 A when the
call is off.
features.caution: Live line voltage in the heater compartment. Clamp only the insulated conductor, keep hands clear of the heater rack and terminals, and lock out before moving any wire.

states.normal: About the rated amps for the voltage actually applied (about 20.8 A per 5 kW at 240 V)
states.low: Partial amps (one bank or element out)
states.zero: Zero amps on the heater leads

zero: no amp draw on heat strips

features.name: Air-handler strip-heat breaker / disconnect
features.ask: Is the dedicated high-amp breaker or pull-out disconnect for the electric heat strips on and supplying 208/240 V?
features.how:
Many air handlers have two separate circuits or cabinet breakers: one feeds the blower and 24 V
transformer, and a second 30–60 A breaker feeds the electric strip banks. Meter L1–L2 right at
the heater breaker lugs.
features.caution: Live line voltage at the breaker lugs. Use a CAT III meter and insulated probes, and lock out before removing any cover you do not have to.

states.ok: On, full 208/240 V at heater lugs
states.off_or_tripped: Off, tripped, or open pull-out on the heater circuit

off_or_tripped: second breaker on air handler off

features.name: Heat strip sequencer / relay
features.ask: How does the electric heat sequencer or contactor behave?
features.how:
With 24 V applied to the sequencer's bottom control terminals (bimetal heater), wait 30–60 seconds
and meter line voltage across the load contacts (should close to 0 V drop). With 24 V removed for
2 minutes, load contacts must open completely.
features.caution: Live line voltage across the load contacts. Use a CAT III meter and insulated probes, and keep hands off the heater rack.

states.ok: Closes within 60 s of 24 V call, opens when call is removed
states.open_with_call: 24 V on sequencer coil for >60 s, but load contacts stay open
states.welded_or_grounded: Contacts welded closed with no 24 V call (or element shorted to grounded frame)

welded_or_grounded: strips stay on with fan off

features.name: Strip-heat thermal high-limit & fusible link
features.ask: Are the thermal high-limit disc switch and the one-shot fusible link on the heater rack closed?
features.how:
Lock out power and check continuity across each snap-disc thermal limit and ceramic fusible link
mounted on the heater frame (or meter across them under call — an open safety shows full line
voltage across its terminals).
features.caution: Metering across a limit under call means live line voltage. Use a CAT III meter and insulated probes, or lock out and check continuity instead.

states.open: High-limit switch open or fusible link blown

open: thermal limit open on heater kit

features.name: Heating element coil resistance
features.ask: With power locked out and leads lifted, what do the nichrome heating element coils read?
features.how:
Each 5 kW 240 V nichrome coil reads about 11–12 Ω end-to-end and ∞ Ω to the metal frame. Visually
inspect the ceramic insulators for a snapped or sagging coil wire.

states.ok: 10–15 Ω per 5 kW coil and open to ground
states.open: Open circuit (∞ Ω — broken nichrome wire)

features.name: Pressures when switched to cooling mode
features.ask: Only if the outdoor air is above about 55 °F, after a shutdown and restart in cooling, do pressures and superheat/subcooling read normal?
features.how:
Only when the outdoor air is above about 55 °F (or the maker's limit for running in cooling). Shut the unit
down and wait about 5 minutes for the pressures to equalize, then restart it in cooling, let it run 10–15
minutes and read pressures, superheat and subcooling. Below that outdoor temperature skip this check:
cooling at low ambient reads abnormal on any unit, so the answer proves nothing. Switching the mode with the
compressor running slams the reversing valve. If it runs normally in cooling but starves or misbehaves in
heating, suspect a directional check valve or the outdoor heating metering device. Most heating-only faults
(ice, defrost, strips, lockout, balance point) also cool fine, so a "cools fine" answer does not point to
one cause. In heating the big vapor service port is discharge, so keep the low hose off it.
features.caution: Do not run the unit in cooling below about 55 °F outdoor (liquid slugging, an iced indoor coil, low-pressure trips). Always shut down and let the pressures equalize before switching modes.

states.no: Fault is present in both modes (or not a directional fault)
states.yes: Cools normally — fault happens only in heating mode

features.name: Directional check valves & heating metering device
features.ask: What do you find at the indoor bypass check valve and the outdoor heating metering device?
features.how:
In heating mode, liquid leaves the indoor coil through a check valve that bypasses the indoor
cooling orifice/TXV, and enters the outdoor coil through the outdoor heating TXV/orifice while the
outdoor check valve closes. Check for a temperature drop or frost across the indoor metering
assembly (means indoor check valve stuck closed) or frost/starving vs flooding at the outdoor
bi-flow/check assembly. Take suction readings at a true suction port, never at the big vapor valve
(discharge in heating).

states.ok: Indoor check valve open, outdoor heating metering device feeding properly
states.outdoor_heating_restricted: Outdoor heating TXV or piston starving / stuck closed in heating
states.indoor_bypass_stuck: Indoor check valve stuck closed in heating (temperature drop or frost across the indoor metering assembly)
states.outdoor_bypass_leaking: Outdoor check valve leaking through in heating (flooding outdoor coil)

outdoor_heating_restricted: bi flow txv stuck in heating
indoor_bypass_stuck: check valve at indoor coil stuck
liquid backing up in indoor coil

features.name: Outdoor coil air path (heating evaporator)
features.ask: Is the outdoor coil's air path clear of drifted snow, freezing-rain shell, leaves, or a tarp, and is the coil face clean?
features.how:
In heating mode the outdoor coil is the evaporator extracting heat from outdoor air. Inspect all
sides and under the hood for drifted snow, an ice shell from freezing rain, matted leaves, or a
winter cover left on, then look at the coil face itself for a mat of cottonwood, grass clippings or dirt.

states.blocked_snow_or_debris: Blocked by snow, glaze, leaves, a cover, or a matted/dirty coil face

features.name: Outdoor temperature vs thermal balance point
features.ask: Is the outdoor ambient temperature below the heat pump's thermal balance point?
features.how:
The balance point is building plus unit, so a tech rarely knows it. Use this test: is it colder outside than
the outdoor temperature at which this unit alone last held setpoint? Below that point building heat loss
exceeds the compressor's heating capacity even when the refrigerant circuit is healthy, so auxiliary heat must
stage on to hold setpoint. Standard heat pumps balance out at roughly 25–35 °F; cold-climate units hold on
to a lower outdoor temperature.

states.no: Outdoor air is above the balance point
states.yes: Deep cold — outdoor air is below the unit's balance point

yes: too cold for heat pump alone

features.name: Mini-split / inverter fault code
features.ask: What fault code or LED blink pattern is the mini-split or inverter unit displaying? Then look up what it means in that maker's service manual.
features.how:
Codes and blink patterns mean different things from one maker to the next, so never read one from memory or
from another brand. Write the code or the number of blinks down exactly, then find it in the maker's service
manual or code table and pick the matching state below.

states.none: No error code displayed
states.comm_error: Indoor-outdoor communication fault code (look it up in that maker's table)
states.ipm_or_drive: Inverter drive / IPM / compressor overcurrent or start-failure code

features.name: Indoor–outdoor serial communication voltage
features.ask: What do you measure on the communication wire between the indoor and outdoor units (labeled S, S2–S3, 2–3 or similar)?
features.how:
Find the signal terminal and its common in the wiring diagram first. Labels vary, and on some terminal
blocks the neighboring terminal is line voltage. Set your meter to DC volts (and check AC volts too), and
read signal to common at both the indoor and the outdoor terminal blocks. A healthy serial line shows an
unsteady DC voltage that visibly sweeps or pulses. Compare with the maker's figure if you have it. A steady
0 V, a flat rail that never moves, or wild noise from a spliced or stranded wire points to a communication
fault.
features.caution: Live check on a terminal block next to line voltage: use a CAT III meter and insulated probes, and find the signal terminal on the wiring diagram before the leads touch anything. Before unplugging the serial wire or touching the board, breaker off, wait the maker's time (not under 5 minutes) and confirm under 10 V DC across P(+)–N(−): the inverter bus holds 300–400 V DC.

states.pulsing_ok: Normal unsteady, sweeping or pulsing DC/AC voltage
states.dead_or_noisy: Steady 0 V, stuck high, open/spliced wire, or outdoor board power supply dead

dead_or_noisy: no pulsing voltage on s wire

features.name: Inverter IPM diode check & DC bus
features.ask: How do the outdoor inverter board's IPM (Intelligent Power Module) diode legs and DC bus test?
features.how:
Breaker off, then wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes) for the high-voltage DC bus
capacitors to bleed down, and confirm the bus reads under 10 V DC across P(+) and N(−) with a CAT III 600 V
meter before anything else. Unplug the compressor (U, V, W) and use the meter's diode mode to test P(+) to
U/V/W and N(−) to U/V/W in both directions. All six IGBT diode legs should read the same drop one way and
open (OL) the other. Compare the legs with each other, not with a fixed number.
features.caution: The inverter board holds 300–400 V DC on the bus capacitors after the breaker is off. Wait the maker's time (not under 5 minutes) and confirm under 10 V DC across P(+)–N(−) with a CAT III 600 V meter before unplugging any harness or touching the board.

states.ok: All 6 IPM diode legs match each other and the DC bus reads normal
states.failed: Shorted or open IPM leg, burned trace, or failed DC bus capacitor/reactor

failed: failed diode check on inverter board

features.name: Inverter compressor windings (U–V–W)
features.ask: With the compressor leads unplugged from the inverter board, how do U–V, V–W, and U–W measure?
features.how:
First make the board safe: breaker off, wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes), and
confirm under 10 V DC across P(+) and N(−) before unplugging the compressor leads. Disconnect the leads from
the board before any megger test, since a megger across a connected board destroys it. Measure
phase-to-phase resistance across U–V, V–W, and U–W with a low-ohms meter, then megger or ohm each pin to
the copper suction pipe. All three phases on a three-phase inverter compressor must read the same (within
a few percent, and usually a few ohms or less) and show infinite resistance to ground. Equal phases and no
ground fault do not clear a seized or demagnetized rotor, so judge that from how the compressor starts.
features.caution: Inverter board bus capacitors hold 300–400 V DC after power-off. Wait the maker's time (not under 5 minutes) and confirm under 10 V DC across P(+)–N(−) with a CAT III 600 V meter before unplugging the compressor leads. Disconnect the leads from the board before any megger test.

states.balanced_ok: All three phases equal (U–V = V–W = U–W) and open to ground
states.imbalanced_or_grounded: Phase-to-phase resistance unequal, open, or grounded

features.name: EEV stepper coil winding resistance
features.ask: With power off and the DC bus verified discharged, what do the EEV stepper coil winding pairs read at the unplugged harness?
features.how:
Make the board safe first: breaker off, wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes), and confirm
under 10 V DC across P(+) and N(−) before unplugging the EEV harness. Test resistance from the common
wire(s) to each of the stepper phase pins on the small 5- or 6-pin plug. Healthy windings read matched values
across all the phases (use the maker's figure; commonly tens to low hundreds of ohms) and ∞ Ω to the valve
body.
features.caution: Inverter board bus capacitors hold 300–400 V DC after power-off. Wait the maker's time (not under 5 minutes) and confirm under 10 V DC across P(+)–N(−) with a CAT III 600 V meter before unplugging the EEV harness or touching the board.

states.ok: All stepper windings matched (maker's figure) and open to the valve body
states.open_or_short: One or more windings open (∞ Ω), shorted, or corroded plug

features.name: EEV power-up initialization & magnet test
features.ask: When you cycle breaker power (or rotate a service magnet on the EEV body), does the EEV click and move refrigerant?
features.how:
At power-up, the board drives the EEV several hundred steps closed to find zero — you should hear
and feel rapid ticking at the valve body for 10–20 seconds. If the coil ticks but refrigerant flow
never changes, remove the coil and spin an EEV service magnet around the brass spindle to check if
the internal rotor/needle is jammed.

states.normal: Ticks at power-up and modulates refrigerant flow
states.clicks_no_flow_change: Coil clicks at power-up, but needle is mechanically stuck (no flow change)

features.name: NTC thermistor resistance vs temperature
features.ask: Do the unit's NTC thermistors (coil, discharge, room, outdoor ambient) match their resistance-vs-temperature table, and are they seated on the coil or tube they should read?
features.how:
Make the board safe first: breaker off, wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes), and confirm
under 10 V DC across P(+) and N(−) before unplugging any sensor. Unplug the suspected thermistor from the
board, measure the actual temperature right at the sensor bulb (or place it in a 32 °F ice-water bath), and
compare its kΩ reading with the manufacturer's kΩ chart. A sensor that has drifted well off the curve tells
the inverter to throttle back or lock out. A resistance that passes only proves the bulb is good: look at
where the bulb sits, because a sensor that has slipped out of its well or off the tube reads air instead of
the coil.
features.caution: Inverter board bus capacitors hold 300–400 V DC after power-off. Wait the maker's time (not under 5 minutes) and confirm under 10 V DC across P(+)–N(−) with a CAT III 600 V meter before unplugging any sensor or touching the board.

states.ok: Resistance matches actual temperature on the chart, and the sensor sits tight on its coil or tube
states.drifted_or_open: Drifted off-curve, open, or shorted (reports false temperature)
states.loose_or_misplaced: Resistance is right at the bulb, but the sensor is loose, out of its well, or not on the coil it should read

features.name: Mini-split flare joints
features.ask: What do you find at the flare nuts (behind the indoor unit and at the outdoor service valves)?
features.how:
Open the line-set wrap behind the indoor wall head and at the outdoor flare ports. Check for compressor
oil sheen on the brass flare nuts and sweep with an electronic leak detector or soap bubbles.

states.oil_or_leak: Oil film, bubbles, detector alarm, or cracked/cocked copper flare

features.name: Mini-split indoor cross-flow blower wheel
features.ask: Shine a flashlight into the indoor unit's supply vane — what is the condition of the cylindrical blower wheel?

states.clean: Clean blades and strong, even air throw
states.caked_surging: Blades packed with biofilm/dust — weak air throw and surging/whooshing noise

caked_surging: barely blowing air from wall unit

features.name: Mini-split condensate pump & float switch
features.ask: How are the mini-split's internal float switch and condensate pump operating?
features.how:
Check the indoor drain pan and mini-pump reservoir for slime, a stuck reed float, an air-bound pump
impeller, or an open safety contact cutting off the head.

states.ok: Float switch closed and pump discharging water cleanly
states.pump_or_float_fault: Pump failed/air-bound, float switch tripped open, or overflow alarm active

features.name: Multi-zone port piping vs wiring match
features.ask: On a multi-zone condenser or branch box, does each indoor head's control wire land on the same port (A, B, C, D) as its refrigerant lines?
features.how:
Turn on only one indoor head at a time and check which liquid/gas line pair changes temperature at
the outdoor manifold or branch box. If calling on head A chills or heats the pipes feeding head B,
the control wires and pipe ports are crossed. Before you tear into the wiring, rule out the normal
one-mode-at-a-time behavior (see the mode check): a head that sits in standby while another head
runs the opposite mode is not crossed.

states.matched: Control wire and refrigerant lines match on every port
states.crossed_pipes_wires: Crossed — calling on head A sends refrigerant to head B's coil

crossed_pipes_wires: head b freezes when head a calls

features.name: Mode asked of each head (multi-zone)
features.ask: On a multi-zone system, is another head running in the opposite mode (one heating, one cooling), with this head waiting in standby?
features.how:
Most multi-zone outdoor units (the ones without heat recovery) can run only one mode at a time. The head
that was called first sets the mode, and a head asking for the other mode waits in standby, often with a
blinking indicator, until the first mode is done. Check what mode each head is set to and which one started
first.

states.same_mode: Every head that is running is in the same mode
states.mixed_modes: One head is heating and another is asking for cooling (or the reverse) and is waiting

mixed_modes: one head heating other head cooling
one zone cool one zone heat
one head wont heat while the other zone is cooling
head wont cool while other head is heating
other zone is in the opposite mode

features.name: Area affected
features.ask: Is the heating problem in a single zone/unit or the whole building loop?

states.normal: Heating normally across zones
states.one_zone: One zone, coil, or room stays cold
states.whole_loop: Whole building or main loop is cold
states.overheating: A zone overheats with its thermostat off (ghost heat)

features.name: Circulator pump
features.ask: What is the circulator pump doing when the loop calls for heat?
features.how:
Listen and feel carefully at the pump housing (or touch a screwdriver tip to the bearing bracket and
the handle to your ear). A wet-rotor pump runs very quietly; check amp draw if unsure.

states.hums: Hums, gets hot, or trips overload without spinning
states.noisy: Running with rattling, gurgling, or gravel noise

features.name: Line voltage at circulator
features.ask: Is there full line voltage at the circulator motor terminals when calling?
features.how:
Meter L1 to N (or L1 to L2 on 208/230/460 V pumps) inside the pump junction box or at the load side of
the switching relay.

features.name: Circulator run capacitor
features.ask: How does the circulator motor's run capacitor test (µF vs rating)?
features.how:
Lock out power, discharge the capacitor in the motor terminal box, disconnect one lead, and measure
capacitance in µF. Replace if more than 7% below rating or swollen.

states.ok: Within rating

features.name: Circulator motor windings
features.ask: What do the circulator motor windings read with power locked out?
features.how:
Disconnect motor leads and ohm across the windings and from each lead to ground. An open winding reads
infinite; a grounded winding reads continuity to the motor shell.

states.ok: Normal winding resistance and open to ground

features.name: Pump coupling, shaft & impeller
features.ask: Inspect the pump coupler, shaft rotation, and impeller — what do you find?
features.how:
Look through the bearing-assembly window on a 3-piece pump to see if the coupler is intact and turning
the pump shaft. On a wet-rotor pump, isolate it first (close both isolation flanges; with no flanges,
drain the loop down below the pump), let it cool below about 120 °F and relieve it to 0 psig at its
drain, and only then remove the center vent plug or pull the cartridge to check if the rotor is seized
or the impeller has spun loose on the shaft. Catch the fluid.
features.caution: Close both pump isolation flanges, let the pump cool below about 120 °F and relieve it to 0 psig at its drain before a vent plug or cartridge comes out. A pump on a live hot loop sprays.

states.ok: Coupling intact, shaft turns freely, impeller tight
states.sheared: Coupling sheared or broken (motor spins, pump shaft stays still)
states.seized: Rotor or pump shaft seized / bound up
states.impeller_slip: Shaft spins, but impeller is stripped, loose, or broken

features.name: Circulator amp draw
features.ask: How does the circulator's running amp draw compare with nameplate FLA?
features.how:
Clamp one motor lead with the pump running at normal flow. Small circulators normally run about 50–90 %
of FLA, so compare with this pump's own known-good running amps if you have them.

states.normal: Roughly 60–100 % of nameplate FLA
states.low: Under about half of FLA, or well under this pump's known-good amps (unloaded — no flow or broken coupling/impeller)
states.high: Over FLA or pulling locked-rotor amps

features.name: Pump differential head
features.ask: How does the pressure rise across the running pump compare with its rated head?
features.how:
Measure discharge minus suction pressure across the pump and convert to feet of head (psig × 2.31 ÷
the fluid's specific gravity; about 1.03–1.06 for 40–55 % glycol, about 0.97 for 180 °F water). Compare
it with the design head on the pump tag or curve. Cold glycol is viscous and derates the curve, so judge
"low" against the pump curve at the fluid temperature.

states.normal: Near design head (on the pump curve at the fluid temperature)
states.zero: Near zero (under 3 ft — pump not moving fluid)
states.low: Low (under 65% of design head)
states.high: High / deadheaded (at shutoff head — flow blocked downstream)

features.name: Loop temperature drop (supply − return ΔT)
features.ask: How does the supply-minus-return temperature drop (ΔT) compare with the design ΔT on the tag or commissioning sheet?
features.how:
Measure supply and return pipe temperatures with clamp/strap probes or an IR thermometer on dull tape.
Read it with every zone or coil calling, the supply at its design or reset temperature and the fans
running. At light load a healthy constant-flow loop reads only 5–10 °F, so do not enter a light-load
reading. Wide ΔT (more than about 8 °F over design) means low water flow; narrow ΔT (under about half
of design) means short-circuiting or no heat transfer.

states.normal: From about 45 % of the design ΔT up to 8 °F over it, read at design load
states.high: High / wide ΔT (more than about 8 °F over design — supply hot, return cold, low flow)
states.low: Low / narrow ΔT (under about 45 % of design — supply and return nearly the same temperature)

features.name: Loop supply temperature
features.ask: How hot is the supply water leaving the header, mixing valve, or heat exchanger?
features.how: Read it on the supply pipe with a separate thermometer, not just the controller display.

states.normal: At expected temperature for the current load (typically 140–190 °F)
states.low: Cold or lukewarm (well below what the space load requires)
states.high: Too hot (above the controller setpoint or the high limit)

features.name: System pressure
features.ask: What does the hydronic pressure gauge read compared with the cold-fill target for this building?
features.how:
Read the boiler/loop pressure gauge; verify with a known test gauge on a drain or boiler drain cock
(hose any discharge to a container) because tridicators often stick. Read it hot and cold: a rise of
more than about 10 psig from cold to operating temperature means the expansion tank is not taking
water. The cold-fill target is the height of the highest point above the gauge (ft) × fluid SG ÷ 2.31,
plus 4–5 psig.
features.caution: If you check the gauge against a test gauge on a drain cock, open it slowly with a hose to a container. The fluid can be hot, and ethylene glycol is poisonous.

states.normal: Steady, at the cold-fill target (a few psi higher hot)
states.low: 5+ psig under the cold-fill target, or under the highest point's static head + 4 psig (under 8 psig is low on any loop)
states.high: Within 5 psig of the relief setting, or 10+ psig over the cold-fill target

features.name: Pressure relief valve
features.ask: What is the pressure relief valve doing — dry, weeping, or running?
features.how: A seat that drips at normal loop pressure is maintenance. A valve that is running or blowing hot water, glycol or steam is an overpressure or overtemperature event, so shut the heat source off first and then find the cause.

states.weeping: Dripping or weeping, loop pressure normal
states.discharging: Running or blowing hot water, glycol or steam (shut the heat source off)

features.name: Expansion tank check
features.ask: What do you find when you check the expansion tank (connection, tap test, and the air side at the Schrader valve)?
features.how:
First look at the tank's connection: is its isolation valve open, and is the connection pipe warm when
the loop is hot? Tap the shell from top to bottom (a bladder tank should ring hollow on the air end).
Then valve the tank off and drain its water side to 0 psig (no valve: cool the loop and relieve it to
0 psig) before you press the Schrader core or put a gauge on it, and stand to the side with eye
protection on. Water from the Schrader means a ruptured bladder or diaphragm. With the water side at
0 psig, the air side should read the cold-fill pressure.
features.caution: Valve the tank off and drain its water side to 0 psig before pressing the Schrader valve or fitting a gauge. A ruptured bladder sprays hot fluid at face height. Stand to the side, eye protection on.

states.ok: Air side holds the cold-fill pressure (tank valved off, water side at 0 psig, gauge on the Schrader)
states.ruptured: Water comes out of the Schrader (bladder or diaphragm failed), or the tank is dead solid top to bottom
states.low_precharge: Schrader dry but the air side reads under the cold-fill pressure (bladder intact)
states.waterlogged: Plain steel compression tank full of water (air cushion gone)
states.isolated: Tank valved off, or its connection pipe is cold, frozen or plugged

features.name: Make-up / fill valve (PRV)
features.ask: How is the automatic fill / pressure-reducing valve (or glycol make-up feeder) behaving?
features.how:
If pressure is low, check that the supply isolation valve is open and the glycol reservoir is not empty.
On a water loop, lift the fast-fill lever to see if fluid feeds in; on a glycol loop use the glycol
feeder, not the domestic fast-fill lever. If pressure is high, close the isolation valve ahead of the
fill valve and bleed pressure down to the cold-fill target through a hose to a container — if it stays
steady with the valve shut, the PRV was passing.
features.caution: Bleed through a hose to a container, never onto the floor. The fluid can be hot, and ethylene glycol is poisonous. On a glycol loop use the glycol feeder, not the domestic fast-fill lever.

states.ok: Feeds to target pressure and shuts off tight
states.blocked: Valved off, inlet screen plugged, failed closed, or glycol tank empty
states.passing: Passing / leaking through — creeps pressure up even when cool

features.name: Sound in pipes or pump
features.ask: What sound do you hear in the hydronic pipes, coils, or pump?

states.gurgling: Gurgling, sloshing, or rushing water sound in pipes/coils
states.gravel: Gravel or marbles rattling at the pump suction (cavitation)

features.name: Bleeding / purging test
features.ask: What comes out when you open the coin vent, purge valve, or pump bleed screw?

ask_for.terminal: What comes out when you open the unit's coin vent or bleed valve at its high point?

features.caution: Hot fluid can spray from a vent or bleed port. Open it slowly with a hose to a container, face away, and collect glycol (ethylene glycol is poisonous).

states.water: Solid stream of water or glycol right away
states.air: Air hisses or sputters out before liquid
states.nothing: Nothing comes out (zero pressure or frozen/blocked line)

features.name: Automatic air vent (hyvent)
features.ask: Inspect the automatic air vent(s) at the air separator and high points — what do you find?

states.ok: Cap loose 1 turn, venting air cleanly, dry
states.stuck_closed: Cap screwed down tight or float stuck shut (trapping air)
states.leaking: Spitting or dripping water/glycol from the vent cap

features.name: Isolation & balancing valves
features.ask: Check the isolation, service, and balancing valves in the loop — how are they set?

ask_for.terminal: Check the unit's own isolation and balancing valves on its supply and return — how are they set?

states.closed: An isolation or service valve is closed (or gate dropped off stem)
states.bypass_open: Bypass valve left wide open or near-branch balancing valves wide open

features.name: Y-strainer / dirt separator
features.ask: Is the Y-strainer or dirt-separator screen plugged with scale, rust, or sludge?
features.how:
Feel or measure for a temperature/pressure drop across the strainer body, then isolate, let it cool,
relieve it to 0 psig, and blow down or pull the screen to inspect.
features.caution: Isolate the strainer, let it cool and relieve it to 0 psig before backing out the plug or cover. Catch the fluid.

states.clogged: Plugged with debris, scale, magnetite, or sludge

features.name: Zone valve operation
features.ask: With the zone calling for heat, what is the zone valve doing?

ask_for.terminal: With the unit calling for heat, what is its control valve (zone valve, or modulating valve and actuator) doing?

features.how:
Push the manual opener lever on the actuator head: if the valve is already open, the lever moves freely
with no resistance; if closed, you feel spring resistance pushing the ball/poppet open.
features.caution: On steam, don't latch a valve open or drive it with a jumper onto a cold coil. Crack it open, listen for hammer, and shut it at once if it bangs. Some zone valve heads are 120 V — read the label before you meter.

states.ok: Opens on call and closes when satisfied
states.stays_closed: Stays closed on call (lever has spring resistance; heats when latched open manually)
states.jammed_closed: Mechanically jammed closed (seized stem/cartridge; no flow even with head removed)
states.stuck_open: Stuck open or latched in manual-open (heats zone when not calling)

features.name: Zone valve end switch
features.ask: When the zone valve is driven full open, does its auxiliary end switch close?
features.how:
Meter continuity (or 24 V drop) across the two end-switch terminals on the valve head while the valve is
fully open. Closed switch = 0 V across it (or 0 Ω isolated).

states.open: Stays open even when valve is full open

open: zone valve opens pump stays off

features.name: 3-way mixing valve
features.ask: How is the 3-way mixing valve positioned when the loop calls for heat?
features.how:
Compare pipe temperatures on all three ports (hot supply in, return bypass in, mixed loop out) and check
whether the actuator drives the stem toward the hot port.

states.ok: Blending hot supply into the loop normally
states.stuck_bypass: Stuck in full bypass / closed to hot port (hot port is hot, mixed outlet stays cool)
states.stuck_hot: Stuck open to the hot port (mixed outlet runs at primary temperature)

stuck_hot: mixing valve stuck open to hot

features.name: Flow-check / check valve
features.ask: How is the flow-check or spring/swing check valve operating?
features.how:
If a zone heats with its pump off, check whether the flow-check thumbscrew is turned down to "manual
open" or trash is holding the weight/clapper up. If a running pump gets no flow through the branch, check
for a stuck-shut clapper or a check valve installed backwards.

states.ok: Opens with pump running and seats when pump stops
states.stuck_open: Stuck open or thumbscrew left in manual-open (gravity/ghost flow)
states.stuck_closed: Stuck closed or installed backwards (blocks pumped flow)

features.name: Heat exchanger approach temperature
features.ask: What is the hot-end approach across the heat exchanger (primary hot inlet minus secondary heated outlet), with the primary control valve wide open?
features.how:
Hot-end approach = the primary fluid entering the plate/tube heat exchanger minus the secondary supply
leaving it, read with the primary control valve at 95–100 % open (drive it open by hand if you can do
so safely) and the secondary at design flow. A modulating primary valve at part load throttles to hold
the secondary setpoint, which makes this number large by design. Data sheets often quote the cold-end
figure, so compare like with like. A clean exchanger typically runs a 5–15 °F hot-end approach; over
20 °F points to fouling or poor primary flow.

states.normal: Normal (20 °F or less, primary valve wide open)
states.high: High (over 20 °F with the primary valve wide open — poor heat transfer across the exchanger)

features.name: Pressure drop across heat exchanger
features.ask: How does the waterside pressure drop (inlet minus outlet psi) across the heat exchanger compare with its data sheet or commissioning value at the same flow?
features.how: Read inlet and outlet pressure with the secondary at design flow, on one gauge or a matched pair.

states.normal: Within about 25 % of the data-sheet or commissioning ΔP at the same flow
states.high: More than ~25–30 % above the data-sheet or commissioning ΔP at the same flow (no absolute figure applies — plates or tubes plugged)

high: high pressure drop across heat exchanger

features.name: Primary-side temperature drop across the exchanger
features.ask: With the exchanger working, how does the primary-side temperature drop (primary in minus primary out) compare with its design?
features.how:
Read primary in and primary out at the exchanger with the primary valve wide open. A drop much wider
than design with the secondary leaving cool means too little primary flow (pump off, valve throttled,
strainer plugged). A drop much narrower than design with the secondary still leaving cool means the
plates are not passing heat (fouled).

states.normal: Close to design
states.wide: Much wider than design (not enough primary flow)
states.narrow: Much narrower than design (heat is not crossing the plates)

features.name: Glycol freeze protection
features.ask: How does the measured glycol freeze point compare with the required freeze protection?
features.how:
Sample from a flowing part of the loop (not the feeder tank or a dead leg), let the drop cool to room
temperature, and put it on a temperature-compensated glycol refractometer; read the freeze point on the
scale matching the loop fluid (PG or EG). Wipe the prism between samples. Never trust color alone.
