features.caution: Sample from a flowing part of the loop and let the drop cool before it goes on the prism; hot fluid scalds. Ethylene glycol is poisonous, so keep it off skin, food and drinking water, and collect what you draw.

states.ok: Protected (freeze point at or below required target)
states.weak: Too weak — freeze point warmer than the target (slush forms at the freeze point and coils stop flowing; burst protection is colder, do not rely on it)
states.rich: Over-concentrated (above ~60 % the freeze point turns back up; thick, poor heat transfer)

features.name: Glycol pH and visual condition
features.ask: What do a pH strip and a jar sample of the glycol show?
features.how:
Draw a sample from a drain port into a container after flushing dead leg water. Inhibited glycol should
read about pH 8.0–10.5 with no sediment or odor; it is usually dyed, so color alone tells you nothing.
Below pH 8.0 means organic acids have formed and the inhibitors are spent.
features.caution: Draw the sample slowly into a container. Hot fluid scalds, and ethylene glycol is poisonous, so keep it off skin and out of drains, and collect it.

states.good: pH 8.0–10.5 and no sediment or odor (color does not matter)
states.degraded: pH under 8.0, dark sludge, or burnt smell

features.name: Frozen or burst pipe / coil
features.ask: Is a pipe or coil iced up, slushy, blocked with ice, or split? (On a glycol loop, being below 32 °F is normal.)
features.caution: Treat every frozen coil or pipe as split. Never thaw it while it is connected to a live supply. Lock out the unit, close and verify both isolation valves, and open its drain or vent first.

states.no: No ice or slush, and intact (cold pipe is normal on a glycol loop)
states.iced: Ice or slush in the fluid, or an ice plug (on a water loop, below 32 °F counts)

features.name: Circulator shaft seal leak
features.ask: Is water or glycol dripping from the weep hole between the pump volute and motor bracket?

states.pump_seal: Dripping or spraying from the pump shaft seal / bracket weep hole

features.name: Terminal unit fan or fin airflow
features.ask: With hot water at the terminal unit, how is air moving across the coil or baseboard fins?

states.good: Fan running at full speed / baseboard fins clean and damper open
states.fan_off: Unit-heater or fan-coil fan motor is dead (coil pipes hot, fan not spinning)
states.fins_blocked: Baseboard/convector fins matted with dust, louver shut, or blocked by furniture
states.coil_fouled: Unit-heater or fan-coil airflow is poor with the fan running (filter plugged, coil fins matted with dust or lint, or coil tubes scaled or air-bound)

fan_off: fan motor not running on unit heater

features.name: Outdoor-reset / supply setpoint
features.ask: What supply water temperature is the outdoor-reset controller calling for vs actual outdoor weather?
features.how:
Read the controller's calculated target supply temperature and its outdoor sensor reading. Compare the
sensor reading with a thermometer outdoors and check the reset curve settings.

states.ok: Setpoint matches outdoor conditions and curve
states.too_low: Setpoint is far too low (outdoor sensor drifted warm, in sun/exhaust, or curve mis-set)

features.name: Primary heat-recovery loop & backup boiler staging
features.ask: On a heat-recovery plant, is the primary jacket-water/waste-heat loop hot, and did the backup boiler stage on?

states.ok: Primary heat source hot (or backup boiler staged on normally)
states.cold_no_stage: Primary heat-recovery loop is cold AND backup boiler did not stage on

cold_no_stage: waste heat down backup boiler off

features.name: Indirect domestic hot water (DHW) check
features.ask: On an indirect water heater, what do you find at the tank coil, DHW priority zone, and tempering valve?

states.ok: Domestic hot water normal
states.fault: Domestic water cold/lukewarm — DHW pump/valve off, scaled coil, or failed tempering valve

features.name: Steam problem area
features.ask: Where is the steam heating or condensate problem showing up?

states.normal: Heating evenly across the building
states.one_unit: A single radiator, convector, or steam coil stays cold
states.main_slow: A whole branch or far end of a steam main heats slowly or stays cold
states.return_issue: Steam blowing from receiver vent, hot return header, or overflowing receiver

features.name: Water hammer (banging pipes)
features.ask: Are the steam pipes or radiators banging, clanking, or pounding (water hammer)?

states.no: Quiet (or light ticking from normal thermal expansion)
states.yes: Loud banging, pounding, or violent water hammer

features.name: Boiler water line
features.ask: Is the boiler water line steady in the gauge glass?
features.how:
Watch the gauge glass for a minute at the normal firing rate and compare it with the normal water line
mark. Dirty, oily or heavily treated boiler water foams and carries over, and so does a line held too
high.

states.bouncing: Bouncing or surging in the glass (priming or foaming)
states.high: Held above the normal line

features.name: Condensate return temperature
features.ask: What is the temperature of the condensate return header or receiver tank?
features.how:
Measure the condensate return pipe entering the receiver with a contact probe or IR thermometer on tape.
Compare it with this plant's own logged baseline: F&T and bucket-trap systems routinely return 195–205 °F
after flashing, while thermostatic-trap systems with bare returns run cooler (150–185 °F). A vented
receiver tops out near 212 °F, so temperature alone cannot separate flash steam from live steam. Confirm
with the vent plume and by listening to the traps.

states.normal: Below about 205 °F (F&T and bucket-trap systems routinely run 195–205, so judge by the vent plume and trap tests)
states.high: 205 °F or more, or 15–20 °F above this plant's own logged baseline

features.name: Condensate receiver vent plume
features.ask: What is coming out of the condensate receiver's atmospheric vent pipe?
features.how:
Distinguish flash steam from live steam: lazy white vapor drifting gently from the vent is normal flash
steam; a strong, noisy jet with a clear gap right at the pipe lip is live steam from a blowing trap.

states.normal: Nothing or lazy drifting vapor (normal flash steam)
states.live_steam: Strong, noisy jet of live steam blowing out
states.water: Liquid water spitting or overflowing from the receiver/vent

water: water pouring out of condensate tank

features.name: Unit steam trap test
features.ask: What do the sound and temperature checks on the radiator/coil steam trap show?
features.how:
Listen first with a mechanic's stethoscope or ultrasonic detector on the trap body: a failed-open trap
hisses or roars continuously with no cycling, and a failed-closed trap is silent. Temperature is a
backup only. Thermostatic traps run 15–30 °F cooler on the outlet; F&T, bucket and disc traps show
little drop, so a small drop alone is not a failure.
features.caution: Test by sound and surface temperature only. Never open a trap cap, strainer plug or union while the line holds steam.

states.ok: Steam held back; condensate flow intermittent or smooth; outlet at or below ~212 °F
states.failed_open: Hissing or roaring continuously, hot on both sides, outlet pipe at about 212 °F
states.failed_closed: Silent and cold on both sides while steam is available in the supply main

features.name: Main or riser drip trap
features.ask: Check the steam main / riser drip leg strainer and drip trap — is it hot and draining condensate?
features.how:
Every steam main low point and riser heel has a drip leg and trap draining into the wet/dry return. If
that drip trap is cold while the main is hot, condensate is backing up into the steam main.
features.caution: Check by sound and surface temperature. Verify the drip leg is isolated and at 0 psig before opening a strainer plug, trap cap or blowdown.

states.ok: Hot and passing condensate cleanly
states.cold_plugged: Cold — trap failed closed or drip-leg dirt pocket/strainer plugged

cold_plugged: bad f and t drip trap

features.name: Radiator / main air vent
features.ask: How does the automatic air vent (on the radiator or end of the steam main) behave when steam comes on?
features.caution: Watch it, do not unscrew it. Never remove a vent, plug or union from anything holding steam. Close the supply valve, let it cool, and confirm 0 psig first.

states.ok: Hisses air out while cold, then closes tight when steam hits it
states.stuck_closed: Never hisses air out — stays cold and keeps the radiator/main air-bound
states.stuck_open: Spits live steam and water into the room after the radiator is hot

features.name: Steam pipe pitch & hangers
features.ask: Check the pitch of the steam main, runout, or radiator with a level — are there sags, pockets, or un-trapped lifts?

states.good: Pitched continuously toward the drain or trap, with no low pockets
states.sagged: Sagging hanger, back-pitched runout, tilted radiator, or condensate lifted to an overhead return

features.name: Radiator / coil steam supply valve
features.ask: Is the manual steam supply valve at the radiator or coil wide open and passing steam?
features.how:
On one-pipe steam, a supply valve must be 100% open or 100% closed — never throttled part-way. Also
check whether the handwheel turns freely with a detached disc sitting on the seat.

states.closed_or_throttled: Closed, partly throttled, or valve disc detached on the seat

closed_or_throttled: disc off stem on steam valve

features.name: Condensate return pump operation
features.ask: What is the condensate return pump doing when the receiver fills?

states.normal: Starts when full, pumps down in ~20–40 s, shuts off
states.off_full: Receiver full or overflowing, but pump motor does not run
states.runs_no_pump: Pump motor runs nonstop, but receiver stays full or overflows
states.short_cycles: Pumps down, shuts off, and immediately refills from the discharge line

features.name: Condensate pump float switch
features.ask: With the receiver tank full, is the float switch closed and sending voltage to the pump motor?
features.how:
Move the float linkage by hand to feel for binding or a waterlogged float ball, then meter voltage into
and out of the float switch.
features.caution: Lock out the pump and let the receiver cool before you reach in or open the cover. The water can be 180–210 °F.

states.ok: Float moves freely and switch closes when tank is full
states.stuck: Float stuck/waterlogged or switch contacts stay open when full

features.name: Condensate pump discharge check valve
features.ask: When the condensate pump stops, does hot water or steam back-flow through the discharge check valve into the receiver?
features.how:
Feel and listen at the discharge check valve right as the pump shuts off. If boiler water/steam rushes
backward through the check, the receiver refills rapidly and the pump short-cycles.
features.caution: Feel and listen only. Boiler-pressure water sits behind this check valve, so do not open it until the isolation valve downstream is closed and the line is relieved.

states.leaks_back: Leaks backward — refills receiver from the discharge line

features.name: Vacuum return gauge reading
features.ask: On a vacuum return system, how much vacuum does the vacuum pump pull (normally 2–6 in. Hg)?

states.normal: Pulls 2–6 in. Hg vacuum and cycles off
states.low: Stays near 0 in. Hg while vacuum pump runs continuously

features.name: Visible steam or return pipe leak
features.ask: Do you see or hear steam hissing or condensate leaking from a pipe, union, valve packing, or flange?
features.caution: Find a steam leak by sound and with a rag on a stick, never with your hand. Steam is invisible close to the leak, and it burns.

states.no: Piping, joints, and valve packings tight
states.yes: Hissing steam or dripping condensate at a union, packing nut, flange, or corroded pipe

features.name: Low-pressure steam main pressure after the reducing valve
features.ask: On a plant that steps high-pressure steam down through a reducing station, what does the low-pressure gauge read against the set pressure?
features.how:
Read the gauge on the low-pressure main at least 10 ft past the reducing valve and compare it with the
pressure the station is set to deliver. Over the setting with the low-side relief lifting, or well under
it at the units, points at the station.

states.normal: Holds the set pressure
states.low: Well under the set pressure (units starved)
states.high: Over the set pressure (low-side relief lifting, or over-pressure at the units)

features.name: Box / cabinet temperature
features.ask: How is the walk-in or reach-in temperature compared with its setpoint?
features.how: Read an independent thermometer inside the box away from the evaporator discharge, not just the door dial or controller display, and not within an hour of a defrost or a long door-open (a freezer's air climbs 5–15 °F in defrost and takes 30–60 min to pull back).

states.normal: Box temperature at setpoint (within ±4 °F)
states.high: Box / cabinet warm (more than 4 °F above setpoint)
states.low: Box too cold / freezing product (more than 4 °F below setpoint)

features.name: Frost / ice pattern in the box
features.ask: Where and what kind of frost or ice do you see on the evaporator and in the box?
features.how: Solid frost packed evenly through the fins points to missed defrost; clear solid ice rising from the pan into the coil and fan blades comes from a frozen drain; fluffy snow and hoarfrost on the ceiling, door frame, and fan guards comes from warm moist air leaking into the box, or from steam when a defrost runs far too long. Ice left in one zone only (bottom rows, one stripe) belongs under "frost on part of the coil", not here.

states.none: Clean — no heavy ice or snow buildup
states.uniform_fin: Solid frost/ice packed evenly across the coil fins
states.pan_backup: Clear solid ice building up from the drain pan into the coil bottom and fan blades
states.snow_door: Fluffy snow and hoarfrost around the door, ceiling, fan guards, and coil face

features.name: Defrost initiation
features.ask: Does the defrost timer or controller initiate defrost on schedule (and when advanced manually)?
features.how: Check the timer dial motor (is it turning?), verify the brass trippers are in place, or trigger a manual defrost on the electronic controller and listen for the defrost relay to click.

states.not_initiating: Never initiates defrost (timer motor stopped, trippers missing, or controller not scheduled)

features.name: Voltage to defrost heaters
features.ask: With the unit forced into defrost, is line voltage reaching the defrost heater circuit?
features.how: Advance the timer or controller into defrost and meter line voltage on the load side of the defrost contactor or timer terminal (typically terminal 3 to N or L2).

states.present: Line voltage present at heater circuit
states.missing: No line voltage at heater terminals in defrost (contactor or timer contact open)

features.name: Defrost heater amp draw
features.ask: With the unit in defrost, what do the electric defrost heaters draw on a clamp meter?
features.how: Clamp the heater feed wire at the condensing unit or evaporator terminal block during defrost and compare with nameplate heater watts ÷ nameplate volts, scaled to the voltage you really have (heater amps follow voltage; a 240 V heater on a 208 V supply draws about 87 % of nameplate with every element good).

states.normal: Full rated amps (all heater elements drawing)
states.low: Partial amps (one or more heater elements open)

features.name: Defrost termination behavior
features.ask: How does the defrost cycle end (termination snap-disc or coil temperature sensor)?
features.how: Watch one defrost end, or read the controller's last-defrost log (a full cycle takes 20–45 min). It should run until the coil reaches ~45–55 °F and the ice is gone, then end on temperature, well before the fail-safe time limit. Skip it on a timer that ends defrost on time alone (no termination snap-disc or probe).

states.normal: Ends on temperature when the coil is clear (~45–55 °F)
states.early: Ends after a few minutes while ice is still on the coil
states.late_never: Never ends on temperature — runs to the fail-safe time limit (coil still iced = not enough heat reached it; coil hot, dry and the box steaming = sensor failed)

early: comes out of defrost too soon
termination thermostat closed on a cold coil

features.name: Defrost safety high-limit switch
features.ask: On a cold coil, is the defrost safety high-limit (snap-disc) thermostat closed?
features.how: With the evaporator below freezing and power locked out (or metered across the limit in defrost), check continuity across the high-limit switch mounted near the top of the coil.

states.open: Open on a cold coil (blocks power to the heaters)

features.name: Hot-gas defrost solenoid valve
features.ask: How is the hot-gas defrost solenoid valve behaving?
features.how: In cooling, the hot-gas line after the solenoid should be cool. In defrost, the coil should energize and the pipe immediately downstream should jump to well over 150 °F — read it with an IR thermometer or a clamp-on pipe probe; don't grab hot-gas piping.

states.normal: Opens in defrost, stays shut and cool during cooling
states.stuck_closed: Fails to open in defrost (pipe stays cold when defrost is called)
states.leaking_cooling: Leaks hot gas into the evaporator during the cooling cycle (pipe stays hot in cooling)

leaking_cooling: hot gas bypass leaking in cooling

features.name: Evaporator drain pan and drain line
features.ask: Is the evaporator condensate drain pan and drain line clear or frozen up?

states.frozen: Frozen solid or plugged with ice in the pan and drain line

features.name: Drain-line / drain-pan heat tape
features.ask: Is the drain-line or drain-pan heater warm and drawing current (or showing normal resistance)?
features.how: Feel the drain line inside the freezer under the insulation and meter the heat tape's amp draw or resistance at the evaporator junction box.

states.open_cold: Cold — heater tape open, unpowered, or pulled out of the drain

features.name: Evaporator fan-delay control
features.ask: With the evaporator coil cold, is the fan-delay snap-disc thermostat or controller relay energizing the fans?
features.how: After defrost ends and the compressor chills the coil below ~25 °F, the fan-delay side of the termination/fan thermostat (or controller F terminal) must close to bring the fans back on.

states.closed_ok: Closes normally once the coil is cold
states.stuck_open: Stuck open on a cold coil — evaporator fans never restart after defrost

stuck_open: fans wont come back on after defrost

features.name: Evaporator fan blade & shroud clearance
features.ask: Do the evaporator fan blades spin freely without hitting ice or the fan shroud?
features.how: With power off, look at the fan ring and spin each blade by hand to check for ice ridges, bent blades, or a shifted motor mount.

states.clear: Blades spin freely with even clearance
states.hitting_ice: Blade locked in ice, bent, or scraping the shroud

features.name: Door switch (fan cutout / light switch)
features.ask: Does the walk-in or reach-in door switch actuate cleanly when the door closes?
features.how: Press the plunger by hand and check that the door frame actually depresses it when latched; a stuck or misaligned switch kills the evaporator fans or holds the interior heater/lights on.

states.ok: Switches cleanly when the door closes
states.stuck_fault: Stuck, broken, or not depressed by the door (holds fans off or lights on)

stuck_fault: fans stay off with door closed

features.name: Door gasket, hinges, closer & latch
features.ask: Does the door pull shut tightly and seal all the way around the gasket?
features.how: Check for torn or brittle gasket corners, sagging hinges, a dead hydraulic closer, and test with a dollar bill or flashlight around the perimeter.

states.tight: Tight seal all around; door closes fully
states.leaking: Torn/gapped gasket, sagging hinge, failed closer, or door not latching shut

features.name: Door frame / mullion anti-sweat heater
features.ask: Is the door perimeter frame / mullion warm and dry, or cold and sweating / freezing the door shut?
features.how: Run your hand along the door jamb and mullion; if it is cold, meter the anti-sweat heater wire for voltage and continuity (and check whether an energy-saver switch is turned off).

states.cold_failed: Cold — sweating heavily or freezing the door gasket to the frame

features.name: Box penetrations, strip curtains & relief port
features.ask: Is outside air pouring in through missing strip curtains, an unsealed pipe hole, or a stuck relief port?
features.how: Look inside with the lights off for daylight around pipe penetrations, check that strip curtains hang flat, that the heated pressure-relief port flaps aren't stuck open, and that the door isn't being propped open.

states.sealed: Envelope tight; curtains and relief port intact
states.open_breach: Heavy air infiltration (missing curtains, open penetration, stuck relief port, or propped door)

features.name: Product loading & interior airflow path
features.ask: Are boxes stacked tight against the evaporator/walls blocking airflow, or was a large hot load just put in?
features.how: Check that cartons sit on pallets/racks with clearance under the evaporator and along the walls, and ask the galley crew if steaming trays or warm pallets were just loaded.

states.ok: Clear air path; normal pre-chilled load
states.blocked_or_hot: Boxes blocking evaporator/return air path, or heavy load of warm product just placed inside

features.name: Box thermostat / controller probe accuracy
features.ask: Does the controller display or thermostat bulb agree with a calibrated thermometer at the probe?
features.how: Strap a trusted digital thermometer tip right next to the box air probe (or stir both in an ice-water bath at 32 °F) and compare readings. Enter that reference reading (taken AT the probe), not a box reading from elsewhere.

states.drifted: Off by 4 °F or more (probe drifted, wet, or capillary bulb out of place)

features.name: Liquid-line pump-down solenoid valve (LLSV)
features.ask: How does the liquid-line solenoid valve behave on call and during off-cycle pump-down?
features.how: When the box satisfies, the LLSV should close and the compressor should pump the low side down once and stay off. On a call for cooling, the coil gets voltage and the valve clicks open.

states.normal: Opens on call, holds tight during off cycle
states.leaking_through: Leaks through when off (suction creeps up and compressor short-cycles during the off cycle)
states.stuck_closed: Stays closed on call (coil open or plunger stuck — unit stays pumped down on LPS)

features.name: Low-pressure control (LPC) settings
features.ask: Are the low-pressure switch cut-in and cut-out settings matched to the refrigerant and box temperature?
features.how:
Read the cut-in and cut-out off gauges against the refrigerant PT chart, not the dial scale. Cut-in (compressor
starts) must sit below the saturation pressure at the box air temperature where the thermostat calls, so the
compressor always restarts when the solenoid opens, and above the highest pressure the pumped-down coil creeps to
with the solenoid shut. Cut-out (pump-down ends) belongs a few psig above zero, never into vacuum. Keep at least
10–15 psi of differential so it doesn't rapid-cycle.

states.correct: Cut-in, cut-out, and differential set properly for the refrigerant
states.wrong_tight: Cut-out set too high or differential too tight (cuts out early or rapid-cycles)

features.name: Crankcase heater (off cycle)
features.ask: With the compressor off in a cold space, is the crankcase heater warm and drawing current?
features.how: Feel the bottom of the compressor shell during the off cycle and meter voltage and resistance across the crankcase heater leads.

states.warm_ok: Crankcase warm in off cycle; heater intact
states.cold_failed: Crankcase cold in off cycle — heater open or unpowered

features.name: Compressor oil sight glass
features.ask: What do you see in the compressor crankcase oil sight glass?
features.how: Check oil level after 10 minutes of running and watch the glass right at start-up for violent foaming.

states.normal: Clear oil steady at 1/4 to 3/4 glass
states.foaming_low: Violent foaming / frothing oil in the sight glass (liquid refrigerant in crankcase)
states.low_empty: Oil level below the sight glass or empty

features.name: Oil-pressure safety control (OPS)
features.ask: Has the semi-hermetic compressor tripped on its oil-pressure safety control?
features.how: Check the reset button on a mechanical oil failure control, or the lockout light on an electronic oil-pressure module.

states.ok: Oil safety not tripped

features.name: Evaporator pressure regulator (EPR / ORIT)
features.ask: If an EPR valve is installed in the suction line, how do pressures read upstream vs downstream of it?
features.how: Compare evaporator outlet pressure (upstream of the EPR) with compressor suction pressure (downstream) against the box temperature target. Enter the compressor-side (downstream) gauge as suction pressure; a stuck-closed EPR makes that reading low while the coil side runs high.

states.normal: Holds target evaporator pressure (or no EPR present)
states.stuck_high: Stuck closed or set too high (evaporator stays warm while compressor suction after the EPR is low)
states.stuck_low: Stuck wide open or set too low (cooler evaporator drops well below freezing and ices up)

stuck_high: high evaporator pressure low compressor suction

features.name: Crankcase pressure regulator (CPR / CROT)
features.ask: If a CPR valve is installed at the compressor suction inlet, is it throttling when the box is already cool?
features.how: Measure suction pressure before and after the CPR valve once the box is down near temperature; a big pressure drop in normal running means the CPR is set too low or stuck throttling. Enter the compressor-side (downstream) gauge as suction pressure.

states.normal: Wide open during normal running (throttles only on hot pull-down)
states.throttling_low: Stuck throttling or set too low (large suction drop across CPR, starving the compressor)

features.name: Head-pressure flooding valve
features.ask: How is the 3-way head-pressure flooding valve operating?
features.how: Touch the line between the valve and the receiver (the R port) and compare it with the condenser-outlet line. In warm air they should match — warm liquid, never near discharge temperature. In cold air with the valve working, the line to the receiver turns hot (discharge gas is being bypassed) while the condenser backs up with liquid and head pressure holds at the valve's setting. A two-valve ORI/ORD set is checked differently (ORI in the condenser outlet, ORD in the bypass line).

states.normal: Holds steady head pressure with a clear liquid sight glass
states.stuck_bypass: Stuck in bypass in warm air (line to the receiver near discharge temperature; high head, warm liquid, flashing glass)
states.no_bypass_cold: In cold air the valve never bypasses — the line to the receiver stays cold and head pressure is low (dome charge lost, or valve stuck toward the condenser)
states.starving_cold: In cold air the valve does bypass (line to the receiver is hot) and the condenser is flooded, but the receiver runs dry — winter charge short

stuck_bypass: flooding valve stuck open to receiver
hot gas bypassing condenser in summer
no_bypass_cold: low head in winter with cold receiver line
starving_cold: low head in winter with headmaster

features.name: Condenser fan-cycling switch / speed control
features.ask: Is the condenser fan-cycling switch or VFD cycling the fan properly with head pressure?
features.how:
Compare high-side pressure with the fan switch cut-in/cut-out settings: in cold air the fan should shut off or
slow down when head drops (a fan that is off in cold air is normal while head sits at cut-out); above cut-in the
switch must close and run the fan.

states.ok: Switches or modulates fan to hold head pressure in band
states.stuck_open: Control stuck open or no output — fan stays off while head pressure is above cut-in
states.stuck_closed: Control stuck closed or at full speed — fan runs nonstop in cold air and head pressure collapses

stuck_open: fan wont start at high head

features.name: Water-regulating valve (WRV) & strainer
features.ask: On the water-cooled condenser, how is the water-regulating valve (and its inlet strainer) working?
features.how: Check whether water flows when head pressure rises, whether the inlet strainer screen is plugged, and whether water shuts off completely a minute after the compressor stops.

states.normal: Opens with head pressure and shuts off when the compressor stops
states.stuck_closed: Stuck closed, set too high, or inlet strainer plugged (no/low water flow, high head)
states.stuck_open: Stuck open or seat eroded (water flows continuously in off cycle, low head pressure)

stuck_open: water runs when compressor is off

features.name: Condenser water / glycol flow
features.ask: How is flow through the water-cooled condenser — how does the leaving water compare with the condensing temperature?
features.how: A water-regulating valve holds head pressure by throttling flow, so the leaving water settles a few degrees under the condensing temperature (about 100–115 °F; one ice maker's manual sets the valve for a 104–115 °F drain) whatever the supply temperature, and a 40–60 °F rise on cold water is normal. Low flow shows as leaving water within ~5 °F of the condensing temperature with head pressure high. On a pump-fed glycol loop the flow is fixed and a 10–15 °F rise is normal.

states.normal: Flow adequate — leaving water at least ~5 °F under condensing temperature, and the valve shuts off with the compressor
states.low_hot: Little or no flow — leaving water within ~5 °F of condensing temperature (or the loop pump is off)
states.continuous_cold: Water runs cold and nonstop with the compressor off, or barely warms while running (valve stuck open)

features.name: Water-cooled condenser approach
features.ask: What is the temperature gap between condensing saturation and the leaving water/glycol (`vc.cond_sat_t - rf.water_out_f`)?
features.how: Compute condensing saturation temperature from high-side pressure and subtract the water/glycol outlet temperature. A clean coaxial or shell-and-tube condenser runs under 15–18 °F; a big gap with normal water flow means scaled or fouled tubes — but an overcharge or air in the system gives the same gap, so check subcooling and standing pressure before you descale.

states.normal: Normal (18 °F or less)
states.high: High (over 18 °F — tubes scaled or fouled)

features.name: Reach-in condensate evaporation pan
features.ask: Check the condensate evaporation pan under the reach-in cabinet — is the heater/loop or wick working?
features.how: Self-contained reach-ins drain into a bottom pan heated by a hot-gas discharge loop, an electric pan heater, or a wicking pad in the condenser air stream.

states.ok: Pan heater/loop warm and wicks intact; evaporating normally
states.overflowing_dead: Pan brimming over onto the floor — pan heater open, wick calcified/missing, or drain hose out of pan

overflowing_dead: reach in leaking water on floor

features.name: Prep-table rail covers, pans & air curtain
features.ask: On the prep table, are all food pans in place with the rail cover closed when idle, and is the air-curtain slot clear?
features.how: A missing food pan drops the cold air curtain out of the rail; leaving the rail hood open all day or jamming oversized pans against the supply/return louver ices the coil and warms the rail.

states.ok: All pans seated, lid closed when idle, air-curtain louver unobstructed
states.open_blocked: Rail lid left open, pan missing from rail opening, or air-curtain slot blocked/iced

open_blocked: lid left open on prep table

features.name: Ice machine water supply & inlet filter
features.ask: Is full water pressure reaching the ice machine inlet valve through a clean water filter?
features.how: Check the filter pressure gauge while the water inlet valve is energized (a clogged cartridge holds static pressure but drops to near zero under flow) and verify the shutoff valve is wide open.

states.good: Full flow and pressure through the water filter
states.none_low: Water shut off, saddle valve plugged, or inlet water filter clogged

none_low: low water pressure to ice maker

features.name: Ice machine sump / trough water level
features.ask: What happens to the water level in the ice machine sump during the freeze cycle?

states.full_normal: Fills to the normal line and holds enough water until harvest
states.empty: Sump empty or runs dry before the ice bridge finishes forming
states.overflowing: Sump overflows continuously down the drain during freeze

empty: runs out of water during freeze
overflowing: water running down drain in freeze

features.name: Ice machine water inlet solenoid valve
features.ask: How does the ice machine water inlet solenoid valve behave when energized and when off?
features.how: During timed fill, meter voltage at the solenoid coil and check that water enters at full rate; during freeze (coil de-energized), make sure no water trickles past the valve seat.

states.ok: Opens on fill call, shuts drip-tight during freeze
states.failed_closed: Voltage at coil on fill call, but no water passes (open coil or plugged inlet screen)
states.leaking_through: Weeps or flows continuously into the sump during the freeze cycle

features.name: Water-level float switch or conductivity probe
features.ask: Is the sump float switch or water-level probe clean and switching accurately?
features.how: Inspect the float stem or metal conductivity pins for white mineral scale or slime buildup, and watch the controller input light as you raise and lower the water level.

states.clean_ok: Clean and switches reliably with water level
states.fouled_stuck: Coated in mineral scale/slime or physically stuck in the up or down position

features.name: Ice machine water circulation pump
features.ask: Is the water circulation pump running and delivering an even sheet of water across the entire evaporator?
features.how: Watch the water distribution tube and evaporator face during freeze; every cell or flute needs a steady flow.

states.running: Strong, even flow across the whole evaporator
states.off_weak: Pump dead, humming/seized, air-locked, or weak uneven trickle (clogged distribution tube)

off_weak: bad water pump on ice machine

features.name: Water curtain / splash shield & trough
features.ask: Is the plastic water curtain hanging straight and keeping water in the trough, or is water leaking out into the bin?

states.intact: Curtain seated properly; all water returns to the sump
states.leaking_bypass: Curtain crooked/missing or trough/hose leaking water out into the ice bin

features.name: Ice machine evaporator surface (scale / plating)
features.ask: What does the evaporator grid or plate surface look like?
features.how: Inspect the cells and bridge area for chalky white mineral scale, pink/brown slime, or flaking nickel plating that locks the ice sheet into the grid.

states.clean: Smooth, clean metal / intact nickel plating
states.scaled_rough: Crusted with mineral scale, biofilm, or flaking nickel plating

features.name: Incoming supply water temperature
features.ask: What is the temperature of the supply water feeding the ice machine?
features.how: Run the supply line or check the water entering the sump with a thermometer. Over about 80 °F (a mixing-valve backfeed, a pipe run over the dish pit) lengthens every freeze; under about 45 °F (a line off an outdoor or snow-melt source) can leave the harvest too cold to release the slab.

states.normal: Normal (about 45–80 °F)
states.hot: Warm or hot supply water (over about 80 °F)

cold: outdoor water line to ice machine

features.name: Ice freeze cycle time
features.ask: How long is the freeze cycle taking from start of freeze to harvest, compared with the maker's figure?
features.how: Time one full freeze with a watch or read the controller's cycle log, then compare it with the cycle-time table in the service manual at today's room and water temperature. Cube makers differ a lot — one crescent cuber's service manual shows 20 min at 70 °F air / 50 °F water, 25 min at 90/70 and 29 min at 100/90 and calls 20–40 min normal, while other makes run 8–20 min — so judge it against the table for that model.

states.normal: Within about 25 % of the maker's figure for these conditions
states.long: More than about 25 % over the maker's figure (over ~35 min if you have no table)
states.short: Under about 60 % of the maker's figure (only judged against a table)

features.name: Ice cube / slab appearance
features.ask: What do the ice cubes or the ice sheet on the evaporator look like?

states.normal: Clear, full cubes with a normal ~1/8 in. bridge
states.hollow_thin: Hollow, thin, shell-like, or incomplete cubes
states.solid_slab: Thick solid slab of ice bridged completely across the evaporator (freeze-up)
states.cloudy_stuck: Cloudy white cubes that hang up in the grid during harvest

solid_slab: ice machine frozen into a block

features.name: Ice harvest initiation & release
features.ask: Does the ice machine initiate harvest when the bridge forms, and does the ice sheet release?
features.how:
Watch the end of the freeze cycle: the thickness probe (or float/timer) should trigger harvest, and the sheet
should slide off within the maker's harvest time (about 1–4 minutes depending on make and conditions).

states.normal: Enters harvest on time and drops the ice sheet cleanly
states.stuck_in_freeze: Never initiates harvest — stays in freeze while the ice slab grows thicker
states.initiates_no_drop: Enters harvest mode, but the ice slab hangs on the evaporator until harvest times out

initiates_no_drop: goes into harvest but ice wont drop

features.name: Ice machine hot-gas harvest valve
features.ask: How does the hot-gas harvest solenoid valve behave in freeze and in harvest?
features.how:
Check the tubing just past the harvest valve with an IR thermometer or clamp-on pipe probe (hot-gas lines run well
over 150 °F — don't grab them): it must stay cool during freeze and jump to hot within seconds of entering harvest.

states.ok: Cool in freeze, piping hot in harvest
states.stuck_closed: Stays cold in harvest (coil open or plunger stuck closed — evaporator never warms)
states.leaking_in_freeze: Hot during the freeze cycle (weeping hot gas into the evaporator during freeze)

stuck_closed: hot gas valve wont open in harvest
leaking_in_freeze: hot corner on evaporator in freeze

features.name: Harvest-assist mechanism (air pump / pusher / purge)
features.ask: During harvest, does the harvest-assist air pump, mechanical pusher rod, or water purge operate?
features.how: Once the evaporator warms and the bond breaks, check that the assist air pump builds pressure (no torn diaphragm or split tube) or the mechanical pusher solenoid extends fully.

states.ok: Operates normally in harvest (or unit uses gravity harvest only)
states.failed: Assist air pump dead/leaking, or mechanical pusher solenoid/probe stuck in harvest

features.name: Harvest-termination thermistor (evaporator temperature sensor)
features.ask: Is the thermistor that watches the evaporator warm up in harvest seated tight and reading right for the tube temperature?
features.how: Power off. Check it is clipped (and insulated) where the maker puts it on the suction tube or evaporator outlet, then read its resistance at the board plug and compare with the maker's temperature table. Open, shorted or far-off readings usually also throw an alarm code.

states.ok: Seated tight and reads right for the tube temperature
states.off: Loose or out of position, or open, shorted or off against the chart

features.name: Ice bin thermostat / curtain switch / eye
features.ask: Is the bin control (curtain switch, optical eye, or bin thermostat bulb) reading the bin status accurately?
features.how: With the bin not full, check whether the curtain is held open by a chunk of ice, the optical sensors are filmed over with scale, or a bin capillary bulb is touching the evaporator/chute and shutting the machine off.

states.ok: Calls when bin is low; shuts machine off when ice reaches the curtain/sensor
states.faulted: Shows "bin full" when the bin is empty, or fails to stop when the bin packs up into the chute

features.name: Control-board alarm or safety-limit code
features.ask: Is the ice machine's control board showing an alarm, safety-limit light or beep code?
features.how: Read the LED pattern, beeps or front-panel code and look it up in the service manual. Most boards latch a freeze-time, harvest-time, low-water or high-temperature safety, and that code is the cheapest way to split the fault list in half.

states.none: No alarm or safety code
states.freeze_safety: Freeze-time safety (the freeze ran past its limit)
states.harvest_safety: Harvest-time safety (harvest ran to its backup timer)

features.name: Unit fan
features.ask: With the unit calling for heat, what is its fan doing?
features.how: Look and listen at the fan. Many unit heaters hold the fan off until the coil is hot, so give a cold unit a few minutes before you call the fan dead.

states.hums: Fan hums, buzzes or turns slowly and won't come up to speed

features.name: Air off the unit
features.ask: With the fan running, how much air comes off the unit compared with a sister unit or its normal throw?

states.weak: Weak airflow — fan runs but little air comes off

features.name: Voltage at the fan motor
features.ask: Is there line voltage at the fan motor leads with the unit calling?
features.how: Meter at the motor leads or the load side of the fan relay or speed switch, not at the unit's supply.
features.caution: Live voltage inside the unit. Meter with a rated meter and keep fingers clear of the fan blade — it can start at any moment.

features.name: Fan motor run capacitor
features.ask: How does the fan motor's run capacitor test (µF against its rating)?
features.how: Take one lead off and read it in µF. More than about 6–10 % under its rating, open, or swollen counts as bad. Shaded-pole and ECM motors (a control module on the motor's end) have no capacitor.
features.caution: Lock out, then discharge the capacitor through a resistor before you touch its terminals.

states.ok: Within rating (or no capacitor on this motor)

features.name: Fan turns by hand
features.ask: With power locked out, how does the fan blade or blower wheel turn by hand?
features.caution: Lock out and tag the unit first. Wait for the blade to stop.

states.stiff: Drags, rough, or stops short (dry or worn bearings)

features.name: Fan blade or blower wheel
features.ask: With the unit locked out, what do the fan blade or blower wheel and its set screw look like?
features.caution: Lock out and tag the unit before you reach in.

states.ok: Clean, tight on the shaft, not rubbing
states.loose: Loose or slipping on the shaft (set screw backed off or shaft worn)
states.dirty: Blades or wheel caked with dirt or lint
states.damaged: Bent, cracked or rubbing the housing or guard

features.name: Fan speed setting
features.ask: What speed is the fan running on, and is that what the unit is meant to run?
features.how: Check the speed switch, the tap the motor is wired to, or the fan-speed setting on the unit's control.

states.ok: On its intended speed
states.low: Stuck on low, wired to the low tap, or set low

features.name: Fan rotation
features.ask: Watch the fan as it starts or coasts to a stop — does it turn the way the arrow on the housing or motor shows?
features.caution: Look from outside the guard; don't reach in to check it.

states.right: Turns the way the arrow shows

features.name: Unit filter
features.ask: What does the unit's filter look like?
features.caution: Turn the unit off before you pull the filter so the fan doesn't pull the debris in.

states.clean: Clean, or no filter on this unit
states.dirty: Loaded with dust or lint, or blinded

features.name: Coil fins and air path
features.ask: What do the coil fins (or the baseboard element) and the air path into and out of the unit look like?
features.how: Look at the coil face with a light, and at the inlet and outlet grilles. On baseboard, lift the cover and look at the fins and the damper flap.
features.caution: On electric baseboard, switch its breaker off before you lift the cover.

states.clean: Fins clean and straight, grilles and damper open, nothing in the way
states.matted: Fins matted with dust or lint, or crushed flat
states.blocked: Grille or damper shut, or furniture, drapes, stock or a cover blocking the air

features.name: Air temperature rise across the unit
features.ask: How much warmer is the air leaving the unit than the air going in?
features.how: Read the air going into the unit and the air leaving it with the same thermometer, after it has run 10 minutes. A healthy unit heats the air about 40–50 % of the way from room temperature up to the hot-water or steam temperature (about 40–50 °F on a 180 °F hot-water unit, 60–80 °F on steam).

states.none: None — air leaves at room temperature
states.low: Low — air leaves barely warm
states.normal: Normal for the water or steam temperature
states.high: High — air leaves very hot but there isn't much of it

features.name: Floor-to-ceiling temperature
features.ask: How much warmer is it at the ceiling than at the floor near the unit heater?
features.how: Read the air at about 5 ft and up near the roof deck, away from the unit's discharge.

states.large: More than about 15 °F — warm air sits up high

large: hot at ceiling cold at floor

features.name: Supply pipe at the unit
features.ask: How hot is the pipe feeding the unit, ahead of its valve (the heating supply on a 4-pipe fan coil)?
features.how: Read it with a strap-on or IR thermometer (IR on a piece of tape or a painted spot). Compare with what the loop or steam main is meant to carry right now. On a 4-pipe fan coil, read the heating supply.
features.caution: Steam and hot-water pipes burn on contact. Use the thermometer, or touch only for an instant with the back of a gloved hand — never on steam.

states.hot: Hot (what the loop or steam main should carry)
states.lukewarm: Lukewarm — warm, but well below what it should be
states.chilled: Colder than the room, maybe sweating (chilled water in the pipe)

features.name: Drop across the coil
features.ask: With the unit calling (and its fan on, if it has one), how does the pipe leaving the coil compare with the pipe feeding it?
features.how: Read both pipes at the unit (the heating coil on a 4-pipe unit) — the supply ahead of the valve and the return (or the condensate line ahead of the trap on steam). A hot-water coil normally drops about 10–30 °F. A steam coil's outlet ahead of the trap stays close to steam temperature.
features.caution: Steam and hot-water pipes burn on contact. Read them with a thermometer.

states.normal: Normal drop
states.wide: Leaving pipe much cooler or cold — little flow through the coil, or condensate backed up in it
states.none: Leaving pipe as hot as the supply — the coil is not giving up heat (hot water or glycol)

none: hot water return as hot as supply

features.name: Heat spread across the coil
features.ask: Scan the coil, radiator or baseboard element with an IR thermometer (or feel it at a safe distance) — how is the heat spread?
features.caution: Steam radiators and coils burn on contact. Use an IR thermometer, or hold a hand near it, not on it.

states.cold_top: Cold at the top or the high end, hot below
states.cold_low: Cold along the bottom or the outlet end, hot at the top
states.patchy: Some tubes, sections or circuits cold, others hot

cold_top: baseboard cold at the high end

features.name: Control signal at the valve actuator
features.ask: With the unit calling for heat, is the control signal reaching the valve actuator?
features.how: Meter at the actuator terminals — 24 V on a two-position valve, or the 0–10 V, 2–10 V or 4–20 mA signal on a modulating one. Compare with what the thermostat or controller says it is sending.
features.caution: Read the actuator's label for its voltage first; some zone valve heads are 120 V. Read 4–20 mA in series on the meter's mA range, never across the terminals.

states.present: Signal present (24 V, or a modulating signal calling it open)
states.missing: No signal, or the signal says closed while the unit calls

features.name: Piping connections at the unit
features.ask: Trace the piping at the unit — does supply feed the coil inlet, and does the control valve's flow arrow point with the flow?
features.how: Follow each pipe back to the main. On steam, supply enters at the top and the trap sits on the bottom outlet. On a globe or zone valve, the arrow on the body shows the direction water must flow.

states.ok: Supply to the inlet, valve arrow with the flow
states.reversed: Supply and return swapped, or the valve fitted against its flow arrow

features.name: Changeover sensor (2-pipe fan coil)
features.ask: On this 2-pipe fan coil, what does the changeover sensor on the supply pipe tell the unit's control?
features.how: Find the strap-on switch or sensor on the supply pipe at the unit. With hot water in the pipe it should read heating. Check that it is clamped tight to bare pipe, and meter it or read the control's mode.

states.ok: Reads heating with hot water in the pipe
states.wrong: Reads cooling with the pipe hot, or loose off the pipe, or open

wrong: fan coil in cooling mode with hot water

features.name: Chilled-water side (4-pipe fan coil)
features.ask: With the unit heating, feel the chilled-water coil's pipes after its valve (the coil side or its return) — is that side shut off? The pipe ahead of a shut valve is always cold.
features.caution: The heating pipes beside the chilled-water coil burn on contact; use a thermometer.

states.closed: Chilled-water pipes at room temperature, valve shut
states.passing: Chilled-water pipes cold or sweating — chilled water is flowing through the cooling coil

passing: chilled water valve open in heating
chilled water coil cold in heat mode

features.name: Vacuum breaker on the steam coil
features.ask: Does the modulated steam coil have a working vacuum breaker on its outlet?
features.how: A vacuum breaker sits on the coil's condensate outlet (or the top of the return header), ahead of the trap. With the valve throttled, a working one lets air in with a short hiss; plugged, painted over or missing, it lets the coil pull a vacuum and hold condensate.

states.ok: Present and working
states.failed: Missing, plugged, painted over, or stuck shut

features.name: Fan-delay switch (strap-on temperature switch or low limit)
features.ask: Check the fan-delay switch that lets the fan run only once the coil is hot — how does it behave?
features.how: It is usually a strap-on temperature switch or snap-disc switch on the supply or return pipe, or a pressure switch on steam. Meter across it with the pipe hot, then with it cold. Check that it is clamped tight to bare pipe.
features.caution: Live line-voltage fan circuit. Meter it with a rated meter; don't bridge the switch to test it.

states.ok: Closes with the pipe hot, opens with it cold (or the unit has none)
states.open_hot: Stays open with the pipe hot — fan never gets power
states.closed_cold: Closed with the pipe cold, jumpered out, or hanging loose off the pipe

open_hot: low limit open with pipe hot

features.name: Unit freeze-stat
features.ask: Has the unit's freeze-stat (low-temperature limit on the coil) tripped?
features.how: It is a capillary or snap-disc across the coil, usually with a reset button. Note whether the air at the coil is actually cold.
features.caution: A freeze-stat trip is the unit protecting its coil. Don't jumper or hold it in; find the cold air first.

states.ok: Not tripped (or the unit has none)
states.tripped: Tripped, with cold air at the coil
states.open_warm: Open even though the air at the coil is well above its setting

open_warm: freeze stat open at room temperature

features.name: Thermostat or sensor location
features.ask: Where is the thermostat or the unit's own temperature sensor, relative to the warm air and outside walls?
features.how: Look for discharge air blowing at it, a sunny or warm wall, a lamp or equipment near it, an outside wall, a door draft, or a return-air sensor on a fan coil whose fan cycles off.

states.ok: On an inside wall, out of drafts and the warm air stream
states.warm_spot: In the warm air stream, on a warm surface or near a heat source (satisfies early)
states.cold_spot: On a cold outside wall, by a door, or in a draft (never satisfies)

features.name: Thermostat-to-unit check
features.ask: Turn this unit's thermostat up and its neighbor's down — does the right unit respond?

states.crossed: The other unit responds (thermostats or valves cross-wired)

features.name: Heating element resistance
features.ask: With power locked out and a lead lifted, what do the heating elements read?
features.how: Ohm each element end to end, then each terminal to the sheath or cabinet. The reading should be close to V² ÷ W from the nameplate (a 1,500 W, 240 V element reads about 38 Ω).
features.caution: Lock out and tag, and verify dead on both legs. A 240 V heater has two live legs, so a single-pole thermostat or one breaker handle turned off can leave the other leg live.

states.ok: Each element reads close to V² ÷ W, open to ground
states.grounded: An element reads to the sheath or cabinet

features.name: Heater current
features.ask: With the heater called, what current does it draw compared with its nameplate?
features.how: Clamp one supply leg (each leg on a three-phase heater). Nameplate watts ÷ volts gives the expected amps on a single-phase heater; on a three-phase heater, watts ÷ (volts × 1.73) on each leg — one leg low or zero means a blown fuse, a dead contactor pole or a lost phase.
features.caution: Live conductors. Open only the cover you need, clamp with a rated meter and PPE, and keep clear of the terminals.

states.normal: Close to nameplate
states.low: Well under nameplate (an element out, or a low supply voltage)
states.zero: Nothing — no current to the elements
states.one_leg: One leg low or zero on a three-phase heater, the others normal

features.name: High limit and thermal cutoff
features.ask: How do the heater's high limit and thermal cutoff behave?
features.how: Meter across each limit. With the heater cool every limit should be closed. Watch the heater run — a limit that opens and recloses every few minutes means it is overheating.
features.caution: Lock out before you ohm a limit. Never jumper a limit to test the heater with it running.

states.closed: Closed, and stays closed while it runs
states.cycling: Opens and recloses while running (heater overheating)
states.open_cool: Open with the heater cool (failed, or a one-shot cutoff has blown)

features.name: Heater contactor or relay
features.ask: With the heater called, what is its contactor or relay doing?
features.how: Meter the coil (24 V or line voltage) and then line voltage in and out of each pole.
features.caution: Live voltage — meter with a rated meter and PPE, or lock out and use continuity.

states.ok: Pulls in on a call and passes full voltage on every pole
states.fails: Doesn't close on a call — coil powered but won't pull in, coil open, or pulled in with a dead pole
states.welded: Stays closed with no call (contacts welded)

features.name: Line-voltage thermostat
features.ask: Turn the line-voltage thermostat to its highest and then its lowest setting — what comes out of its load side?
features.how: Meter the load terminals to ground or neutral (or across the two load legs on 240 V). At the highest setting it should pass full voltage; at the lowest it should pass none.
features.caution: Line voltage at the wall. Meter with a rated meter, or lock out and use continuity.

states.closes: Passes power at the highest setting, none at the lowest
states.open: No power out even at the highest setting
states.stuck_closed: Power out even at the lowest setting

features.name: Heater nameplate voltage vs supply
features.ask: Does the heater's nameplate voltage match the supply it's on?
features.how: Read the nameplate, then meter the supply at the heater. Output goes with the square of voltage — a 240 V heater on 208 V gives about three-quarters of its rated heat, a 480 V heater on 277 V only about a third.
features.caution: Live supply at the heater. Meter it with a rated meter and PPE.

states.heater_higher: Heater rated above the supply (240 V heater on 208 V, 480 V on 277 V)
states.heater_lower: Heater rated below the supply (208 V heater on 240 V)

features.name: What covers the radiant panel or floor
features.ask: Is the radiant floor or panel covered or cut off from the room?

states.clear: Open to the room as designed
states.covered: Thick rugs or pads, new flooring, stored stock, or (on a ceiling panel) the insulation above it missing

features.name: Where the unit leaks
features.ask: Where is the water or glycol coming from at the unit?

states.none: Not from the unit (from somewhere else)
states.valve: Valve stem packing, a union or a fitting
states.coil: The coil itself — a pinhole, a corroded return bend, or a split tube
states.vent: The coin vent or automatic air vent

features.name: Compressor
features.ask: Is the compressor running?
features.how: Listen and feel at the condensing unit — a running compressor hums steadily and the discharge line gets hot within a minute or two.

states.hums: Hums, clicks or trips — tries but won't start

features.name: Condenser fan
features.ask: Is the condenser fan running at full speed?

ask_for.vc.hp: Is the outdoor fan running at full speed?
ask_for.vc.walkin: Is the condenser fan doing what its control calls for? (Running when head is above cut-in; off or slow in cold air with head at cut-out is normal for fan cycling or a VFD.)
ask_for.vc.reachin: Is the condenser fan doing what its control calls for? (Running when head is above cut-in; off or slow in cold air with head at cut-out is normal for fan cycling or a VFD.)
ask_for.vc.ice: Is the condenser fan doing what its control calls for? (Running when head is above cut-in; off or slow in cold air with head at cut-out is normal for fan cycling or a VFD.)

features.name: Evaporator fan / blower
features.ask: Are the evaporator fans (the indoor blower on A/C) running and moving full air?

ask_for.vc.hp: Is the indoor blower running and moving full air?

features.name: Contactor
features.ask: What is the contactor doing (with the unit calling)?
features.how: Look at the plunger, then meter line voltage in and out across each pole.

states.ok: Pulled in, full voltage through
states.burnt: Pulled in but contacts burnt — voltage drop across them
states.welded: Stuck closed — stays in with no call

features.name: 24 V at the contactor coil
features.ask: Is there 24 V across the contactor coil terminals?

features.name: Run capacitor
features.ask: What does the run capacitor test at (µF vs rating)?
features.how: Power off, discharge it through a resistor (not a screwdriver), then test each section (HERM–C, FAN–C) with a µF meter. Bulged tops or oil leaking mean replace.

states.ok: Within rating (−7 % to +10 % of the µF on the label)

features.name: Start capacitor, relay or PTC
features.ask: Do the start capacitor, potential relay or PTC test good?
features.how: Power off, then discharge the capacitors through a resistor. Start cap in range and not bulged; relay coil continuity and contacts not pitted or stuck; PTC cold resistance a few ohms (open or very high when cold is bad).

states.ok: Test good
states.bad: Open, burnt, low µF, relay contacts pitted or stuck

features.name: Compressor windings
features.ask: What do the compressor windings read (C–R, C–S, R–S, each to ground)?
features.how: Power off and locked out. R–S should equal C–R + C–S. Any terminal to ground should read open (megohms). If C–R and C–S read open but R–S reads normal, the internal overload is open — let it cool.
features.caution: Never megger a compressor that is under vacuum.

states.ok: Normal readings
states.overload_open: C–R and C–S open, R–S normal (hot — internal overload open)

features.name: Three-phase supply at the compressor
features.ask: Are all three legs present and balanced at the compressor contactor?
features.how: Open the panel with the power off. Then, with the call on and proper PPE, meter L1–L2, L2–L3 and L1–L3 on the line side of the contactor and again on the load side. Within 2 % of each other is good; one pair far low, or a leg that drops across a pole, is a lost leg. With the compressor running, clamp each leg — more than 10 % apart is bad.
features.caution: Live metering — rated PPE and meter, one hand, and treat every terminal as live until proven dead.

states.ok: All three present and balanced
states.phase_loss: One leg missing or far off
states.unbalanced: Present but unbalanced (over 2 % volts or 10 % amps)

features.name: Phase sequence at the compressor
features.ask: Does a phase-sequence tester (or the unit's phase monitor) say the rotation is correct?
features.how: Rotation meter on the line terminals, power on. A scroll compressor with two legs swapped runs backwards — loud, pumps nothing, and trips its protector after a few minutes.
features.caution: Live metering — rated PPE and meter, one hand, and treat every terminal as live until proven dead.

features.name: Compressor overheated
features.ask: Is the compressor cycling off on its internal overload, or hotter than the same model normally runs (use a thermometer, not your hand)?

features.name: Compressor sweating or frosting (floodback)
features.ask: Is the crankcase frosted, or sweating all the way up the shell (not just the lower shell on a humid day)?

states.yes: Frost on the crankcase / sweating up the whole shell — liquid floodback
states.no: No frost; shell dry or only a damp lower shell

features.name: Compressor noise
features.ask: Does the compressor knock, rattle or bang?

states.normal: Normal hum

features.name: Evaporator ice / frost
features.ask: How much ice or frost is on the evaporator coil?

states.none: None, or the normal light frost between defrosts (on an A/C coil any frost is abnormal)
states.partial: Frost on part of the coil only

features.name: Condenser coil
features.ask: Is the condenser coil dirty, matted, or blocked?

ask_for.vc.hp: Is the outdoor coil dirty, matted or blocked?

features.name: Air path to the condenser
features.ask: Is the condenser's air path clear (no walls, snow, stacked units or hot-air recirculation)?

ask_for.vc.hp: Is the outdoor coil's air path clear (snow, drifts, walls, a cover)?

features.name: Evaporator coil
features.ask: Is the evaporator coil dirty or matted on the air-entering face?

ask_for.vc.hp: Is the indoor coil dirty or matted?

features.name: Air filter
features.ask: Is the air filter dirty or collapsed?

features.name: Ducts and registers
features.ask: Are supply registers and dampers open and the ducts intact?

states.ok: Open and intact
states.restricted: Closed registers or dampers, crushed or undersized duct
states.leaking: Disconnected or leaking duct (return pulling in attic or outdoor air)

features.name: Condensate drain
features.ask: Is the condensate drain open, or is the pan full / float switch tripped?

states.clogged: Clogged — pan full or float switch tripped

features.name: Sight glass
features.ask: What does the liquid-line sight glass show with the system running steady?
features.how: Give it 10–15 minutes of steady running. A few bubbles right after start-up or during head-pressure control swings are normal.

features.name: Receiver level
features.ask: Where is the liquid level in the receiver with the system running steady?
features.how: Read the receiver's level glass (or the two glasses) after 10–15 minutes of steady running — not during pump-down, defrost or a start-up. Without a glass, in cold weather the shell feels or reads cooler below the liquid line. A flooding head-pressure valve holds liquid back in the condenser in cold air, so the level runs lower in winter than in summer.

states.low: Low or empty (below the bottom glass)
states.normal: In range (between the glasses)

features.name: Moisture indicator
features.ask: What color is the moisture indicator in the sight glass?

features.name: Oil spots
features.ask: Is there oil residue at a joint, valve, Schrader, or on the coil?

features.name: Refrigerant leak
features.ask: Did a leak search (electronic detector, bubbles or UV dye) find a leak?

features.name: Cold spot on the liquid line
features.ask: Is there a cold, sweating or frosted spot on the liquid line (at the drier, a valve or a kink)?

features.name: Cold outdoor air
features.ask: Is it running with cold outdoor (condenser) air — below about 55 °F?

features.name: Suction pressure (evaporator temp)
features.ask: How does the suction pressure / evaporator saturation temperature compare with normal?
features.how: Saturation temperature from the suction pressure (dew point for blends), compared with the air entering the coil — about 35 °F below return air on A/C, about 10 °F below box air on refrigeration, and on a heat pump in heating roughly 3–18 °F below the outdoor air (read suction at a true suction port, not the big vapor valve).

states.low: Low
states.normal: Normal
states.high: High

features.name: Head pressure (condensing temp)
features.ask: How does the head pressure / condensing temperature compare with normal (an A/C usually condenses 20–30 °F above the outdoor air, 15–20 °F on a high-efficiency unit)?
features.how: Condensing temperature from the high-side pressure, compared with the air entering the condenser — on a heat pump in heating that is the indoor coil, normally about 20–40 °F above return air.

states.low: Low
states.normal: Normal
states.high: High

features.name: Superheat
features.ask: What is the superheat compared with its target (a TXV usually holds 8–12 °F at the evaporator outlet and more at the compressor end)?

states.low: Low
states.normal: Normal
states.high: High

features.name: Subcooling
features.ask: What is the subcooling compared with its target?

states.low: Low
states.normal: Normal
states.high: High

features.name: Discharge line temperature
features.ask: How hot is the discharge line 6 in. from the compressor?
features.how: Read it 6 in. from the compressor and compare it with the condensing temperature. It runs about 60–90 °F above it on R-410A and R-134a, 50–75 °F on R-404A medium-temp, and 85–125 °F on low-temp and R-22 (typical — the maker's data wins). Above 250 °F the oil starts to break down whatever the condensing temperature is. Within about 25 °F of the condensing temperature means liquid is coming back.

states.low: Low (liquid coming back)
states.normal: Normal
states.high: High for the condensing temperature (or over 250 °F)

features.name: Compressor amps
features.ask: What does the compressor draw compared with its RLA?

states.low: Low (under 50 % of RLA, under 35 % on a freezer)
states.normal: Normal
states.high: High (over RLA)

features.name: Air temperature drop across the evaporator
features.ask: What is the return-minus-supply air temperature split compared with its target?

states.low: Low (too little drop)
states.normal: Normal
states.high: High (too much drop)

features.name: Air temperature rise across the condenser
features.ask: How much does the air warm up going through the condenser?

states.low: Low
states.normal: Normal
states.high: High

features.name: Temperature drop across the filter-drier
features.ask: Is there a temperature drop from inlet to outlet of the liquid-line filter-drier?

states.normal: Under 3 °F
states.high: 3 °F or more (restricted)

features.name: Standing pressure (system off)
features.ask: With the system off and equalized, does the standing pressure match the refrigerant's PT at that temperature?
features.how: Off at least an hour (overnight is best), with the coil and condenser shaded and at the same temperature as the air around them. If the condensing unit and the evaporator are at different temperatures (winter, outdoor unit), the pressure follows the colder liquid-holding part — use that temperature and treat the result as a hint, or wait for them to equalize.

states.high: Higher than the PT chart (by more than 4 psi or 4 %, whichever is larger)
states.low: Lower than the PT chart (by more than 4 psi or 4 %, whichever is larger)

features.name: Refrigerant identifier
features.ask: What does a refrigerant identifier (or a careful standing-pressure check) say about the charge?

features.name: Compressor pumping test
features.ask: Does the compressor pull the suction down and hold it (pump-down / efficiency test)?
features.how: Close the liquid valve with the compressor running and watch the suction gauge. A healthy compressor reaches about 0 psig in a minute or two on a small system. Stop it there, then watch whether suction climbs back — with everything closed, a rise of more than a few psi a minute means leaking valves. The climb-back part is not valid on a piston, cap tube or bleed-port TXV — they equalize by themselves; use the pull-down only.
features.caution: Stop the compressor at about 0 psig. Never run a scroll or hermetic compressor into a vacuum — it arcs at the terminals and loses oil.

states.ok: Pulls down and holds
states.weak: Can't pull down — or, with the liquid valve closed on a non-bleed TXV, pressures equalize in a minute or two

features.name: TXV bulb test
features.ask: Does the TXV respond when you warm or cool its sensing bulb?
features.how: Warming the bulb (hand or warm rag) should open the valve — suction pressure rises, superheat falls. Cooling it (ice water) should close it down.

states.no_response: No response (stuck, or the bulb lost its charge)

features.name: TXV bulb mounting
features.ask: Is the TXV bulb tight on a clean section of suction line and insulated?

states.poor: Loose, uninsulated or in the wrong place

features.name: Low-pressure switch
features.ask: Is it cycling off on the low-pressure switch?

ask_for.vc.walkin: Is it cutting out on the low-pressure switch while the box is still calling? (The normal pump-down cut-out at the end of a cycle does not count.)

features.name: High-pressure switch
features.ask: Is it tripping the high-pressure switch (or needing a manual reset)?

features.name: Total external static pressure
features.ask: What is the total external static pressure across the air handler compared with its rating?

states.low: Low
states.normal: Normal
states.high: High

causes.name: No run signal reaching the starter or drive — HOA switch in Off, drive in local/stop, broken wire, bad relay or starter coil
causes.confirm: The controller is commanding the fan and every safety reads closed, but the starter coil (or the drive's run terminal) never sees the signal.
causes.fix:
Start at the controller's fan output and follow the signal: HOA or local/remote switch, the start relay,
each safety, then the starter coil or the drive's run/enable terminals. Fix the break you find — a switch
left in Off or a drive left in local after service is the usual answer. If the coil sees voltage and the
starter still won't pull in, the coil is open; replace the starter or coil. On a drive, check the
run-command source parameter matches how it's wired (terminal vs keypad vs network).
causes.safety: Lock out before opening the starter. A VFD's bus capacitors stay charged after power is removed — wait the maker's time (several minutes) and verify with a meter. Tracing the signal is live work — qualified person only, with a properly rated meter and PPE, and the door closed where possible; otherwise lock out and use continuity.

causes.name: A safety or interlock in the fan start circuit is open — duct smoke detector, high/low static switch, damper end switch, filter or door switch
causes.confirm: Meter across each device in the start circuit — the open one has voltage across it. Smoke detectors and static switches usually show a trip light or flag.
causes.fix:
A tripped safety is a messenger — find out why before resetting. Duct smoke detector: confirm there is no
fire or smoke, clean the sampling tube and head, then have it reset through the fire-alarm authority per
site procedure (the panel too if it latched) — don't clear a life-safety alarm on your own. High-static
switch: something closed downstream — fire/smoke damper, isolation damper, VAV boxes — or the switch is
set too close to normal static. Low-static (or airflow) switch: a fan or belt problem upstream. Damper end
switch: the damper didn't open — actuator, linkage, frozen blades, or the switch out of adjustment. Door
or filter switch: close the door, change the filters. Replace a device only after you have shown that the
condition it guards is fine and the contact is still open.
causes.safety: Never jumper, tape, bridge or reset-and-walk-away any device in the start circuit — smoke or fire interlock, firestat, freezestat, high- or low-static switch, end switch, airflow switch. Replace a suspect device, don't bypass it; a test jumper only while you stand at the unit, and take it out before you leave. A duct-detector alarm is cleared with the fire-alarm authority per site procedure, after you have confirmed there is no smoke.

causes.name: Motor overload relay tripped — fan overloaded, bearing drag, single-phasing, low voltage, or overload set too low
causes.confirm: Overload relay flag shows tripped; with it reset the motor draws over FLA, growls on one lost phase, or spins hard by hand.
causes.fix:
Before resetting, check the overload's dial or heater size against the motor FLA (a mis-sized overload trips
for nothing). Never raise the setting to stop trips (NEC 430.32: no more than 125 % of FLA for a motor
marked service factor 1.15 or 40 °C rise, 115 % otherwise) — a motor that needs more than that is
overloaded. Check all three phases and the voltage under load. Lock out and spin the wheel — a dragging
bearing or a rubbing wheel loads the motor. Check the belt isn't over-tight and the fan isn't moving far
more air than design (a forward-curved wheel overloads when the duct is wide open or a panel is off). Trips
only in deep cold? Air at −40 °F is about 26 % denser, so the same fan draws about 26 % more power and
makes about 26 % more static (worse for a fan in the outdoor-air stream: blow-through unit, exhaust, or
preheat down). Compare the amps with FLA at the coldest hour; the fix is a larger motor, lower speed, or
restoring preheat — not a higher overload setting. Then reset once and clamp the amps on every leg as it
runs.
causes.safety: Lock out at the starter and the fan disconnect before touching the starter or spinning the wheel. Metering a live starter is qualified-person work with a rated meter and PPE.

causes.name: Fan motor failed — winding open or grounded, thermal protector open, or seized bearings
causes.confirm: Voltage reaches the motor terminals but it won't run, and the windings read open, unbalanced or to ground (a VFD ground-fault trip points the same way). A protector that resets after cooling means it's overheating — find why.
causes.fix:
Lock out, disconnect the leads and read the windings lead-to-lead and to ground. Replace a motor that reads
open, badly unbalanced or grounded — match HP, RPM, frame, voltage, and inverter-duty if it runs on a VFD.
Before the new one goes in: check the motor leads for chafe and moisture, and spin the fan shaft so a seized
fan bearing doesn't kill the next motor. If the old motor's protector was opening on heat, check voltage,
phases, airflow over the motor and the load.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag. Verify dead at the motor leads — a drive output can be live with the keypad showing stopped.

causes.name: Single-phasing — one leg of the three-phase supply lost (blown fuse, loose lug, bad contact)
causes.confirm: One phase pair reads far below the others at the motor or drive input; a running motor growls and trips its overload.
causes.fix:
Work back from the motor terminals: fuses in the disconnect and starter (one blown fuse is the classic),
then lugs and contacts for heat damage. Replace the fuse set and the burnt parts. Find why the fuse blew —
a motor on its way out, a loose connection, or an upstream fault. A drive usually rides through briefly
and then faults on undervoltage or phase loss.
causes.safety: Lock out before touching lugs; a lost leg can still leave the other two live.

causes.name: Contactor or starter failed — pitted, burnt or welded pole, loose lug, open fuse
causes.confirm: The contactor pulls in but a pole drops the voltage — line voltage in and little or none out on one leg, or a fuse reads open — while the motor tests good with its leads off.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Inspect the poles and lugs for pitting, heat and a welded set; replace the contactor as a set,
check the coil voltage and the amps afterwards, and find why (loose lug, undersized contactor,
short-cycling).
causes.safety: Lock out and tag; verify dead with a tested meter. A welded pole can leave the motor live with the coil dropped.

causes.name: Fan motor capacitor failed — run or start capacitor weak, open or bulged (a single-phase motor hums, won't start, or starts slowly and runs hot)
causes.confirm: A single-phase fan motor hums or won't start and spins freely by hand; the capacitor tests well under its label µF (or open) or is bulged or leaking; the motor windings test good.
causes.fix:
Lock out and discharge the capacitor through a resistor before touching it. Meter µF with the leads off
(within about ±6 % of the label); a bulged or leaking can fails regardless. Replace it with the same µF
and an equal or higher voltage rating. Spin the wheel by hand first — a dragging bearing kills
capacitors, so a new one in front of a bad bearing won't last.
causes.safety: A capacitor holds a charge after the power is off. Lock out, then discharge it through a resistor.

causes.name: Belt broken or thrown — motor runs, fan wheel doesn't turn
causes.confirm: Motor turning, wheel still; belt lying in the fan section or hanging off the sheaves.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Fit the right belt (number from the old one or the sheave data), align the sheaves with a
straightedge and tension it. Look for why it broke: misaligned or loose sheaves, a seized fan bearing, a
sheave with a damaged groove, or a belt that was already worn. Re-tension after the first day of running.
causes.safety: Lock out before reaching into the belt guard — a fan can start on a schedule.

causes.name: Wheel loose on the shaft or coupling failed — motor turns, wheel doesn't (sheared key, set screws backed out, hub or taper-lock slipped, flexible coupling gone)
causes.confirm: The motor runs and draws light amps, but the wheel stands still or turns far slower than the motor shaft — a sheared key, backed-out set screws, a slipped hub or taper-lock, or a cracked or missing coupling.
causes.fix:
Lock out and block the wheel. Check the key, set screws or taper-lock and the hub bore; set the wheel at
the right position in the inlet cone with a new key and thread-locker on the set screws, torqued to the
maker's value. Replace a spun hub or shaft. On a flexible-coupling drive replace the coupling and check
