the shaft alignment. Don't bump the motor to test it while the wheel is loose or the coupling is off — a
free wheel can spin up from airflow and loose parts can fly.
causes.safety: Lock out and block the wheel before reaching in.

causes.name: VFD dead — no display (input fuses, disconnect, failed power section)
causes.confirm: No display with line voltage at the drive's input terminals — the drive or its input fuses. No voltage at the input — the disconnect, breaker or feeder.
causes.fix:
Check the disconnect and breaker, then meter the drive's input terminals on all three phases. With input
present and a dark keypad, check the drive's internal input fuses and the keypad cable (a loose cable
looks like a dead drive). A drive that has lost its power section is replaced — size by motor amps, not
HP, and match the voltage.
causes.safety: The DC bus holds a lethal charge after power is cut — wait the maker's time and verify across the bus terminals before touching anything inside.

causes.name: VFD overcurrent or motor-overload fault — mechanical overload, belt over-tight, bearings, wheel rubbing, acceleration too fast, motor data wrong, or a failing motor
causes.confirm: The fault log shows overcurrent or overload; the motor draws over FLA when it does run, or trips on every start.
causes.fix:
Lock out and spin the wheel — a dragging bearing, a rubbing wheel or an over-tight belt loads the motor.
Check the motor nameplate data entered in the drive (FLA, voltage, RPM) and the overload setting. Trips
only on starting: lengthen the acceleration time. Tripped at start on an idle fan that is spinning (wind
or stack effect through a backdraft damper)? Enable the drive's catch-a-spinning-load (flying start) or
DC-brake-before-start, and fix the backdraft damper. Trips at full speed with a free wheel: the fan may be
moving far more air than design (open duct, missing panel, dampers wide open) — read the amps against FLA.
Trips only in deep cold? Air at −40 °F is about 26 % denser, so the same fan draws about 26 % more power
and makes about 26 % more static (worse for a fan in the outdoor-air stream: blow-through unit, exhaust,
or preheat down). Compare the amps with FLA at the coldest hour; the fix is a larger motor, lower speed or
max Hz, or restoring preheat — don't raise the overload setting. If nothing mechanical turns up, test the
motor and its cable: lock out, wait out the bus-discharge time and verify zero, disconnect the motor leads
at the drive's output (T1/T2/T3), then megger the motor and the cable separately. Never megger through
the drive. A motor breaking down also trips on current.
causes.safety: Lock out and wait for the drive's bus to discharge before working in the drive or on the motor leads.

causes.name: VFD line-side fault — undervoltage or phase loss (dips, a blown fuse, generator transfer), or DC-bus overvoltage (line high, or deceleration too fast for a big wheel)
causes.confirm: Fault log shows undervoltage, phase loss or bus overvoltage; the trips line up with power events, generator transfers, or with the fan being commanded to slow down or stop.
causes.fix:
Undervoltage or phase loss: meter all three input phases under load and check the input fuses; if the
supply itself dips (generator loading, utility), report it and consider the drive's ride-through and
auto-restart settings. Bus overvoltage while slowing: the wheel is driving the motor as a generator —
lengthen the deceleration time, enable coast-to-stop, or add a braking resistor if the maker allows. Bus
overvoltage at steady speed: the line is high — check the supply voltage and transformer taps. Tripped at
start on an idle fan that is spinning (wind or stack effect through a backdraft damper)? Enable the
drive's catch-a-spinning-load (flying start) or DC-brake-before-start, and fix the backdraft damper.
causes.safety: Metering the drive's input is live work — qualified person, properly rated meter and PPE. Before opening the drive or touching its terminals, lock out, wait out the bus-discharge time and verify zero.

causes.name: VFD overtemperature — heatsink fins clogged, drive cooling fan dead, enclosure filter plugged, or the room too hot
causes.confirm: Fault log shows overtemperature; the heatsink is packed with dust or the drive's own fan is dead; trips come on hot afternoons or after long running.
causes.fix:
Power down and let the bus discharge. Blow out the heatsink fins and the enclosure filters, replace the
drive's cooling fan if it's slow or dead, and clear anything stacked against the vents. If the room or
enclosure runs hot, add ventilation or move the drive. Check the drive isn't running a motor larger than
its rating.
causes.safety: Wait for the bus capacitors to discharge before opening the drive.

causes.name: VFD running below command — in Hand/local at a low speed, maximum-frequency or limit parameter set low, current limit folding back, or the speed reference lost or scaled wrong
causes.confirm: The BAS commands a speed the drive doesn't reach, or the drive sits at one speed no matter what the BAS asks.
causes.fix:
Check Hand/Auto on the keypad and whether the reference source is the terminal, keypad or network the BAS
actually uses. Compare the maximum frequency, upper limit and reference scaling parameters with the
design values for this fan (don't assume 0–100 % is 0–60 Hz; many drives scale between a minimum and a
maximum frequency). Meter the speed reference at the terminals (0–10 V or 4–20 mA) while the BAS changes
it. A drive folding back in current limit has a load problem — see the overcurrent cause.
causes.safety: The terminals and parameters are on a drive with charged capacitors. Before opening it, lock out, wait out the bus-discharge time and verify zero. Reading the keypad needs none of that.

causes.name: Fan status (run proof) wrong — current switch or differential-pressure switch out of adjustment, or its wiring faulted, so the BAS thinks the fan is off (or running) when it is not
causes.confirm: The wheel turns and the motor draws normal amps while the BAS shows the fan off or failed (or the reverse); heating or other equipment may be locked out because it believes there is no airflow.
causes.fix:
Compare the BAS status with the wheel and the motor amps. Adjust a current switch to trip between the idle
and running amps (and check the lead passes through the sensor the right number of times), set a
differential-pressure switch between the off and running readings, and check the status wiring and the BAS
input. Once the status is right, clear any lockout it caused.
causes.safety: Setting a current switch means working near live leads — qualified person, rated meter and PPE.

causes.name: Belt slipping or worn — loose, glazed, stretched, wrong size, or oiled
causes.confirm: Low static with low amps on a motor that runs fine; the belt deflects too far, shows glazed sides, cracks or black dust under the drive, and squeals on start.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Replace a glazed, cracked or bottomed-out belt (match the number; replace matched sets together).
Align the sheaves and tension to the maker's deflection, then re-tension after a day's run — new belts
stretch. Check the sheave grooves for wear (a worn groove eats belts) and look for oil on the belt from a
leaking bearing.
causes.safety: Lock out before reaching into the belt guard.

causes.name: Fan speed set wrong — variable-pitch sheave opened or closed too far, wrong replacement sheave, or a sheave loose or misaligned on its shaft
causes.confirm: Fan RPM (photo-tach on reflective tape fitted while locked out) doesn't match the balance report or design; a sheave rocks on its shaft or the belt runs off-center.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Tighten a loose sheave (key, set screws, bushing) and align both with a straightedge. Compare the
fan RPM with the design or balance report; set the variable-pitch sheave or fit the right fixed sheave to
get there. Never set the speed above the fan's maximum RPM (fan nameplate or submittal) — a wheel over its
limit can fly apart. Power rises with the cube of speed, so 10 % faster is about 33 % more load: set it to
the balance report, then clamp the amps against FLA.
causes.safety: Lock out the fan at its disconnect before opening the belt guard or working at the sheaves. Never reach at a running shaft with a tach.

causes.name: Fan running backward — phase leads swapped after motor, starter or drive work
causes.confirm: The wheel turns against the arrow on the housing; the fan moves some air but far below design with low static.
causes.fix:
Lock out and swap any two motor leads (at the motor or the starter — on a VFD, at the drive's output
terminals, or use the drive's rotation parameter). Confirm the arrow, then check amps and static. A
centrifugal wheel still blows air backward, so trust the arrow, not the airflow.
causes.safety: Lock out; verify dead before swapping leads. On a drive, wait out the bus-discharge time and verify zero at the output terminals first (or use the drive's rotation parameter and leave the leads alone).

causes.name: Filters loaded — high pressure drop starving the fan
causes.confirm: Filter pressure drop at or past its final rating; filters dark and bowed; amps low and the fan's own static rise at or somewhat above design (a loaded filter bank moves it only 5–20 %).
causes.fix:
Change the filters (whole bank, right size and MERV). Reset the dirty-filter switch or alarm. If they load
fast, look for the source — construction dust, a return pulling from a dirty space, snow or moisture
caking them — and fix the filter rack seal so dirt doesn't bypass the next set.
causes.safety: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the filter section — a running fan pins or throws the door and pulls at loose clothing.

causes.name: Snow or rain drawn in through the intake — filters wet, iced or packed, coil face plugged
causes.confirm: Filters wet, frozen or packed with snow; snow or rime on the coil face; water on the floor of the mixing section after a blow.
causes.fix:
Stop the fan and lock out first. Pull the loaded filters and dry-clear the coil face (soft brush or
vacuum). Don't put water on a coil face or louver at below-freezing temperatures — it refreezes in the
fins and blades and makes ice underfoot. Thaw ice with warm air (a heater or a heat gun on low, held back
from seals, insulation and filters) with the fan locked out and the outdoor-air damper closed — never a
torch or open flame. Dry the section and check the drain. Then slow the intake air so snow drops out
before the filters: a snow hood or louver with a bottom drain, lower intake velocity, a snow baffle or
settling plenum, and a drain in the mixing box. In a storm go to minimum outdoor air only if the building
stays at or above neutral pressure; never put a makeup unit on recirculation while exhaust fans or
fuel-fired equipment are running.
causes.safety: A freezestat tripped by snow on the coil is doing its job — don't bypass it. Stop the fan and lock out before opening the filter, coil or mixing section; a running fan pins or throws the door and pulls at loose clothing.

causes.name: Coil fins matted with dirt on the air side — filters bypassing, missing or long overdue
causes.confirm: Entering face of the coil matted; filters missing, undersized or gapped so dirt got past them.
causes.fix:
Clean the coil with coil cleaner and low-pressure water from the leaving side toward the entering side,
straighten fins, and clear the drain pan. Fix the reason: fill gaps in the filter rack, use the right
filter size, replace missing or collapsed filters, and set a change interval.
causes.safety: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the coil section. Open the drain first, and keep wash water and cleaner off motors, drives, controls and wiring (cover them).

causes.name: Outdoor intake blocked — snow drift, ice on the louver or screen, debris, or a clogged hood screen
causes.confirm: Intake hood, louver or screen drifted over, iced, or packed with debris; outdoor-air fraction low with the damper open.
causes.fix:
Dry-clear first (soft brush, vacuum; scrape from outside the louver). Don't put water on a louver, damper
or coil face at below-freezing temperatures — it refreezes inside the blades, drains and fins (a worse
plug) and makes ice underfoot. Thaw with warm air (heater or heat gun on low, held back from seals,
insulation and filters) with the fan locked out and the outdoor-air damper closed — no open flame. Check
louver drains and the bird screen. Where it keeps happening: a snow fence or hood extension, a heated
louver, a larger screen, or relocating the intake out of the drift line. A 100 % outdoor-air unit starves
completely when its intake blocks — check its freezestat and coil afterward. In a storm go to minimum
outdoor air only if the building stays at or above neutral pressure; never put a makeup unit on
recirculation while exhaust fans or fuel-fired equipment are running.
causes.safety: Work at the intake with a second person, fall protection near roof edges, and the fan locked out — a running fan pulls hard at a louver, and drifts and ice are slippery. Keep a heat gun clear of seals, insulation and filters (fire risk).

causes.name: A damper in the air path is closed — fire/smoke damper dropped, isolation or balancing damper shut, VAV boxes all at minimum
causes.confirm: Fan static far above design with clean filters and coils; a fire damper indicator shows closed, an isolation damper is shut, or every VAV box is at minimum.
causes.fix:
Find the closed damper: fire/smoke damper access doors (after confirming there was no fire event, fit a
new fusible link of the same temperature rating — a melted link is replaced, not reset; reset a smoke
damper only after the fire-alarm panel is cleared by the authorized person), isolation and balancing
dampers (someone may have shut one), and the VAV boxes' damper commands. On VAV systems, check the duct
static setpoint and that the boxes can open; the high-static switch is there to protect the duct when
they can't.
causes.safety: Never prop or wire a fire damper open.

causes.name: Fan wheel loaded with dirt or damaged — blades caked, wheel slipped on the shaft, bent blades
causes.confirm: Low static and low amps with a good belt and correct rotation; the wheel is caked, or it has walked on the shaft and the blades no longer line up with the inlet cone.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Clean the blades (dirt comes off in flakes — bag it), check every blade for cracks and bends, and
check the wheel's hub set screws and position in the inlet cone. A damaged or badly out-of-balance wheel
is replaced; the fan is re-balanced after a cleaning if it vibrates.
causes.safety: Lock out and block the wheel before working inside the housing.

causes.name: Fan or motor bearing failing — dry, worn, or misaligned
causes.confirm: Growl or rumble that follows the shaft speed, a housing running much hotter than its twin at the other end of the machine (read with an IR thermometer from outside the guard) or over the maker's limit, or a shaft that feels rough when spun by hand, locked out, with the belt off.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Pillow-block fan bearings: check the set screws and locking collars, grease per the schedule (don't
over-grease sealed bearings), and replace a bearing that growls or runs hot — in pairs, with the shaft
checked for wear. Motor bearings: replace the motor or have it re-bearinged. Check sheave alignment and
belt tension afterward; a tight belt loads the bearings. Repeated failures on a drive-fed motor: fit a
shaft-grounding ring or an insulated bearing and check the drive's grounding. Use the maker's
low-temperature grease and don't mix thickener types — stiff grease at −40 °F raises start amps and noise.
causes.safety: Lock out before putting a hand on the shaft.

causes.name: Fan vibration — wheel out of balance (dirt build-up, lost weight, damaged blade), loose on the shaft, or sheaves misaligned
causes.confirm: Vibration you can feel in the housing that rises with speed; dirt or a missing balance weight on the wheel, a sheave off-line, or the wheel loose on the shaft.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Clean the wheel, look for a missing clip weight or a damaged blade, check hub set screws and the
position in the inlet cone, and align the sheaves. Check the isolators and flexible connections aren't
bottomed out or bypassed. If it still shakes with a clean, tight wheel, have it balanced in place — running
it unbalanced destroys the bearings. Vibration only in one speed band on a drive? Set the drive's skip
frequencies around it.

causes.name: Heating valve not opening — actuator dead, no control signal, or stem stuck
causes.confirm: Hot supply at the valve, controller commanding it open, stem not moving, and the pipe after the valve cold. The actuator test says which part.
causes.fix:
On a preheat coil facing cold air, protect the coil first: stop the supply fan, drive the outdoor-air
damper closed (or isolate the intake if it is stuck open), and force the heating valve open with its manual
override or by powering the actuator directly. If the coil is plain water and heat will not be back soon,
drain it. Then meter the signal at the actuator. No signal: controller output, wiring, or the actuator's
own power — fix upstream. Signal present and no stroke: replace the actuator (match the signal type,
stroke, torque and fail position — a preheat valve should fail open). Actuator strokes but the stem
doesn't: free or replace the valve; a stem that has sat closed all summer corrodes. On a spring-return
actuator, confirm it drives the right way. Reset the freezestat only after the coil is warm, and look the
coil over for bulged bends and split tubes before restoring flow.

causes.name: No hot water or glycol reaching the coil — plant down, loop pump off, loop valve closed, or loop temperature too low
causes.confirm: Valve wide open with setpoint not met and the supply pipe cold or lukewarm — the coil is doing what it can with what it's given.
causes.fix:
If this coil faces outdoor air, protect it first: stop the supply fan, drive the outdoor-air damper closed
(or isolate the intake if it is stuck open — wind-driven air through an open or leaking damper still
freezes a coil with the fan off), and keep the heating valve open. A plain-water coil (no glycol) freezes
anyway when the loop stops; if heat will not be back soon, drain it. This unit is fine; go to the plant:
boiler or heat exchanger firing, loop pump running and turning the right way, loop isolation and balancing
valves open, loop temperature and any reset schedule (a reset curve set too low starves preheat coils in
deep cold). Air in the loop or a dead zone pump shows the same way. Keep the fan off until heat is back,
and look the coil over for bulged bends and split tubes before restarting the pump or reopening valves.

causes.name: Coil air-bound — air trapped at the top of the coil (failed vent, low loop pressure, after a drain-down)
causes.confirm: Hot supply, cold return, air hissing from the coil vent before water.
causes.fix:
Vent the coil at its high point — open the vent slowly, hose to a bucket, face shield on a hot loop —
until solid water or glycol runs, and again after an hour of running. Check the loop fill pressure (air
gets in when the top of the system drops below atmospheric) and the automatic vents. Coils at the top of a
system or after a drain-down may need venting a few times. Top up glycol strength if you added water.
causes.safety: A hot loop is under pressure and scalds — open the vent slowly, hose to a bucket, face shield on.

causes.name: Strainer or coil tubes plugged — flow starved by dirt, scale or sludge
causes.confirm: Hot supply, return far colder than it should be, valve wide open, solid water at the vent — and a strainer screen packed with debris.
causes.fix:
Isolate, drain the strainer and clean or replace the screen. If the screen is clean and flow is still
starved, back-flush the coil. Look for the source of the dirt (new piping, a corroding loop, old glycol
breaking down) and check the glycol's inhibitor and pH.
causes.safety: Isolate both sides and relieve pressure before opening a strainer; hot glycol scalds. A steam coil's strainer holds live steam and condensate — isolate and relieve first.

causes.name: Steam coil waterlogged — trap stuck closed or plugged, condensate return blocked or backed up (a coil that holds condensate heats poorly, hammers and freezes)
causes.confirm: Steam supply hot at the valve, but the bottom of the coil is cold, the coil bangs or gurgles, and the air rise is poor — the trap, strainer or return line is holding condensate in the coil.
causes.fix:
Isolate and relieve the steam and condensate sides before working on traps or strainers. Check the trap
(cold and not cycling means stuck closed or plugged), its strainer, the condensate return line and any
check valve or lift, and the vacuum breaker on a modulating steam valve — without one the coil can pull to
vacuum at low load and hold condensate. A waterlogged coil in cold air freezes and splits: look it over
before restoring steam.
causes.safety: Steam and condensate scald. Isolate and relieve before opening a trap, strainer or union.

causes.name: Heating valve leaking through — seat worn, actuator not closing fully, or a three-way valve piped wrong
causes.confirm: Valve commanded closed, pipe after it hot, and the air warms across the coil with no call — supply air above setpoint, often with the cooling coil working against it.
causes.fix:
Confirm the actuator reaches the fully closed stop (stroke and signal span). If it does and the valve still
passes, the seat or plug is worn — rebuild or replace the valve (check the close-off rating against the
pump head). On a three-way valve, check the ports are piped to the arrows. Clean a bypass or check valve
that is letting hot water around.

causes.name: Coil frozen and split — tubes, headers or return bends burst (water or glycol release when it thaws)
causes.confirm: Bulged return bends, split tubes near the headers, water or glycol on the floor of the coil section — usually found after a freezestat trip, a plant outage or a damper failure.
causes.fix:
Isolate the coil on both sides before it thaws and be ready for the release — a split coil dumps the loop
as the ice melts. Thaw gently (warm air, never a torch). Plug or replace the coil; one split means its
neighbors were stressed too. Any torch work only after the coil is isolated, drained, flushed and purged,
with the site's hot-work permit and a fire watch. Pressure-test with water, or low-pressure nitrogen
behind a barrier, to the coil's test rating, never with shop air in a closed section. Then fix what let it
freeze: damper that stayed open, valve or pump that failed, glycol too weak (or no glycol in a water
coil), stratification, or a sequence that opened the dampers before the coil was warm.
causes.safety: Isolate and relieve the coil; glycol on the floor is slippery and a hot loop scalds. Lock out the fan so the coil isn't fed cold air while it's open.

causes.name: Plain-water coil in air that goes below freezing — no glycol, so only flow and the freezestat stand between the coil and a split (one plant, pump or valve hiccup freezes it)
causes.confirm: A hot-water coil with no glycol in it faces air that goes below freezing; the freezestat has tripped, or the coil is split, after a plant, pump or valve hiccup — nothing in the loop but water.
causes.fix:
Protect the coil first as for any freeze trip (fan off, outdoor damper closed, heating valve forced open)
and look it over for bulged bends and split tubes before restoring flow. A water coil in air that goes
below freezing is protected only by flow and the freezestat: add glycol sized for the coldest air, or write
a drain-down step into the shutdown procedure and keep the freezestat, damper and valve interlocks proven.
Until then, treat any plant, pump or valve outage as a freeze emergency for this coil.
causes.safety: Isolate and relieve the coil before opening it; a thawing coil can dump its loop. Lock out the fan so the coil isn't fed cold air while it's open.

causes.name: Electric heat not energizing — airflow switch not made, stage contactor or relay, element open, fuse or high-limit open
causes.confirm: Call for heat present, little or no amp draw on the stages, no rise across the heater.
causes.fix:
Confirm airflow first — the airflow or sail switch must make before any stage can energize, and weak airflow
keeps it open. Then follow each dead stage: control signal to the stage relay or SCR, contactor pulling in,
fuses, the high-limit and the manual-reset limit, and the element's resistance (an open element reads
infinite). Replace open elements and tripped one-shot limits; find why a limit tripped (airflow, dirty
filters, element sagging onto the frame).
causes.safety: Lock out — heater circuits are line voltage and often fed from a separate disconnect. Never jumper the airflow (sail) switch or a high limit to force heat or to test; those two keep the elements from igniting the duct.

causes.name: Chilled-water valve not opening — actuator dead, no control signal, or stem stuck
causes.confirm: Cold chilled water at the valve, controller commanding it open, stem not moving, pipe after the valve warm.
causes.fix:
Meter the signal at the actuator; no signal means the controller output or wiring. With signal and no
stroke, replace the actuator (signal type, stroke, torque, fail position). If the actuator strokes and the
stem doesn't, free or replace the valve.

causes.name: No chilled water reaching the coil — chiller off, pump down, loop valve closed, or loop too warm
causes.confirm: Valve wide open with setpoint not met and the supply pipe warm — the plant isn't delivering.
causes.fix: Go to the plant — chiller status and alarms, chilled-water pump, loop isolation valves, and the chilled- water setpoint or reset. The air handler is doing what it can.

causes.name: Chilled-water valve leaking through — overcooling, reheat fighting it
causes.confirm: Valve commanded closed, pipe after it cold and sweating, air cooled across the coil with no call; heating runs to make up for it.
causes.fix: Confirm the actuator reaches the closed stop and the signal span is right; if it does, rebuild or replace the valve (check the close-off rating). On a three-way valve, check the piping against the port arrows.

causes.name: DX cooling coil not cooling — a refrigerant-side fault (diagnose it under A/C cooling)
causes.confirm: Airflow, filters and coil face are fine, yet the air barely cools across the DX coil with cooling commanded.
causes.fix:
The air side is cleared. Switch this app to the A/C cooling system and diagnose there: compressor and
condenser fan running, charge, metering device, condenser coil, pressures and superheat. Make sure the
cooling call actually reaches the condensing unit first.

causes.name: Condensate drain, trap or pan problem — drain plugged, trap seal lost or too shallow for the fan's negative static, or the drain line frozen
causes.confirm: Water in the drain pan or on the floor under the cooling coil section while the coil cools normally; the drain is plugged, the trap has no water seal (or is too shallow for the fan's suction), or the line is iced.
causes.fix:
Clear the drain (pour water in and watch it go). The trap's inlet leg must be at least the unit's negative
static in inches plus 1 in. — prime it; a trap that is too shallow is sucked dry and the pan overflows.
Insulate or heat-trace any drain line that runs through cold space.
causes.safety: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the coil section. Standing water in a pan is a slip hazard and a mold risk — clean and dry it.

causes.name: Outdoor-air damper stuck open — blades jammed, spring return failed, or a manual override left in
causes.confirm: Damper commanded closed or to minimum but the blades sit open; outdoor-air fraction far above the command; in cold weather the freezestat trips and the heating valve pins at 100 %.
causes.fix:
First protect the coil: stop the supply fan, drive the outdoor-air damper closed (or isolate the intake if
it is stuck open), and force the heating valve open with its manual override or by powering the actuator
directly. If the coil is plain water and heat will not be back soon, drain it. Then release the
actuator's manual override if someone set it. With the fan locked out, support the damper, unhook the
linkage and swing the blades by hand: bound blades need the ice, dirt or bent blade dealt with and the
pivots freed; a spring-return actuator that no longer returns is replaced. Check the end stops so
"closed" really closes, and the blade seals. Reset the freezestat only once the coil is warm and the
damper is closed, and look the coil over for bulged bends and split tubes before restoring flow.
causes.safety: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the mixing section — a running fan pins or throws the door. Spring-return actuators and damper blades store energy; support the damper before unhooking the linkage and keep fingers out of the linkage when releasing an override.

causes.name: Outdoor-air damper stuck closed — frozen or iced shut, blades jammed, or spring-returned with no power
causes.confirm: Damper commanded open but the blades stay shut; outdoor-air fraction near zero; the damper end switch may keep the fan from starting.
causes.fix:
With the fan locked out, support the damper, unhook the linkage and try the blades by hand. Frozen or
iced: dry-clear first, then thaw with warm air (heater or heat gun on low, held back from seals,
insulation and filters; no flame) — don't put water on a louver or damper at below-freezing temperatures,
because it refreezes inside the blades. Dry, and look at why moisture got there — snow in the intake, a
leaking louver drain. Jammed: clear debris, free the pivots, straighten or replace bent blades. Blades
free but the actuator doesn't drive: see the actuator cause. Check the damper's power and signal are
enabled by the sequence (some stay closed until the coil is warm — that's correct).
causes.safety: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the mixing section. Support the damper before unhooking the linkage — spring-return actuators and blades store energy. Keep a heat gun clear of seals, insulation and filters.

causes.name: Outdoor-air damper leaks when closed — worn or iced blade and jamb seals, warped blades, actuator not closing hard enough (cold air pours into the mixing box with the fan off and cold-soaks the coil)
causes.confirm: The damper shuts on command but daylight or a draft shows along the blade edges and jambs, or frost sits on the seals; the coil cold-soaks while the fan is off and the freezestat trips at start-up.
causes.safety: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the mixing section. Support the damper before unhooking the linkage — actuators and spring returns store energy.

causes.name: Damper actuator failed, no control signal, or linkage slipped — blades don't follow the command
causes.confirm: Blades swing freely by hand, but the actuator doesn't stroke on command (or strokes while the blades stay put because the linkage or crank arm has slipped).
causes.fix:
Meter the signal and power at the actuator while the BAS commands it. No signal: the controller output,
wiring or the actuator's transformer. Signal present, no stroke: replace the actuator — match signal type,
torque for the damper area, fail-safe direction (outdoor dampers normally fail closed), and the stroke.
Actuator moves but blades don't: tighten the crank arm and set screws on the jackshaft, replace a worn
linkage rod, and re-stroke so the blades reach both stops. Check the end switch makes when open.
causes.safety: Stop the fan and lock out before opening the mixing section — never open the door with the fan running. Support the damper before unhooking the linkage; actuators and spring returns store energy.

causes.name: Return-air damper stuck — closed (unit pulls nearly all outdoor air) or open (short on outdoor air)
causes.confirm: Outdoor damper tracks its command but the return damper doesn't; the outdoor-air fraction is far from the command in the direction the return damper forces.
causes.fix:
Same drill as the outdoor damper: manual override, linkage, blades by hand, actuator and signal. On linked
outdoor/return dampers, check the linkage geometry so one closes as the other opens. A return damper
stuck closed in cold weather is a freeze risk — fix it before restoring the fan to automatic.

causes.name: Mixed-air sensor wrong — failed, drifted, or a single-point sensor sitting in a stratified stream
causes.confirm: The BAS mixed-air value falls outside the return/outdoor pair (a blend can't), or disagrees with a traverse of the plenum by more than a few degrees.
causes.fix:
Check the sensor's resistance against its curve at a known temperature and its wiring. If it reads right at
its tip but the plenum is stratified, the problem is placement — install an averaging mixed-air sensor
across the full plenum (serpentine, not straight), away from the outdoor stream. A wrong mixed-air value
drives the economizer and preheat wrong, so fix it before tuning anything else.

causes.name: Supply-air sensor failed or drifted — the controller chases a wrong reading
causes.confirm: The BAS shows supply air at setpoint while a reference thermometer in the duct says otherwise (or the BAS value sits flat or impossible).
causes.fix:
Check the sensor's resistance at a known temperature against its curve, its wiring and the controller's
input type and offset. Replace a drifted or failed sensor and mount it where the air is mixed (several
diameters past the fan or coil, not against the duct wall). Clear any software offset someone added to
hide the drift.

causes.name: Outdoor- or return-air sensor wrong — in the sun, on a warm wall or in an exhaust plume, iced, failed, or carrying a software offset (preheat and freeze logic act on a wrong temperature)
causes.confirm: A reference thermometer in the shade at the intake disagrees with the BAS outdoor (or return) temperature by more than a degree or so — the sensor sits in the sun, on a warm wall, in an exhaust plume, is iced, or has failed — and the preheat enable, lockout or freeze-staging logic is acting on the wrong number.
causes.fix:
Compare with a reference in the shade at the intake; relocate the sensor away from sun, exhaust and
building heat; check the preheat enable and lockout setpoints and any offset someone added in the BAS.
Replace a drifted or failed sensor and trend it against the reference.

causes.name: Economizer changeover wrong — outdoor sensor off (sun, ice, failed), changeover setpoint or enthalpy logic set wrong, or the sequence backwards
causes.confirm: The dampers follow their command, but the command is wrong for the outdoor conditions — free cooling with warm outdoor air, or compressors or chilled water running when the outdoor air could do the job.
causes.fix:
Compare the outdoor sensor with a reference in the shade; relocate it out of the sun and away from exhaust,
or replace it. Check the changeover: dry-bulb high limit (commonly 70–75 °F today; 55–65 °F is the old
figure) or differential logic (outdoor warmer than return) and its sensors, the lockout for heating, and
that the sequence opens the dampers before adding mechanical cooling. A unit heating with the dampers open
past minimum (and no CO₂ demand ventilation calling for it) has the same logic wrong the other way.

causes.name: Minimum outdoor air set wrong — too low (stale air, negative building) or too high (freezestat trips, heat can't keep up)
causes.confirm: Dampers track their command and the intake is clear, yet the measured outdoor-air fraction at minimum position is far from the design minimum.
causes.fix:
Compare the measured fraction with the design minimum fraction (ventilation schedule or balance report),
not with the blade position. Measure the outdoor-air fraction at minimum position (mixed, return and
outdoor temperatures, or a flow station) and set the minimum position until it matches the design
ventilation rate. Blade position is not airflow — a 20 % blade angle isn't 20 % air. On units with a
separate minimum damper or a flow-controlled minimum, check its setpoint and sensor. Record the new
position. In deep cold, make sure the preheat coil can carry the minimum you set.

causes.name: Mixed-air stratification — a cold outdoor-air stream reaching the coil or freezestat unmixed (poor mixing box, outdoor and return air entering side by side, low velocity at reduced fan speed)
causes.confirm: A traverse of the plenum or coil face shows a cold stream or layer far below the average mixed-air temperature; the coil average looks fine while one part sits near freezing.
causes.fix:
Give the air somewhere to mix: baffles or a mixing plate, opposed-blade dampers arranged so the outdoor and
return streams collide, more distance or a turn before the coil, or a mixing-box retrofit. On VFD units,
raise the minimum fan speed in cold weather — mixing dies at low velocity. Move the freezestat capillary
so it covers the whole leaving face (it trips on the coldest foot, so more coverage means more
protection); use an averaging element only for the mixed-air control sensor. Keep the preheat coil's valve
open in deep cold instead of letting it throttle.

causes.name: Glycol too weak for the air it sees — diluted by make-up water or filled short
causes.confirm: Refractometer reading gives a freeze point above (or within a few degrees of) the coldest air the coil can see.
causes.fix:
Find the dilution: an automatic make-up feeder on a glycol loop, water added after a leak or a drain-down.
Bring the concentration up with the same glycol type and inhibitor package to a freeze point at least
9 °F (5 °C) below the design low (burst protection needs less, but a coil that loses flow in −40 °F air
takes the air's temperature, so size for the freeze point). Re-test after mixing. Check the inhibitor and
pH while you're at it — old glycol turns acidic.

causes.name: Control sequence wrong — dampers open before the coil is warm, no warm-up or preheat enable, freezestat not driving the valve open, a point left in override, or a bad program change
causes.confirm: Hardware all checks out — dampers, valve, plant, glycol, freezestat — and it still trips or misbehaves, usually at start-up or after a controls change; the BAS shows points in override or a sequence that opens dampers cold.
causes.fix:
Walk the sequence on the BAS against the design: at start the heating valve should open and prove a warm
coil before the outdoor damper leaves closed; the freezestat should drive the valve open and the damper
closed when it trips; morning warm-up should run on return air; the preheat setpoint should suit the
outdoor temperature. Clear overrides left from testing, restore the schedule, and check the last program
change. Trend the start-up once to prove it.

causes.name: Freezestat nuisance trip — set above its design value, element touching cold metal, sitting ahead of the preheat coil or hanging in the outdoor stream, element damaged, or a short bulb-type stat on a wide coil
causes.confirm: Coil warm, plant fine, dampers tracking, no cold stream on a traverse — yet it trips; the element rests on the casing or in the outdoor stream, is kinked, or the setpoint is above what the mixed air normally runs.
causes.fix:
If the stat is set above its design value, bring it back to the design setting (commonly 35–38 °F — use
the drawing's figure) and route one long capillary zig-zagged across the leaving-air face of the first
water (preheat) coil on standoffs, never touching metal, never in the outdoor stream, never in the
mixed-air plenum ahead of a preheat coil. Replace a kinked or leaking element (it's a filled capillary — a
kink is a dead spot). Where a bulb or short stat is used on a wide coil, fit a long capillary type that
covers the face. Never lower the setpoint below the design value (35 °F unless the drawing says
otherwise), add a time delay, or jumper the stat to stop a trip. A trip that survives a correct setting
and routing is real: find the cold air (stratification, a leaking damper, valve or plant, weak glycol).

causes.name: Control loop hunting — gains or deadband wrong, oversized valve, noisy sensor, or two loops fighting
causes.confirm: Trend shows supply temperature and valve or damper position swinging in a steady rhythm; sensors agree with a reference and the valve follows its command.
causes.fix:
Trend the loop for an hour. Slow it down: reduce the proportional gain, lengthen the integral time, widen
the deadband, or add a ramp on setpoint changes. A valve that is far too big for the load hunts near
closed — add a smaller valve in parallel or change the valve. Make sure two loops don't fight (supply
temperature vs. static, or a preheat loop vs. the main coil) by staggering their setpoints.

causes.name: Duct-static control wrong — static sensor or tubing faulted (pinched, iced, leaking or disconnected tube, transducer out of zero, probe in the wrong place) or a bad setpoint or reset, so the drive follows a wrong command
causes.confirm: The drive follows its speed command exactly, but the duct-static reading disagrees with a manometer on the same tap, or the tubing is kinked, iced, leaking or disconnected — so the fan runs flat out (noise, doors, high-static trips) or crawls (weak air).
causes.fix:
Zero the transducer with both ports open; compare it with a manometer on the same tap; check the tubing end
to end for kinks, water and ice, leaks and a probe pointing against the flow; check the setpoint and reset
limits. In the cold, condensate in a sensing line that runs through an unheated space freezes — slope the
tubing to drain and keep it warm.

causes.name: Simultaneous heating and cooling from the sequence — setpoints overlapping, no deadband, reheat fighting the cooling coil, or both valves commanded at once
causes.confirm: Both valves (or heat and DX) commanded on at the same time, each doing what it's told — the sequence asks for it.
causes.fix:
Give the loops a deadband: heating setpoint a few degrees below the cooling setpoint, and a single output
sequenced heat–economizer–cool so only one acts at a time. Check reheat boxes aren't heating while the
supply is being cooled below what the zones need (raise the supply setpoint or add reset). Clear overrides
and check that both outputs aren't mapped to the same loop.

causes.name: Exhaust running without enough makeup air — makeup or supply unit down or throttled, intake iced, outdoor damper closed; the space goes negative
causes.confirm: Exhaust fans running while the makeup or supply unit is off, tripped, or taking far less outdoor air than the exhaust removes; doors pull hard, cold air whistles in at cracks.
causes.fix:
Get the makeup or supply unit running at its design outdoor air (its own fan, freezestat, filters and
intake first), and interlock the exhaust to it so exhaust can't run without makeup. Check that the makeup
unit's damper and intake pass the design flow. In cold climates a negative building pulls frost into walls
and makes doors a hazard — treat it as urgent. A strongly negative building (doors hard to open, whistling
at cracks) can also backdraft fuel-fired appliances: check CO at the boiler and generator rooms, and shut
the exhaust fans off or open a door or makeup path until makeup air is restored.
causes.safety: A negative building can pull flue gas back down the vents of boilers, furnaces, water heaters and generators — carbon monoxide. Check CO before anyone works in those rooms.

causes.name: Building over-pressurized — exhaust fan down, or supply, return and relief out of balance (relief or return damper stuck, return fan tracking wrong)
causes.confirm: Doors push open, air blows out at cracks; an exhaust fan is off, or the relief/return path is stuck while the outdoor damper brings in more than leaves.
causes.fix:
Exhaust fan off: motor, belt, interlock, schedule, or its backdraft/isolation damper frozen shut — restore it.
Exhaust running: check the relief or exhaust damper opens with the outdoor damper, the return fan's
tracking or building-pressure control, and whether the outdoor air was raised above what the exhaust
removes. Balance supply vs. exhaust to a slight positive (about +0.02 in. w.c.) and no more.

causes.name: Recovery core frosted or iced — defrost not working (defrost sensor or timer failed, recirculation or bypass damper stuck or iced, exhaust restricted, condensate drain frozen)
causes.confirm: Ice on the core's exhaust face in cold weather; supply airflow dropping off and the supply arriving colder; the defrost never starts, never finishes, or the damper that should open for it doesn't move.
causes.fix:
Confirm what starts the defrost (sensor, timer or pressure switch) and whether the recirculation or bypass
damper strokes when it is commanded. Thaw the core with warm air and the supply fan off — no tools on the
fins — and clear the drain, then fix what stopped the defrost: a failed defrost sensor or timer, a damper
that does not stroke or is iced, an exhaust path that is restricted (filters, a frozen exhaust hood or
grille), or a drain that froze. Don't keep running a frosted core in the cold — the ice restricts airflow
and can crush the core.
causes.safety: Stop both fans and lock out before opening the core section.

causes.name: Recovery wheel not turning — drive belt off or worn, wheel motor or drive failed, or the rotation sensor wrong
causes.confirm: The supply and exhaust fans run and the airflow is normal, but the wheel stands still (or the belt lies off) and the supply air leaves the unit near the outdoor temperature.
causes.fix:
Lock out both fans. Check the drive belt (a stretched, cracked or off belt is the usual failure — replace
it), the pulley and the wheel motor; the wheel should turn freely by hand. Check the rotation sensor or
controller signal that tells the BAS the wheel is turning, and the wheel seals for drag. Restart and watch
the wheel through a full turn.
causes.safety: Lock out both fans and keep hands clear of the rim and the belt.

causes.name: Recovery filters or core plugged — dirt, lint or grease restricting one or both airstreams
causes.confirm: Filters dark and bowed, or dust, lint or grease packed in the core's passages; the fans struggle, airflow is down and the recovery is poor.
causes.fix:
Replace or clean the filters on both airstreams (the exhaust side loads first in kitchens and shops).
Clean the core only the way the maker allows — many enthalpy wheels and membrane cores can't take water,
solvents or a pressure washer — and fix what loaded it (missing filters, a dirty return, grease).
causes.safety: Stop both fans and lock out before opening the core section.

causes.name: Recovery bypass or recirculation damper stuck — open or leaking (supply passes around the core) or closed or iced shut (no defrost, no free cooling)
causes.confirm: The bypass or recirculation damper does not go where the controller sends it — stuck open in cold weather (cold supply, poor recovery) or stuck closed (the core frosts because defrost can't open it).
causes.fix:
Drive the damper from the controller and watch it stroke. Clear ice or debris from the blades and seals,
free the linkage, replace a failed actuator (match torque, signal and fail position), and check the end
stops so closed really closes. Confirm the bypass and defrost logic is using a good outdoor sensor.
causes.safety: Stop the unit and lock out before reaching at the damper; actuators and springs store energy.

causes.name: Recovery condensate or defrost water not draining — drain or trap plugged, drain line frozen, pan cracked, or the unit out of level
causes.confirm: Water on the floor under the recovery core, or in its pan, in cold weather — the drain or trap is plugged or iced, the pan is cracked, or the unit is out of level — and a frozen drain also keeps the core iced.
causes.fix:
Clear the drain, trap and pan (pour water in and watch it go). Check the trap seal is deep enough for the
unit's pressure, the drain slopes away, the pan isn't cracked and the unit is level. A drain line through
cold space needs heat trace or insulation. Thaw a frozen line with warm air, not an open flame.
causes.safety: Stop both fans and lock out before opening the core section. Standing water is a slip hazard.

causes.name: Supply and exhaust airflows out of balance — fan speed or damper setting changed, or one filter or duct restricted
causes.confirm: Measured supply and exhaust airflows differ a lot; the building runs negative (supply low) or positive (exhaust low) and the core is clean and turning.
causes.fix:
Measure both airflows at the ducts and compare with the balance report. Look for what changed: fan speed or
damper settings, a loaded filter or plugged grille on one side, a kinked flex duct, a stuck balancing
damper. Reset to the balance report (supply and exhaust close to equal, the building slightly positive if
the design says so) and recheck the building pressure.
causes.safety: Stop both fans and lock out before opening a filter or core door.

causes.name: Ignition transformer or solid-state igniter weak or dead
causes.confirm: Motor runs and oil reaches the nozzle, but no arc (or a thin, intermittent one) across good electrodes. A solid-state igniter that works cold and quits warm is also a failed igniter.
causes.fix:
Check line voltage at the igniter primary during the start first — no voltage is a primary control or wiring
problem, not an igniter. With voltage in and no arc, replace the transformer or igniter (match the burner;
solid-state igniters replace iron-core transformers on many newer burners). Clean the spring contacts and the
electrode buss bars, then recheck the electrode settings before the first light.

The failed tries may have left raw oil in the chamber. Before the next try, look into the chamber with the
burner off. Liquid oil, or a glowing or smoldering floor, means no relight — remove the oil, let it cool and let
the vapor clear, and ventilate it (TM 5-642 ¶3-11b(9) says to ventilate after any misfire; open the fire or
observation door if the unit has one). Then reset the primary once.
causes.safety: 10,000–14,000 V at the output. Never test a solid-state igniter by arcing it with a hand-held screwdriver; use a tester. Reset the primary once — if it locks out again, find the cause before another reset. Raw oil in the chamber puffs on relight, so there is no relight over liquid oil.

causes.name: Electrodes out of adjustment, carboned, or porcelain cracked
causes.confirm: Drawer assembly out — gap or position off the spec card, tips burnt back, carbon bridging, or a crack or carbon track across the porcelain that bleeds the spark to ground.
causes.fix:
Reset the electrodes to the burner's spec (gap and position to the nozzle), out of the oil spray; replace
cracked or carbon-tracked porcelains and bent or burnt tips. Carbon on the tips means they sit in the spray,
the nozzle leaks at its seat, or the pump isn't cutting off cleanly at shutdown (TM 5-642 ¶3-13d(3)) — fix
that too or they'll carbon again. Tighten the clamps and check the buss bars and transformer springs make
firm contact. Replace the nozzle while you're in there.
causes.safety: Delayed ignition from weak electrodes puffs burning gas and soot out of every leak in the appliance. After a misfire, look into the chamber with the burner off and ventilate it. Liquid oil, or a glowing or smoldering floor, means no relight until the oil is removed, the chamber has cooled and the vapor has cleared. Reset the primary once — if it locks out again, find the cause before another reset.

causes.name: Nozzle plugged, dirty or worn
causes.confirm: Streaky, one-sided or smoky flame; delayed light-off; or no flame at all with pump pressure normal and a plugged orifice or strainer on the bench.
causes.fix:
Replace the nozzle with the same gph, spray angle and pattern the appliance plate calls for; a nozzle is
replaced in the field, not cleaned (TM 5-642 ¶3-13b, c). Replace the nozzle-line strainer or the pump strainer
if it's loaded. Hold the adapter with a second wrench and seat the new nozzle firmly on a clean seat in one go;
don't overtighten it, and use no sealant on the threads. Set electrodes, then run a smoke test and set the
air. A nozzle that plugs again soon has dirty fuel or a bad filter behind it: check the fuel sample and
filter.
causes.safety: A nozzle that dribbles or sprays badly may have wet the chamber. Before the next start look in with the burner off — liquid oil means no relight until it is removed and the vapor has cleared. Reset the primary once; if it locks out again, find the cause before another reset.

causes.name: Wrong nozzle or pump pressure — overfired, wrong angle or pattern, flame hitting the chamber
causes.confirm: Nozzle stamping (gph, angle, pattern) doesn't match the appliance plate and burner spec, or the pump is set well above the pressure the nozzle is rated at; the flame reaches the chamber wall or floor.
causes.fix:
Fit the nozzle the appliance and burner literature call for and set pump pressure to the burner's spec —
flow rises with pressure (TM 5-642 table 3-1), so 140 psi through a nozzle sized for 100 overfires it. A
too-large nozzle also heats the boiler so fast it short-cycles on the limit (TM 5-642 ¶3-13d(5)(e)). Check
the chamber for damage from the impinging flame and clean the carbon out. Re-tune with the analyzer.

causes.name: Pump pressure low — worn pump, regulator mis-set or pump strainer plugged
causes.confirm: Pressure below the burner's spec with normal vacuum and clean supply — the regulator won't bring it up, or the pressure sags as the pump warms (worse once it is warm, on light fuel).
causes.fix:
Adjust the regulator to spec first; if it won't hold, the gear set or regulator is worn — replace the fuel
unit (match one-pipe/two-pipe, rotation and the bypass plug). Clean the pump strainer. Big droplets from low
pressure make a smoky flame, so retune after the pressure is right. If vacuum is high too, fix the supply
restriction before condemning the pump.

On kerosene-class fuel, check that the lot carries a lubricity additive (TM 5-642 ¶3-11a); a fuel unit that
wears out early may be a fuel problem, not just a bad pump.
causes.safety: Low pressure makes big droplets and a rough or late light-off. If it has been puffing or locking out, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil before the next start, and reset the primary once only.

causes.name: Fuel pump seized or failed (no pressure)
causes.confirm: No pressure and no oil at the nozzle; the motor hums or trips with the coupling on and spins free with it off (seized pump), or the pump turns but pumps nothing (stripped gears). If it only hums in the cold and runs once it is warm, suspect thick fuel before the pump.
causes.fix:
Pull the coupling: if the pump shaft won't turn by hand, replace the fuel unit. Find out why it seized —
water or rust in the fuel, running dry after an empty tank, dirt past a bad strainer — and fix that, or the
new one follows it. Prime and bleed the new pump at the bleed port into a container, check pressure and cutoff,
then set the air.

On kerosene-class fuel, check that the lot carries a lubricity additive (TM 5-642 ¶3-11a); a fuel unit that
wears out early may be a fuel problem, not just a bad pump.
causes.safety: Reset the primary once after the repair. If it locks out again, find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l), and look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil first.

causes.name: Motor-to-pump coupling broken or slipping
causes.confirm: Motor runs normally, no pressure and no oil; the coupling is cracked, stripped or lying in the housing.
causes.fix:
Replace the coupling and check why it failed — a pump that drags or seized momentarily, or the coupling set
with end pressure on the pump shaft (TM 5-642 ¶3-13e wants it seated without pushing on the pump). Spin the
pump by hand before fitting the new coupling. Bleed into a container, check pressure, then relight.
causes.safety: Reset the primary once after the repair. If it locks out again, find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l), and look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil first.

causes.name: Burner motor failed — open winding, bad bearings, capacitor or thermal overload
causes.confirm: Line voltage at the motor leads on a call but it hums and trips, or sits silent; shaft turns freely with the coupling off.
causes.fix:
Press the motor's thermal reset button if it has one and watch whether it trips again. Test the capacitor on
PSC motors, spin the shaft for rough bearings, ohm the windings. Replace with the same frame, rpm, rotation
and shaft; make sure the new motor isn't fighting a seized pump (spin the pump first). A motor that runs hot
and trips may be over-coupled to the pump or starved of air by a soot-packed fan wheel.
causes.safety: Lock out power before touching the motor or coupling. After the repair reset the primary once; if it locks out again, find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).

causes.name: Oil solenoid or delay valve not opening (dead coil, no power, stuck)
causes.confirm: Pump pressure normal but no oil reaches the nozzle; the valve coil has no voltage on a start, or has voltage and never clicks open.
causes.fix:
No voltage to the coil: trace it to the primary control's valve terminal or the delay timer. Voltage but no
click: replace the valve or coil (match voltage and the delay the burner wants — TM 5-642 ¶3-14b has the
delay valve opening at least 4 s after the motor). Check the nozzle line and nozzle strainer while it's apart;
a plugged line looks the same from outside.
causes.safety: Reset the primary once after the repair. If it locks out again, find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l), and look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil first.

causes.name: After-drip — pump cutoff or oil valve leaking, or air in the nozzle line
causes.confirm: At shutdown the flame hangs on, smokes or rumbles, or oil drips from the nozzle; the pump gauge doesn't drop sharply to a held cutoff pressure.
causes.fix:
Bleed any air out of the nozzle line and give a new installation a few days — trapped air compresses and
squirts oil at shutdown (TM 5-642 ¶3-13d(1)(d)). If the pump's cutoff doesn't snap shut (gauge drifts instead
of holding), replace the fuel unit or add/replace the oil solenoid valve; if the solenoid passes oil, replace
it. Clean carbon out of the chamber and off the electrodes, and replace a nozzle that leaks at its seat.
causes.safety: Oil that drips at shutdown collects in the chamber. Before a relight, look in with the burner off. Liquid oil, or a glowing or smoldering floor, means no relight until the oil is removed, the chamber has cooled and the vapor has cleared.

causes.name: Oil leaking — pump shaft seal, filter gasket, fitting or nozzle line
causes.confirm: Wet oil at the pump shaft, filter can, flare fittings or nozzle line, and the smell to go with it. With the tank above the burner, a weeping shaft seal can also mean too much inlet head on the seal.
causes.fix:
Fix the leak at its source: new filter gasket (lubricate it with oil), reflare or replace a weeping flare
(no compression fittings on oil lines), tighten or replace the nozzle line. A leaking shaft seal means a new
fuel unit — and check that the bypass plug matches the piping, because a plug on a one-pipe system blows the
seal within minutes. Clean up with absorbent; oil-soaked floor and insulation keep the smell for weeks.

Tank above the burner: check the inlet head against the pump's seal rating (the pump's data sheet gives it), and
fit an anti-siphon (oil safety) valve if a broken line could drain the tank through the pump.
causes.safety: Oil on a hot burner housing or in the chamber is a fire hazard. Close the oil supply valve at the tank and kill burner power while you work.

causes.name: Pump bypass plug wrong for the piping (after a pump change)
causes.confirm: Pump recently changed. One-pipe with the plug in — the shaft seal blows and oil runs out of the pump. Two-pipe with the plug out — it never primes, pressure is low or bouncy, air keeps showing up.
causes.fix:
One-pipe: remove the bypass plug from the return port and plug the return port itself. Two-pipe: install the
bypass plug and connect the return line. Replace a fuel unit whose seal already blew. Prime at the bleed port
into a container until the oil runs clear, then check pressure and cutoff.
causes.safety: Oil sprayed from a blown seal onto a hot housing is a fire hazard. Close the oil supply valve at the tank and kill burner power before you start. After the repair reset the primary once; if it locks out again, find the cause before another reset, and look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil first.

causes.name: Air leak into the suction line — fitting, filter gasket, gauge port, valve packing
causes.confirm: Vacuum reads near zero for the lift or falls away when the burner stops; pump whines; pressure needle bounces; air keeps appearing at the bleed port. Overhead piping above the tank's oil level admits air at any loose joint (TM 5-642 ¶3-13d(4)).
causes.fix:
Find the leak: tighten or reflare every fitting from the tank to the pump, new filter-can gasket, cap or
plug the vacuum-gauge port, repack or replace the shutoff valve, check the pump cover gasket and the
vacuum-gauge port plug. Isolate by section with a vacuum gauge — a tight section holds vacuum when the pump
stops. With very light fuels an overhead line lets dissolved air collect; a two-pipe arrangement minimizes
that (TM 5-642 ¶3-13d(4)(d)), and an air separator (de-aerator) in the supply line cures chronic air as a
matter of practice. Bleed thoroughly into a container after the repair.
causes.safety: Air in the oil makes the flame sputter and drop out, and every failed try can leave oil in the chamber. Reset the primary once; if it locks out again, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).

causes.name: Fuel supply restricted — clogged filter or strainer, partly closed valve, kinked or crushed line
causes.confirm: Vacuum well above what the lift explains, or over the pump's limit (about 6 in. Hg one-pipe, 10 two-pipe single-stage, 15 two-stage), pressure sagging, pump noisy; a loaded filter or strainer, or a valve or line that isn't fully open.
causes.fix:
Change the filter and clean the pump strainer; open valves fully; straighten or replace a crushed line. If
vacuum is still high, the lift or run is too much for that pump — convert a one-pipe to two-pipe, or fit a
two-stage pump. Sludge in the filter means the tank needs treatment or cleaning, and water drained off the
bottom. Bleed into a container and check pressure afterward.
causes.safety: Reset the primary once after the repair. If it locks out again, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).

causes.name: Out of fuel, or the supply valve / fire valve is closed
causes.confirm: Tank sticks dry or below the pickup (gauges stick — stick it), or a supply valve or the fusible-link fire valve is closed. An empty tank sucks air (vacuum near zero); a closed valve pulls a high vacuum.
causes.fix:
Fill the tank (or open the valve — but find out why the fire valve tripped before resetting it). Running dry
pulls tank-bottom sludge and water into the filter and pump: change the filter, clean the strainer, bleed the
pump until the oil runs clear, and expect a second filter change soon. Reset the primary once after the
bleed; repeated resets fill the chamber with oil.
causes.safety: After an empty-tank episode the chamber may hold unburned oil from the lockout tries. Before the first light, look in with the burner off — liquid oil, or a glowing or smoldering floor, means no relight until the oil is removed, the chamber has cooled and the vapor has cleared. Then ventilate it, stand clear of the front of the unit on the first try, and reset the primary once only.

causes.name: Fuel waxed or gelled in the cold
causes.confirm: Cold outdoor tank or line, high vacuum, a filter coated in white wax and a cloudy or jelled fuel sample. It runs again when the sun hits the tank or the line is warmed. On kerosene-class fuel it takes deep cold, below about −40 °F, or the wrong fuel in the tank.
causes.fix:
Warm the filter and line gently (warm water, warm rags, heat trace, or move the filter indoors; a heat gun only
on a dry metal line with no fuel leaking and the burner locked out) — never a flame — and change the waxed
filter. Then stop it recurring: move the filter indoors onto the warm side of the wall, heat-trace or insulate
the outdoor run, and match the fuel to the weather.

No. 2 oil: blend kerosene / No. 1 into the tank (the usual winter blend is 10–50 %), or switch to an arctic
grade. Kerosene-class fuel (kerosene, No. 1, JP-8, AN8, arctic diesel): wax means it is colder than that lot's
cloud or freeze point, or the wrong fuel is in the tank — read the cloud or freeze point off the delivery
paperwork, keep the tank, filter and suction line warm, and do not blend No. 2 into it. Anti-gel additive
only works mixed into fuel that hasn't waxed yet.
causes.safety: Reset the primary once after the thaw. If it locks out again, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).
causes.notes: No. 2 oil clouds around +10 to +20 °F untreated. Kerosene, No. 1, JP-8, AN8 and arctic diesel stay fluid to about −40 °F, but below that, in outdoor tanks and lines, they can cloud too — so this cause is live on every grade. When the fuel is known to be kerosene-class, the cold sign is tightened to deep cold, and the waxed filter and cloudy sample still have to be there.

causes.name: Water or ice in the fuel
causes.confirm: A clear water layer or ice crystals in a settled sample; slush or ice on the filter element in the cold; the flame sputters and drops out as water slugs reach the nozzle.
causes.fix:
Pump or drain the water off the tank bottom (every outdoor tank breathes and condenses; snow gets in loose
fills). Change the filter — a water-absorbing cartridge helps — clean the pump strainer, replace the nozzle,
and bleed into a container until the oil runs clean. Fix the way water gets in: fill cap gasket, vent cap, a
tank that sits in the sun by day and chills at night. Water also feeds microbial sludge in warm months, so
treat the tank if the sample shows growth. In the cold, ice crystals plug a filter the same way wax does at any
fuel grade.
causes.safety: Water slugs put the flame out and the primary locks out, and each failed try can leave oil in the chamber. Reset the primary once; if it locks out again, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).

causes.name: Outdoor fuel line or filter frozen, iced or snow-crushed
causes.confirm: Exposed line or filter in deep cold, vacuum pegged, and warming the suspect section brings the oil back; the fuel sample itself may look fine because the water froze in the low spot of the line.
causes.fix:
Thaw gently (warm water on the filter can, warm rags or heat trace; a heat gun only on a dry metal line with no
fuel leaking and the burner locked out — never a flame), then find the ice: a low spot or trap in the line
where water settles, a filter can outdoors, a line crushed under snow or ice load. Drain water from the tank,
drop the filter indoors, pitch the line so it drains back to the tank with no traps, heat-trace and insulate
what has to stay outside, and keep the run clear of drifting snow. Change the filter after the thaw. If the
line was never frozen and the vacuum stays high, check the tank vent before anything else.
causes.safety: Reset the primary once after the thaw. If it locks out again, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).

causes.name: Tank vent iced over or blocked — the tank pulls a vacuum and the pump starves
causes.confirm: Vacuum high with a clean filter and a clear fuel sample, and warming the line changes nothing; frost, ice or snow packed in the vent cap or screen, no whistle at the vent, and air rushing in when the fill cap is cracked. The vacuum drops and the burner runs once the vent is cleared.
causes.fix:
Clear the vent cap and screen (warm water or warm rags, no flame), check the vent line for a pinch, a low spot
that holds water or a crushed section, and make sure the vent ends where snow and drifting spray cannot reach it
— a hooded, screened cap on a pitched line, kept clear of rime. Then recheck the pump vacuum and bleed the pump
into a container. Do not replace the fuel unit for this.
causes.safety: A tank pulling a hard vacuum can be dented or collapsed, and cracking the fill cap lets air rush in. Loosen the cap slowly, with no flame or spark near the vent. Reset the primary once after the repair; if it locks out again, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause before another reset.

causes.name: Fuel too thick in the deep cold (not waxed) — pump starves, motor overloads on a cold start, spray is poor
keywords: slow to start in the cold
causes.confirm: Deep cold, an outdoor tank or long outdoor suction run, vacuum high with a clear sample and a clean filter, no wax anywhere; the motor hums or trips on a cold start and the burner runs once the pump has warmed, with a ragged, stringy flame until the fuel warms.
causes.fix:
Thick fuel is not waxed fuel — it flows, just badly. Keep the fuel unit, filter and suction line warm (heat trace,
an insulated indoor filter housing, the shortest possible outdoor run, larger tubing, or a two-stage pump) and
do not condemn the pump until it has been run warm. Check the lot's viscosity or cold-flow data on the delivery
paperwork if the problem comes back in the same weather.
causes.safety: A motor that hums and trips on a cold start is stalled. Leave it off with the power locked out rather than cycling it, because a motor held at stall overheats; warm the pump, then try once. If the primary locks out, reset it once, and if it locks out again look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause before another reset.

causes.name: CAD cell dirty, misaligned, failed or its leads bad — flame not proven
causes.confirm: The burner lights and burns well but the control drops it at the end of its own safety time (15 seconds is common; the primary's sheet gives it); the cell reads over the control's limit (typically 1,600 Ω) with the flame on, and much lower once cleaned or replaced.
causes.fix:
Pull the cell: wipe the face, seat it firmly in its bracket sighting straight down the air tube at the flame,
check the leads and the F–F terminals for corrosion or a pinched wire. Re-read it with the flame on — still
high, replace the cell. A smoky flame or a nozzle that sprays off-pattern also hides the flame from the cell,
so if the reading improves after a tune-up the cell was never the fault. Clean the flame sensor every heating
season (TM 5-642 ¶7-9e).
causes.safety: Reset the primary once after the cell is cleaned or replaced. If it drops out again, do not keep resetting — every try pumps oil for the safety time, so look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause first (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).
causes.notes: CAD-cell ohm limits are manufacturer practice, not in the Army manuals; the control's own instruction sheet rules.

causes.name: CAD cell sees light with no flame — light leak, shorted cell, glowing refractory or smoldering oil
causes.confirm: The control refuses to start or locks out before ignition; the cell reads low (under ~20 kΩ) with the burner off and the air tube covered.
causes.fix:
Cover the air tube and re-read: if the reading climbs, light is reaching the cell — close the inspection door,
seal gaps around the transformer and air tube, and look into the chamber with the burner off for a glowing floor
or smoldering oil left by earlier failed starts. If you find any, there is no relight until it is out, the oil
is removed and the vapor has cleared. If the reading stays low covered, the cell or its leads are shorted —
replace. Check the primary control's instructions; some run a flame-present test before each start.
causes.safety: A cell that sees "flame" with the burner off may be looking at a glowing floor or smoldering oil. Keep the burner off and the chamber closed up until it has cooled, and do not relight until the oil is removed and the vapor has cleared. Reset the primary once; if it locks out again, find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).

causes.name: Stack relay helix sooted or stuck, or its contacts failed
causes.confirm: Helix bound with soot so it never pulls the hot contacts in (the burner drops out when the stack control's own safety timing runs out) or never releases (won't restart until it's tapped); contacts pitted. A stack-control lockout comes later than a CAD-cell lockout — usually a minute or more after light-off (the control's sheet gives the time), where a CAD primary locks out within its own 15 to 45 second safety time.
causes.fix:
Pull the relay, clean the helix and the smoke-pipe hole, set the drive arm per the control's sheet and reseal
the hole — air leaks there upset it (TM 5-642 ¶7-9k). Make sure the element sits in flowing flue gas, not a
dead pocket. Worn contacts or a tired relay: replace, or convert the burner to a CAD-cell primary. Heavy soot
on the helix means the fire has been dirty — tune it.

After a lockout let the stack control's safety element cool before you reset it (the control's sheet gives the
wait), and never hold the relay in. Do not restart until the cause is found (TM 5-642 ¶3-11b(7), ¶7-9h, ¶7-9l).
causes.safety: Do not block the control's motor or ignition switches in or out, and do not hold the relay in — the safety features stop working and the safety element overheats (TM 5-642 ¶7-9h, ¶3-11b(7)). Reset once; if it locks out again, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause before another reset.

causes.name: Primary control failed — relay, safety switch or board won't send the burner out
causes.confirm: Line voltage into the control and a call at T–T, nothing out to the motor and igniter — even after a reset and with the CAD cell reading dark.
causes.fix:
Confirm polarity and a sound neutral first, and that the CAD cell reads dark (a cell that sees light stops a
start). Then replace the control with one matched to the flame sensor and safety timing the burner needs, and
set the thermostat anticipator to the control's rating. Don't block or hold a relay in — the safety features
stop working (TM 5-642 ¶7-9h). Nuisance safety trips are often low voltage or reversed polarity, not the
control (¶3-13d(6)).
causes.safety: Never block or hold a relay in to make it run — the safety features don't work while it is held (TM 5-642 ¶7-9h). After a lockout reset once only; a lockout that comes back means find the cause before another reset (¶7-9l).

causes.name: Reversed polarity or bad neutral/ground at the burner (after rewiring or a generator switch-over)
causes.confirm: White reads line voltage to ground, or black reads near zero; the control misbehaves or locks out for no flame-related reason, often starting right after wiring work or a transfer to generator power.
causes.fix:
Correct hot and neutral at the service switch, the junction box and the primary's terminals, and make the
ground path solid. TM 5-642 ¶3-13d(6)(b) notes that a reversed hot and ground leaks enough through the
control to cause safety shutdowns. On generator-fed buildings check the transfer switch neutral bonding too.
causes.safety: With hot and neutral swapped or the ground open, the burner's metal parts can be live. Meter before you touch. After the wiring is corrected reset the primary once; if it locks out again, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).

causes.name: Low or sagging supply voltage — nuisance lockouts and slow starts
causes.confirm: Voltage at the burner during the start more than 10 percent under nameplate, or a recording voltmeter left on for 24 hours or more (TM 5-642 ¶3-13d(6)(a)) catching dips at light-off, with nothing else wrong at the burner.
causes.fix:
Find where the drop is: panel versus burner under load, loose or burnt connections, an undersized or overlong
run, a shared load starting. If the source is low (station power or a generator under load), report it — low
voltage slows the motor and the igniter and trips the primary. Do not replace the primary or the cell first.
causes.safety: Reset the primary once. A lockout that keeps coming back at light-off is a reason to meter and find the cause, not to keep resetting (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l), and each failed try can leave oil in the chamber, so look in with the burner off for liquid oil first. A hot connection that drops voltage under load can burn.

causes.name: Call not reaching the burner — zone-valve end switch, circulator or flow interlock, proving switch, relay, outdoor reset
causes.confirm: The thermostat is calling and the zone or relay shows it, but nothing closes T–T at the primary; the burner starts the moment T–T is jumpered.
causes.fix:
Work back from T–T: zone-valve end switch (valve opens but the switch doesn't make — common), zone relay or
switching relay contacts, circulator/flow-switch interlock, outdoor-reset or warm-weather shutdown holding the
burner off, a broken wire. At a plant with ducted intakes also check the switches that stop a burner on
purpose: the combustion-air louver or damper end switch (iced or drifted shut), a draft-proving or
stack-damper switch, and a low-oil or low-fuel pressure switch. Replace the part that doesn't pass the call.

Confirm the circulator is running before you jumper T–T on a boiler, keep the jumper on for a few seconds only,
and take it off. Don't leave T–T jumpered.
causes.safety: An open proving or flow interlock is doing its job until you know why it is open. Never jumper one to get the burner running.

causes.name: High limit (aquastat / pressuretrol / furnace limit) open while not hot — failed, mis-set or sensor out
keywords: sensing bulb out of the well
causes.confirm: Line voltage stops at the limit while the boiler water, steam pressure or plenum is well below the dial setting; the element is loose, out of its well, or the switch simply won't close.
causes.fix:
Check the setting and differential first (someone may have turned it down), then that the sensing bulb is
fully in its well with heat-transfer compound, or the pressuretrol's pigtail siphon isn't plugged. A switch
that stays open cold is replaced — mercury-type controls must be level (TM 5-642 ¶7-11b(1)).

Prove it with a meter, not a jumper: line voltage across the open contacts with the boiler cold means the limit
is open, and you read the actual boiler temperature or pressure at the same moment. Never jumper a limit,
pressuretrol or low-water cutoff to get heat. A bad control is replaced.
causes.safety: A jumpered limit or pressuretrol is how a boiler overheats or over-pressurizes. Never jumper one to test it or to get heat.
