causes.name: Boiler cycling on its high limit because heat isn't leaving it — circulator, zone valves, air-bound loop
causes.confirm: Burner fires fine, boiler sits at the limit and cycles on it, yet the building is cold — the water isn't moving (circulator, zone valves, air, closed valve) or the steam isn't leaving (closed header valve, flooded main).
causes.fix:
The burner side is healthy; go to the distribution side — circulator running and moving water (feel the
supply and return, check the pump), zone valves opening, air in the loop, closed isolation valves; on steam,
header and main valves, water line and pressuretrol. Fix the flow and the cycling stops. Confirm the limit
itself opens at its setting and the relief valve isn't being asked to do the limit's job.

causes.name: High limit / pressuretrol not shutting the burner off — boiler overheating or over-pressure
causes.confirm: Boiler well past its setting (steaming, relief or safety valve lifting, plenum scorching) and the limit still has the burner running; on steam, often a pigtail siphon packed with scale so the pressuretrol never sees the pressure.
causes.fix:
Shut the burner off at the service switch and let it cool. Clean or replace the pressuretrol's pigtail siphon
and check the control's bellows; replace an aquastat or limit whose contacts have welded; make sure a
furnace limit isn't bypassed or its element pulled out of the airstream. Replace a relief or safety valve that
lifted more than once — its seat is cut. The hand-lift test belongs to the regular test schedule, at the
pressure the maker and TM 5-642 ¶4-41c specify (80 to 85 percent of the popping point), with the discharge piped
to a safe drain. Don't lever-test a valve on a boiler that is already over-pressured. Never raise a limit or
safety-valve setting to stop the nuisance.
causes.safety: An overheating boiler can rupture or scald. Don't add cold water to a hot boiler. Treat a relief valve that has been discharging steam or boiling water as a scald hazard.

causes.name: Low-water cutoff tripped on genuinely low water — leak, failed feeder, return not coming back
causes.confirm: LWCO contacts open and the glass is empty (steam) or the boiler pressure is at zero (hot water); the burner is held off until water is restored.
causes.fix:
Let the boiler cool before adding water. Then find where the water went (TM 5-642 ¶4-78): a leak or broken
section, a return pump or feeder that failed, a broken or blocked return, a valve closed in the return,
a gauge glass valved off or drained (false low), or priming and surging from dirty water carrying it out.
Refill to the normal line, check the feeder with the broken-union test (¶4-35), and watch the level through
a full cycle before leaving. Blow down a float-type LWCO weekly in service.
causes.safety: Low water is the most serious condition a boiler plant faces (TM 5-642 ¶4-78). Never feed cold water into a hot, dry boiler — it can crack sections or flash to steam. Never bypass the cutoff.

causes.name: Low-water cutoff holding the burner off with the water level fine — dirty probe, sludged float, bad control
causes.confirm: Contacts open, but water shows at the right level in the glass (after blowing it down) or the hot-water boiler is full and pressurized.
causes.fix:
Burner off and locked out, the boiler cool and at zero pressure, and the water drained below the connection,
before you pull a probe or open a float chamber. To blow a float chamber down, close the top and bottom
connection valves, then open the blowoff (TM 5-642 ¶4-34).

Probe type: pull the probe and clean the scale off it; check the control's test button and the wiring; replace
the control if it still won't make with a clean probe in water. Float type: blow it down until the water runs
clear, then open the float chamber and clean out the mud if the switch still won't make (TM 5-642 ¶4-34,
¶4-35c). A bouncing water line trips a cutoff intermittently — see surging. Steam boilers need two
independent cutoffs; don't jumper either (¶7-13b).

Before you leave, retest the cutoff (drain slowly until the burner drops out) and refill to the normal line.
causes.safety: Never jumper the cutoff to keep the burner running while you chase the fault. A cutoff that has just been cleaned and not retested is the one most likely to be trusted wrongly.

causes.name: Low-water cutoff failed to cut out (stuck, bridged, bypassed or not fitted) — burner firing with low or no water
causes.confirm: Glass empty (steam) or pressure at zero (hot water) with the burner still firing and the cutoff contacts closed; a jumper across the cutoff, or no cutoff on the boiler.
causes.fix:
Burner off at the service switch now (TM 5-642 ¶4-78). Do not open the feed or make-up line — cold water on a
hot, dry boiler cracks sections or flashes to steam. Let it cool completely, then inspect for dry-fire damage
(cracked or warped sections, weeping joints, a sagging crown) before refilling. Find why the cutoff did not
trip (probe bridged with scale, float stuck, welded contacts, a jumper, wrong wiring), replace it, remove any
jumper, and prove it with a slow-drain test. A steam boiler needs two independent cutoffs, so test both (¶7-13b).
causes.safety: Never add water to a hot, dry boiler. Treat the boiler as damaged until it has been inspected.

causes.name: Steam boiler surging, priming or foaming — dirty or oily water, high water line, overfiring
causes.confirm: Water line bounces an inch or more while steaming, oily film or foam in a drawn sample, nuisance LWCO trips, wet steam and hammer in the mains.
causes.fix:
Skim the boiler through the skim tapping with a slow fire until the water runs clean; blow down from the bottom
a little at a time until it runs clear, watching the glass — stop at the low-water mark and never leave a
blowdown valve open; on a new or repiped boiler expect to skim several times to clear cutting oil. Check the
water line isn't carried too high and the firing rate isn't above the boiler's rating (oversized nozzle).
Gauge-glass taps at a turbulent spot can fake a bounce (TM 5-642 ¶4-77a) — compare with the LWCO behavior. Fix
the leaks that keep bringing fresh water (and oxygen and dirt) into the boiler.
causes.safety: A bottom blowdown on a small steam boiler can drop the water out of the glass and trip the cutoff. Watch the glass the whole time, and have the blowdown piped to a safe drain.

causes.name: Steam boiler flooding — feeder leaking or over-feeding, return backing up, hand bypass left open
causes.confirm: Water above the top of the glass, wet steam or hammer; the broken-union test (TM 5-642 ¶4-35b) shows the feeder valve trickling with the boiler full, or a hand bypass passing.
causes.fix:
Shut the feed, drain to the normal line, then prove where the water came from: broken-union test on the
feeder (a partly plugged feed line holds the valve off its seat — ¶4-35b(2)(a)), a leaky hand-bypass globe
valve, a swing check in the return that's failed, a condensate pump returning a slug, a tankless coil leaking
into the boiler, or city pressure needing a reducing valve. Repair that part, don't just keep draining.

causes.name: Operating control set wrong — aquastat or pressuretrol too low or differential too tight
causes.confirm: Burner runs clean but only in short bursts and the building never catches up; dial set well under the system's design (hot-water limit far below 180 °F, pressuretrol cut-out barely above cut-in, furnace limit low).
causes.fix:
Set the controls to the system's design values and a sensible differential (TM 5-642 ¶3-13d(5)(d): a limit set
too low shuts the burner down before the building can get warm; ¶6-39b: furnace limit about 175–200 °F). Ask
who turned it down and why — sometimes it was covering an overheating or relief problem that needs fixing
instead. On steam, a pressuretrol that cycles the burner every few minutes wants a wider differential.

causes.name: Operating control set too high — aquastat or pressuretrol turned up, relief or safety valve lifting
causes.confirm: Dial or setpoint well above the system's design (hot-water limit well over 200 °F, a steam pressuretrol cut-out turned up toward the 15 psi safety valve, a furnace limit above 200 °F), and the control is opening where it is set — the boiler really is that hot.
causes.fix:
Set it back to design (aquastat 180–200 °F, pressuretrol cut-in ½–1 psi with a 1–2 psi differential, furnace
limit 175–200 °F per TM 5-642 ¶6-39b) and ask why it was turned up — an undersized radiator, a weak circulator
or a failing exchanger usually sits behind it. Replace a relief or safety valve that has lifted. Never raise a
limit or valve setting to stop a nuisance.
causes.safety: A setpoint near the relief valve's rating leaves no margin. Do not raise a valve setting.

causes.name: Short cycling from the thermostat side — anticipator, wiring, location or an oversized unit
causes.confirm: Burner starts and stops every few minutes with the limit never opening and the operating control set right; the call itself comes and goes.
causes.fix:
TM 5-642 ¶3-13d(5): check the thermostat's anticipator is set to the primary control's amp draw and the heater
element screwed in tight; look for reversed or badly spliced wires at the stat and the primary; check the
stat's location (sun, drafts, a supply register) and its differential. A grossly oversized nozzle or boiler
also heats too fast — compare the nozzle with the load.

causes.name: Flue or chimney blocked or restricted — soot, debris, fallen liner, snow or ice at the cap
causes.confirm: No draft at the breech, pressure over the fire, smoke and soot at the draft regulator and inspection door; soot or debris at the chimney base, a collapsed liner, or a cap sealed with frost and ice.
causes.fix:
Shut the burner off, air out the room, and test for CO before anything else. Clear the smoke pipe, breeching and
chimney base; check the cap and the top of the liner for ice, frost and snow (cold flues frost shut from the
inside in deep cold — a low stack temperature makes it worse); repair a fallen or crushed liner. Then tune the
burner: the soot that blocked it came from a dirty fire. TM 5-642 ¶4-87 lists the boiler-room-smoke checks:
closed damper, stopped breeching or stack, soot-closed passages, leaky settings, too many sharp turns.
causes.safety: A blocked flue dumps combustion products — including CO — into the building. Don't run it until the flue is clear and draft is proven. If the burner has puffed or locked out, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil before the next start. A tripped spill or rollout switch is a safety too — find the cause before you reset it, and never jumper or bypass it.

causes.name: Poor chimney draft — cold or oversized chimney, downdraft, leaks, barometric regulator mis-set or stuck open
causes.confirm: Flue clear but draft at the breech is weak or reverses with the wind; flame pulses; smoke and odor on start-up; the barometric gate hangs open or the chimney is leaky, cold, or exposed.
causes.fix:
Set the barometric regulator (weight and level) so the breech holds the draft the burner wants, with the gate
just floating. Seal chimney and cleanout leaks (TM 5-642 ¶3-13d(1)(b)), add a cap or extend the chimney if wind
reverses it, line an oversized cold masonry flue, or add a draft inducer listed for the appliance and
interlocked with draft proving. Too little draft puts pressure in the firebox and pushes odors and smoke out
(¶3-11b(11)). Re-tune the burner once draft is right.
causes.safety: A poorly drafted burner puts CO in the building. With a CO complaint, shut it down, ventilate, and prove the draft and the flue before another start. If the burner has puffed or locked out, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil before the next start. A tripped spill or rollout switch is a safety — find the cause before you reset it, and never jumper it.

causes.name: Excessive draft — tall chimney in extreme cold, regulator stuck shut or missing, over-strong inducer
causes.confirm: Breech draft far past the burner's spec with the regulator gate shut or absent; O2 high and stack temperature high for the air setting; worse the colder it gets.
causes.fix:
Chimney draft grows with the gap between flue and outdoor temperature, so a stack that behaves at 40 °F pulls
hard at −40 °F. Free up or replace the barometric regulator and weight it to hold the breech at spec; a very
tall stack may need a double-acting (or second) regulator, or a motorized draft damper interlocked with the
burner. Excess draft pulls extra air through the fire, lowers CO2 and efficiency and magnifies any leak (TM
5-642 ¶3-11b(11)); it can also lift the flame off the retention head at light-off. Re-tune the air afterward.
causes.safety: A flame that lifts off the head at light-off can drop out and leave oil in the chamber. After a lockout reset the primary once; if it locks out again, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil and find the cause before another reset (TM 5-642 ¶7-9l).

causes.name: Combustion air starved — intake drifted shut, louvers closed, tight room, exhaust fans pulling it negative
causes.confirm: Intake louvers closed or drifted full of snow, a sealed-up boiler room, or exhaust fans that pull the room negative; the burner smokes and the CO climbs when the room depressurizes.
causes.fix:
Open and clear the combustion-air path — dig out and screen a drifted intake, open louvers, add an outside-air
duct sized for the firing rate — and make sure exhaust fans and dryers can't pull the room negative while the
burner runs (interlock or make-up air). TM 5-642 ¶4-87c: enough door, window or other openings must be in use
for combustion air. Re-tune after.
causes.safety: A starved burner makes CO and a flue under positive room-pressure spills it. Ventilate before working.

causes.name: Too little combustion air at the burner — air shutter closed down, dirty fan wheel, air tube or head carboned
causes.confirm: Low O2 (high CO2) with a smoke spot of 2 or more and CO rising; dark, lazy flame. Room air is fine — the restriction is at the burner.
causes.fix:
Clean the burner fan wheel, air tube, retention head and the inlet screen; check the shutter and band haven't
slipped. Then set the air by the book: close the air until a trace of smoke shows, open it until the smoke just
disappears, then add a little more (TM 5-642 ¶3-11b(10)) and confirm with the analyzer — O2 about 4–6 %, smoke 1
or less, CO under 100 ppm. A burner that won't reach 5 % O2 without smoking is a replacement candidate
(¶3-23e). Brush out the soot it made.
causes.safety: A rich burner puts CO in the building. With a CO complaint, shut it down, ventilate, and prove the draft and the flue before another start.

causes.name: Too much combustion air — shutter wide open, lean fire, hard light-off
causes.confirm: O2 well over 8 % with the draft normal and no flue leak at the sample point; a sparky, stringy, noisy flame; delayed or rough light-off; raw oil on the chamber floor. It often shows up when the weather turns cold on a burner that draws outside air.
causes.fix:
Close the air shutter and band in steps toward the smoke-trace point and back off just past clean (TM 5-642
¶3-11b(10), ¶3-13d(2)(a) — too much air makes a poor fire and soaks the brick with raw oil). Make sure a leaky
appliance setting or a sample taken past the barometric isn't faking the high O2 (¶3-13f, ¶3-23b). Target
O2 4–6 %, smoke 1 or less. Excess air carries heat up the stack — efficiency comes back as the O2 drops.

If the burner draws outside air, a shutter that was right in a warm room runs lean at −40 °F (cold air is about
a quarter denser, so the same fan delivers about a quarter more air by weight) and rich again in summer. Set
the air with the analyzer at the season's intake temperature and recheck when the weather swings. Enter the
actual intake temperature as the room / combustion air temperature.
causes.safety: A lean fire that lights hard puffs. If the light-off has been rough, look into the chamber with the burner off for liquid oil before the next start, and reset the primary once only.

causes.name: Heat exchanger / flue passages sooted up
causes.confirm: Stack temperature high for the firing rate, passages narrowed with soot at the cleanout, draft falling off over the fire, soot blowing out of the appliance.
causes.fix:
Shut down, brush and vacuum the flue passages, combustion chamber, smoke pipe and chimney base; replace the
gaskets and seal the cleanouts. Then find and fix what made the soot — air setting, nozzle, draft, combustion
air — and tune with the analyzer, or it's back in a month. Soot insulates: an eighth of an inch costs several
points of efficiency and shows up as stack temperature. TM 5-642 ¶4-79a(1), ¶4-87b.
causes.safety: Soot-blocked passages push CO and smoke out of the appliance. With a CO complaint, shut it down, ventilate, and prove the draft and the flue before another start. A tripped spill or rollout switch is a safety — find the cause before you reset it, and never jumper it.

causes.name: Stack too cool — cold boiler or return water, uninsulated outdoor stack, oversized boiler, condensing flue
causes.confirm: Net stack under about 275 °F with rust streaks, moisture or white deposits in the smoke pipe and chimney base; usually cold boiler or return water, an outdoor stack that loses its heat, or a boiler far bigger than its load running cold and short (or fired below the plate rating).
causes.fix:
Flue gas that falls below its dew point drops acid water in the pipe and chimney, and the sulfur in the oil
makes it acid (TM 5-642 ¶4-98a). Find out why the gas is cool before you touch the nozzle.
- Boiler or return water running cold (a low operating limit, outdoor reset, long cold starts): raise the
setpoint toward the design value (180 °F is typical) or add return-water protection that holds the boiler
maker's minimum return temperature, which the boiler's manual gives.
- An uninsulated outdoor stack in deep cold: insulate it or fit an insulated stainless liner.
- Too much excess air: trim to O2 4–6 %.
- A boiler far bigger than its load: confirm the nozzle matches the plate. Downsizing within the maker's range
lengthens the runs but lowers the stack temperature, so it does not cure a wet flue by itself.

Repair corroded pipe before it leaks flue gas.

causes.name: Combustion chamber / refractory damaged or oil-soaked
causes.confirm: Through the port — cracked, collapsed or burned-through refractory, or a floor black with carbon and raw oil; rumbling and puffing for minutes after a light-off is the soaked lining cooking off (TM 5-642 ¶3-11b(9)).
causes.fix:
Do not fire into oil-soaked refractory or onto a wet chamber floor. Burner and oil supply off, let it cool, soak
up and remove any liquid oil, scrape out the carbon, and replace any refractory or blanket that is saturated — it
cannot be burned out safely in a small gun-fired chamber (TM 5-642 ¶3-11b(9) describes letting oil-soaked soft
brick burn off with the relief door open; a small unit has no relief door, so do not copy that).

Repair or replace the chamber (wet-blanket or pre-formed liners for most gun burners) and re-set the air tube
insertion. Then fix what soaked it: failed ignitions, after-drip, a nozzle spraying onto the wall. A damaged
chamber lets the flame hit cold iron, which smokes and shortens the boiler's life.
causes.safety: Raw oil in the chamber turns a normal light-off into a puffback. Do not relight until the chamber is dry and clean. For the first light after the repair, keep the inspection door and port closed, everyone clear of the front of the unit and one person at the switch; if it does not light on that one try, stop and look again.

causes.name: Water-side scale or sludge — kettling, hot spots, heat not getting into the water
causes.confirm: Rumbling, percolating or banging while the burner runs, stack temperature high with clean flue passages, and a history of fresh make-up water (leaks) or hard water.
causes.fix:
Scale insulates the water side: find and stop the make-up water first (every gallon brings new minerals), then
flush and, where the maker allows, chemically clean the boiler and rinse thoroughly; open handholes and remove
sludge from the mud ring and lower sections (TM 5-642 ¶4-85b, ¶4-88). Treat the water afterward. Kettling in
a hot-water boiler can also be low flow through the boiler — check the circulator and bypass before descaling.

causes.name: Tankless coil scaled or plugged — little domestic hot water
keywords: no hot water at the tap
causes.confirm:
Boiler holds temperature and heats the building, but the tap runs lukewarm or the flow is poor: scale
inside the coil (low flow) or outside it (poor heat transfer); or the low-limit/reverse-acting aquastat isn't
keeping the boiler hot between heating calls.
causes.fix:
Check the low-limit setting first (the boiler must be held around 160–180 °F for the coil to work). Then flow-test
the coil: poor flow means scale inside — acid-flush with a circulating pump and a descaler the coil maker
approves, or replace the coil (and its gasket). Fit a mixing valve on the outlet and a flow restrictor if the
coil is undersized for the draw. A coil that drips into the boiler shows up as rising boiler pressure.

causes.name: Tankless coil leaking domestic water into the boiler — pressure climbs, relief valve weeps
causes.confirm: Boiler pressure keeps climbing with the make-up water valve shut and the burner off; the relief valve weeps or lifts at normal boiler temperature.
causes.fix:
Isolate the coil (shut the domestic cold feed to it) and watch — pressure that stops climbing confirms it.
Replace the coil or plug it off and install an indirect or separate water heater. Replace a relief valve that
has been weeping for long; its seat is scored. A waterlogged expansion tank or a passing fill valve gives a
similar pressure rise, so rule them out first (see the expansion tank and fill valve causes). Only a leaking
coil keeps climbing with the make-up valve shut — that's why the fill-valve-shut test matters.

causes.name: Relief valve weeping at normal pressure — worn or fouled seat
causes.confirm: Dripping or weeping with the boiler pressure and temperature well under the valve's rating — the seat is scored or has debris on it.
causes.fix:
Do not lever-flush it as a repair. TM 5-642 ¶4-41c allows a hand lift only when the pressure is 80 to 85
percent of the popping point, and a boiler that is well under the valve's rating is not there. If the maker
allows a lever lift to clear debris, do it at working pressure with the full-size discharge pipe in place and
everyone clear of the outlet. If it still weeps, replace the valve with one of the same pressure rating and
capacity — never tighten the spring (¶4-41c) or plug the outlet. Pipe the discharge to a safe spot. If the
pressure ever reads high, the valve is doing its job: look at the expansion tank, fill valve, tankless coil or
limit instead (see the expansion tank and fill valve causes).
causes.safety: A relief or safety valve is the last line against a boiler rupture. Replace, don't disable. A lever lift throws boiler-temperature water or steam, so keep clear of the outlet.

causes.name: Expansion tank waterlogged or lost its air charge — pressure climbs as the water heats
causes.confirm: Pressure is normal cold but climbs toward the relief setting as the boiler heats, and the relief valve weeps or lifts hot; the tank rings dull or solid all over, the air valve spits water or holds no air, and the pressure holds steady with the fill valve shut.
causes.fix:
Isolate the tank and drain its water side before you test the air side. A bladder tank that spits water at the
air valve has a ruptured bladder — replace the tank rather than pumping it up, and set the new tank's air
precharge to the cold fill pressure (about 12 psi) before it goes onto the wet system. On a plain steel
compression tank, drain it and restore its air cushion, then find out why it keeps losing air. If the tank
tests good but the pressure still climbs to the relief setting on every heat-up, it is too small for the
water in the system. Replace a relief valve that has popped repeatedly; its seat is cut.
causes.safety: The water in the tank is hot and under pressure. Let the system cool and the pressure down before you isolate or drain the tank. A relief valve is the last line against a rupture; replace it, don't disable it.

causes.name: Fill (make-up) valve passing or set high — pressure creeps up even with the boiler cool
causes.confirm: Pressure creeps up toward the relief setting even with the boiler cool, the expansion tank tests good, and closing the shutoff ahead of the fill valve stops the rise.
causes.fix:
Close the shutoff ahead of the fill valve and bleed the boiler back to the cold fill pressure (about 12 psi); if
it then holds, the fill valve is passing. Clean the valve's seat and strainer (scale under the seat lets supply
water creep through) or replace the pressure-reducing fill valve, and set its cold fill pressure to match the
expansion tank's air precharge. A relief valve that has popped repeatedly is replaced, not re-seated.
causes.safety: A relief valve is the last line against a rupture; replace it, don't disable it. Let the boiler cool and the pressure down before you work on the fill valve.

causes.name: Furnace starved for airflow — dirty filter, slow blower, closed registers — tripping its limit
causes.confirm:
Burner runs, the plenum gets very hot, the limit opens and the burner cycles; filter loaded, blower slow
or belt slipping, or registers shut (TM 5-642 ¶6-40g: outlet air over 160 °F for long is nearly always
airflow).
causes.fix:
Replace the filter and clean the blower wheel; check belt tension, pulley setting and that the blower isn't
running backward (¶6-36, ¶6-40a); open registers and dampers and fix crushed or blocked ducts. Then check
plenum temperature and the limit setting (about 175–200 °F — ¶6-39b). A furnace that still trips with full
airflow is overfired: check the nozzle against the plate.

causes.name: Furnace blower motor failed or weak — motor, capacitor, belt, bearings
causes.confirm: Voltage at the blower motor once the plenum is hot but it doesn't run (or barely turns); the burner then cycles on the limit with the plenum scorching.
causes.fix:
Power off: spin the wheel for seized bearings, check the belt and pulleys, test the capacitor, ohm the windings,
press the motor's overload reset if it has one (TM 5-642 ¶6-40a(3)). Replace the motor (match hp, rpm, frame,
rotation and the speed taps or ECM program) or the belt and bearings. A too-tight belt or binding thrust
collars overload the motor (¶6-36a).
causes.safety: Do not run the burner without airflow. Leave the furnace off (use other heat) until the blower runs; the limit is a backup, not the control.

causes.name: Fan control not switching the blower on (or on far too late)
causes.confirm: Plenum hot, no voltage out of the fan control to the blower; the blower runs when its switch is set to manual/on. The fan contacts are burnt or the control's element is tired or set too high.
causes.fix:
Replace the fan-limit control (don't repair switches in the field — TM 5-642 ¶7-11a(8)); set fan-on about 115 °F
and fan-off about 100 °F with a 10–20 °F differential (¶7-11a(4)), limit about 175–200 °F. Mount the element
where it sees the plenum air, not the crown sheet. Until the part arrives, run the blower from the manual fan
switch so it moves air whenever the burner fires, with the limit still in the circuit. Do not jumper across
the limit terminals: TM 5-642 ¶6-40e treats that as an emergency-only measure, and ¶6-40d says not to operate a
forced warm-air furnace without the blower control.
causes.safety: Never run the burner with no blower control and no manual fan; the heat exchanger overheats and the limit is the only thing left. Don't bypass the limit to get heat.

causes.name: Blower running constantly — fan control stuck on, set too low, or switch left on manual
causes.confirm: The blower never stops, blowing cool air between burner cycles; the fan control's contacts are welded, the fan-off setting is below room temperature, or the manual fan switch is on.
causes.fix:
Check the thermostat fan switch and the control's manual lever first. Set fan-off about 100 °F (TM 5-642 ¶6-39a,
¶7-11a(4)); a control whose contacts won't open has been cooked by overheating — replace it and find the
overheating (airflow, overfiring). Frequent blower starts and stops shorten motor life: widen the differential
10 °F (¶6-40f).

causes.name: Cracked heat exchanger — combustion gases into the supply air
causes.confirm: Flame jumps or rolls when the blower starts, CO or an O2 drop in the supply air with the analyzer, soot streaks or a visible crack with a light and mirror; a CO alarm in the building. TM 5-642 ¶4-87 names a leak in the furnace's heat exchanger as a source of CO in the building.
causes.fix:
Shut the furnace down, tag it out and ventilate. Replace the heat exchanger or the furnace — there is no
field repair. Find out why it cracked: years of limit trips from poor airflow, overfiring, flame impingement,
or thermal shock from a blower that never ran. Fix that on the replacement.
causes.safety: Carbon monoxide. Red-tag it, and do not run it again until the heat exchanger is replaced.

causes.name: No line power — breaker off or tripped, disconnect off, or a fuse blown
causes.confirm: No voltage across the line terminals at the unit's disconnect, then work back toward the panel.
causes.fix:
Find where the power stops: panel breaker, disconnect switch, fuses (in the disconnect and inside the unit),
then the wiring between. Before resetting a tripped breaker or replacing a fuse, ask why it opened: check
the loads for a short to ground (meg or ohm each motor, compressor and heater to ground). If it trips
again right away, treat it as a shorted load, not a bad breaker.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag before opening any panel. Verify dead with a tested meter.

causes.name: Short or ground fault in a load (keeps tripping the breaker)
causes.confirm: With power locked out, meter (or megger) each load to ground — compressor terminals, motor leads, heaters — and look for scorched wiring.
causes.fix:
Isolate the load that reads to ground or shorted (disconnect its leads one at a time). Repair chafed
wiring; replace the shorted motor, heater or compressor. A compressor reading to ground also needs an acid
test of the oil before a new one goes in. Never keep resetting a breaker on a dead short.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag. A grounded compressor can blow its terminals out — don't run it to "see".

causes.name: No control power — control transformer, control fuse or a shorted 24 V circuit
causes.confirm: Line voltage on the transformer primary but no 24 V on the secondary (transformer bad), or a blown low-voltage fuse on the board.
causes.fix:
If the control fuse is blown, find the short before replacing it: a nicked thermostat wire, a shorted
contactor or relay coil, or a wire rubbing the cabinet. Measure each coil's resistance (most 24 V coils
read 5–20 Ω; near zero is shorted). Replace a transformer that has primary voltage but no secondary, and
check its VA rating against the load.

causes.name: Thermostat or controller not calling (setpoint, mode, schedule, failed control or broken wire)
causes.confirm: No call signal at the unit while the space is away from setpoint; jumpering the call (e.g. R to Y or R to W) at the unit starts it.
causes.fix:
Check mode, setpoint, schedule, batteries and any lockout or holiday setting. If the stat calls but the
unit doesn't see it, trace the wire for a break. Replace a thermostat or controller that won't close its
output, and check its sensor or probe (a sensor reading wrong makes the control think it's satisfied).

causes.name: Low supply voltage (source, generator, undersized or long wiring)
causes.confirm: Voltage at the unit under load more than 10 % below nameplate; compare with the voltage at the panel to find where it drops.
causes.fix:
If the drop is between the panel and the unit, look for a loose or corroded connection or undersized
wire. If the panel itself is low, it is a supply problem (utility or station power plant / generator
loading) — report it. Low voltage overheats motors and compressors, so fix it before replacing parts.

causes.name: Loose or burnt power connection
causes.confirm: Discolored or melted terminal, a lug that turns when tightened, or voltage that drops across a connection under load.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Inspect lugs, terminal blocks, contactor and disconnect terminals for heat discoloration and
pitting. Cut back and re-terminate burnt conductors, replace damaged terminals, and torque to spec.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag; verify dead before touching terminals.

causes.name: Low-voltage fuse blown by a shorted thermostat or outdoor control cable
causes.confirm: With the thermostat off the wall and power off, a call terminal reads near 0 Ω to C, and the short clears when one cable is lifted.
causes.fix:
Find the damage on that run: a staple through the cable, insulation rubbed through on a cabinet edge or the
outdoor unit's sheet metal, a cable chewed or cut outside, a wet splice. Repair or replace the run; don't
tape a bare spot on an outdoor cable. Replace the fuse with the same rating, never a larger one. Then run
every call (Y, W, G, O/B) and check the fuse holds.

causes.name: Low-voltage fuse blown by a shorted coil (contactor, relay, zone valve or reversing-valve coil)
keywords: fuse blows when contactor pulls in
causes.confirm: The fuse blows the moment one call comes on, and the coil on that call reads under about 2 Ω with a lead lifted.
causes.fix:
Replace the shorted coil, or the whole contactor or relay if the coil isn't sold alone. Match the coil
voltage. Look for why it failed: water dripping on it, a coil run on high voltage (wrong transformer tap),
or a contactor that chattered for a long time. Fit a fuse of the same rating and run every call.

causes.name: Control transformer failed — line voltage on the primary, no 24 V out
causes.confirm: Line voltage across the primary leads and 0 V across the secondary, measured at the transformer.
causes.fix:
Before you fit a new transformer, ohm the 24 V circuit for a short (call terminals to C with the thermostat
off). A transformer with no fuse ahead of its load often dies from a short that is still there. Replace it
with one of the same primary voltage and at least the same VA. Add an inline fuse in the secondary if the
circuit has none.
causes.safety: The primary is line voltage. Lock out before you change it.

causes.name: Control power lost before the transformer — a switch, fuse, breaker or loose lead
causes.confirm: Line voltage at the unit's disconnect or power terminals, none at the transformer primary leads.
causes.fix:
Work from the unit's power terminals toward the transformer: a burner service or emergency switch, a
control-circuit fuse or breaker, a door or limit switch in the primary leg, then the lead terminals. Find
why a switch or fuse was open before you restore it.
causes.safety: The primary is line voltage. Meter with a CAT III meter and insulated probes; lock out before you touch the terminals.

causes.name: Control transformer overloaded or undersized — 24 V sags on a call, contactor chatters
causes.confirm: R to C reads normal with no call and drops under 22 V once the loads pull in; the voltage at the coil follows the transformer down (no extra drop in the wiring).
causes.fix:
Add up the VA of everything on the secondary: the contactor and relays, zone dampers, a humidifier, a
thermostat, accessory boards. Fit a larger transformer, or move the added loads to their own transformer
(and keep them apart from the first one, or phase them). A transformer that runs hot to the touch is past
its rating.
causes.safety: Lock out and dead-test before you change the transformer; its primary is line voltage.

causes.name: Transformer on the wrong primary tap for the supply (208 vs 240 V) — 24 V reads high or low
causes.confirm: The primary lead in use doesn't match the voltage you metered on the primary, and the secondary reads outside 22–28 V.
causes.fix:
Lock out and move the primary to the tap that matches the measured supply. Cap the unused lead. Then check
the secondary is 24–28 V under load. A secondary that has run high for a long time can cook coils, so ohm
the contactor and relay coils too.
causes.safety: Lock out and dead-test before you move a tap.

causes.name: Two transformers tied together out of phase — fuses blow, controls act up
causes.confirm: With the C terminals tied, about 48 V reads between the two R terminals.
causes.fix:
Keep the two transformers' circuits apart where the design allows: take out the R-terminal jumper on a
two-transformer thermostat, or use a relay to keep the circuits apart. Where they must share a common, swap the primary or
secondary leads on one transformer so R to R reads near 0 V. Then replace any blown fuse and recheck.

causes.name: Blower-door safety switch open — door not seated or the switch failed
causes.confirm: Line voltage at the unit's power terminals but none on the transformer primary, and the switch plunger isn't made with the door on.
causes.fix:
Seat the door so it pushes the plunger fully in; bent doors and lost screws are the usual reason after a
filter change. If the plunger is made and the switch still reads open, replace the switch. Never tape or
jumper it: it keeps hands out of a live cabinet with a blower that can start.

causes.name: Loose or corroded low-voltage connection — the coil gets too few volts and chatters or drops out
causes.confirm: R to C at the transformer reads normal, but the coil reads more than 2 V lower with the call on; stepping along the circuit finds the joint where the volts are lost.
causes.fix:
Cut back and remake the bad joint. Outdoors, use gel-filled connectors or a sealed splice. Tighten loose
terminal screws, and replace any aluminum or very thin conductor in the run. Check the coil's voltage
again with the call on.
causes.safety: Lock out and dead-test before you remake a joint at the unit; the contactor's line side stays live with the call off.

causes.name: A safety or control jumpered out and left that way
causes.confirm: A jumper, wire nut or pinned switch bridges a safety (pressure switch, float, limit, rollout, door switch) or a control.
causes.fix:
Take the jumper out. Then find why someone put it in: the safety was tripping for a reason. Fix that reason
(dirty coil, clogged drain, airflow, draft) or replace a switch that tests failed. Check what running
without the safety may have damaged: a compressor that overheated, water on a ceiling, a scorched limit.
causes.safety: A bypassed safety lets the equipment run into the condition it guards against. Don't leave a unit running with any safety jumpered.

causes.name: High-pressure switch failed open (or its wire loose) — open at normal head pressure
causes.confirm: Head pressure reads normal (or the system is off and equalized), yet the switch still reads open with a lead lifted.
causes.fix:
A high-pressure trip is nearly always real, so rule out a dirty condenser, a failed fan and overcharge
first. Check the switch wires and spade terminals; a loose one reads the same as an open switch. Replace
with the same cut-out setting and the same reset type (manual or automatic). A switch on a valve-core
fitting must have a core depressor, or it never sees pressure and will not trip. Confirm there is a valve
core behind the old switch before you unscrew it, and leak-check the fitting.
causes.safety: The fitting is under system pressure. Wear eye protection; if there is no valve core behind the switch, recover the refrigerant first.

causes.name: Low-pressure switch failed open or set too high — open at normal suction, or trips every cold start
causes.confirm: Suction reads normal with the unit running (or the system is equalized above the cut-out), yet the switch reads open. A switch that only trips in the first minute of a cold start points at a missing start-up bypass.
causes.fix:
A low-pressure trip is usually real: confirm the charge and the indoor airflow first. Replace a switch that
reads open at normal suction, with the same setting and reset type; a switch on a valve-core fitting needs
a core depressor. Many control boards ignore the low-pressure switch for the first minutes of a start;
check that this is set or wired as the maker intends. Don't lower a cut-out to hide a low-suction problem.
causes.safety: The fitting is under system pressure. Wear eye protection; if there is no valve core behind the switch, recover the refrigerant first.

causes.name: Condensate float switch open with the pan dry — float stuck, out of level, or wired wrong
causes.confirm: The float switch reads open (24 V across it with the call on) while its pan holds no water.
causes.fix:
Free a float stuck in slime or debris, level a pan-mounted switch, or replace it. Check it is wired in the
leg the maker shows (usually breaking Y or R to the outdoor unit). Prove it with the power off: lift the
float by hand and ohm the switch open and closed. If you must use water, pour it only with the disconnect
off. Never jumper a float switch to keep the unit running; a jumpered float is how a ceiling gets flooded.
causes.safety: The pan sits beside line-voltage blower and heater wiring. Power off before you pour water or reach in.

causes.name: Rollout or spill switch failed — trips with nothing found wrong
causes.confirm: A full inspection finds the draft, flue, passages, combustion air and light-off all good, and the after one reset and a cool-down it trips again on the next start with every reading still normal.
causes.fix:
A rollout or spill switch that trips is nearly always telling the truth. Prove the draft, flue and
combustion air once more with an analyzer before you blame the switch. Then replace it with one of the same
rating and reset type, never an automatic-reset switch in place of a manual one. If the new switch trips
too, go back to the draft and the flue.
causes.safety: A rollout or spill trip means flame or flue gas left its path. Find the reason before the first reset, reset once only, and never bypass it. Test for CO in the room and at the flue.

causes.name: Outdoor control board in lockout after repeated safety trips — runs only after a power reset
causes.confirm: The board shows its lockout code; cutting power for a minute clears it and the unit runs again.
causes.fix:
Read the code before you reset it. The lockout counts trips of a pressure switch or another safety, so the
real fault is whatever trips it: a dirty condenser or failed fan (high pressure), low charge or a frozen
coil (low pressure). Reset, then watch the pressures through a full cycle.

causes.name: Relay coil open — 24 V on the coil, the relay doesn't pull in
causes.confirm: 24 V across the coil terminals with the call on, the relay stays out, and the coil reads open with a lead lifted.
causes.fix:
Replace the relay (or the coil, if it's sold alone) with the same coil voltage and contact rating. If the
new coil also fails soon, look for high control voltage or water on it.

causes.name: Relay contacts pitted or burnt — pulled in, but the load gets low or no voltage
causes.confirm: The relay is pulled in but several volts or more read across a closed contact while the load runs.
causes.fix:
Replace the relay; don't file the contacts. Check the load's current against the contact rating. A motor
with a failing capacitor or tight bearings pulls high current and burns the contacts again.
causes.safety: Lock out before you change it; the contacts switch line voltage.

causes.name: Relay stuck closed — burner, blower or pump runs with no call
causes.confirm: With the call off there is no voltage on the relay coil, yet the relay stays in and the load runs.
causes.fix:
Lock out and replace the relay. Look for why the contacts welded: a load drawing more than the contact
rating, or contacts that chattered on low control voltage. On a boiler, check that the high limit still
shut the burner off while the relay was stuck.
causes.safety: The load can start at any moment while the relay is stuck. Lock out before you work on it.

causes.name: Call stuck on — 24 V stays on the coil with the thermostat satisfied
causes.confirm: With the thermostat off, 24 V still reads on the contactor or relay coil. If it goes away with the thermostat off the wall, the thermostat is stuck; if it stays, the cable is shorted.
causes.fix:
Pull the thermostat off: if the call drops, replace the thermostat. If it stays, find the short between R
and the call wire in the cable (often at a staple or where it enters the unit) and repair the run. On an
A/C that ran nonstop, check the indoor coil for ice before you leave.

causes.name: Contactor buzzing loudly while pulled in — dirty or rusted pole faces, or a cracked shading ring
causes.confirm: The contactor buzzes loudly with normal voltage on its coil; the noise is in the magnet, not the compressor.
causes.fix:
Replace the contactor. A loud magnet hum means the armature isn't seating flat, and it will chatter and
pit its contacts soon. Look for dirt or insects in it, and check the coil voltage under load.
causes.safety: Lock out and dead-test before you change it; the contactor's line side stays live with the call off.

causes.name: Restart delay timing out — a normal 3–5 minute wait (longer after a power event), not a fault
causes.confirm: The unit starts on its own a few minutes after the call or after power returns, then runs normally.
causes.fix:
Nothing to repair. Wait out the delay before you troubleshoot a no-start, and tell the occupant about it.
Don't bypass the timer; it protects the compressor from restarting against high pressure.

causes.name: Delay timer (anti-short-cycle or time-delay relay) failed open — never times out
causes.confirm: 24 V goes into the timer but nothing comes out after 10 minutes.
causes.fix:
Check that the safeties wired through the timer read closed first. Then replace the timer, or the board it
sits on. Don't leave a jumper across the timer: it removes the compressor's short-cycle protection.
causes.safety: Lock out and dead-test before you change it; the contactor's line side stays live with the call off.

causes.name: Unit or zone control board failed — 24 V and a call in, no output
causes.confirm: 24 V and the call read at the board's input terminals, every safety input to the board reads closed, and nothing comes out after any start delay.
causes.fix:
Check the board's own fuse and status light, and that every safety input to it reads closed: a board holds
its outputs off while a safety is open. Then replace the board with the same part or an approved
replacement, set its switches or settings to match the old one, and run every call. After a power event,
look for surge damage elsewhere and fit surge protection if the unit has none.
causes.safety: Lock out before you change the board; line voltage is on it.

causes.name: Thermostat set wrong — mode, setpoint, fan, schedule or a hold
causes.confirm: The mode, setpoint, fan setting, schedule or hold doesn't match the call the occupant wants; setting it right brings the call on.
causes.fix:
Set the mode, setpoint and fan, clear any hold or vacation mode, and fix the schedule. Show the occupant how
it is set. If the settings keep changing, look for a second person or a remote app adjusting it.

causes.name: Thermostat set up wrong for the equipment — system type, stages, fan in heat
causes.confirm: The installer menu doesn't match the equipment (for example set as a heat pump on a furnace, or one stage on a two-stage unit).
causes.fix:
Set the system type, stages, auxiliary heat and fan control to match the equipment, then run each call (Y,
Y2, W, W2, G) and check the right parts start.

causes.name: Thermostat failed — set right but won't close its output
causes.confirm: With the thermostat set right and 24 V on R, nothing comes out on the call terminal; jumpering R to the call at the unit starts it.
causes.fix:
Replace the thermostat. Match the type (heat pump or conventional, stages, needs a C wire or not). Set the
installer menu for the equipment, then run each call.

causes.name: Thermostat wire broken or loose — the call leaves the thermostat but doesn't reach the unit
causes.confirm: 24 V on the call terminal at the thermostat, none at the unit's terminal board.
causes.fix:
Check both ends for a wire pulled out of its terminal or broken under the screw. Then ohm the conductor end
to end (power off, both ends lifted). Use a spare conductor in the cable if one is broken, or pull a new
cable.

causes.name: Thermostat batteries dead — display blank or warning, the call drops out
causes.confirm: Fresh batteries bring the display back and the call comes on.
causes.fix:
Fit fresh batteries of the type marked in the thermostat. If they die again within months, the thermostat
may be drawing on them because it has no C wire; add one if the equipment has a C terminal.

causes.name: No C wire — the thermostat steals power and browns out (blank or restarting display, chatter)
causes.confirm: The thermostat needs a C wire and none is connected; with a C wire landed (or a temporary one from the equipment) the faults stop.
causes.fix:
Land a C wire: use a spare conductor in the cable, pull a new cable, or fit an adapter the thermostat maker
approves. Check R to C reads 24 V at the sub-base afterwards.

causes.name: Thermostat miswired — wires on the wrong letters, R and C crossed, or the R-terminal jumper wrong
causes.confirm: A conductor lands on different letters at the thermostat and at the equipment, or the jumper between the R terminals (Rh and Rc) is wrong for the number of transformers.
causes.fix:
Re-land each wire by function, not by color: follow it to the equipment terminal it actually lands on.
Put the R-terminal jumper in for one transformer, out for two. Replace a blown fuse and run every call.

causes.name: Heat anticipator or cycle rate set wrong — short cycles, or long cycles with big swings
causes.confirm: The anticipator dial doesn't match the W-circuit current (clamp with 10 wraps, divide by 10), or the cycle-rate setting doesn't match the equipment type.
causes.fix:
Set the anticipator to the measured W current. On a digital thermostat set the cycle rate for the
equipment (the installer menu lists types such as forced air, hot water, steam). Short cycles with every
setting right point back at the thermostat's location.

causes.name: Mechanical thermostat off level or dirty — switches several degrees off the dial
causes.confirm: The base is off its level marks, or dust and lint sit on the coil and contacts, and the call switches several degrees away from the dial setting.
causes.fix:
Level the base on its marks and clean the coil and contacts with a soft brush (no abrasive on the
contacts). A mercury thermostat that is cracked or no longer needed should be replaced; take the bulb for
proper disposal, never the trash.
causes.safety: A mercury bulb is a hazardous waste. Don't break it.

causes.name: Thermostat or sensor in a poor location — sun, supply air, a draft, a cold wall or a heat source
causes.confirm: The sensor reads its own spot correctly, but that spot runs warmer or colder than the space it is meant to control.
causes.fix:
Move the thermostat or sensor to an inside wall in the space it serves, about 5 ft up, out of sun and
supply air. Seal the wire hole behind it with foam or putty. In a walk-in, mount the probe in the box air,
away from the evaporator discharge and the door.

causes.name: Temperature sensor failed or drifted (10 kΩ NTC) — the control acts on a false reading
causes.confirm: The sensor's resistance, with a lead lifted, is off the chart at the temperature it sits in (or reads open or shorted).
causes.fix:
Replace the sensor with one of the same type and curve; the controller expects that curve. If it reads open
or shorted only at the controller end, the wire run is at fault: ohm the sensor at the sensor end too.

causes.name: Sensor good but the reading is off — wrong sensor type set, an offset, or long-wire resistance
causes.confirm: The sensor ohms correctly on its chart, yet the controller shows a different temperature.
causes.fix:
Check the input's sensor type (for example 10 kΩ Type II vs Type III, or a different resistance) and any
offset in the controller or thermostat setup. On a long sensor run, add the wire resistance to what you
measured. Correct the setup; don't use an offset to hide a wrong sensor type.

causes.name: Heat pump heats on a cooling call — thermostat O/B setting wrong for the valve
causes.confirm: The thermostat's O/B setting doesn't match the valve (by the diagram or a meter on the coil), and the unit heats on a cooling call.
causes.fix:
Set O/B to match the valve, then run cooling and heat and check the vapor line at the indoor unit in each
(cold in cooling, hot in heat).

causes.name: Reversing-valve coil voltage wrong in cooling — O wire open or not landed, or a B wire live
keywords: no 24 volts to the reversing valve
causes.confirm: The O/B setting is right, but the coil gets no 24 V on a cooling call (O valve) or 24 V when it shouldn't (B valve).
causes.fix:
Trace the O (or B) conductor from the thermostat to the outdoor unit: a broken wire, one not landed at the
outdoor board, or a B wire shorted to R. If 24 V reaches the coil and the valve still won't shift, ohm the
coil and check the valve itself.

causes.name: BAS point left in override or hand — the equipment ignores the schedule and the sequence
causes.confirm: The point shows an operator override or hand at a level above the program, and the equipment does exactly what that override says.
causes.fix:
Before you release anything, find out who set the override and why (the BAS log, shift notes, or ask the
plant operator). At McMurdo it may be holding a pump or valve on for freeze protection, or off for a
tagged-out job. If it is, fix that reason first. Then release the override at the level that holds it, or
put the hand-off-auto switch in auto, and watch the program take over. Hand mode can also be standing in
for a safety input someone bypassed.
causes.safety: An override can be the only thing keeping a loop from freezing. Check lockout tags and freeze risk before you release it.

causes.name: Occupancy schedule wrong — holiday or exception left in, wrong times, or a clock off by an hour
causes.confirm: The schedule (or an exception in it) puts the system unoccupied while people are in, or occupied while the building is empty, with the controller clock right.
causes.fix:
Correct the schedule and clear stale holidays and exceptions. Check the daylight-saving rule. Note the
building's real hours with the occupant, and set warm-up or cool-down to start early enough.

causes.name: Occupancy sensor or after-hours button faulted — space held occupied, or never sees anyone
causes.confirm: The occupancy input doesn't change when you walk in and out of its view or press the button.
causes.fix:
Clear what blocks the sensor's view, aim it away from hallways, or replace it. Check the input at the BAS
changes state, and that the off-delay is set as the design calls for.

causes.name: Controller lost its program or clock after a power event — default program or wrong time
causes.confirm: After the outage the controller shows a default program, a reset clock, or setpoints that don't match the saved database.
causes.fix:
Reload the program from the saved backup and set the clock (or let it sync from the network). Check the
controller's memory backup (battery or flash) so it survives the next outage, and make sure the backup on
file is current.

causes.name: Controller offline on the BAS network — runs its own default schedule
causes.confirm: The workstation shows the controller offline, or its values haven't updated, while the controller itself has power.
causes.fix:
Check the controller's power, then the network: a loose or broken trunk wire, a missing end-of-line
termination, an address clash after a board swap, or a router or switch that didn't restart after the
outage. While it's offline, it runs on its local default schedule, so compare that schedule with the
building's hours.

causes.name: BAS commands it on, but nothing leaves the controller output (dead output, blown output fuse)
keywords: bas says on but nothing runs
causes.confirm: The command point reads on, but no signal reads at the controller's output terminals.
causes.fix:
Check the output's fuse and its power or common supply on the controller. Replace a dead output, or move the
point to a spare output and update the program. Find what killed it: a shorted field device, or a load
larger than the output's rating, which needs its own relay between the output and the load.
causes.safety: Some outputs switch line voltage. Lock out the controller's supply before you change an output or its fuse.

causes.name: BAS signal leaves the controller but doesn't reach the device — broken wire or failed relay
keywords: bas says on but nothing runs
causes.confirm: The signal reads at the controller terminals but not at the device, or the relay in the run gets its coil signal and its contacts don't close.
causes.fix:
Trace the run between the controller and the device: terminal blocks, splices, any relay in the run.
Repair the wire or replace the relay, then command the point on and off and watch the device follow.

causes.name: Valve or damper actuator failed — the signal reaches it and it doesn't move
causes.confirm: The correct signal reads at the actuator's terminals, and the actuator doesn't stroke (or its feedback doesn't follow).
causes.fix:
Check the actuator's own power. Then, once you know what the valve or damper will do to the system when it
moves, try its manual override. If the actuator turns but the valve stem doesn't, the linkage or coupling
has slipped or the valve is stuck. Replace a dead actuator with one of the same signal, stroke and fail
position, and check the feedback span afterwards.
causes.safety: A spring-return actuator can move as soon as it is freed. Confirm what the valve or damper will do to the system before you free it, and keep clear of the linkage. Never hand-drive a burner's fuel valve or combustion-air damper; leave that to the maker's procedure.

causes.name: Reversing valve stuck in cooling on a heat call — 24 V is still on an O-type coil (O shorted to R, or a stuck relay at the thermostat or defrost board)
causes.confirm:
The unit runs in cooling on a heat call, the thermostat is set to match an O-type valve (energized in
cooling), and metering the coil leads on the heat call shows 24 V that should not be there.
causes.fix:
Find where the 24 V is coming from by working back from the coil: pull the O wire at the air handler and then
at the thermostat, and watch the voltage on the coil leads. Look for O shorted to R (a nicked or stapled
thermostat cable, a pinched wire at a splice), a thermostat or sub-base relay stuck on, or a stuck relay on
the outdoor defrost board holding 24 V on the coil. Repair or replace whatever holds the voltage on, then
confirm the valve moves to heating on the next heat call.

causes.name: Reversing valve stuck in cooling on a heat call — no 24 V reaching a B-type (heat-energized) coil (open B wire, thermostat or defrost-board relay)
causes.confirm:
The unit runs in cooling on a heat call, the thermostat is set to match a B-type valve (energized in
heating), and the coil leads read 0 V when the heat call needs them energized.
causes.fix:
Trace the B circuit from the thermostat through the air handler splice and the outdoor defrost board to the
solenoid leads, metering as you go. The voltage drops out at the open wire, loose terminal, thermostat output
or board relay that is at fault. Repair the break, then confirm the valve shifts to heating on the next heat
call.

causes.name: Reversing-valve solenoid coil open or burned out (a heat-energized valve, so it sits in cooling on a heat call)
causes.confirm:
24 V is present right at the reversing-valve solenoid leads on the heat call, but the coil reads open (∞ Ω)
or has no magnetic pull on a screwdriver tip.
causes.fix:
Lock out power, unclip or unscrew the retaining nut on the 4-way valve pilot solenoid, and slip on a
replacement coil of the same voltage matched to the valve body (no refrigerant recovery needed). Secure the
wires away from the hot discharge line so the insulation cannot melt.
causes.notes:
An open coil can only leave the valve in cooling on a heat call when the valve is energized in heating
(B-type). On an O-type valve the coil is off in heating anyway, so an open coil there shows up the other way
round, as heating when cooling is called.

causes.name: Reversing valve mechanically stuck (main slide jammed or pilot capillary plugged)
causes.confirm:
The coil gets the right voltage for the mode called and tests good (strong magnetic pull if it is a 24 V
coil), but switching the coil with the compressor running produces no whoosh and the valve slide never
shifts.
causes.fix:
Before condemning the valve, check the charge and the pressure difference across it: a valve will not shift
without enough charge and a pumping compressor. Then, with the compressor running, cycle the coil while rapping
the valve body gently with a rubber mallet (never dent the brass body with a steel hammer, or it will
permanently bind). If it still will not shift or sticks again, recover the charge, remove the solenoid coil and
shield the pilot tubes, wrap the new 4-way valve in wet rags while brazing with a nitrogen purge, replace the
filter-drier, evacuate to 500 microns, and weigh in the charge.
causes.safety: R-32 and R-454B are mildly flammable (A2L). Use an A2L-rated recovery machine and leak detector, keep open flame and hot tools away from any leak, ventilate, and evacuate or purge with nitrogen fully before brazing.

causes.name: Ductless unit blowing cool air on a heat call — 4-way valve coil not energized (no line voltage from the board relay or harness) or the coil is open
keywords: mini split blowing cold in heat
mini split cools in heat mode
wall unit cold air in heating
4 way valve not energized mini split
causes.confirm:
The head is on a heat call but blows cool air while the outdoor fan blows warm air. At the board's 4-way coil
connector (power on, call made) either the voltage the wiring diagram calls for is missing, or it is there and
the coil, checked with power off, reads open against the maker's figure.
causes.fix:
Read the maker's wiring diagram to see which mode energizes the coil. If the voltage is missing, check the
board relay output, the harness and connector (heat damage, corrosion, a loose pin), and any stored fault code
(look it up in the maker's manual) before replacing the outdoor board. If the voltage is there and the coil
reads open, replace the coil with the exact part for the valve (no refrigerant recovery needed) and keep its
leads clear of the hot discharge line.
causes.safety: The 4-way coil circuit is line voltage. Lock out and verify dead before unplugging or swapping the coil, and use a CAT III meter for the live check.

causes.name: Reversing valve stuck mid-position or leaking internally (hot discharge gas bypassing into suction)
keywords: hot gas bypass in 4 way valve
causes.confirm:
Touch-and-measure test on the 4-way valve body: the center tube leaving the valve toward the compressor is
more than 3–4 °F (often 8–20 °F) warmer than the evaporator return tube entering the valve, accompanied by
high suction pressure and low head pressure.
causes.fix:
First try cycling the solenoid several times under load to see if the slide seats fully. If the
suction-path temperature rise across the 4-way valve stays above 3–4 °F, the PTFE slide is scored
or warped (often from brazing too hot without wet rags or overheating on high discharge temp).
Recover the refrigerant, remove the solenoid coil and shield the pilot tubes, braze in a new reversing valve
with wet heat-sink wraps and a nitrogen sweep, replace the filter-drier, evacuate, and recharge by weight.
causes.safety: R-32 and R-454B are mildly flammable (A2L). Use an A2L-rated recovery machine and leak detector, keep open flame and hot tools away from any leak, ventilate, and evacuate or purge with nitrogen fully before brazing.
causes.notes:
NIST TN 1648 Table 5.3.1 shows internal 4-way/compressor leakage raises evaporator saturation
temperature, lowers superheat, and drops condensing temperature and indoor air temperature rise. The
leak also bleeds discharge gas into suction, so the pump-down test fails the same way it does for weak
compressor valves. The 4-way valve suction rise check is what separates a leaking reversing valve from
weak compressor valves.

causes.name: Thermostat reversing-valve (O/B) setting does not match the valve (set to O on a B valve, or to B on an O valve)
keywords: cools in heat and heats in cool
new thermostat blowing cold in heat
causes.confirm:
Calling for heat runs the unit in cooling (and calling for cool runs it in heating), right after a
thermostat replacement or reset, and the installer menu has the O/B setting opposite to what the valve coil
needs (confirmed from the wiring diagram or by metering the coil leads in both modes).
causes.fix:
Change the reversing-valve O/B setting in the thermostat's installer menu to match the valve: O if the coil is
energized in cooling, B if it is energized in heating. Confirm which one you have from the wiring diagram or
the meter, not from the brand name. Then verify the outdoor unit shifts into heating on a heat call.

causes.name: Defrost control board failed (timer IC or relay dead — never initiates defrost)
causes.confirm:
Outdoor coil is encased in ice, 24 V power (R and C) and Y are present on the defrost board, the
defrost sensor tests good (closed/in-range), and shorting the TEST pins still fails to start defrost.
causes.fix:
Inspect the defrost board for cracked solder joints or a burned outdoor-fan relay. Thaw the outdoor
coil carefully with warm water (never chip ice off fins with a screwdriver), replace the defrost
control board, set the timer jumper (30/60/90 min), and verify a forced test-pin defrost shifts the
4-way valve, stops the outdoor fan, and energizes W2.

causes.name: Defrost coil sensor, defrost thermostat or outdoor ambient sensor open / drifted warm (never detects a freezing coil)
causes.fix:
Replace the defrost snap-disc thermostat or NTC coil thermistor, clip it tightly to the designated
bottom liquid/distributor return bend where frost forms first, insulate the bulb from wind if specified,
and thaw the coil before returning the unit to service. On a demand-defrost board, test the outdoor ambient
sensor the same way and replace it if it has drifted, since the board compares coil to ambient.

causes.name: Defrost initiates, but reversing valve fails to shift (fan stops and W2 calls, outdoor coil stays cold)
keywords: fan stops in defrost but coil stays cold
reversing valve wont shift in defrost
causes.confirm:
When defrost triggers, the outdoor fan stops and W2 energizes, but the reversing valve never moves to the
cooling position that sends hot discharge gas into the outdoor coil.
causes.fix:
Check whether the defrost board's reversing-valve relay is actually switching the O/B terminal during
defrost. If the board switches 24 V properly, check the solenoid coil and wiring to the 4-way valve;
if the board's O/B relay contact is burned open or stuck, replace the defrost board. If the board and the
coil both check out, run the shift test: the valve itself may be mechanically stuck.

causes.name: Outdoor fan stays running during defrost (welded fan relay on defrost board or miswired fan)
causes.confirm:
During a defrost cycle, the reversing valve shifts to heat the outdoor coil, but the outdoor condenser
fan keeps spinning and blowing subfreezing air across the coil so the ice cannot finish melting.
causes.fix:
With the unit off, pull the fan lead from the defrost board's OF/FAN relay terminal and check if the
relay contacts on the board are welded closed (0 Ω between line in and fan out with no power). Replace
the defrost board if the relay is welded, or correct any field wiring where a tech landed the fan
motor directly on the contactor load side instead of through the defrost board.

causes.name: Defrost runs too long or never terminates until the 10-minute backup limit (sensor stuck closed or unclipped)
causes.confirm:
All ice melts off within a few minutes and the outdoor coil is steaming hot, yet the unit stays in
defrost with the fan off until the 10-minute backup timer expires or the high-pressure switch trips.
causes.fix:
Check if the defrost termination sensor fell off the tube and is hanging in cold air. If it is clipped
tight to the hot liquid tube (>70 °F) and still reads closed (snap-disc) or high-resistance cold
(thermistor), replace the termination sensor.

causes.name: Nuisance defrost cycles in cold dry weather (timer set too short or a sensor reading falsely cold)
causes.confirm: Unit enters defrost every 30 minutes even when the outdoor coil is completely bare and dry.
causes.fix:
On time-temperature defrost boards in dry climates (like polar/high-altitude stations), move the
timer pin from 30 minutes to 60 or 90 minutes. On a demand-defrost board or an inverter unit, check that the
coil thermistor has not drifted to a higher resistance, and that the outdoor ambient sensor has not drifted,
since either can fool the board into seeing a frost difference on a clean coil.

causes.name: Outdoor basepan drain plugged or basepan heater failed — solid ice shelf in bottom of unit
causes.confirm:
Upper coil rows clear during defrost, but meltwater cannot escape the bottom pan — forming a thick
glacier that engulfs the lower refrigerant passes and can split the bottom return bends or hit the
fan blade.
causes.fix:
With the unit off, melt the basepan ice completely with warm water (never a heat gun, and never pry against
the copper return bends, which may already be split). Clear leaves and mud from the drain slots, remove
rubber shipping plugs if left in on a mini-split, verify the unit sits level on risers above the snow line,
and test/replace the electric basepan heater and its thermostat on cold-climate units.

causes.name: Cold air blows from vents during defrost (W2 / defrost tempering wire open or disconnected)
causes.confirm:
The outdoor unit defrosts normally (shifts into cooling to melt outdoor frost), but the indoor air
handler never receives the 24 V W/W2 signal from the outdoor defrost board to energize tempering
strip heat, so 55 °F air blows into the rooms. Only a fault when the air handler has strips wired to the
defrost output.
causes.fix:
Connect and trace the W / W2 defrost tempering wire from the outdoor defrost board's W out terminal
to the indoor air handler's W1/W2 strip-heat terminal, and confirm the electric heat strips stage on
whenever a defrost cycle runs.

causes.name: Thermostat left on Emergency Heat, or the compressor lockout set above today's outdoor temperature (the strips are doing all the work)
keywords: heat pump not running strips on
causes.confirm:
The thermostat shows Emergency Heat, or its installer menu locks the compressor out below an outdoor
temperature that is higher than today's. The compressor is off, the strips draw their normal amps, the air is
lukewarm to hot at the supply, and the unit runs constantly.
causes.fix:
Take the thermostat out of Emergency Heat. If the compressor lockout is the cause, lower it to what the
equipment allows (the maker's minimum outdoor temperature for compressor operation) and check the aux-heat
lockout and stage delays in the same menu. Explain to the customer that Emergency Heat is for a failed heat
pump, because it runs the strips only and costs far more to run.

causes.name: Aux heat sequencer or relay failed open (24 V on control coil, load contacts never close)
causes.confirm:
24 V has been on the sequencer's low-voltage terminals for over 60 seconds, line voltage is present
and limits are closed, but the sequencer's high-voltage load contacts remain open (240 V across the
contacts, 0 A on the heater leads).
causes.fix:
Lock out power, label each wire by terminal (M1/M2, M3/M4, H1/H2), and replace the failed bimetal
heat sequencer or contactor with one of matching staging timing and contact rating. Verify all slip-on
spade terminals fit tightly so they do not overheat.

causes.name: Aux heat thermal high-limit switch open or one-shot fusible link blown
causes.confirm:
Heater circuit has 240 V and a 24 V call, but the snap-disc high-limit switch or ceramic fusible link
in series with the heater element reads open (∞ Ω with power off).
causes.fix:
Never bypass a thermal limit or fusible link. Before replacing an open limit or blown fuse link, find
why the heater rack overheated: check for a plugged filter, failed indoor blower, closed supply
registers, or a welded sequencer that ran the strips with the blower off. Replace with the exact
temperature-rated OEM limit assembly.
causes.safety: Never jumper a heater high-limit or fusible link — uncooled nichrome strips can ignite duct liner.

causes.name: Electric heating element coil burned open (broken nichrome wire)
causes.confirm:
Full 208/240 V is present directly across the heating element end terminals with the sequencer closed,
but that element bank draws 0 A and reads open (∞ Ω) with power locked out.
causes.fix:
Lock out power, slide the heater rack out of the air handler, inspect the ceramic stringers for a
broken or melted nichrome coil and check that no broken tail is touching the cabinet, and restring or
replace the heater element assembly. Check indoor airflow so the new element does not overheat.

causes.name: Outdoor aux-heat lockout thermostat or balance-point setting set too low (locks out strips in cold weather)
causes.confirm:
The building is losing ground in cold weather while the heat pump runs nonstop, the strips work fine
when jumped at the air handler, and the thermostat or outdoor ambient lockout is blocking W2.
causes.fix:
Raise the auxiliary-heat lockout / balance-point temperature in the thermostat's installer setup (e.g.
from 15 °F up to 35–40 °F), or adjust/replace a drifted outdoor ambient lockout thermostat so auxiliary
heat can assist below the building's true balance point.

causes.name: Air-handler strip-heat breaker or disconnect off / tripped (separate circuit from blower)
causes.confirm:
The indoor blower and 24 V controls have power (from Circuit 1), but the second 30–60 A breaker or
pull-out feeding the electric strip banks is switched off or tripped (0 V across heater L1–L2).
causes.fix:
With power off, ohm the heater banks and wiring to ground first to make sure a grounded element or
shorted wire did not trip the breaker. Then restore the heater breaker, command Emergency Heat / W2,
and verify balanced amp draw on all strip stages.

causes.name: Electric heat strip stuck ON continuously (welded sequencer/relay or element shorted to grounded frame)
causes.confirm:
Clamp meter shows current on the electric heater leads with the thermostat off or in cooling, caused
either by a sequencer contact welded shut (240 V, full amps) or a sagging nichrome coil touching the
grounded metal rack (120 V to ground on one leg, ~half amps even with the sequencer open).
causes.fix:
Lock out power immediately — an energized strip with the blower off will cycle on the high-limit until
the limit fails. Ohm each element terminal to the metal frame (to catch a grounded coil) and across
each sequencer contact with 24 V disconnected (to catch a welded contact). Replace the failed
sequencer or grounded element rack, and inspect the high-limit switch for heat fatigue.
causes.safety: Lock out all air-handler breakers before opening the heater compartment; a grounded strip stays hot on one leg even when the sequencer is open.

causes.name: Outdoor (heating) metering device stuck closed or restricted — starves in heating, cools normally
causes.confirm:
In heating mode suction pressure dives and outdoor-coil superheat is very high, but when the outdoor air is
warm enough to run it, switching the unit into cooling brings pressures, superheat, and subcooling right
back to normal. Liquid backs up behind the starved device, so subcooling runs high, which is what separates
it from an undercharge.
causes.fix:
Inspect the outdoor heating TXV sensing bulb (must be tight and insulated on the outdoor suction
header) and warm the bulb to see if the valve opens. If the power head is dead, the inlet screen is
plugged, or the outdoor heating piston is clogged, recover the charge, clean or replace the outdoor
metering assembly and bi-flow filter-drier, evacuate to 500 microns, and weigh in the charge.
causes.safety: R-32 and R-454B are mildly flammable (A2L). Use an A2L-rated recovery machine and leak detector, keep open flame and hot tools away from any leak, ventilate, and evacuate or purge with nitrogen fully before brazing.

causes.name: Indoor bypass check valve stuck closed in heating (forces the condensed liquid through the indoor metering device)
keywords: temperature drop across indoor metering device
frost on indoor metering device in heat
causes.confirm:
Unit cools fine, but in heating suction is low and superheat is high. Head pressure reads normal to low at the
liquid port, because that port sits downstream of the stuck valve, and the high-pressure switch does not trip.
There is a sharp temperature drop (or frost) across the indoor metering assembly where the bypass check valve
is failing to open.
causes.fix:
Lightly tap the brass check-valve body while switching between cooling and heating to see if a stuck
PTFE ball or flapper frees up. If it stays restricted in heating, recover the charge, replace the
indoor check-valve / piston housing (or bi-flow TXV), install a new bi-flow filter-drier, evacuate,
and recharge by weight.
causes.safety: R-32 and R-454B are mildly flammable (A2L). Use an A2L-rated recovery machine and leak detector, keep open flame and hot tools away from any leak, ventilate, and evacuate or purge with nitrogen fully before brazing.
causes.notes:
A liquid-line restriction leaves condensing temperature about where it was and drops subcooling (NIST TN 1648
Table 5.4.1), so this fault is easy to miss on the head reading. Do not expect a high head or a high-pressure
trip from it.

causes.name: Outdoor check valve leaking through in heating (bypasses outdoor metering device and floods compressor)
causes.confirm:
In heating mode, superheat at the compressor drops near zero with a sweating/frosted accumulator and
high suction pressure because liquid is bypassing around the outdoor TXV/orifice through a failed
outdoor check valve.
causes.fix:
Do not leave the unit running with liquid floodback. Recover the refrigerant, replace the leaking
outdoor check valve (using wet heat-sink rags so the new seat is not heat-damaged during brazing) and
the bi-flow filter-drier, evacuate to 500 microns, and weigh in the charge.
causes.safety: R-32 and R-454B are mildly flammable (A2L). Use an A2L-rated recovery machine and leak detector, keep open flame and hot tools away from any leak, ventilate, and evacuate or purge with nitrogen fully before brazing.
