causes.name: Low indoor airflow in heating — dirty filter, closed or crushed ducts, or a dirty indoor coil (the indoor coil is the condenser)
causes.confirm:
With the indoor coil acting as the condenser, a loaded filter, closed or crushed ducts, or a matted indoor
coil show up as high external static, weak air at the registers and an air rise above the normal band
(over about 38 °F ducted), with head pressure climbing toward the high-pressure cutout. A mild restriction
moves the numbers only a little, so rest the call on what you can see: the filter, the static reading, the
registers and the coil face.
causes.fix:
Check the indoor air filter first, then inspect supply registers, return dampers, the indoor coil face
(and secondary heat exchanger if dual-fuel), and indoor blower speed/capacitor. Restore full indoor
CFM (~400 CFM per ton) before resetting the high-pressure switch.
causes.notes:
NIST TN 1648 Table 5.1.1: reducing indoor (condenser) airflow in heating mode strongly raises
indoor air temperature rise (+32% at the largest fault, about 30% less air), condensing saturation
temperature (about +5 °F) and discharge temperature (+4%) while barely changing evaporator saturation
temperature. Those are small moves, so the head and rise often still read normal until the restriction is
severe.

causes.name: Indoor blower not running or running slow in heating (motor, run capacitor, relay or control board) — the indoor coil overheats and the head climbs
keywords: indoor blower not running heat pump
no air from vents heat pump
air handler fan not coming on
causes.confirm:
The compressor and outdoor fan run on the heat call but the indoor blower is not turning, or turns slowly and
moves little air, while the head climbs and the high-pressure switch trips. With a clean filter and low
static, the airflow problem is the blower, not the ducts.
causes.fix:
Voltage at the motor decides it: present means the motor or its run capacitor, absent means the blower relay,
the control board or the fan-delay logic. With voltage at the motor, test the capacitor, spin the shaft for
seized bearings, and ohm the windings and thermal protector. On an ECM motor check the control signal and the
motor's own plug before condemning it. With no voltage, check the fan relay, the board output and the
thermostat G call. Do not leave the compressor running with no indoor airflow, because it will trip on high
pressure.
causes.safety: Keep the heat strips off until the blower runs. A strip with no airflow overheats the heater rack and can open the limit or the fusible link.

causes.name: Outdoor coil (heating evaporator) blocked by snow drift, freezing-rain glaze, leaves, a cover, or a matted, dirty coil face
causes.confirm:
The outdoor coil is starved of air by drifted snow, an ice shell from freezing rain, leaves, a cover, or a
mat of dirt and cottonwood on the coil face, pulling evaporator saturation temperature way down and dropping
indoor condensing pressure and supply air rise.
causes.fix:
Shovel snow clear with at least 24 in. of breathing room around all sides of the outdoor unit, melt
any freezing-rain shell with warm water, remove debris or covers, and install a snow hood / wind
baffle or higher snow stand if drifts regularly bury the coil. If the coil face is matted, power off and
clean it from the inside out with coil cleaner and low-pressure water, then comb the fins.
causes.notes:
NIST TN 1648 Table 5.2.1: outdoor (evaporator) airflow blockage in heating mode produces the largest
capacity loss (−24%) of any single fault, with a steep drop in evaporator saturation temperature and
condensing temperature, and rising superheat and discharge temperature.

causes.name: Outdoor fan not running or running slow in heating (motor, run capacitor, defrost-board fan relay, DC fan driver, or ice locking the blade)
keywords: outdoor fan motor bad in heating
causes.confirm:
Compressor is running in normal heating (not in a defrost cycle), the outdoor fan blade is still or turning
slowly, and suction pressure and outdoor coil temperature plummet instead of rising as they would in cooling
mode.
causes.fix:
Check whether 208/240 V is leaving the defrost board's outdoor-fan relay (OF/FAN) to the motor. If
voltage reaches the motor, test the fan run capacitor, check whether ice in the shroud is locking the
blade, and ohm the motor windings. If voltage stops at the defrost board while not in defrost, the
board's NC fan relay contact has burned open — replace the defrost board. On a ductless or inverter unit
the outdoor fan is usually a DC motor driven from the board: there is no capacitor to test, so check the
board's fan output, the motor connector and the motor against the maker's data.

causes.name: Outdoor ambient below the heat pump's thermal balance point (pressures normal for deep cold — needs aux heat)
keywords: too cold outside for heat pump
causes.confirm:
Outdoor coil is clean and clear of ice, suction grades normal for the outdoor air (the coil runs only about
3–18 °F below it), superheat and subcooling are on target, and the compressor is running flat out below the
building's balance point.
causes.fix:
Do not add refrigerant to try to raise suction pressure in cold weather — that will seriously
overcharge the system when weather warms up. Verify that auxiliary electric strip heat or backup
hydronic/furnace heat is enabled and staging on to supplement the heat pump below its balance point.

causes.name: Mini-split indoor–outdoor communication error (open/spliced signal wire, miswiring, or dead outdoor board supply)
causes.confirm:
Indoor head displays a communication fault code (look it up in the maker's table) or a blinking indicator LED,
and metering the serial link terminal (labeled S, S2–S3, 2–3 or similar) to the common shows steady 0 V, a
stuck DC voltage, or a dead outdoor board instead of the normal unsteady, sweeping DC signal.
causes.fix:
1. Verify 208/240 V line power at the outdoor terminals L1–L2 and check that the indoor-to-outdoor
   interconnect cable lands terminal-for-terminal (1 to 1, 2 to 2, 3/S to 3/S — never crossed).
2. Inspect the interconnect run for wire-nut splices (most manufacturers forbid splices on the serial
   link), nicked insulation, or high-voltage induction; pull a continuous cable of the gauge and
   conductor count the install manual calls for if it is spliced.
3. Disconnect the signal wire at the outdoor board and measure the board's open-circuit DC output: if
   the outdoor board has line power and good fuses/thermistor/rectifier but outputs 0 V DC with no
   status LEDs, replace the outdoor main board.
causes.safety: Inverter outdoor board: breaker off, wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes), then confirm under 10 V DC across P(+) and N(−) with a CAT III 600 V meter before unplugging any harness (compressor U/V/W, EEV, thermistor, serial) or touching the board. Unplug the compressor leads from the board before any megger test. A live DC bus reads roughly 300–400 V DC: insulated probes, one hand, and never while unplugging.

causes.name: Inverter compressor drive / IPM fault (shorted IGBT module, failed DC bus capacitor or reactor)
causes.confirm:
Compressor windings U–V–W test balanced and clean to ground, but the unit faults out on a drive or IPM code
(as the maker's table defines it) and the diode test across P(+)/N(−) to U, V, W on the outdoor inverter
board shows a shorted or open leg. A DC bus well below the maker's normal figure supports it, but that is a
live 300–400 V DC measurement, so see the safety note before taking it.
causes.fix:
Lock out power and wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes) for the DC bus capacitors to
discharge, then verify under 10 V DC before touching the board. Always test the compressor windings (U–V–W
balance and megger to ground, with the leads off the board) before installing a new inverter PCB so a shorted
compressor does not immediately blow the replacement IPM. Apply fresh thermal paste uniformly under the IPM
heat sink and torque the mounting screws evenly.
causes.safety: Inverter outdoor board: breaker off, wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes), then confirm under 10 V DC across P(+) and N(−) with a CAT III 600 V meter before unplugging any harness (compressor U/V/W, EEV, thermistor, serial) or touching the board. Unplug the compressor leads from the board before any megger test. A live DC bus reads roughly 300–400 V DC: insulated probes, one hand, and never while unplugging.

causes.name: Inverter BLDC compressor winding fault or seized/demagnetized rotor
causes.confirm:
With the U, V, W harness unplugged from the inverter board, phase-to-phase resistances (U–V, V–W,
U–W) are unequal, open, or read to ground — or, with all three phases equal and clean to ground, the
compressor sputters and stalls (seized or demagnetized rotor, high start current) on a board whose IPM
and DC bus test good.
causes.fix:
Replace the inverter compressor (and inspect/diode-check the IPM board at the same time, as a grounded
winding often takes out an IGBT leg). Flush or clean the circuit if the oil is dark or acidic, install
a new filter-drier, evacuate to below 500 microns, and weigh in the exact factory charge.
causes.safety: Inverter outdoor board: breaker off, wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes), then confirm under 10 V DC across P(+) and N(−) with a CAT III 600 V meter before unplugging any harness (compressor U/V/W, EEV, thermistor, serial) or touching the board. Unplug the compressor leads from the board before any megger test. A live DC bus reads roughly 300–400 V DC: insulated probes, one hand, and never while unplugging.

causes.name: Mini-split EEV stepper coil open, shorted or unplugged
causes.confirm:
EEV makes no initialization clicking sound when breaker power is cycled, and ohming the 5- or 6-pin
EEV stepper plug shows an open or shorted winding pair.
causes.fix:
With the board made safe first (see the safety note), unclip the failed stepper motor head from the brass EEV
body (no refrigerant recovery is required to swap the external coil), plug the new stepper coil into the
board, secure its locking clip so it seats squarely on the spindle, and cycle power to hear the
initialization step sequence.
causes.safety: Inverter outdoor board: breaker off, wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes), then confirm under 10 V DC across P(+) and N(−) with a CAT III 600 V meter before unplugging any harness (compressor U/V/W, EEV, thermistor, serial) or touching the board. Unplug the compressor leads from the board before any megger test. A live DC bus reads roughly 300–400 V DC: insulated probes, one hand, and never while unplugging.

causes.name: Mini-split EEV valve body mechanically stuck (needle seized closed or open)
causes.confirm:
All four stepper coil windings ohm balanced and the coil clicks at power-up, but the valve needle does
not open or close (starving with frost at the outdoor EEV outlet, or flooding right through).
causes.fix:
With the board made safe first (see the safety note), remove the stepper coil and rotate a cylindrical EEV
service magnet around the brass spindle while gently tapping the valve body to free grit or copper oxide on
the needle threads. If it frees up, reinstall the coil and power-cycle to home it. If the internal rotor
remains seized, recover the charge, take the stepper coil off so the heat cannot reach it, braze in a new
EEV body wrapped in wet heat-sink rags with a nitrogen purge, evacuate deeply, and weigh in the factory
charge.
causes.safety: Inverter outdoor board: breaker off, wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes), then confirm under 10 V DC across P(+) and N(−) with a CAT III 600 V meter before unplugging any harness (compressor U/V/W, EEV, thermistor, serial) or touching the board. R-32 and R-454B are mildly flammable (A2L): use an A2L-rated recovery machine and leak detector, keep open flame and hot tools away from any leak, ventilate, and evacuate or purge with nitrogen fully before brazing.

causes.name: NTC thermistor drifted out of curve, or loose off its coil (coil, discharge, ambient or room sensor reporting a false temperature)
causes.confirm:
Unplugging the thermistor and comparing its kΩ resistance against a calibrated thermometer (or a 32 °F
ice-water bath) shows it is off the manufacturer's resistance-vs-temperature curve, or it reads right at the
bulb but the bulb is loose or out of its well and not touching the coil it should read, causing the inverter to
throttle down compressor Hz, lock out prematurely, or defrost wrongly (never, or all the time).
causes.fix:
With the board made safe first (see the safety note), replace the drifted NTC thermistor (confirm
whether the position uses a 5 kΩ, 10 kΩ, 15 kΩ, 50 kΩ, or 200 kΩ @ 25 °C curve — discharge sensors use a much
higher resistance rating than coil/air sensors), seat it all the way into its copper well with thermal grease,
and clip it tight. If the sensor tests good, re-seat it on the exact coil spot and clip the maker's way.
causes.safety: Inverter outdoor board: breaker off, wait the maker's stated time (never less than 5 minutes), then confirm under 10 V DC across P(+) and N(−) with a CAT III 600 V meter before unplugging any harness (compressor U/V/W, EEV, thermistor, serial) or touching the board. Unplug the compressor leads from the board before any megger test. A live DC bus reads roughly 300–400 V DC: insulated probes, one hand, and never while unplugging.

causes.name: Mini-split flare-joint refrigerant leak (cracked flare, wrong torque, or thermal expansion)
causes.confirm:
Oil residue, soap bubbles, or an electronic leak-detector alarm at the indoor whip union or outdoor
service-valve flare nuts, often accompanied by frost on the small two-phase liquid line and weak
output. Subcooling has collapsed, which is the tell that separates a shortage from a restriction.
causes.fix:
Recover any remaining refrigerant, undo the leaking flare union, cut back the old flare, slide the
forged 45° mini-split flare nut on first, ream lightly, form a fresh concentric flare with an orbital
flaring block, apply a tiny drop of the refrigerant oil the maker calls for (or Nylog) to the flare face, and tighten
with a torque wrench to the maker's spec (typically 1/4 in.: 11–14 ft-lb; 3/8 in.: 25–30 ft-lb; 1/2 in.:
36–45 ft-lb; 5/8 in.: 45–55 ft-lb). Pressure-test with dry nitrogen to the unit's nameplate design test
pressure, never above it (older R-22 ductless units are lower), pull a deep vacuum below 500 microns, and weigh
in the nameplate charge plus or minus the manual's ounces per foot for the actual line-set length
(mini-splits have no liquid-line sight glass and expand inside the outdoor unit, so always charge by weight).
causes.safety: R-32 and R-454B are mildly flammable (A2L). Use an A2L-rated recovery machine and leak detector, keep open flame and hot tools away from any leak, ventilate, and evacuate or purge with nitrogen fully before brazing.

causes.name: Mini-split indoor cross-flow blower wheel packed with biofilm and lint (barely any air throw, surging noise)
causes.confirm:
Looking into the discharge louver with a flashlight shows the curved tangential blades of the
cylindrical blower wheel filled with dark biofilm/lint; even a 1/16 in. coating spoils the aerodynamic
scoop of a cross-flow wheel so air barely leaves the head and surges rhythmically.
causes.fix:
Lock out power, remove the plastic cabinet shroud and louvers, bag the indoor head with a mini-split
wash bib (protecting the right-side control board and louver stepper motors from water), or pull the
blower wheel out by loosening the left bearing cup and right motor set-screw. Wash the wheel blades
and coil clean with low-pressure water and coil cleaner, dry thoroughly, and reassemble.

causes.name: Mini-split condensate pump or pan float switch failed (overflow lockout or water dripping down wall)
causes.confirm:
Indoor pan is full of water or the head shuts off on a drain-float error; the mini-pump reservoir
float is stuck with slime, the diaphragm pump buzzes without pumping, or the safety switch is open.
causes.fix:
Flush the indoor drain pan and clear biofilm from the small float reservoir and reed magnet. Check
that the discharge vinyl tubing is not kinked or siphoning back without a vent. Replace a noisy or
burned-out mini-pump, and pour water into the pan to verify both pump cut-in and high-water cutoff.

causes.name: Multi-zone branch box or outdoor port wiring crossed (pipes go to head A, control wires go to head B)
causes.confirm:
Calling for cooling or heating on Indoor Head A opens the EEV for Port A at the outdoor unit / branch
box, which is piped to Indoor Head B — so Head B's coil floods (freezing solid in cooling or baking in
heating with its fan off) while Head A blows room-temperature air and never satisfies.
causes.fix:
Run one zone at a time (or use the outdoor unit's wiring/piping check mode if equipped) to map which
control cable (A, B, C, D) matches which pair of liquid and gas flares. Move the control cables at the
outdoor unit or branch box so every port's electrical plug matches its refrigerant lines.
causes.notes:
Rule out the normal one-mode-at-a-time behavior of a non-heat-recovery multi-zone unit first (see the
mode-conflict cause): a head waiting in standby while another head runs the opposite mode is not crossed.

causes.name: Multi-zone heads asking for opposite modes (normal behavior, not a fault — the outdoor unit serves one mode at a time and the second head waits)
keywords: one head heating one head cooling
causes.confirm:
One head is running in the mode it was first called for while another head, set to the opposite mode, sits in
standby (often blinking) and delivers nothing. Nothing is broken: the outdoor unit can serve only one mode at a
time.
causes.fix:
Nothing needs repair. Set all the heads to the same mode, or let the first mode finish before the other head
takes its turn, and explain this to the customer. If they need heating in one room and cooling in another at
the same time, that takes equipment that can run both modes at once (a heat-recovery type, per the maker's
literature), which is an equipment choice.

causes.name: Circulator motor failed (open, shorted, or grounded winding)
causes.confirm:
Full line voltage is present at the motor leads on a call for heat, but the motor stays dead or trips
the breaker, and ohm/megger checks show an open, shorted, or grounded winding.
causes.fix:
Lock out power. On a wet-rotor circulator, replace the motor head / cartridge assembly (or complete pump
if isolation flanges are fitted). On a 3-piece or base-mounted pump, replace the motor on the resilient
cradle and align the coupling. Check for water leaking from the shaft seal into the motor before
energizing the replacement.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag out power before opening the motor junction box.

causes.name: Circulator run capacitor failed
causes.confirm:
The wet-rotor circulator hums and gets hot without moving water, the rotor turns freely with a
screwdriver, and the capacitor inside the terminal box reads below rating or open.
causes.fix:
Lock out power, discharge the capacitor, and replace it with one of the exact same µF rating and equal
or higher voltage rating (typically 4–10 µF, 370/440 VAC on small wet-rotor pumps). Verify amp draw and
flow once restarted.
causes.safety: Lock out power and discharge the capacitor before touching its terminals.

causes.name: Switching relay, zone board, or pump contactor not sending voltage to circulator
causes.confirm:
The thermostat or zone end switch is calling the relay board, line voltage is present on the board's
supply terminals, but no line voltage leaves the pump relay contacts to the circulator.
causes.fix:
Check the plug-in ice-cube relay, soldered board relay (look for cracked solder joints on the back of
the PCB), or pump contactor contacts. On a socketed relay panel, swap the suspect ice-cube relay with a
known good zone slot to verify, then replace the relay or control board.
causes.safety: Line voltage and 24 V share the same switching relay enclosure — lock out before removing the board.

causes.name: Circulator rotor or bearing assembly seized
causes.confirm:
The pump motor hums and runs hot with a good capacitor, and the wet-rotor shaft (behind the center bleed
plug) or 3-piece bearing shaft cannot be turned by hand.
causes.fix:
Lock out power. On a wet-rotor pump, close both pump isolation flanges (with no flanges, drain the loop
down below the pump), let the pump cool below about 120 °F and relieve it to 0 psig at its drain before
the center vent screw comes out, and catch the fluid. Then try freeing the rotor shaft with a flathead
screwdriver; if it grinds or re-seizes from magnetite/sludge, replace the replaceable cartridge and
clean the dirt separator. On a 3-piece pump, replace the seized bearing assembly, oil the wicks per the
nameplate with SAE 20 non-detergent oil, and install a new coupler.
causes.safety: A pump on a live hot loop sprays when its vent plug comes out. Isolate, cool and relieve first; eye and hand protection is the last line, not the control. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: Circulator coupling sheared or broken
causes.confirm:
The motor runs quietly at low (unloaded) amps, but looking through the bracket window shows the flexible
coupler broken and the pump shaft stationary, with zero differential pressure across the pump.
causes.fix:
Lock out power. Before installing a new coupler, spin the pump shaft by hand to make sure a seized
bearing assembly didn't snap the old coupler, and check the rubber motor-mount grommets (sagged motor
mounts misalign the shafts and eat couplers). Replace the coupler and any sagged motor mounts.
causes.safety: Keep hands and tools clear of the bracket window until the motor is locked out.

causes.name: Circulator impeller broken, stripped, or loose on shaft
causes.confirm:
The motor and pump shaft both spin, the volute is bled full of liquid (no air), isolation valves are
open, yet differential pressure across the pump is near zero and motor amps are unloaded.
causes.fix:
Isolate the pump, drain the volute, and pull the cartridge or bearing/impeller assembly. Replace the
cartridge or impeller, retrieve any broken plastic vanes trapped in the volute throat or downstream
check valve, and verify full differential head on restart.
causes.safety: Isolate the pump, let it cool below about 120 °F and relieve it to 0 psig before draining the volute or pulling the cartridge. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: Circulator running backwards (wrong motor rotation after pump or motor work)
causes.confirm:
A three-phase pump or motor was just replaced or rewired. The pump runs smoothly but moves little: its
differential head is well under the curve with no air at the bleed, and the shaft turns against the arrow
on the pump casing.
causes.fix:
Lock out power and reverse the motor per the motor maker's instructions (on a three-phase motor, swap any
two of the three leads at the starter or disconnect). Bump-start it and check that the shaft or motor fan
turns the way the arrow on the casing points (on a pump with an exposed shaft, a rubber-tipped pencil
touched to the shaft shows the direction), then recheck the differential pressure against the pump curve
and the loop ΔT.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag out power before changing leads, and keep hands clear of the coupling and fan while checking rotation.

causes.name: Circulator volute air-locked (air pocket in pump)
causes.confirm:
A centrifugal circulator cannot pump air: the pump runs quietly or with a swishing/rattling sound (a
wet-rotor pump often sounds normal), builds near-zero head, the pipe is hot right up to the pump and cold
2 feet past it, and cracking the bleed screw or flange vents trapped air.
causes.fix:
Shut the circulator off (a running pump churns the air bubble in the eye of the impeller), purge the
loop or crack the pump's bleed plug slowly, with a hose to a container and your face turned away, until
a solid stream of water/glycol comes out. Verify system fill pressure is at target, and restart the pump.
causes.safety: Hot fluid at the bleed port: crack it slowly with a hose to a container, face away. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: Isolation or service valve left closed (or gate dropped off stem)
causes.confirm:
A closed main or pump-side valve deadheads the pump (high differential pressure, low amps, warm pump
housing); a closed branch valve leaves pump head near normal and kills just that branch. Either way,
inspection finds a closed ball/butterfly handle or a gate valve whose stem turns without lifting the gate.
causes.fix:
Slowly open the closed isolation valve while watching system pressure and temperature (avoid slugging a
hot boiler with a sudden rush of cold water). If a gate valve disc has separated from its stem, isolate
the section and replace the valve with a full-port ball or butterfly valve.
causes.safety: Open isolation valves slowly to prevent thermal shock to hot cast-iron boiler sections.

causes.name: Y-strainer or dirt separator plugged with scale or debris
causes.confirm:
Loop ΔT is wide (supply hot, return cool), pump differential head is elevated against the restriction,
and blowing down or pulling the Y-strainer basket reveals heavy scale, rust flakes, or construction
debris.
causes.fix:
Isolate the strainer, relieve pressure, pull the screen, and scrub it clean (replace if the mesh is
torn or collapsed). Blow down the dirt/magnetic separator, check glycol condition and pH if sludge is
present, and verify loop ΔT returns to design.
causes.safety: Relieve pressure and let hot water/glycol cool before backing out the strainer plug. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: Air trapped in hydronic zones or coils (air-bound branch)
causes.confirm:
Gurgling or rushing water sounds in the pipes, radiators cold at the top or a zone loop cold past a high
point, and opening the coin vent or purge station releases trapped air.
causes.fix:
Hold loop pressure at the cold-fill target while purging. Isolate the zone from the rest of the system
(close the valve between the zone and the other loops), open its drain or hose bib to a container, and
run make-up through until the discharge is bubble-free; hot fluid scalds. On glycol loops, purge using a glycol transfer pump drawing from and returning to a clean glycol
bucket so you don't dilute the loop with raw water or dump glycol down a drain.

Then find out why the air got in. Air that keeps coming back is a symptom: check the fill pressure against
the highest point's static head + 4–5 psig, which way the pump pushes relative to the expansion tank
connection, whether an air separator sits on the supply at the hottest point ahead of the pump, and
weeping vents or seals drawing air in (see "Air keeps returning").
causes.safety: Purge discharge can be hot: open drains slowly, with a hose to a container. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: Air keeps returning (fill pressure too low, pump pushing toward the tank, no separator at the hottest point, or weeping vents and seals drawing air in)
causes.confirm:
The loop was purged clean and the air is back within days or weeks, with no recent opening of the system.
Compare the cold fill pressure with the highest point's static head + 4–5 psig, find out which way the
pump pushes relative to the expansion tank connection, and look for weeping vents, seals or fittings that
draw air in as the loop cools.
causes.fix:
Raise the cold fill above the highest point's static head + 4–5 psig; set the pump to pump away from the
expansion tank connection; put an air separator on the supply at the hottest point ahead of the pump (keep
a manual vent beside any automatic one); and repair weeping vents, seals and fittings. Then purge once
and watch whether the air stays gone.
causes.safety: Purge discharge can be hot: open drains slowly, with a hose to a container. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: Automatic air vent (hyvent) or air separator failed (cap closed, float stuck, or leaking)
causes.confirm:
Inspection at the air scoop/microbubble separator or high-point vent shows the tire-style cap screwed
down tight, a float gummed shut that won't hiss when depressed, or water/glycol dribbling from the vent
cap.
causes.fix:
If the cap was screwed tight on a working vent, back it off one full turn so air can escape. If the
internal float is fouled with sludge or spitting liquid, close the isolation check fitting (or isolate
the header), thread in a new automatic air vent, and leave a manual coin vent or ball valve ahead of
high-point vents on glycol systems so a weeping vent can be isolated.
causes.safety: Never unscrew a vent from a hot, pressurized line: close the valve under it first, let it cool and relieve it. Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Low system pressure — make-up fill valve (PRV) closed, plugged, or glycol feeder empty
causes.confirm:
Hydronic gauge reads well below the cold-fill target (under 8 psig is low on any loop), high points draw
in air or fail to circulate, and the make-up valve is valved off, has a plugged inlet strainer, or the
glycol make-up feeder tank is empty.
causes.fix:
On a glycol loop, refill the pressurized glycol feeder tank with premixed inhibited glycol at the target
concentration (never top off an Antarctic/cold-region glycol loop with raw domestic water, or you dilute
freeze protection, and never hard-pipe a glycol loop to domestic make-up). On a water loop, clean the PRV
inlet screen, verify the fast-fill lever brings pressure up to the cold-fill target, or replace a
stuck-closed PRV, then bleed air from the high points.
causes.safety: Never feed cold make-up liquid rapidly into a hot cast-iron boiler; let it cool below 140 °F first. Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Hydronic piping, fitting, or coil leak dropping system pressure
causes.confirm:
System pressure drops steadily when the make-up valve is shut off, and visual inspection finds water or
dyed glycol dripping from a union, soldered joint, radiant manifold, or terminal coil (not the relief
valve or pump seal).
causes.fix:
Isolate the leaking branch or zone so the rest of the building keeps heating, repair the pipe/fitting or
brazed coil joint, pressure-test the repair, recharge with matching water or premixed glycol to design
fill pressure, and purge trapped air.
causes.safety: Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Pressure keeps falling with no visible leak (hidden leak, plate exchanger crossover, unseen weeping vent, or low expansion tank precharge sagging cold)
causes.confirm:
The gauge keeps sagging and the feeder level or make-up meter keeps dropping (watch it over 24 hours with
the loop held at a steady temperature), yet nothing is wet. Pressure that sags only when the loop is cold
points at a low expansion tank precharge instead.
causes.fix:
Work it by sections: isolate branches and mains one at a time and see which section holds pressure. Look
at buried and insulated runs, the plate exchanger for crossover (see "Plate heat exchanger crossover or
gasket leak"), weeping auto-vents and relief valve seats, and check the expansion tank precharge cold.
Repair, pressure-test, and refill with matching water or premixed glycol.
causes.safety: Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Expansion tank waterlogged or ruptured (bladder failed, tank full of water, or air precharge lost)
causes.confirm:
Read hot, system pressure climbs well past its cold value (more than about 10 psig) and lifts the relief
valve as the loop heats up. Read cold, the pressure can look normal and the relief dry, so go to the tank
itself: a plain steel tank taps dead and solid, and on a bladder tank pressing the Schrader releases water
(ruptured) or shows no air pressure (flat precharge).
causes.fix:
Valve the tank off, cool the loop, and drain the tank's water side to 0 psig before you touch the
Schrader valve.

If the Schrader spits water, the bladder or diaphragm is ruptured: replace the tank, and set the new
tank's air side to the cold-fill pressure BEFORE connecting it to the wet system.

If the Schrader is dry and only the precharge is low (bladder intact), do not replace the tank. With the
water side at 0 psig, set the precharge equal to the cold-fill pressure and reopen the valve. Never add
air to a tank that still has system pressure on the water side; the gauge then just reads system
pressure.

On a plain steel compression tank (overhead), drain the waterlogged tank and restore its ~1/2 air cushion.
Also test the relief valve after repeated pops in case scale lodged on its seat.
causes.safety: Cool and depressurize before swapping the tank; hot fluid sprays from a ruptured tank or an opened connection. Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Expansion tank cut off (valve closed, connection frozen or plugged) or too small for the fluid and temperature span
causes.confirm:
Pressure rises more than about 10 psig from cold to hot and the relief lifts. The tank valve is shut, or
the tank connection pipe is cold when the loop is hot; or the connection is open and the air side tests
fine, but the tank is too small for the fluid and temperature span.
causes.fix:
Open the tank valve (and lock or tag it open), or clear the connection, and set the precharge to the
cold-fill pressure. If the connection is frozen, treat it like any frozen pipe (see "Frozen or burst
hydronic coil or branch pipe") before thawing.

If the connection is open and the tank is fine, work out the tank's acceptance volume again for the
coldest fill temperature and the glycol percent.
causes.safety: A loop with its expansion tank cut off can lift the relief valve on every heat-up. Shut the heat source off before working on the connection, and cool and depressurize before opening it. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.
causes.notes: A glycol loop that swings from about -40 to +180 °F expands roughly twice as much as a 60-180 °F water loop (on the order of 7 % against 3 %), so a tank sized for water is too small here.

causes.name: Make-up / pressure-reducing fill valve (PRV) passing or set too high
causes.confirm:
System pressure creeps up toward the relief setting and weeps the relief valve even with the loop cool,
the expansion tank air cushion tests good, and closing the manual shutoff valve ahead of the PRV stops
the pressure rise.
causes.fix:
Flush or clean the PRV seat and strainer (scale under the rubber disc lets street water creep through),
or replace the pressure-reducing fill valve and adjust its cold fill pressure to match the expansion
tank precharge and the building's static height.

A glycol loop must not be hard-piped to potable make-up. Remove the tie-in or install an RPZ backflow
preventer with an air gap, and use a dedicated glycol feeder. If glycol may have reached potable lines,
isolate and notify water quality per station procedure.
causes.safety: A single check valve cannot stop ethylene glycol (poisonous) backing into potable water when loop pressure rises above supply pressure. Treat any glycol-to-potable tie-in as a cross-connection.

causes.name: Pressure relief valve weak or debris on seat (weeping at normal pressure)
causes.confirm:
The relief valve drips or weeps while a verified pressure gauge shows loop pressure steady near the
cold-fill target, cold and hot and well under the valve's set pressure, and the expansion tank air
cushion is intact.
causes.fix:
With system pressure confirmed normal, check that the discharge pipe is open and ends within 6 in. of a
drain or catch drum, then briefly lift the relief test lever to flush any grit off the seat (hot water or
glycol will come out). If it continues to weep, shut the heat source off, let the loop cool below about
120 °F and drain below the valve, then replace the relief valve with an ASME-rated hot-water relief valve
of the same set pressure (stamped on the old valve) and equal or greater BTU/hr capacity. Never put a
shutoff between the heat source and the relief valve.
causes.safety: Never plug, cap, or reduce the pipe size of a safety relief valve discharge. Check that the discharge pipe ends within 6 in. of a drain or catch drum before lifting the lever; hot water or glycol will come out. Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Zone valve actuator or motor head failed (stays closed on call)
causes.confirm:
One zone is cold with 24 V present at the zone valve actuator leads; the manual lever has full spring
resistance (valve closed), and latching the manual lever open sends hot water into the zone.
causes.fix:
Latch the manual opener lever to "MAN OPEN" so the zone gets heat right away (vital in subzero weather).
On many zone valves the lever opens the port but does not make the end switch, so confirm the circulator
is actually running (another zone calling, or jumper the end-switch terminals, or run the pump in HAND)
and that the zone pipe warms. Tag the lever as latched.

Then replace the synchronous motor or snap-on actuator power head without draining the loop. Verify 24 V
drives it open and the spring returns it closed when the call drops, and release the lever after the
repair.
causes.notes: How the manual lever behaves differs between valve models. Check the maker's data for the valves on this site.

causes.name: Zone valve auxiliary end switch failed open
keywords: zone valve opens boiler wont fire
pump wont start on one zone
causes.confirm:
On a call from that zone alone, the zone valve drives all the way open (manual lever goes floppy), but
the end switch remains open on a meter so the circulator and heat source never start — until another
zone calls and its pump moves water through both.
causes.fix:
Verify by momentarily jumpering the two end-switch terminals at the valve head (the circulator/boiler
should start immediately). Replace the snap switch or the complete actuator head.

causes.name: Zone valve body mechanically jammed closed
causes.confirm:
Even with the actuator head removed from the valve body, the stem, ball, or poppet cartridge is seized
shut and no hot water enters the zone while the circulator is running.
causes.fix:
Isolate and drain the zone branch, unbolt or unthread the seized conversion cartridge (or replace the
complete valve body), clean magnetite and scale out of the valve seat, and verify smooth stem travel
before snapping the actuator head back on.
causes.safety: Let the branch cool and relieve it to 0 psig before draining the zone or opening the valve body. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: Zone valve stuck open, latched in manual-open, or miswired open (overheating zone)
causes.confirm:
A zone overheats whenever another zone calls for heat because its zone valve is latched in the "MAN
OPEN" slot, its internal ball/poppet is stuck off the seat, or its actuator is miswired to constant 24 V.
causes.fix:
Check the manual opener lever first — if it was left hooked in the "MAN OPEN" notch after bleeding air,
release it. Next, disconnect one thermostat lead at the valve: if the valve now closes, trace the
thermostat wire or relay board for a short or cross-wiring. If it stays open with 24 V removed and the
lever unlatched, rebuild or replace the sticking valve cartridge.
causes.safety: Isolate the zone and relieve it to 0 psig before opening the valve body, and let it cool first. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: 3-way mixing valve or actuator stuck in bypass
causes.confirm:
The primary header entering the 3-way valve is hot, the loop circulator is running, the controller is
calling for heat, but the 3-way valve stays closed to the hot port and recirculates cool return water
(narrow loop ΔT, cold supply).
causes.fix:
Place the 3-way actuator in manual override (declutch button or handwheel) and open it toward the hot
port in steps, watching the supply temperature, and stop below the lowest limit in the loop (plastic or
radiant piping, DHW, the relief setpoint). Fully open sends primary temperature into the building loop;
engine jacket water is typically 180–200 °F. Return the actuator to AUTO after the repair. Meter the
control signal (24 V floating, 0–10 VDC, or 4–20 mA) at the actuator; replace the failed actuator or
free/rebuild the seized mixing valve plug.
causes.safety: Manual override removes temperature control. Watch the supply temperature the whole time, and never leave the valve in override unattended.

causes.name: Supply temperature above setpoint (aquastat or high-limit failed, 3-way valve stuck full hot, controller output stuck)
causes.confirm: A separate thermometer on the supply pipe reads above the controller setpoint or the high limit, and the control output is stuck high.
causes.fix:
Shut the heat source or the primary valve, then check the aquastat/high-limit well and sensor, and the
3-way valve and its actuator (free it or replace it). Find out why the control did not shut the source off
before the loop goes back into service.
causes.safety: Scald and flash hazard at the relief discharge. Treat a discharging relief valve as an overtemperature event and shut the heat source down.

causes.name: Flow-check or check valve stuck open (ghost / gravity flow overheating zone)
causes.confirm:
A zone gets hot even with its thermostat off and its circulator silent because buoyant hot water
thermosiphons past a flow-check whose thumbscrew was left in "OPEN" or whose seat is held open by scale.
causes.fix:
Turn the top thumbscrew on the weighted flow-check counterclockwise all the way to the normal automatic
position. If it still passes gravity flow, rap the valve body lightly or isolate and clean/replace the
check valve cartridge or spring check.

If there is no check valve at all, add a heat trap (loop the take-off down 8–12 in. before it rises) or a
spring check.
causes.safety: Isolate the branch, let it cool and relieve it to 0 psig before pulling a check valve cap or cartridge. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: Flow-check or spring check valve stuck closed (or installed backwards)
keywords: pump runs no flow in zone
causes.confirm:
The zone circulator runs, the branch is bled free of air and isolation valves are open, but the pipe is
hot right up to the check valve and cold immediately downstream of it (or the flow arrow points against
the pump).
causes.fix:
On a weighted flow-check, turn the top stem clockwise to manually lift the weight and break it free of
the seat, then return to automatic. If a spring/swing check is seized or installed backwards after
recent work, isolate the branch and reorient or replace the check valve.
causes.safety: Isolate the branch, let it cool and relieve it to 0 psig before pulling a check valve cap or cartridge. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: Hydronic loop short-circuiting or unbalanced (open bypass or unthrottled near branches)
causes.confirm:
Supply and return main temperatures are nearly identical while every zone is calling and the heat source
is hot (a narrow ΔT at light load is normal, so check at design load), because an open manual bypass
valve or wide-open balancing valves on near branches let hot water dump straight into the return,
starving distant coils.
causes.fix:
Close any manual bypass valve that was left open, or adjust the differential-pressure bypass valve to
open only when zones close. Balance circuit setters from the closest branch to the farthest so every
branch sees its design flow and design ΔT.

causes.name: Plate or shell-and-tube heat exchanger fouled or scaled
causes.confirm:
Primary hot supply entering the heat exchanger is at full temperature and its control valve is wide open,
but the secondary loop leaves more than 20 °F cooler (high hot-end approach) and the primary side gives
up less heat than design (narrow primary drop). Scale and film cost heat transfer long before they move
the pressure drop, so a normal ΔP does not clear the plates; debris plugging the ports shows as a large
ΔP rise over the data sheet.
causes.fix:
Backflush the plate heat exchanger by reversing valve paths if a backflush manifold is piped in;
otherwise isolate and circulate an inhibited descaling/cleaning solution through the plates (or pull the
plate pack, clean the chevron channels, and re-torque the frame to the nameplate tie-bolt dimension).
Clean the upstream Y-strainer so debris doesn't immediately re-plug the inlet ports.
causes.safety: Isolate both sides, drain, relieve to 0 psig and cool below about 110 °F before loosening the frame. The tie bolts store force: back them off evenly, never one side. Plate edges cut. Descaling acid needs protective gear and gasket/plate compatibility (no chlorides on stainless); neutralize it and collect the spent cleaner and glycol, do not drain them.

causes.name: Heat exchanger starved on the primary side (primary pump off, valve closed or throttled, primary strainer plugged)
causes.confirm:
The approach is high with the primary valve commanded open, but pressure drop across the plates is normal
and the primary side drops far more temperature than design, because too little primary fluid is getting
through: the primary pump is off or has lost flow, the control valve or its actuator is closed or
throttled, or the primary strainer is plugged.
causes.fix:
Check the primary pump (running, right rotation, flow proven), then the control valve and its actuator
(drive it open and see whether the approach closes up), and the primary strainer. Fix whatever restricts the
primary flow, then re-read the approach with the valve wide open.
causes.safety: Isolate, cool and relieve to 0 psig before pulling the primary strainer or opening a valve body. Collect any glycol in labeled drums (ethylene glycol is poisonous); never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea.

causes.name: Plate heat exchanger crossover or gasket leak (or plates burst by freezing)
causes.confirm: Glycol or inhibitor shows up in the primary loop, or the secondary loses glycol or pressure with no external leak; fluid at the frame seams.
causes.fix:
Pressure-test one side with the other drained (fluid appearing on the dry side means crossover). Replace
plates or gaskets, then verify glycol percent and inhibitor on both sides.
causes.safety: Isolate both sides, drain, relieve to 0 psig and cool below about 110 °F before loosening the frame; the tie bolts store force, so back them off evenly. Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.
causes.notes: A pinhole or gasket failure moves fluid from the higher-pressure side to the lower. A stagnant exchanger at subzero ambient can ice-burst its plates, which then cross-leak.

causes.name: Glycol concentration too low — freeze and slush risk
causes.confirm:
Refractometer reading shows the freeze point is warmer than the site's required target (the design low
minus the safety margin), so slush can form in outdoor or makeup-air coils.
causes.fix:
Find out how raw water entered the loop (passing domestic make-up PRV, a water hose used for purging, a
leaking DHW heat exchanger, or a leaking main plate heat exchanger). Isolate any raw-water tie-in (a
glycol loop must not be hard-piped to domestic make-up; use a dedicated glycol feeder), drain enough
weak solution from the loop into labeled drums, and pump in concentrated inhibited glycol of the
SAME chemistry (never mix EG and PG) until the mixed loop tests at or below the required freeze point
(about 50 vol % EG or 54 vol % PG for −40 °F). Never go above 60 %.

To go from C1 % to C2 % by replacing x of a V-gallon loop with neat glycol, x = V × (C2 − C1) ÷ (100 − C1).
Use the same basis (volume or weight) for all three numbers. Check: V = 1000, 30 to 55 gives x = 357.

Circulate for at least 1–2 hours before re-sampling from a flowing point; stratified concentrate reads
wrong.
causes.safety: In polar or subzero plants, weak glycol is a life-safety hazard: a coil that goes to slush stops flowing, then freezes solid, and at subzero ambient that is well under an hour. Weak glycol is also under-inhibited (below roughly 25-30 % the corrosion and bio protection is gone; per the fluid maker's data). Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Glycol thermally degraded or inhibitor depleted (low pH, sludge, corrosion)
causes.confirm:
A sample from the loop tests acidic (pH below 8.0 on a test strip) and looks dark brown/black with
suspended magnetite or smells burnt/sour from overheating or air ingress.
causes.fix:
Acidic glycol actively eats iron, copper, and pump seals — do not just add fresh glycol on top of burnt
sludge. If pH is 7.5–8.0 and the fluid is still free of sludge and burnt smell, re-inhibit per the fluid
manufacturer's buffer addition chart. If pH is below 7.5 or the fluid is dark and sludgy, drain it into
labeled drums, flush with a system cleaner (collect the flush too), clean all strainers and dirt
separators, fix the air-ingress or local overheating spot, and recharge with fresh premixed inhibited
glycol.
causes.safety: Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Glycol over-concentrated (above ~60 %) — freeze point back up, thick and slow
causes.confirm: Refractometer reads off the top of the scale or above 60 %; the loop was topped off with neat concentrate or filled from an undiluted drum.
causes.fix:
Drain a measured volume into labeled drums and replace it with the pre-mix (same chemistry) until the
freeze point reads at or just below the required target (typically 50–55 %).

Richer is not safer: above about 60 % the freeze point turns back up, and the fluid gets thick and
transfers heat poorly. The same replace-and-remix formula as for weak glycol applies (see "Glycol
concentration too low").
causes.safety: Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Frozen or burst hydronic coil or branch pipe
causes.confirm:
A branch pipe, baseboard loop, or unit-heater/air-handler coil exposed to subfreezing air is iced, slushy
or blocked with ice, or is below the loop fluid's freeze point, with zero flow (or split open and leaking
as it thaws).
causes.fix:
Shut the outside-air damper or seal the cold draft immediately. Treat every frozen coil or pipe as split
until a pressure test proves otherwise.

Lock out power to the unit and fan. Close and verify BOTH isolation valves to the frozen section and crack
its drain or highest vent (relief for thaw expansion, and a path for any release). Put a pan or hose to a
drum under it; do not let glycol reach electrics or the floor drain.

Thaw from the open end toward the plug with a heat gun, warm air or warm rags. After it is clear,
pressure-test before reopening the supply.

Braze or replace any split tube, verify the glycol freeze point across the whole plant, and keep
circulators running continuously during extreme cold.
causes.safety: Never thaw a frozen coil or pipe while it is connected to a live supply: the ice plug may be the only thing holding a split tube closed. Never use an open torch on a sealed ice-plugged pipe; trapped steam pressure between two ice plugs can rupture the tube violently. Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Circulator pump cavitating (low suction pressure, hot fluid, or restricted pump inlet)
causes.confirm:
A sharp rattling sound like gravel or marbles inside the pump volute accompanied by fluctuating lower
discharge pressure; partially throttling the pump DISCHARGE valve quiets the noise immediately.
causes.fix:
Cavitation happens when pressure at the impeller eye drops below the fluid's vapor pressure: (1) raise
system static fill pressure (or move the expansion tank connection to the suction side of the pump —
always pump away from the expansion tank); (2) fully open any throttled valve or clean any plugged
strainer on the pump SUCTION side; (3) lower excessive loop temperature if near boiling at current loop
pressure.

causes.name: Circulator mechanical shaft seal leaking
causes.confirm:
Water or crusty glycol residue is dripping from the weep hole at the bottom of the bearing bracket
between the pump volute and the motor.
causes.fix:
Isolate the pump, relieve pressure, and replace the mechanical seal kit (ceramic stationary seat +
carbon spring rotary seal) and volute gasket — or swap in a complete replacement bearing assembly. Check
the shaft sleeve for grooves and test loop fluid for abrasive magnetite or acidic glycol that chewed up
the old seal face.
causes.safety: Isolate the pump, let it cool below about 120 °F and relieve it to 0 psig before opening it. Collect every drain, purge, bleed and relief discharge in labeled drums; never to a floor drain, the ground, ice or sea. Ethylene glycol is poisonous: keep it from food, drinking water and animals and wash skin. Propylene glycol is low-toxicity, not harmless, and spent loop fluid carries metals and inhibitors. Follow the station spill and waste procedure and report spills.

causes.name: Unit-heater or fan-coil blower motor failed (hot coil, fan dead)
causes.confirm:
Supply and return pipes right at the unit heater or fan coil are hot, but the fan motor is not spinning
(leaving return water nearly as hot as supply).
causes.fix:
Check whether a strap-on pipe aquastat (low-limit fan delay) is open even though the pipe is hot, then
meter line voltage and the run capacitor at the fan motor. Replace the strap-on aquastat, run capacitor,
or seized fan motor.
causes.safety: Lock out unit-heater power before reaching past the fan guard.

causes.name: Baseboard / convector fins dirty, damper closed, or airflow blocked
causes.confirm:
The copper tube inside the baseboard or convector is hot from end to end, but natural convection is
choked off by a closed top louver, heavy dust/carpet blocking the bottom air gap, or furniture pushed
tight against the cover.
causes.fix:
Flip the baseboard top damper open, clear at least 1–2 inches under the bottom skirt and move furniture/
drapes away, and vacuum or brush lint out of the aluminum fins. Fin-tube baseboards are convection
heaters — if air can't enter the bottom and leave the top, heat stays in the water.

causes.name: Unit-heater or fan-coil coil fouled (filter plugged, fins matted with dust or lint, tubes scaled or air-bound)
causes.confirm:
The supply and return pipes at the unit are hot and the fan runs, but airflow off the coil is weak: the
filter is loaded, the fin face is matted with dust or lint, or the coil is cold in patches because its
tubes are scaled or air-bound.
causes.fix:
Lock out the unit. Replace or clean the filter, comb and vacuum the fin face from the air-leaving side
(and wash it with a coil cleaner approved for the fin material), and bleed air from the coil. If part of
the coil stays cold with a clean fin face and good airflow, flush or descale the tubes. Recheck the
airflow and the coil's temperature drop.
causes.safety: Lock out unit power before reaching past the fan guard, and keep water and cleaner off the motor and controls.

causes.name: Outdoor-reset sensor or supply setpoint control fault (target supply temp too low)
causes.confirm:
Pumps and valves work normally, but the reset controller is holding loop supply water lukewarm (e.g.
110 °F in subzero weather) because the outdoor thermistor drifted low in resistance (reading warm) or
the reset curve / high limit was turned down.
causes.fix:
Disconnect the outdoor thermistor and measure its resistance against its 10 kΩ / 1 kΩ temperature chart;
replace a drifted sensor or relocate one mounted in direct sun or near an exhaust hood. If the sensor is
temporarily unavailable, enable manual setpoint override at a temperature that stays under the lowest
limit in the loop (plastic or radiant piping, DHW) so the building stays warm.

causes.name: Primary heat-recovery loop cold and backup boiler failing to stage on
causes.confirm:
On a waste-heat / generator jacket-water recovery loop, the primary hot supply entering the building or
plant HX has dropped cold, and the auxiliary/backup boiler did not automatically stage on to pick up the
load.
causes.fix:
Start or enable the backup boiler in manual/local lead mode right away to protect the building and
glycol loop from freezing, but prove flow through it first (pump running, flow switch made) and bring
the return temperature up gradually (use the boiler bypass) rather than hitting a hot boiler with a
subzero return. Then troubleshoot the staging changeover aquastat/PLC interlock, the backup boiler's
isolation valve actuator, and check with the power plant on primary jacket-water loop status and
primary pumps.
causes.safety: In polar heat-recovery loops, loss of primary heat with no backup boiler staging can freeze building utilities — bring backup firing online first.

causes.name: Indirect domestic hot water (DHW) fault — zone off, scaled coil, or bad tempering valve
causes.confirm:
Space heating works, but domestic hot water at the taps is cold or lukewarm: checking the indirect tank
shows either the DHW aquastat/circulator isn't circulating boiler water through the tank coil, the coil
is scaled (boiler loop hot in/out with zero ΔT while tank is cold), or the tank outlet pipe is hot right
into the ASSE 1017 tempering valve and cold leaving it.
causes.fix:
Compare the pipe leaving the top of the indirect tank with the mixed pipe leaving the thermostatic
tempering valve: if the tank outlet is hot (storage should sit at about 140 °F or above) and the mixed
outlet is cold, rebuild or replace the stuck tempering valve. If the tank itself is cold, test the tank
aquastat, DHW zone valve/circulator, and purge air or descale the indirect heat-exchanger coil.
causes.safety: After any tempering-valve work, measure the delivered temperature at the farthest tap with a thermometer; it must be no hotter than about 120 °F. Do not bypass the valve or raise setpoints to chase warmth. Store at about 140 °F or above for Legionella control (the tempering valve is what makes that safe). Indirect coils on glycol loops must be double-wall; after a coil leak, test the potable side.

causes.name: Steam trap failed open — blowing live steam into the condensate return
causes.confirm:
Listening with a stethoscope or ultrasonic detector finds a trap that hisses or roars continuously, with
its outlet pipe at about 212 °F. One blowing trap in a large system often leaves the receiver vent and the
return header looking normal; with several, live steam may jet out of the receiver vent and the
condensate return reads well above this plant's baseline.
causes.fix:
Isolate the failed trap (supply valve shut, return side valved off), let it cool and confirm 0 psig, then
open the trap body and replace the thermostatic bellows/capsule (on radiator and F&T traps) or inverted
bucket/disc assembly. Check that any 3-valve trap bypass is closed tight. Fixing a blowing trap stops
return back-pressure that blocks other units from draining and stops live steam from vapor-binding the
condensate/vacuum pumps.
causes.safety: Condensate return lines with a failed-open trap carry live steam. Verify the branch or main is isolated and at 0 psig, and let it cool, before opening any trap cap, strainer plug or union.

causes.name: Steam trap failed closed or plugged — radiator or coil cold and waterlogged
causes.confirm:
Steam supply pipe is hot right up to the radiator, convector, or unit heater, the manual supply valve is
open, but the trap and return line are cold because condensate and air are backed up inside the unit.
causes.fix:
Isolate the unit's steam supply valve, let the flooded radiator/coil cool, and confirm 0 psig. Then drain
the trapped water through the trap's drain plug or a full-port valve to a safe drain with a pipe or hose,
not into a bucket under the line. Clean the inlet Y-strainer and replace the failed thermostatic element
or clogged float-and-thermostatic (F&T) trap internals.
causes.safety: Verify the branch is isolated and at 0 psig before opening any trap cap, strainer plug or union, and blow down slowly through a full-port valve to a safe drain. In subfreezing air handlers or unit heaters, a failed-closed steam trap floods the coil with water that freezes and bursts the tubes within minutes.

causes.name: Steam radiator or main air vent stuck closed (air-bound radiator or slow main)
causes.confirm:
On a one-pipe radiator or steam main, steam cannot enter until air is pushed out: the supply main is hot
and the vent never hisses air and stays cold. With the supply valve shut and the unit cool, blow through
the vent: a good one passes air freely when cold, and one that will not pass air is plugged. Reopen the
valve slowly; steam should fill the unit from the supply end in a minute or two, and the vent should hiss,
then close.
causes.fix:
Close the radiator supply valve (for a main vent, shut the boiler down and let the main reach 0 psig), let
it cool until you can hold the vent, then unscrew it and thread in a new properly sized radiator or main
vent (never boil/soak old vents in vinegar if the internal float or orifice is corroded — replace it). At
the far end of long steam mains, install high-capacity main vents 6–15 inches back from the end elbow and
6 inches above the main so steam reaches all risers evenly.
causes.safety: Never unscrew a vent, plug or union from anything holding steam. Close the supply valve, let it cool, and confirm 0 psig before opening.

causes.name: Steam radiator or main air vent stuck open (spitting live steam and water)
causes.confirm:
After the radiator heats up completely, the air vent fails to snap shut and continues hissing live steam
or sputtering hot water into the room.
causes.fix:
Shut the radiator supply valve and let the radiator and vent cool until you can hold them (10–20
minutes for cast iron), then replace the stuck-open air vent, making sure the new vent sits dead
vertical so its internal float can rise and seat properly.
causes.safety: A vent spitting steam is under pressure. Shut the supply valve and let the unit cool before you touch the vent.

causes.name: Sagging, back-pitched pipe, or lifted condensate return causing water hammer
causes.confirm:
Violent banging or pounding in the steam main, runout, or radiator on warm-up, and checking with a level
shows a broken hanger, bellied horizontal pipe, radiator pitched away from its drain end, or a return
line lifting condensate up to an overhead return.
causes.fix:
Restore a continuous slope toward the drain end of the pipe (steeper rather than shallower, and steeper
still on counterflow runouts where the condensate runs against the steam) by replacing broken pipe
hangers, shimming the far feet of one-pipe radiators so condensate drains back down the supply valve, and
adding a drip trap or condensate pump at any low point instead of trying to lift condensate with steam
pressure.
causes.safety: Severe steam water hammer can crack cast-iron fittings and valves — open main steam valves slowly on cold start-up.
causes.notes: Published pitch figures differ between sources, and TM 5-642 gives none. Use the plant's piping standard or the maker's data; a main with any sag holds condensate.

causes.name: Boiler priming or carryover (water line too high, dirty or oily boiler water, over-firing) sending wet steam
causes.confirm:
Water hammer shows up although the pipe pitch is sound and the drip traps are working, the gauge-glass
water line bounces or sits too high, and wet steam (water slugs) is carried out into the header. Check the
boiler water for oil, grease or heavy dirt.
causes.fix:
Bring the water line down to the normal mark, blow down per the maker's procedure to remove oil, grease
and dirt (surface skim if fitted), cut the firing rate to what the load needs, and clean the boiler
(boil-out) if oil or grease is present. The oil-boiler checks on water level and water condition apply
here too.
causes.safety: Blow down only per the maker's procedure, slowly and to a safe drain, and keep the water line in the glass the whole time.

causes.name: Steam main or riser drip trap failed closed or plugged (flooded main and water hammer)
keywords: bad f and t trap on main
causes.confirm:
Loud water hammer in the steam header and slow/wet steam to downstream branches while the main drip leg
and float-and-thermostatic (F&T) drip trap at the end of the main or base of the riser are cold.
causes.fix:
Isolate the drip branch and confirm it is cool and at 0 psig. Then blow down the dirt pocket slowly
through a full-port valve to a safe drain with a pipe or hose, clean the Y-strainer ahead of the drip
trap, and rebuild or replace the failed F&T drip trap. Never allow condensate to pool in a high-velocity
steam main.
causes.safety: Verify the branch or main is isolated and at 0 psig before opening any trap cap, strainer plug, union or drip-leg blowdown. Blow down slowly through a full-port valve to a safe drain with a pipe or hose, not a bucket under the line.

causes.name: Steam radiator or coil supply valve closed, throttled on one-pipe, or disc off stem
causes.confirm:
A single radiator or convector is cold (or gurgling/banging at the inlet on a one-pipe system) because
its manual supply valve is shut, left half-throttled on a one-pipe radiator, or the brass disc has come
detached from the stem and stays seated when the handwheel is turned.
causes.fix:
On a one-pipe steam radiator, open the supply valve 100% all the way (throttling a one-pipe valve traps
leaving condensate against incoming 60-mph steam and causes loud hammering). If the handwheel spins
without lifting the disc off the seat, shut down steam, unscrew the valve bonnet, and reattach or
replace the valve assembly.
causes.safety: Never unscrew a valve bonnet, union or plug on a line holding steam. Shut it off, let it cool, and confirm 0 psig first.

causes.name: Condensate pump float switch stuck or linkage binding
causes.confirm:
The condensate receiver is full or overflowing onto the floor, line power is present at the disconnect,
the float switch contacts are open, and lifting or tapping the float rod starts the pump.
causes.fix:
Inspect the float ball for pinholes (a waterlogged copper or plastic float won't rise), straighten any
bent float rod rubbing the receiver wall, adjust the upper and lower stop collars, or replace the Square
D / NEMA float switch. On duplex receivers, verify the lag/alternator float switch also trips before the
vent overflows.
causes.safety: Lock out the pump and let the receiver cool before you reach in or open the cover; the water can be 180–210 °F.

causes.name: Condensate pump motor failed or thermal overload tripped
causes.confirm:
The receiver is full, the float switch is closed and delivering full line voltage directly to the motor
leads, but the condensate pump motor is silent (open overload/winding) or humming and locked up.
causes.fix:
If the receiver is a duplex unit, switch the selector to the standby pump to drain the receiver right
away. Lock out the failed pump, check whether the impeller is jammed with scale before resetting a
thermal overload, and replace the motor + shaft seal assembly if the windings are open or grounded.
causes.safety: Lock out power and let the receiver cool (its water can be 180–210 °F) before unbolting the vertical motor from the condensate receiver cover.

causes.name: Condensate pump clogged, vapor-bound, running backward or blocked at the discharge (runs without pumping)
causes.confirm:
The condensate pump motor runs continuously with the receiver full, but discharge pressure is low and
the tank level barely drops — either because scale/rust has plugged the inlet strainer/impeller, because
condensate near 200 °F or more is flashing to steam in the pump eye (vapor binding), because the motor
is turning the wrong way, or because the discharge line is blocked. Gauge the pump discharge against
boiler pressure, and check rotation with a rubber-tipped pencil touched to the shaft.
causes.fix:
Check receiver temperature first: if condensate is hot enough to flash in the pump eye (around 200 °F or
more, often from a blowing steam trap), cooling the receiver and fixing the failed-open trap cures the
vapor lock. Otherwise, lock out the pump, clean the inlet strainer, clear rust scale from the impeller
vanes, check rotation on 3-phase motors against the arrow on the casing, and verify discharge valve
opening and that the discharge line is clear.
causes.safety: Let the receiver cool and lock out the pump before opening the receiver cover or pump inlet; the water can be 180–210 °F. Verify the discharge line is isolated and at 0 psig before opening it.

causes.name: Receiver flooded by a stuck-open make-up valve (pump cycles normally but cannot keep up)
causes.confirm:
The pump starts, pumps down and stops normally, yet the receiver overflows or stays full, and the water in
it is cooler than usual because cold make-up keeps pouring in. Shutting the make-up valve lets the level
fall.
causes.fix:
Shut the make-up valve and see whether the level falls; then check the make-up float and the valve seat,
and adjust or replace them. The other receiver-overflow causes (wrong pump rotation, low discharge
pressure, a clogged outlet) belong with the pump that runs without pumping.
causes.safety: Let the receiver cool and lock out the pump before opening the receiver cover; the water can be 180–210 °F.

causes.name: Condensate pump discharge check valve leaking back (boiler water backing into receiver)
causes.confirm:
The condensate pump pumps the receiver down and shuts off, then you immediately hear and feel hot boiler
feedwater rushing backward through the discharge check valve, refilling the receiver and re-triggering
the pump every few minutes (while boiler water level drops on shutdown).
causes.fix:
Close the manual isolation valve downstream of the discharge check valve, let the line cool and
depressurize, and clean scale off the swing/spring check clapper or replace the check valve.
causes.safety: Pressurized hot boiler water sits immediately downstream of the condensate discharge check — close the downstream isolation valve before opening the check.

causes.name: Vacuum return pump failing to pull vacuum (air leak in return or hot-condensate vapor lock)
causes.confirm:
The vacuum return unit runs nonstop on vacuum control, but the compound gauge stays near 0 in. Hg
instead of pulling 2–6 in. Hg and shutting off.
causes.fix:
Per TM 5-642: (1) check condensate temperature — a vacuum pump fed hot condensate (over about 180–190 °F
from leaking traps) cannot pull a vacuum, because seal water that hot cannot hold the 2–6 in. Hg the
system wants; switch the pump to float-only control temporarily and fix the blowing traps; (2) isolate
return branch valves one at a time to locate air leaks in corroded return piping, union gaskets, or
radiator valve packings; (3) inspect the pump impeller/venturi clearances and discharge check valve.
causes.safety: Lock out the pump and let it cool before opening it; condensate and seal water can be 180–210 °F. Verify the lines are isolated and at 0 psig before opening any union or check valve.

causes.name: Steam pipe, union, valve packing, or return line leak
causes.confirm:
Visible wisp/hiss of live steam at a valve stem packing nut, union, or flange gasket, or condensate
dripping from a corroded horizontal return line.
causes.fix:
For a leaking radiator or gate valve stem, back off the packing nut with steam off, wrap graphite/PTFE
valve stem packing around the stem, and snug the packing nut just enough to stop the leak without
binding the stem. For corroded horizontal condensate return piping (often grooved along the bottom from
carbonic acid), cut out and replace the rotted section with Schedule 80 black steel pipe.
causes.safety: Never tighten a union or flange under live steam pressure — isolate and depressurize the line first.

causes.name: Steam pressure-reducing station not holding its set pressure (pilot line plugged, diaphragm failed, cut seat, stem binding, or wrong spring or weight setting)
causes.confirm:
The gauge on the low-pressure main (10 ft or more past the valve) sits well under the set pressure while
the high-pressure side is up (valve not passing: pilot line plugged, stem binding, strainer plugged), or it
climbs over the setting and lifts the low-side relief (cut seat, or the valve held open).
causes.fix:
With the station isolated and at 0 psig, clean the strainer ahead of the valve and the pilot line (refill
the pilot line with water to protect the diaphragm), check the diaphragm, the stem and the seat and disk
for cuts or binding, and reset the spring or weight to the required pressure. Cut seats and valve heads
mean the valve is oversized. Overhaul or replace the valve per the maker's data.
causes.safety: Isolate and relieve both sides of the station before opening it. A station that is not holding its setting can overpressure the low-pressure system, so confirm the low-side relief valve is free and piped to a safe place.

causes.name: Defrost timer or controller not initiating defrost (timer motor dead, trippers missing, or schedule off)
causes.confirm: Frost is packed evenly through the coil fins; the timer dial isn't turning, has no ON trippers installed, or won't switch contacts when rotated into the defrost notch.
causes.fix:
Rotate the timer into defrost by hand to verify the heaters and termination work once triggered. Replace a timer
whose synchronous motor has stopped or whose contacts are pitted, reinstall missing brass trippers (typically
3–4 per day for freezers), or enable the defrost schedule in the electronic controller. Thaw the coil completely
before returning the box to service. If a forced defrost does nothing at all (no relay click, the compressor keeps
running), the timer's or controller's output relay is dead — replace the timer or controller.

causes.name: Electric defrost heater element open or burned out
causes.confirm: With the unit in defrost, line voltage is present at the heater feed and through the safety limit, but clamp-meter current is zero (or well under nameplate when only one of several elements is open), and the defrost ends on its time limit with ice still on the coil.
causes.fix:
Lock out and tag every source (the evaporator heaters, fans and drain heater are usually on their own breaker, not the
condensing unit's) and prove the terminal block dead. Melt the ice off the coil with warm water or a fans-only manual
defrost, then ohm each element (V² ÷ W: about 53 Ω for 1,000 W at 230 V, 106 Ω for 500 W — compare with the nameplate)
and megger each element to its sheath: an element that reads open or to ground is the one to replace. Make sure the new
rod is clipped down in its slots so it cannot bow out or scorch wiring, and verify full rated amp draw in defrost.
causes.safety: Lock out power before unplugging or pulling heater rods; hot elements can blister hands and steam-burn eyes.
