Inside a walk-in: prop the door, check that the inside release works before you rely on the door, never let it latch behind you, and tell someone you are in the box. Thawing leaves ice and water on the floor.

causes.name: Defrost heater contactor or relay failed (open coil or burned contacts — no voltage to heaters)
causes.confirm: The timer or controller initiates defrost (compressor stops), but no line voltage reaches the load side of the defrost contactor or timer terminal 3.
causes.fix:
Check control voltage across the defrost contactor coil during defrost: if voltage is present and it doesn't pull
in (or drops line voltage across burned contacts), replace the contactor or relay. If no coil voltage arrives
from the defrost clock, replace the clock mechanism. Thaw the coil and verify full heater amps.

causes.name: Defrost termination thermostat or coil sensor failed closed (terminates defrost too early with ice left on coil)
causes.confirm: The unit enters defrost and the heaters work, but the termination snap-disc or coil probe kicks it back into cooling after a few minutes while the coil is still below 32 °F and packed with ice.
causes.fix:
On a cold iced coil (below 25 °F), the termination side of a mechanical snap-disc termination thermostat (4-wire or 3-wire) should be open
between its common and termination terminals (read the wiring diagram for the labels) until ~48–55 °F; if it reads closed cold, replace it. On an electronic controller, check
the coil probe resistance against its temperature chart and move the probe to the last place ice melts (usually
top center of the coil away from a heater rod).

causes.name: Defrost termination thermostat or sensor failed open (never terminates on temperature, overheating the box)
causes.confirm: Every defrost cycle runs all the way to the timer's mechanical fail-safe (45–60 min) even after the coil is bone-dry and hot, filling the box with steam (it freezes as hoarfrost on the ceiling, fan guards and door frame) and driving box temperature up.
causes.fix:
Warm the termination snap-disc or coil sensor above 60 °F and check whether it closes to energize the timer release
solenoid (terminal X) or tells the controller the coil is warm. Replace a failed snap-disc or drifted thermistor,
verify it is clipped tightly to the coil tube, and set the fail-safe to a sensible backup — a little over
the longest normal defrost (roughly 30–45 min electric, 15–25 min hot gas).

causes.name: Defrost safety high-limit (snap-disc) failed open on a cold coil
causes.confirm: Line voltage reaches the evaporator in defrost and the heater elements ohm out good, but the series safety high-limit switch at the top of the coil reads open even with the coil frozen solid.
causes.fix:
Confirm it is open on a COLD coil: a limit that opened hot did its job, so find what let the coil overheat (a stuck
termination, fans running or heaters left on) before replacing it. Replace a limit that is open when cold with the exact
temperature and amp rating. Never jumper or
bypass a defrost safety limit permanently — if a termination switch sticks later, an unguarded heater can melt
the drain pan or start a fire.
causes.safety: Never leave a defrost high-limit switch jumpered; it is the fire safety for electric defrost heaters.

causes.name: Hot-gas defrost solenoid valve failed closed (no hot gas enters the evaporator in defrost)
causes.confirm: In defrost, the hot-gas line downstream of the defrost solenoid stays cold (IR thermometer or pipe probe) while the compressor discharge ahead of it is hot, and the defrost ends on its time limit with the coil still iced.
causes.fix:
Meter voltage at the hot-gas solenoid coil during defrost and check coil resistance. If the coil is energized and
the valve won't open (tap it, or lift the plunger with a test magnet), replace the coil. If the body is stuck, pump
down or recover first (no venting), then rebuild or replace the valve and the drier. Also check that sufficient head
pressure exists to push hot gas into the evaporator.
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Hot-gas defrost solenoid valve leaking through during the cooling cycle
causes.confirm: During normal cooling (solenoid coil de-energized), the hot-gas defrost pipe downstream of the solenoid stays hot on an IR thermometer or pipe probe (well over 150 °F) and suction pressure stays elevated.
causes.fix:
Confirm the solenoid coil is not getting stray voltage during cooling. Pump the section down or recover, open the
valve and clean or replace the scored PTFE seat and plunger kit (or replace the valve and add a strainer ahead
of it).
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Drain-pan or drain-line heater failed — frozen drain backing clear ice up into the coil and fans
causes.confirm: Solid clear ice fills the drain pan and climbs up the bottom of the coil while the drain line is frozen solid and the drain heat tape reads open or cold.
causes.fix:
Thaw the pan and drain line completely with warm water or steam (never chip near coil tubes with an ice pick).
Check the drain line pitch and trap outside the box, replace the open drain-line heat tape or pan heater, wrap it
with foil tape and insulation all the way out of the freezer wall, and verify amp draw.
causes.safety: Lock out the drain-heater and evaporator circuits before you thaw (water and steam near heater terminals). Inside a walk-in: prop the door, check that the inside release works before you rely on the door, never let it latch behind you, and tell someone you are in the box. Thawing leaves ice on the floor.

causes.name: Evaporator fan-delay thermostat (snap-disc) or controller relay stuck open (fans stay off after defrost)
causes.confirm: The compressor is running and the evaporator coil is well below 20 °F, but the fan-delay switch (or controller fan relay) stays open so no voltage reaches the fan motors.
causes.fix:
With the coil cold (below 15–20 °F), meter across the fan-delay contacts (F to 4 on a 3-wire snap-disc control, or the fan
relay on an electronic controller). If line voltage enters the switch and doesn't come out on a freezing coil,
replace the termination/fan-delay thermostat (or the controller) and verify its sensing face is clipped tight to the
suction header.

causes.name: Evaporator fan blade locked in ice, bent, or hitting the fan shroud
causes.confirm: Visual inspection shows a fan blade jammed against an ice ridge in the orifice ring or rubbing a shifted shroud (often tripping the fan motor's thermal protector).
causes.fix:
Lock out power immediately so the stalled fan motor doesn't burn out. Melt away all ice around the shroud and
pan, check the motor mounts and set-screw hub, replace any cracked or bent fan blade (a bent blade vibrates and
kills motor bearings), and fix the drain or infiltration issue that put ice in the fan ring.
causes.safety: Lock out power before reaching near evaporator fan blades; a thermally tripped fan motor can restart without warning. Inside a walk-in: prop the door, check that the inside release works before you rely on the door, never let it latch behind you, and tell someone you are in the box.

causes.name: Walk-in or reach-in door switch stuck or misaligned (holding evaporator fans off or box lights on)
causes.confirm: Closing the door doesn't actuate the plunger switch (or the switch contacts are stuck), leaving the evaporator fans off with the door shut or keeping hot incandescent box lights burning 24/7.
causes.fix:
Adjust or shim the door switch bracket so the closed door depresses the plunger reliably, or replace a sticking
plunger switch (moisture inside freezer door switches often freezes them). Verify fans start the instant the
door latches and interior lights turn off.

causes.name: Door gasket torn or leaking, or door closer / hinges not pulling the door shut
causes.confirm: Gaps are visible along the door perimeter (flashlight or dollar-bill test fails), the magnetic gasket is split, or a worn cam-lift hinge / closer leaves the door cracked open.
causes.fix:
Replace torn or hardened door gaskets, adjust cam-lift hinges and the latch strike so the gasket compresses
evenly all the way around, and repair or replace the hydraulic door closer. Clear the fluffy frost off the
evaporator and doorway after sealing.

causes.name: Door frame or mullion anti-sweat heater failed (door sweating or freezing shut to the jamb)
causes.confirm: The door perimeter frame or reach-in center mullion is ice-cold, sweating into puddles on the floor (or freezing the freezer door gasket solid to the frame, tearing the gasket when pulled).
causes.fix:
First check whether a mullion "energy-saver / humidity" rocker switch was flipped off. If voltage is present at
the heater leads in the junction box or hinge pillar and the heater wire reads open (infinite ohms), pull the
snap-in trim plate and replace the perimeter anti-sweat heater wire.
causes.safety: A door frozen to its frame may also have an iced or stiff inside release: test the release from inside with the door held open before you go in. Inside a walk-in: prop the door, check that the inside release works before you rely on the door, never let it latch behind you, and tell someone you are in the box.

causes.name: Heavy moist-air infiltration (missing strip curtains, open pipe penetration, stuck relief port, propped door)
causes.confirm: Fluffy snow and hoarfrost coat the ceiling, fan guards, and coil face; outside air enters through an unsealed conduit/line-set hole, a stuck-open pressure-relief port, missing strip curtains, or doors propped open.
causes.fix:
Seal all pipe and conduit penetrations with vapor-tight foam and silicone on the warm side (warm air carries the
moisture), free up and check the heater on the pressure-relief port, hang full-overlap low-temp strip curtains,
and brush/defrost the snow load off the evaporator.
causes.safety: Inside a walk-in: prop the door, check that the inside release works before you rely on the door, never let it latch behind you, and tell someone you are in the box. Brushing snow off a coil: lock out the fans first.

causes.name: Boxes stacked against the evaporator/walls blocking airflow, or large hot product load placed in box
causes.confirm: Cartons are stacked right in front of the evaporator fan throw or against the return intake behind the unit (or pallets of warm/uncovered food were just loaded into the box).
causes.fix:
Move product at least 18 in. clear of the evaporator discharge and 6 in. below the ceiling, and keep a gap along
the walls and floor racks so air can loop around the load. Have the galley cool hot pans in an ice bath or blast
chiller and cover them before putting them in a holding cooler.

causes.name: Box thermostat or electronic controller probe drifted out of calibration
causes.confirm: A calibrated thermometer placed right next to the box air probe disagrees with the controller display or thermostat dial by 4 °F or more (or the probe resistance doesn't match its Ω-vs-°F chart).
causes.fix:
Check the probe connection for moisture in the splice (water wicking into a sensor wire lowers resistance and
makes an NTC thermistor read falsely warm or cold). Apply a calibration offset ONLY after verifying the probe is
stable; otherwise replace the NTC/PTC sensor or mechanical thermostat and seal the splice with adhesive-lined
heat shrink.

causes.name: Liquid-line pump-down solenoid valve leaking through (compressor short-cycling during the off cycle)
keywords: compressor kicks on in off cycle
causes.confirm: With the box satisfied and the liquid-line solenoid de-energized, suction pressure slowly creeps back up to the LPC cut-in point and the compressor pumps down for 10–30 seconds every few minutes.
causes.fix:
First tell it from a leaking compressor valve: front-seat the receiver king valve with the solenoid HELD OPEN (manual
lift stem, or a temporary jumper on the coil) and pump the liquid line and coil down to 2–5 psig. If suction still
creeps up with the king valve shut, the compressor's valves or discharge check are leaking, not the solenoid.
Pumping down with the solenoid closed leaves liquid trapped between the king valve and the solenoid, and that can burst
the line when it warms or when you braze beside it. With the section pumped down and the remainder recovered (no
venting), clean or replace the solenoid valve (debris or solder scale under the PTFE seat is the usual culprit),
replace the upstream strainer/drier, and verify suction pressure stays flat after pump-down.
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Liquid-line solenoid valve failed closed or open coil (pumps down and stays off on low pressure)
causes.confirm: The box controller is calling for cooling, but the compressor is off on the low-pressure switch with low suction pressure because the liquid-line solenoid hasn't opened.
causes.fix:
Meter voltage across the liquid-line solenoid coil leads with the thermostat calling: if voltage is present and
the valve doesn't click (or a permanent test magnet opens it immediately), replace the open coil. If a magnet
won't open it either, the stem is mechanically jammed — pump down and rebuild or replace the valve.
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Low-pressure control (LPC) cut-in/cut-out set wrong or differential too tight
causes.confirm: Gauges show the low-pressure control cutting the compressor out while box temperature is still above setpoint, or cutting back in almost immediately because the differential wheel is set too narrow.
causes.fix:
Set the LPC using your gauges, not just the stamped scale (scales drift). Pump-down system: set cut-in just below the
saturation pressure at the box temperature where the thermostat CALLS (R-404A: about 82 psig for a 38 °F cooler call,
28 psig for a -5 °F freezer call) so the compressor always restarts when the solenoid opens, but above the pressure the
pumped-down coil creeps to in the off cycle; set cut-out a few psig above zero (never into vacuum). Referencing the
warmest allowable box temperature instead leaves the compressor off after the thermostat has called and the box floats
warm. Non-pump-down off-cycle defrost cooler: set cut-in at ~36–38 °F coil saturation so the coil thaws every cycle.

causes.name: Crankcase heater failed on a cold-ambient unit (off-cycle migration, oil foaming and slugging on start)
causes.confirm: In a cool mechanical space or outdoors, the compressor crankcase is cold during the off cycle; on start-up the oil sight glass foams violently and the compressor bangs/slugs as liquid refrigerant boils out of the oil.
causes.fix:
Meter voltage and resistance across the belly-band or insertion crankcase heater. Replace an open heater, make
sure it is wired to stay energized whenever the compressor is off (or continuously), and consider adding
automatic pump-down if the unit doesn't already have a liquid-line solenoid. After the new heater is in, leave it
energized with the compressor locked out for at least 12 hours (longer in a very cold space) until the shell is warm
to the touch, then start with gauges on and watch the sight glass — never start a cold, foamy compressor just to see
if it runs.

causes.name: Evaporator pressure regulator (EPR / ORIT) stuck closed or set too high (holds coil too warm)
keywords: warm box low suction after epr
causes.confirm: A gauge at the evaporator outlet (upstream of the EPR) reads high saturation pressure while compressor suction pressure downstream of the EPR pulls down low, keeping the coil too warm to cool the box.
causes.fix:
Put a gauge on the EPR's inlet Schrader port and turn the adjustment screw counterclockwise to lower the
evaporator pressure setting toward the design coil saturation temperature (~10–12 °F below box setpoint). If the
inlet pressure won't drop as you back the spring off, the pilot port or main piston is stuck — pump down or recover first (no venting),
then clean or replace the EPR.
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Evaporator pressure regulator (EPR) stuck wide open or set too low on a cooler (freezes coil and product)
causes.confirm: Evaporator pressure upstream of the EPR drops straight down with compressor suction pressure well below the EPR's setpoint, icing a medium-temp coil or freezing sensitive produce.
causes.fix:
Turn the EPR adjustment clockwise while watching the inlet gauge to raise minimum evaporator pressure (e.g., to a
24–28 °F coil saturation for a produce cooler). If pressure upstream still tracks low suction, debris is holding
the EPR piston open — pump down and clean or replace the valve.
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Crankcase pressure regulator (CPR / CROT) set too low or stuck throttling (starves compressor suction)
causes.confirm: Even when compressor amps are well below RLA, gauges before and after the CPR at the compressor inlet show a large pressure drop across the valve, holding evaporator pressure up and starving the compressor.
causes.fix:
Compare compressor amp draw with nameplate RLA and adjust the CPR clockwise in small steps until it stops
throttling during normal pull-down while still capping suction pressure below the compressor's maximum operating
suction pressure (MOP) right after defrost. Pump down or recover first (no venting), then replace a binding CPR cartridge.
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Head-pressure flooding valve stuck in bypass (sending hot gas to receiver in warm ambient)
keywords: bubbles in sight glass warm weather
causes.confirm: With condenser entering air warm (above ~65 °F), the line between the valve and the receiver is near discharge temperature while the condenser outlet line is only a little above ambient, driving head pressure up and flashing the sight glass.
causes.fix:
Check the charge first: an overfilled receiver or a leftover winter flood charge floods the condenser and fakes the same
symptoms, so don't condemn the valve until the charge is right. Then compare the line from the valve to the receiver with
the condenser outlet line — hot against warm means the valve is bypassing. Tap the body once; if it stays stuck (debris, eroded
seat), pump down or recover first (no venting) and replace it with the same pressure setting from the nameplate or catalog
(typically 180–240 psig on R-404A; a dome-charged valve is not field-adjustable). A valve that lost its dome charge does the
opposite: it stays open to the condenser and never floods in cold air (its own cause: flooding valve not bypassing in cold air).
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Winter flooding charge short — the valve is bypassing but the receiver runs dry in cold air (−40 °F)
causes.confirm: Running in cold outdoor air (below 40 °F down to −40 °F), the line from the valve to the receiver is hot (the valve is bypassing discharge gas) and the condenser is flooded, but the receiver runs dry — the sight glass foams continuously and head pressure still collapses.
causes.fix:
1. Rule out a leak before adding anything: oil at joints, receiver level against last season's, a leak search. A system
   that has lost charge needs the leak found and repaired first (EPA 608 recordkeeping and leak-repair rules apply by
   charge size).
2. If the valve is bypassing and the unit is simply short of its winter flood charge, add the maker's winter-charge allowance
   in small steps by weight until the glass clears at steady cold-weather head pressure. Record every pound added (date, lb,
   refrigerant) and label the unit.
3. Check that the receiver holds the whole charge at no more than about 80 % full when the condenser empties in warm air; if
   it can't, take the extra charge back out in spring or the unit runs high head all summer. Insulate the receiver and liquid
   line — a -40 °F receiver condenses the bypass gas and drags receiver pressure down.
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Head-pressure flooding valve not bypassing in cold air — dome charge lost or valve stuck toward the condenser
keywords: low head in winter cold receiver line
causes.confirm: Cold outdoor air, low head pressure, and the line between the valve and the receiver stays cold, so nothing is being bypassed and the condenser never floods. A short charge fools the valve the same way, so check the charge too.
causes.fix:
A valve that lost its dome charge (or stuck toward the condenser) passes everything through the cold condenser and never
holds head pressure. Verify the charge is right first, then pump down or recover (no venting) and replace the valve with the
same pressure setting from the nameplate or catalog (a dome-charged valve is not field-adjustable and its dome cannot be recharged
in the field).
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Condenser fan control stuck on — fan-cycling switch closed or VFD at full speed (head pressure collapses in cold air)
causes.confirm: In cold air the high-side gauge sits well below the fan cut-out, yet the condenser fan runs full speed (the switch contacts stay closed, or the VFD stays at 100 %).
causes.fix:
With the high-side gauge on, check that the contacts open below cut-out (or the VFD drops to its minimum). Replace a pitted
or stuck pressure switch, or fix the VFD's transducer, setpoint or minimum-speed setting. Fan cycling alone seldom holds
head far below about 0 °F: at -40 °F add a flooding valve with its winter charge, or at least a wind baffle, if head still
collapses.
causes.safety: A cycling condenser fan can start without warning — lock out before reaching near the blade.

causes.name: Condenser fan control stuck off — fan-cycling switch open or VFD with no output (fan will not start at high head)
keywords: condenser fan wont start high head
causes.confirm: Head pressure is well above the cut-in setting and the fan stays off; meter across the switch — full line voltage across it with head above cut-in means it is open (or the VFD shows no output).
causes.fix:
Shut the compressor off before it trips on high pressure again. Check the switch setting and contacts, the VFD's
transducer and output, and the fan relay and wiring; replace the failed switch or drive. Never leave a jumper in place.
causes.safety: A cycling condenser fan can start without warning — lock out before reaching near the blade.

causes.name: Water-cooled condenser water-regulating valve stuck closed, set too high, or inlet strainer plugged
causes.confirm: Head pressure is sky-high and the water leaving the condenser is a scalding trickle (or zero); lifting the water-regulating valve stem by hand restores flow and drops head pressure immediately (the leaving water can be scalding; never jumper out the high-pressure switch to keep running).
causes.fix:
Shut the water supply valve and pull and clean the Y-strainer screen ahead of the water-regulating valve first
(rust and pipe scale plug it constantly). Then check the WRV adjustment and capillary bellows: if the bellows has
lost its charge or the disc is seized, rebuild or replace the water-regulating valve (its sensing line taps the high side, so pump down or recover
before you disconnect it).
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Water-cooled condenser water-regulating valve stuck open or seat eroded (flows continuously in off cycle)
keywords: wrv leaking water in off cycle
causes.confirm: Cold water continues rushing through the condenser to drain several minutes after the compressor shuts off, and running head pressure sits below target.
causes.fix:
Turn the WRV adjustment screw to raise the opening pressure. If water still runs with the compressor off, debris
is lodged under the seat or the brass seat/rubber disc is wire-drawn — shut off water, disassemble the valve, and
install a seat-and-disc rebuild kit or replace the WRV.

causes.name: Water- or glycol-cooled condenser tubes scaled or fouled (high approach with normal flow)
causes.confirm: Water is flowing normally (the leaving water sits well below condensing temperature and the water-regulating valve is not starved), yet condensing temperature is more than 18–20 °F above the leaving water because mineral scale coats the tube walls.
causes.fix:
First rule out the other causes of high head on the same water: high subcooling and a standing pressure above the PT chart point
to overcharge or air in the system, not scale (the approach alone can't tell them apart). If flow is normal and the approach is
high, circulate a descaling solution rated for the tube metal and approved by the condenser maker through the water side, then flush
and neutralize thoroughly.

causes.name: Condenser water or glycol flow lost (loop pump off or air-locked, closed isolating valve, plugged strainer, supply shut off)
causes.confirm: Head pressure is high, the leaving water or glycol is within a few degrees of condensing temperature, the water-regulating valve (if there is one) is not stuck, and nothing moves through the condenser.
causes.fix:
Shut the compressor off before the high-pressure switch trips again, then walk the water side from the condenser back: loop
pump running and turning the right way, isolating and balancing valves open, strainer clean, air purged, loop pressure and
expansion tank right, any 3-way or diverting valve in the right position; on a once-through supply, the shutoff valve and
supply pressure. Restore flow before you condemn the condenser or the valve.

causes.name: Semi-hermetic oil-pressure safety lockout (low oil, oil logged in evaporator, floodback dilution, or bad oil pump)
causes.confirm: The semi-hermetic compressor is off on its manual-reset oil failure control (reset button out on a mechanical control, lockout light on an electronic one); when reset, net oil pressure (oil pump pressure minus crankcase suction pressure) stays below 9–12 psid for 90–120 seconds.
causes.fix:
Never repeatedly reset an oil safety without gauges on the crankcase and oil pump port!
1. If the oil sight glass is empty: look for a refrigerant leak that carried oil out, or oil trapped in a cold
   evaporator / un-trapped suction riser (run a manual defrost to warm the coil and watch if oil returns before
   adding oil, or the crankcase will overfill).
2. If the sight glass is full and foaming violently: liquid refrigerant is flooding back (check TXV superheat,
   iced coil, or failed crankcase heater).
3. If the crankcase is full of clean oil and net oil pressure is still zero: the oil pump or pickup screen is
   failed.
causes.safety: Never jumper out an oil-pressure safety to keep a compressor running. If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Self-contained reach-in condensate evaporation pan overflowing (pan heater open, wick bad, or loop bypassed)
causes.confirm: The cabinet cools fine, but the condensate pan underneath the reach-in is brimming over onto the floor because its electric heater is open, its wicking pads are calcified/missing, or the hot-gas loop was bypassed.
causes.fix:
Wet-vac the pan dry, clean out slime and mineral crust, and check how the pan evaporates water: replace calcified
cardboard/fiber wicking pads in front of the condenser fan, or ohm the electric pan heater and its float/thermal
switch and replace if open. Also check door gaskets — a leaking door gasket makes more condensate than a working
pan heater can boil off!

causes.name: Prep-table rail hood left open, food pans missing, or rail air-curtain slot blocked/iced
causes.confirm: Food pans in the top rail read above 41 °F while pans are missing from the rail cutouts, the insulated hood is left open next to a hot grill, or oversized pans/ice block the cold air-curtain slot.
causes.fix:
Install every pan and divider bar in the rail (even empty pans must stay in place to close the air curtain),
unblock and defrost the supply/return air louvers along the rail, and train the kitchen crew to close the
insulated rail hood whenever not actively plating.

causes.name: Ice machine water supply shut off, saddle valve plugged, or inlet water filter clogged
causes.confirm: The water inlet valve energizes on fill, but little or no water enters the sump and the water filter gauge drops to zero under flow (or the supply stop valve is shut).
causes.fix:
Open the supply shutoff valve fully (replace any piercing saddle valve with a full-port ball tee), swap the
plugged water filter cartridge, flush the new cartridge to drain before connecting to the inlet valve, and clean
the inlet solenoid's mesh screen.

causes.name: Ice machine water inlet solenoid valve failed closed (open coil or plugged inlet screen — sump won't fill)
causes.confirm: Full water pressure is present at the inlet fitting and the controller sends voltage to the water inlet solenoid during fill, but no water passes through the valve.
causes.fix:
Shut off the water supply, disconnect the supply line and inspect the small mesh screen inside the inlet valve
body for sediment or carbon fines from a failed filter. If the screen is clean and voltage is present at the
coil with no flow, replace the water inlet solenoid valve assembly.

causes.name: Ice machine water inlet solenoid valve leaking through during freeze (warms sump and stretches freeze cycle)
causes.confirm: During the freeze cycle (with zero volts on the water inlet solenoid coil), fresh supply water continues running into the sump and overflowing down the standpipe drain.
causes.fix:
Verify the water inlet solenoid is not energized during freeze (stray voltage on the coil or a stuck relay holds it
open), then clean the seat or replace the weeping water inlet valve. A valve that leaks through the whole freeze keeps
feeding supply-temperature water into the chilled sump and can flood the bin if the drain clogs.

causes.name: Ice machine water-level float switch or conductivity probe fouled with mineral scale or stuck
causes.confirm: Mineral crust or slime coats the float stem or metal water-level probe pins, causing the machine to either stop filling early (dry sump) or fault out waiting for a water level it already reached.
causes.fix:
Pull the float assembly or conductivity probe housing, soak in ice-machine-safe descaler (phosphoric/citric acid),
wipe the stainless pins bright, and rinse thoroughly. On reed-type float switches, ohm the switch while sliding
the magnet float up and down and replace if it sticks or chatters.
causes.safety: Ice-machine cleaner and descaler are acids: gloves and eye protection, run them only in the machine's clean cycle with the bin emptied, rinse fully, and never mix them with sanitizer (hypochlorite) — the mix gives off chlorine gas.

causes.name: Ice machine water circulation pump failed, air-locked, or weak (no water flow over evaporator)
causes.confirm: The sump is full of water and the machine is in freeze, but little or no water flows out of the distribution tube across the evaporator grid.
causes.fix:
First pop the water distribution tube out and clean scale/slime out of its spray holes. If the pump isn't pumping:
meter voltage at the pump plug, spin the cooling fan/impeller by hand to check for seized bearings or scale on
the impeller, bleed any air lock in the discharge hose, or replace the circulation pump.

causes.name: Water curtain out of place or trough/hose leaking water out (sump runs dry before bridge forms)
causes.confirm: The sump fills to the mark at the start of freeze, but water splashes past a crooked curtain or leaks from a cracked trough/dump valve into the ice bin, starving the pump before the bridge finishes.
causes.fix:
Re-hang the plastic water curtain on both pivot pins so its bottom lip sits inside the trough, inspect the sump
trough and vinyl hoses for cracks, and verify the dump/purge valve (if used) seals tightly during the freeze
cycle.

causes.name: Heavy mineral scale on evaporator plate/grid or flaking nickel plating (slow freeze and sticking cubes)
causes.confirm: Chalky white mineral scale coats the evaporator cells and bridge area (acting as an insulator in freeze and a mechanical anchor in harvest), or bare copper shows where nickel plating has peeled.
causes.fix:
Run a full clean-and-descale cycle with nickel-safe ice machine cleaner (never use hydrochloric/muriatic acid or
wire brushes on nickel-plated evaporators!), scrub stubborn corners with a nylon pad, then sanitize. If the
nickel plating is blistering or peeling off the grid so ice locks into the bare metal, the evaporator must be
replaced.
causes.safety: Ice-machine cleaner and descaler are acids: gloves and eye protection, run them only in the machine's clean cycle with the bin emptied, rinse fully, and never mix them with sanitizer (hypochlorite) — the mix gives off chlorine gas.

causes.name: High incoming supply water temperature (long freeze cycles and low daily ice output)
causes.confirm: Everything on the refrigeration and water side checks out normal, but the water entering the machine measures above about 80 °F (often from a failed mop-sink mixing valve check valve or a line routed over a ceiling heater).
causes.fix:
Trace the cold water supply pipe: repair any leaking hot/cold mixing valve check valve in the galley that is
pushing hot water backward into the cold main, or reroute/insulate the supply line away from steam pipes and
kitchen hoods.

causes.name: Ice freezes into a solid slab and never harvests (thickness probe scaled/misadjusted or float harvest switch stuck)
causes.confirm: A full bridge forms and keeps growing into a solid block of ice over the evaporator without the controller ever switching from freeze to harvest.
causes.fix:
Switch the machine off and melt the slab off with warm water (never pry on the evaporator grid!).
- On conductivity thickness probes: clean the mineral film off the probe tip and its ground with
  nickel-safe cleaner, check the gap to the grid (about 1/8 in. is the factory setting), and run the maker's probe test
  (jumper or water-contact method) — it should start harvest after the maker's sensing delay (roughly 7–10 seconds).
- On float-switch machines (where the lower float ends the freeze): clean the float stem and test the
  switch with the machine's output test; on other makes use the maker's thickness-sensor test.

causes.name: Ice machine hot-gas harvest solenoid valve failed closed (enters harvest, but evaporator stays freezing cold)
keywords: hot gas valve bad on ice machine
causes.confirm: The controller enters harvest mode and turns off the water pump, but the tubing downstream of the hot-gas harvest valve and the evaporator stay cold so the ice slab never melts free.
causes.fix:
During harvest, meter line voltage at the hot-gas solenoid coil: if voltage is present and the valve stays cold,
check coil continuity and test with a solenoid magnet. Replace an open coil, or recover/pump down and replace a
mechanically stuck hot-gas harvest valve.
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Ice machine hot-gas harvest valve leaking through during freeze (slow freeze, high suction, hollow cubes)
keywords: hot gas valve leaking in freeze
causes.confirm: Five minutes into the freeze cycle (harvest coil de-energized), the discharge bypass tube downstream of the hot-gas harvest valve stays hot on an IR thermometer or pipe probe and one corner of the evaporator refuses to freeze properly.
causes.fix:
Confirm no stray voltage is on the harvest solenoid coil during freeze. Recover the refrigerant charge, replace
the leaking hot-gas harvest valve and liquid-line filter-drier, evacuate to 500 microns, and weigh in the exact
nameplate charge (ice machines are critically charged!).
causes.safety: If the nameplate refrigerant is R-290, R-600a (A3) or an A2L blend: no flame, grinder or arcing probe near an open or leaking circuit, ventilate first, recover with flammable-rated equipment, purge with dry nitrogen before and while brazing, and charge only the nameplate weight.

causes.name: Ice machine harvest-assist air pump, probe, or mechanical pusher solenoid failed
causes.confirm: In harvest, the hot-gas valve opens and the evaporator warms enough to loosen the ice sheet, but the harvest-assist air pump isn't blowing (or the mechanical pusher solenoid doesn't push the slab off) before harvest times out.
causes.fix:
On air-assist units: check that the small air compressor vibrates in harvest, inspect the silicone air tube for
splits or pop-offs, and replace the pump if its diaphragm is torn. On mechanical push-rod units: clean scale off
the harvest-assist plunger so it slides freely in its sleeve, and ohm the solenoid coil.

causes.name: Ice bin thermostat, curtain switch, or optical bin sensor stuck (false "bin full" shutdown or overfilling bin)
keywords: bin full light on empty bin
causes.confirm: The machine sits idle on "Bin Full" while the bin is empty (or keeps making ice after the bin is packed all the way up into the evaporator drop chute).
causes.fix:
- Mechanical curtain/lever switch: check that the water curtain hangs free and operates the magnet reed switch
  when swung open and closed; ohm the switch.
- Optical/ultrasonic bin sensors: wipe mineral scale off both lenses with descaler and a soft cloth.
- Capillary bin thermostat: make sure the bulb isn't touching the cold evaporator frame (which tricks it into
  shutting off early), and verify it opens when packed in ice and closes when warmed in your hand; replace if
  dead.

causes.name: Outdoor condenser has no head-pressure control and is running in cold air (starved TXV, low suction, iced coil)
keywords: outdoor condensing unit no flooding valve
trips on low pressure in winter
causes.confirm: Head pressure follows the outdoor air — condensing temperature only 10–20 °F over ambient and far below ~85 °F (about 180 psig on R-404A) — and the unit has no flooding valve, fan-cycling switch or variable-speed fan. The liquid line flashes and the TXV starves until the weather warms.
causes.fix:
Don't treat it as low charge: adding refrigerant to a head problem that follows the weather overcharges the unit the first warm
day. Fit low-ambient head-pressure control sized for the coldest air: a flooding valve with the maker's winter charge and a
receiver that holds the whole charge (fan cycling alone seldom holds head much below 0 °F), an insulated receiver
and liquid line, a crankcase heater and a wind baffle.

causes.name: Supply water or room air too cold for hot-gas harvest (evaporator warms slowly, slab hangs or harvest runs long)
causes.confirm: The harvest valve opens and its outlet pipe gets hot, the evaporator is clean, yet the plate warms far slower than the maker's harvest time. Supply water is under ~45 °F or the room under ~50 °F, and the slab drops normally once either is warmed.
causes.fix:
Bring the room and water into the maker's operating range (typically about 45–100 °F air and 45–90 °F water): move the machine to a
heated space and don't feed it straight off an outdoor or snow-melt line (run the supply through the warm room first). Then
confirm the TXV bulb is tight and the valve isn't stuck open (either keeps the plate cold in harvest) and, if the board allows,
lengthen the harvest timer one step. Remote-condenser machines also need their low-ambient (flooding valve) kit.

causes.name: Harvest-termination thermistor loose, out of position, drifted, open or shorted (harvest ends too soon, or runs to the backup timer)
causes.confirm: The harvest valve opens and the evaporator warms, but the board ends harvest before the slab is free (sensor reading warm or loose) or runs to its backup timer with melted, wet ice (sensor reading cold or open); the thermistor's resistance doesn't match the maker's chart at the tube temperature, or the board shows a thermistor or backup-timer alarm.
causes.fix:
Power off. Re-seat the thermistor tight against the tube where the maker locates it, insulate it, and check its resistance against
the maker's chart (open or shorted = replace). Don't lengthen the harvest timer to hide a bad sensor.

causes.name: Defrost heater breaker or fuse tripped (shorted or grounded element, wet junction box, chafed lead)
causes.confirm: The compressor and fans run, but the heater branch breaker or fuse is open (or trips the moment defrost starts); with the heater leads off, the breaker holds and one or more elements read a short to the sheath with a megohmmeter.
causes.fix:
Lock out and tag the heater circuit. Disconnect the heater leads and megger each element to its sheath (megohms is good); replace the
grounded element, dry out and repair a wet junction box, and replace chafed leads. Reset once with the leads reconnected; if it trips again
the fault is still in the wiring. Never upsize the breaker or fuse.
causes.safety: A grounded heater element is a shock and fire hazard — never reset a breaker repeatedly on it.

causes.name: Off-cycle (air) defrost can't clear the coil — box held under ~34 °F, fans stopping in the off cycle, or compressor restarting too soon
causes.confirm: A medium-temp cooler with no heaters or hot gas ices up while the box sits near or under 34 °F, because the compressor barely rests and the coil never warms above freezing between cycles.
causes.fix:
Raise the setpoint (or fix the probe or thermostat that holds the box too cold) so the coil can reach 35–40 °F in the off cycle; make
sure the evaporator fans keep running with the compressor off (air defrost needs them); check the LPC cut-in so the compressor stays
off until the coil is above freezing, or add a timed off-cycle. If the box has to run below 34 °F it needs electric or hot-gas defrost.

causes.name: Hot-gas defrost too weak or slow — low head in cold air, hot-gas regulator or check valve sticking, or short charge
keywords: coil still iced after hot gas defrost
hot gas defrost takes too long
causes.confirm: The hot-gas valve opens and its outlet line gets hot, yet the coil warms slowly or stalls and the defrost ends on its time limit with ice left; head pressure collapses when defrost starts in cold air.
causes.fix:
Check that head pressure holds during defrost (the low-ambient control must stay in service), that the hot-gas pressure regulator or
defrost bypass is set per the maker, that the check valves around the TXV and in the pan loop aren't stuck, that the liquid-return
path isn't blocked, and that the charge is enough for a defrost (hot-gas defrost uses charge). Don't just lengthen the fail-safe time.

causes.name: Electronic controller settings wrong or reset (setpoint, defrost interval, length or termination, fan delay, drip time)
causes.confirm: A parameter read-out disagrees with the maker's sheet or a saved copy (interval, duration, termination temperature, fan delay, drip time, setpoint or differential, defrost type), often after a power event or someone using the keypad, while the probe checks out.
causes.fix:
Read every parameter against the maker's table or a saved copy, restore the site values, lock the keypad and save a copy. If a forced
defrost does nothing at all, the output relay or controller is bad instead.

causes.name: Box running too cold — setpoint or differential set low, thermostat or relay stuck on, or product in the evaporator's cold air stream
causes.confirm: The box sits more than 4 °F under setpoint with the probe reading true; the controller output never opens (welded relay or contactor, stuck thermostat) or the setpoint or differential is low, or cartons sit in the evaporator discharge.
causes.fix:
Check the setpoint and differential, then meter the controller output and relay or contactor to see whether it opens at cut-out (on a
pump-down system, also that the liquid-line solenoid closes). Move product at least 18 in. from the evaporator discharge and off the coil
face. If the box still can't hold above 33 °F with the control satisfied, add or reset an EPR or fan cycling.

causes.name: Drain line freezes with the heater working — no trap or trap outside the freezer, poor slope, cold gap, or air drawn up the line
causes.confirm: The heat tape is warm and draws current, but the line still freezes solid in one spot (a run with no heat, a dip that holds water, a gap where the tape isn't touching the pipe, or a missing or cold trap letting cold air up the line).
causes.fix:
Thaw the line, then fix the cause: continuous pitch (at least 1/4 in. per foot) with no dips, heat tape in contact the whole way to the
floor drain, a trap outside the box in the warm space (never inside), the air break sealed, and the pan heater element seated. Don't
just re-thaw it every week.
causes.safety: Lock out the drain-heater circuit before the thaw, and see the walk-in entry precautions (prop the door, test the inside release).

causes.name: No hot water or steam reaching the unit — the loop, pump, boiler or steam main is not delivering
causes.confirm: The pipe feeding the unit is cold or barely warm ahead of the unit's own valve, and other units on the same loop or main are short too.
causes.fix:
The unit is not the problem yet: work upstream. Switch to the Hydronic system (circulator, zone valve, air
in the main, boiler or heat-recovery source) or the Steam system (boiler pressure, main vents, reducing
station). If only this unit's branch is cold, look for a closed branch valve or an air-bound high point on
the runout. Come back to the unit once hot water or steam is at its valve.

causes.name: 2-pipe fan coil still on chilled water — the building has not been changed over to heating
causes.confirm: The supply pipe at the unit is colder than the room and may sweat. The whole 2-pipe riser or building carries chilled water.
causes.fix:
A 2-pipe system heats or cools, not both. Ask the plant operator whether changeover to heating has been
done and when. If it has, check the changeover valves at the plant and that the chiller is off and the heat
exchanger or boiler is on line. Expect a few hours for a big loop to swing from chilled to hot. Don't open
hot water into a chiller circuit.

causes.name: 2-pipe fan coil's changeover sensor loose, off the pipe or failed (unit thinks it's in cooling)
keywords: unit in cooling with hot water
causes.confirm: Hot water is in the supply pipe, but the unit's control reads cooling. The strap-on switch or sensor is loose, sitting on insulation, or meters wrong.
causes.fix:
Clamp the sensor tight to bare supply pipe ahead of the valve (on the side that sees water even when the
valve is shut, or the unit will never sense the change). Replace a switch or sensor that reads wrong with
the pipe hot. Then check the unit runs its heating sequence: valve opens on a call for heat, fan follows.

causes.name: 4-pipe fan coil's chilled-water valve passing or stuck open while it heats
keywords: heating and cooling at the same time
causes.confirm: The unit heats weakly while the chilled-water pipes at the cooling coil are cold or sweating. The cooling valve passes water with no cooling call.

causes.name: Unit's isolation or balancing valve closed or throttled shut
causes.confirm: Supply is hot up to the unit, the coil and return are cold, and a ball, gate or balancing valve on the unit's supply or return is shut or set at zero.
causes.fix:
Open it slowly. If it is a balancing valve, set it back to the position on the balancing report (or its
memory stop) instead of wide open, or the units beyond it will starve. If a gate valve's handle turns but
flow doesn't come back, the gate has dropped off the stem: isolate and replace the valve.

causes.name: Steam supply valve at the unit closed, throttled on one-pipe, or disc off the stem
causes.confirm: Steam is hot up to the valve, the unit stays cold, and the valve is shut or part-open, or its handwheel turns with no change (disc off the stem).
causes.fix:
Crack the valve open and let the unit warm and drain, listening for hammer, before you open it fully (shut it
at once if it bangs). On one-pipe steam a supply valve is either fully open or fully closed; throttling it
traps condensate in the radiator and causes hammer. If the handwheel turns freely without lifting the disc,
isolate the branch, let it cool and replace the valve.
causes.safety: Never open a steam valve bonnet or union while the line holds pressure. Close, cool and confirm 0 psig.

causes.name: Supply and return reversed at the unit, or the control valve fitted against its flow arrow
causes.confirm: Since it was installed or re-piped, the unit has never heated right. Tracing the pipes shows the return main on the coil inlet, a steam unit fed from the bottom, or a valve fitted against its arrow (often chatters or bangs as it nears shut).
causes.fix:
Re-pipe so supply enters where the unit's tag says (top on a steam coil, with the trap on the bottom outlet)
and the valve body arrow points with the flow. On a hot-water coil reversed flow costs capacity and puts the
vent at the wrong end; on steam it floods the coil and hammers. Check the vent and trap are at the right ends
afterwards.
causes.safety: Isolate both pipes and relieve to 0 psig before re-piping; on steam, let it cool first.

causes.name: Coil, radiator or baseboard air-bound (air trapped at its high point)
causes.confirm: Air hisses or sputters from the unit's coin vent or bleed before water comes. The coil or radiator is cold at the top and warm below.
causes.fix:
Bleed the unit at its highest vent, slowly, with a rag or a hose to a container, until solid water or glycol
comes. Do it again after it has run an hour. If it keeps coming back, the loop is the problem — low fill
pressure, a failed automatic vent, or a leak drawing air in (Hydronic system, "Air keeps returning"). On a
glycol loop, top up with premix, not water.
causes.safety: Hot water and glycol scald. Open the vent slowly and keep your face clear.

causes.name: Coil tubes or the unit's strainer plugged with sludge, scale or debris
causes.confirm: Supply hot, valve open, bleeds solid water, yet some tubes or sections stay cold and the return runs far colder than it should.
causes.fix:
Isolate the unit, relieve it and clean any strainer ahead of the valve. Back-flush the coil from the return
side into a container, not a floor drain: keep glycol for recovery, and put a backflow preventer on any hose
from the domestic water. If sections stay cold, the coil is scaled or sludged — replace it or have it
cleaned. Then find the source: old glycol breaking down, corrosion in the loop, or no dirt separator.
causes.safety: Isolate both pipes and relieve to 0 psig before opening a strainer or a union. Catch and keep glycol.

causes.name: Coil frozen or split (cold air reached it with no heat on, or a freeze-stat didn't trip)
causes.confirm: Ice or slush in the coil, bulged return bends or a split tube, often in a vestibule, a loading dock or next to an outdoor air opening. On steam, the bottom of the coil freezes first where condensate held.
causes.fix:
Isolate and drain the coil before thawing. Thaw slowly with warm air, then pressure-test before you put it
back in service; replace a split coil. Then find out how cold air reached a coil with no heat on it: a stuck
outdoor air damper, a fan running with the valve shut, a door held open, condensate held in a steam coil,
or weak glycol. On steam, see the vacuum breaker and trap causes.
causes.safety: Treat a frozen coil as split. Isolate it before it thaws, or it floods the space.

causes.name: Leak at the unit — valve packing, union, air vent or a corroded coil
causes.confirm: Water, glycol or steam dripping from the unit's valve stem, a union, its vent, or the coil itself, not from a pipe elsewhere.
causes.fix:
A packing leak on hot water: snug the packing nut a quarter turn with the valve open, or repack it; on steam,
close, cool and confirm 0 psig first. A union or fitting: isolate, relieve and remake it. A vent: clean or replace it. A pinhole or corroded return bend: isolate the
unit and replace the coil (a patch rarely lasts). Check the loop's water or glycol treatment if coils are
pitting from the inside.
causes.safety: Hot water and glycol scald. On steam, don't touch a leaking packing nut or vent while it holds pressure.

causes.name: Control valve actuator or zone valve head failed (valve stays closed on a call)
causes.confirm: The control signal reaches the actuator, but it doesn't move. Opening the valve by hand (manual lever or override) brings heat on hot water or glycol; on steam, crack it open slowly and listen for hammer.
causes.fix:
Check the actuator's own fuse or end stop if it has one, then replace the motor head or actuator to match the
valve body (same stroke, signal and spring-return direction). On a zone valve with a removable head, change
the head only. Make sure the manual lever is released afterwards.
causes.safety: Lock out the head's power before you pull it. Most heads come off without draining the line, but never open the valve body or bonnet under pressure; on steam, cool and confirm 0 psig.

causes.name: Control valve stem or body seized closed, or the plug off the stem
causes.confirm: The actuator strokes (or the head comes off) but the stem won't move, or it moves and no water passes even fully open.
causes.fix:
Isolate the unit and work the stem by hand; scale often frees with a few strokes. If it won't free, replace the
cartridge or the valve body. Check the loop's treatment if valves are scaling up across the building.
causes.safety: Isolate both sides and relieve the pressure before you pull a cartridge or bonnet; on steam, cool and confirm 0 psig.

causes.name: Control valve stuck open, leaking through, or left in manual open (unit heats with no call)
causes.confirm: The room overheats with no call. The valve is warm on both sides with the actuator shut, or its manual lever is latched open.
causes.fix:
Release a latched manual lever. If the actuator is closed and the valve still passes, the seat is cut or
scaled — replace the cartridge or valve. If the actuator is being told to open with no call, it's the control
(see "Thermostat on a cold wall" and "Thermostats crossed").
causes.safety: Isolate and relieve the pressure before you open the valve body; on steam, cool and confirm 0 psig.

causes.name: No control signal at the valve actuator (controller output, wiring, or the unit's 24 V transformer)
causes.confirm: The thermostat or controller calls for heat, but no 24 V or modulating signal arrives at the actuator. On hot water or glycol, powering the actuator directly at the voltage on its label (some zone valve heads are 120 V) opens the valve and brings heat. On steam, don't power it open onto a cold coil; the missing signal is the finding.
causes.fix:
Trace back from the actuator: the controller's output terminal, the wiring, any relay between them. On a
building automation point, check that it isn't left in manual or overridden closed. Repair the wire or
replace the output relay or controller.
causes.safety: A 120 V zone valve head is line voltage; lock out before you touch its wiring. On steam, never power a valve open onto a cold coil.

causes.name: Thermostat or unit sensor in the warm air path (satisfies before the room is warm)
causes.confirm: The unit runs a few minutes and shuts off while most of the room stays cold. The sensor sits in the unit's discharge, on a warm surface or near another heat source.
causes.fix:
Move the thermostat to an inside wall at about 5 ft, out of the discharge and away from lights and equipment,
or aim the unit's louvers away from it. On a fan coil with a return-air sensor and a cycling fan, the sensor
reads its own warm cabinet when the fan stops; set the fan to run on while occupied, or use a wall sensor.

causes.name: Thermostat on a cold outside wall or in a draft (unit runs on and overheats the room)
causes.confirm: The room is warm but the thermostat still calls. It sits on a cold outside wall, by a door, or in a draft from a leaky wall box.
causes.fix:
Seal the wall box behind the thermostat (a cold draft through the conduit fools it), then move it to an
inside wall if it still reads low. Check its reading against a thermometer beside it.

causes.name: Thermostats or valves cross-wired between units (one room's thermostat runs the other unit)
causes.confirm: Turning one room's thermostat up starts the unit in the next room. Usually just after new units, thermostats or controls were installed.
causes.fix:
Label both ends of each thermostat and valve wire and correct the terminations at the controller or relay
panel. Then test each zone on its own.

causes.name: Fan-delay switch or low-limit interlock stuck open (coil hot, fan never starts)
keywords: fan wont start with hot coil
causes.confirm: The coil or element is hot and the unit calls, but no voltage reaches the fan. The strap-on temperature switch, pressure switch or snap-disc fan switch stays open with the pipe hot.
causes.fix:
Check it is clamped to bare pipe. Prove it without a jumper: lock out and ohm the switch with the pipe hot (it
should read closed), and read the voltage at the motor with the unit live. Replace the switch with one of the
same closing temperature. Never jumper it, even to test: the fan would blow cold air when the loop is cold,
and on steam it can freeze the coil.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag before you ohm the switch or reach into the fan section.

causes.name: Fan-delay switch stuck closed, jumpered or off the pipe (fan blows cold air when the loop is cold)
causes.confirm: The fan runs and blows cold air while the supply pipe is cold. The fan-delay switch is closed with the pipe cold, jumpered out, or hanging off the pipe.
causes.fix:
Refit the switch to bare pipe and replace it if it reads closed cold. Then work why the pipe is cold — the
loop or steam main is not delivering (see "No hot water or steam reaching the unit"). The cold blast is only
the symptom the switch is meant to stop.

causes.name: Freeze-stat tripped by cold air at the coil (outside-air damper open, coil starved of heat, or a draft)
causes.confirm: The freeze-stat is tripped and the air at the coil really is cold. Look for an outside-air damper open, a door held open beside the unit, or no hot water at the coil.
causes.fix:
Before resetting, check the coil for ice or split tubes. Close or repair a stuck outside-air damper, find out
why the coil had no heat (valve, air-bound, loop cold), then reset. A unit that trips every cold morning has a
real cold air path — fix that rather than moving the stat.
causes.safety: Never jumper a freeze-stat. Isolate a coil you find split before it thaws.

causes.name: Freeze-stat failed open or out of calibration (trips with warm air at the coil)
causes.confirm: The freeze-stat stays open with the air at the coil well above its setting. The capillary is kinked, broken, or lost its charge.
causes.fix:
Replace it with one of the same setting (usually about 35–38 °F) and route the capillary across the coil face,
off cold metal. Test it before you leave by chilling the element.
causes.safety: Lock out before you replace it. Never jumper a freeze-stat to keep the unit running.

causes.name: Fan motor failed (open winding or burnt out)
causes.confirm: Full voltage at the motor leads, the fan turns freely by hand and the capacitor tests good, but the motor doesn't run. The windings read open.
causes.fix:
Replace the motor with one of the same voltage, speed, rotation, frame and mounting. An ECM motor (a control
module on its end) has no capacitor: with line voltage and its control signal both present, replace the module
or the motor. On a fan coil it is often
quickest to swap the whole fan deck and repair the old one at the shop. Re-tighten the blade or wheel on the
shaft and check rotation before you close it up.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag before you reach in.

causes.name: Fan motor run capacitor failed
causes.confirm: The fan hums or sits still with voltage on it, turns freely by hand (and may run if you spin it), and the capacitor reads low or open.
causes.fix:
Replace the capacitor with the same µF and an equal or higher voltage rating. If the motor still won't start,
check its windings.
causes.safety: Discharge the capacitor before you touch its terminals.

causes.name: Fan motor bearings dry, worn or seized (motor drags, overheats and cycles on its overload)
causes.confirm: The fan drags, grinds or won't turn by hand with power locked out. The motor may run hot, stop on its internal overload and restart later.
causes.fix:
Oil the bearings if the motor has oil ports and turns freely afterwards. A motor that stays stiff or grinds
needs replacing. Fan-coil and unit-heater motors need periodic oiling where they have ports.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag before you spin or oil the motor.

causes.name: Fan relay, speed switch or the unit's control board not powering the fan
causes.confirm: The unit has power and a call, the safeties and fan-delay switch are closed, but no voltage leaves the fan relay, speed switch or board to the motor.
causes.fix:
Follow the fan circuit from the supply through the switch or relay to the motor. Check the relay coil gets its
signal, then the contacts pass voltage. Replace a burnt speed switch, a relay that won't close, or a board whose
fan output stays dead with the call present.
causes.safety: Live voltage in the fan circuit. Lock out before you touch the relay, speed switch or board.

causes.name: Fan blade loose on the shaft, blower wheel caked with dirt, or blade rubbing
causes.confirm: The motor runs at speed but little air comes off. The blade slips on the shaft, the wheel is caked with dirt, or the blade rubs the housing.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Clean a caked wheel in place or pull it and wash it. Re-seat a loose blade on the shaft's flat and
tighten the set screw; replace a worn shaft or blade. Straighten or replace a bent blade, and re-center it so it
doesn't rub.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag before you reach in.

causes.name: Fan on the wrong speed (stuck on low, wrong motor tap, or set low)
causes.confirm: The fan runs but only on low. The speed switch, the motor tap or the control's fan-speed setting is on low, or a speed relay is stuck.
causes.fix:
Set the speed the unit is designed to run on, re-terminate the motor on the right tap, or replace a stuck speed
switch or relay. A motor that runs slow on every tap is failing.
causes.safety: Lock out before you move a motor tap or open the speed switch.

causes.name: Fan turning backwards (after a motor change, or two leads swapped on a three-phase motor)
causes.confirm: The fan runs at speed with normal amps but moves little air, and it turns against the arrow on the housing or motor. Usually right after a motor change or rewiring.
causes.fix:
On a three-phase motor, swap any two of the three motor leads. On a single-phase motor, follow the motor's
wiring diagram to reverse it, or fit a motor of the right rotation. Check that a propeller blade or blower
wheel was not fitted the wrong way round on the shaft.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag before you change motor leads.

causes.name: Unit filter plugged
causes.confirm: Weak air off a unit whose fan runs normally, a filter loaded with dust or lint, and the airflow comes back with the filter out.
causes.fix:
Replace or wash the filter. Fan coils in housing, hospitals and dusty shops need more frequent changes. Then look
at the coil face behind it — a filter left too long lets lint pack the fins too.

causes.name: Coil fins matted with dust or lint, or crushed
causes.confirm: The coil face or baseboard fins are matted with dust or lint, or crushed flat, while the filter (if any) is clean.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Vacuum the fins from the air-leaving side, then brush or wash with low-pressure water or coil cleaner
if the unit allows it. Comb out crushed fins. Clean baseboard fins with a soft brush and vacuum. Fix the filter
routine so it doesn't come back.

causes.name: Air path blocked — grille or damper shut, or furniture, drapes, stock or a cover in the way
causes.confirm: The baseboard damper is closed, a grille is shut or covered, or furniture, drapes or stock sit tight against the unit.
causes.fix:
Clear the air path: open the baseboard damper, open the grilles, and keep furniture and stock a few inches clear
of baseboard and a few feet clear of a unit heater's inlet and throw. Drapes should stop above a baseboard, not
over it. On electric heat a blocked heater trips its limit and is a fire hazard — clear it before you leave.
causes.safety: Electric heaters covered by drapes, bedding or stock are a fire risk. Clear them every time.

causes.name: Warm air stratifying at the ceiling (unit heater hung too high, louvers aimed up, or no downturn)
causes.confirm: The unit heater heats normally, but the air near the roof is much warmer than at the floor. The unit hangs above its rated mounting height or its louvers blow flat or up.
causes.fix:
Aim horizontal louvers down toward the floor and along outside walls, all units blowing the same way round the
space. Fit a downturn nozzle on a vertical unit. If the unit hangs above its rated height, lower it or add a
recirculation duct from near the floor to its inlet, or a ceiling fan to push the warm air down.
causes.safety: Work at height from a lift or a secured ladder, with the unit locked out before you touch the louvers.

causes.name: Steam trap at the unit failed closed, or its strainer plugged (coil waterlogged)
causes.confirm: Steam is hot up to the unit, the bottom of the coil and the line to the trap are cold, and the trap is silent and cold on both sides.
causes.fix:
Isolate the unit and let it cool to 0 psig. Clean the strainer ahead of the trap first — a plugged screen is
the most common cause. Then service the trap: replace the thermostatic element, the float or bucket mechanism,
or the whole trap. Check the trap is big enough for the unit's start-up load and sits at least a foot below
the coil outlet.
causes.safety: Never open a trap, strainer or union while the line holds steam. Close, cool and confirm 0 psig.

causes.name: Steam trap at the unit failed open (blowing steam into the return)
causes.confirm: The trap hisses or roars without cycling and its outlet is as hot as the steam. The unit itself may heat fine while units further along starve and the return runs hot.
causes.fix:
Isolate, cool to 0 psig and replace the trap's internals or the trap. A blowing trap wastes steam and can
pressurize the return so other traps can't drain. Test the other traps on the same return while you are there.
causes.safety: Never open a trap while the line holds steam. Close, cool and confirm 0 psig.

causes.name: Steam unit's or radiator's air vent stuck closed (unit air-bound, won't fill with steam)
causes.confirm: Steam reaches the unit, but part of it stays cold and its air vent never hisses as it heats. On a two-pipe unit, a thermostatic air vent on the coil is shut.
causes.fix:
Close the supply, let it cool and replace the vent (a clogged or painted vent rarely cleans up well). Fit it at
the end opposite the supply, above the water line.
causes.safety: Watch it, don't unscrew it hot. Close the supply, cool and confirm 0 psig before removing a vent.

causes.name: Modulated steam coil holding condensate — vacuum breaker missing, plugged or stuck shut
causes.confirm: The coil hammers and its bottom runs cold when the valve throttles, then heats when the valve is wide open. There is no vacuum breaker on the coil outlet, or it is plugged or painted over.
causes.fix:
Fit or replace a vacuum breaker at the coil's condensate outlet ahead of the trap, and make sure the trap drains
by gravity to a vented return. With a modulating valve, the steam in the coil can fall below the return pressure
and condensate won't leave on its own. In freezing air, this is how steam coils split.
causes.safety: Close the steam supply, let it cool and confirm 0 psig before you open the coil outlet or fit a vacuum breaker.

causes.name: Steam unit's condensate piping wrong — no drop to the trap, outlet pocketed or lifted, or unit not pitched
causes.confirm: Hammer and a cold bottom on the coil while the trap tests good. The outlet runs level or rises to the trap, there is no drop between coil and trap, or the radiator tilts away from its return.
causes.fix:
Re-pipe so the condensate drops at least a foot from the coil outlet to the trap, and the trap discharges down to
the return. Shim or re-hang the radiator so it pitches toward its outlet. Never lift condensate after a modulated
coil without a pump.
causes.safety: Close the steam supply, let it cool and confirm 0 psig before you open any condensate piping.

causes.name: Electric heating element open (one or all elements burnt out)
causes.confirm: Power reaches the elements, but they draw little or no current and an element reads open end to end.
causes.fix:
Replace the element or the heater section with one of the same voltage and wattage. Then ask why it failed: a
heater rated below its supply, a blocked or covered heater, or a fan that stopped. A new element on the same fault
won't last.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag, and verify dead on every leg before you touch the element terminals.

causes.name: Electric heating element shorted to its sheath or cabinet (shock and fire hazard)
causes.confirm: With power locked out and a lead lifted, an element reads a low resistance to its sheath or the cabinet.
causes.fix:
Take the heater out of service and replace the element or the heater section with one of the same voltage and
wattage. Look for moisture, a rubbed lead or a cracked element seal that let it ground.
causes.safety: A grounded element can energize the cabinet. Keep the breaker off and tagged until it is replaced.

causes.name: Three-phase electric heater with one leg out (a blown fuse, a dead contactor pole or a lost phase)
causes.confirm: On a three-phase heater one supply leg reads low or zero amps while the other two are normal, and the elements ohm good.
causes.fix:
Lock out and check the heater's fuses, then each contactor pole (voltage in and out on every leg with it pulled
in), then the supply at the disconnect. Replace a blown fuse with the same rating only after finding why it
blew (a grounded element, loose lug or failing pole).
causes.safety: Lock out and tag, and verify dead on all three legs before you touch fuses or contactor terminals.

causes.name: Electric heater overheating and cycling on its high limit (fan weak or stopped, or the heater blocked)
causes.confirm: The heater heats, a limit opens and recloses every few minutes, and the cabinet runs very hot. The airflow across it is weak or the heater is covered.
causes.fix:
Treat the limit as the messenger. Restore the airflow: a dead or slow fan, a dirty filter or fins, a closed
damper, or something covering the heater. Then check the heater isn't rated below its supply voltage. Replace the
limit only if it opens with the heater running cool.
causes.safety: An electric heater cycling on its limit is overheating. Don't jumper the limit.

causes.name: Electric heater high limit or thermal cutoff open (failed, or a one-shot cutoff blown)
causes.confirm: The elements read good, but a limit or thermal cutoff reads open with the heater cool. A manual-reset limit has its button out.
causes.fix:
Find out why it opened before replacing it — a one-shot cutoff blows only when the heater got far too hot (fan
failure, a covered heater, a welded contactor). Fix that, then reset or replace the limit with one of the same
rating.
causes.safety: Never bypass a limit to get heat.

causes.name: Heater contactor or relay not closing (coil open or contacts burnt)
causes.confirm: The heater is called, but its contactor doesn't pull in, or it pulls in and a pole passes no voltage.
causes.fix:
Check the coil voltage and resistance. Replace a contactor with an open coil or burnt contacts, rated for the
heater's current (resistive load). Look at its wire terminals for heat damage and re-terminate.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag, and verify dead on every leg before you touch the contactor; turning the call off does not kill its line side.

causes.name: Heater contactor contacts welded shut (heater won't shut off)
causes.confirm: The heater stays on with no call. The contactor stays closed with its coil dead.
causes.fix:
Replace the contactor. Check why it welded: an undersized contactor, loose terminals, or a heater drawing more
than it should. Check the limits work, since they were the only thing stopping it.
causes.safety: A heater that won't shut off is a fire risk. Kill its breaker until it's fixed.

causes.name: Line-voltage thermostat failed open (won't pass power at any setting)
causes.confirm: Line voltage reaches the thermostat, but none comes out of its load side even at the highest setting.
causes.fix:
Replace it with a line-voltage thermostat rated for the heater's voltage and current. Use a double-pole one on
240 V so the off position kills both legs. Check the wire terminals for heat damage.
causes.safety: Line voltage at the wall — lock out the breaker before you open the thermostat.

causes.name: Line-voltage thermostat stuck closed (heater runs at every setting)
causes.confirm: The heater runs at every setting, and the thermostat passes full voltage even at its lowest.
causes.fix:
Replace the thermostat with one rated for the heater's current. A stat that welded may have been undersized for
the load — check the heater's amps against its rating.
causes.safety: Line voltage at the wall — lock out the breaker before you open the thermostat.

causes.name: Electric heater rated for a higher voltage than its supply (240 V heater on 208 V gives about 75 % heat)
causes.confirm: The heater works but is weak. Its nameplate says 240 V (or 480 V) and the supply at it reads 208 V (or 277 V). Output follows the square of voltage — about three-quarters of its rating for a 240 V heater on 208 V, about a third for a 480 V heater on 277 V.
causes.fix:
Replace the heater or its elements with ones rated for the actual supply, or add heaters to make up the shortfall.
The reverse — a heater rated below its supply — overheats and burns out elements, so check that while you are at
it.
causes.safety: Lock out and tag before you open the heater. Meter the supply with a rated meter.

causes.name: Radiant floor or panel covered or cut off from the room (rugs, new flooring, stock, missing insulation above)
causes.confirm: The radiant loop carries hot water and heats evenly, but the room stays cool. Thick rugs or pads, new flooring, or stored stock sit on the floor, or the insulation above a ceiling panel is missing.
causes.fix:
Lift the covering and see whether the room recovers. Thick pads and rugs can cut a floor's output a lot; use thin
ones. Over a ceiling panel, restore the insulation on top so the heat goes down into the room.

causes.name: Radiant loop supply too cool — the mixing or reset target is set too low, or its outdoor sensor reads wrong
causes.confirm: The radiant manifold supply runs only lukewarm, and the mixing or reset control is asking for that low a temperature — its curve is set too low or its outdoor sensor reads warm — while the boiler side is hot.
causes.fix:
Read the mixing or injection control's target and its outdoor sensor. Raise the curve or fix the sensor, then
check the mixing valve or injection pump actually follows the control (see the Hydronic system's mixing valve
and reset causes). Keep floor surface temperature limits in mind when you raise it.

causes.name: Low refrigerant charge (leak)
causes.confirm: Superheat high with subcooling low (fixed orifice), or subcooling low with the TXV wide open (high superheat); bubbles in the sight glass; then find the leak.
causes.fix:
Find the leak before adding refrigerant: electronic detector along every joint, valve core and coil, bubbles
to pinpoint, UV dye if it's slow. Repair, pressure-test with dry nitrogen, evacuate to 500 microns with a
decay test, and weigh in the nameplate charge plus the manufacturer's line-set adjustment (liquid-charge
blends), then trim to the subcooling (TXV) or superheat (piston) target. With a receiver there is no
subcooling target — trim to a clear sight glass and a receiver level in range at steady head pressure.
Replace the filter-drier whenever the system is opened.
causes.safety: R-32, R-454B (A2L) and R-290/R-600a (A3) are flammable — no ignition sources, ventilate, use a rated recovery machine and leak detector, and follow the nameplate before brazing.
