Pressure-test with nitrogen through a regulator and never above the lowest test pressure on the nameplate; never use air or oxygen. Fill a recovery cylinder to 80 % by weight at most.
causes.notes: With a TXV a small shortage hides — the valve opens up and holds superheat, so subcooling falling is the first tell. Superheat only climbs once the valve is wide open.

causes.name: Refrigerant overcharge
causes.confirm: High head pressure and high subcooling with a clean condenser and a fan that runs, and a standing pressure that matches the PT chart (rules out air in the system).
causes.fix:
Recover refrigerant to a recovery cylinder in small amounts until subcooling (TXV) or superheat (fixed
orifice) reaches target at steady conditions. With a receiver, recover until the receiver sight-glass level
is in range and head pressure is right for the ambient (a flooded condenser reads high head when overfull).
Don't vent. If the charge history is unknown, recover it all and weigh in the nameplate charge plus the
manufacturer's line-set adjustment, then trim to the subcooling (TXV) or superheat (piston) target — with a
receiver, to the sight-glass level.
causes.safety: R-32, R-454B (A2L) and R-290/R-600a (A3) are flammable — no ignition sources, ventilate, use a rated recovery machine and leak detector, and follow the nameplate before brazing. Pressure-test with nitrogen through a regulator and never above the lowest test pressure on the nameplate; never use air or oxygen. Fill a recovery cylinder to 80 % by weight at most.

causes.name: Air or non-condensables in the system
causes.confirm: With the system off and equalized at a known temperature, the standing pressure is well above the PT chart for that temperature.
causes.fix:
Recover the charge, find how air got in (poor evacuation, a leak on the low side running in vacuum, a
contaminated cylinder), replace the drier, pull a deep vacuum with a decay test, and weigh in fresh
refrigerant (the nameplate charge plus the manufacturer's line-set adjustment). Venting any refrigerant —
CFC, HCFC or HFC — is prohibited, so don't purge off the top of the condenser; recover it.
causes.safety: R-32, R-454B (A2L) and R-290/R-600a (A3) are flammable — no ignition sources, ventilate, use a rated recovery machine and leak detector, and follow the nameplate before brazing. Pressure-test with nitrogen through a regulator and never above the lowest test pressure on the nameplate; never use air or oxygen. Fill a recovery cylinder to 80 % by weight at most.
causes.notes: NIST leaves non-condensables out of its running chart — the standing-pressure test is the clean way to catch it.

causes.name: Wrong or mixed refrigerant
causes.confirm: Standing pressure doesn't match the nameplate refrigerant's PT at a known temperature, and service records or a refrigerant identifier point to a top-off with something else.
causes.fix:
Recover the whole charge into a cylinder marked as mixed/contaminated (it can't be reused), evacuate, and
recharge with the nameplate refrigerant by weight (the nameplate charge plus the manufacturer's line-set
adjustment). Check the oil type matches too.
causes.safety: R-32, R-454B (A2L) and R-290/R-600a (A3) are flammable — no ignition sources, ventilate, use a rated recovery machine and leak detector, and follow the nameplate before brazing. Pressure-test with nitrogen through a regulator and never above the lowest test pressure on the nameplate; never use air or oxygen. Fill a recovery cylinder to 80 % by weight at most.

causes.name: Liquid-line restriction (plugged drier or strainer, kinked line, stuck solenoid or partly closed valve)
causes.confirm: Temperature drop across the drier (3 °F or more) or a frosty/sweaty spot on the liquid line, with high subcooling and high superheat.
causes.fix:
Find the spot where the temperature drops: drier, strainer, solenoid, service valve, kinked or crushed tubing.
Recover or pump down, replace the drier (and core/strainer), straighten or replace the tubing, and check
the solenoid opens fully (coil voltage, stem). Evacuate and recharge with the nameplate charge plus the
manufacturer's line-set adjustment, then trim to the subcooling (TXV) or superheat (piston) target.
causes.safety: R-32, R-454B (A2L) and R-290/R-600a (A3) are flammable — no ignition sources, ventilate, use a rated recovery machine and leak detector, and follow the nameplate before brazing. Pressure-test with nitrogen through a regulator and never above the lowest test pressure on the nameplate; never use air or oxygen. Fill a recovery cylinder to 80 % by weight at most.
causes.notes: NIST SP 1087 found a mild restriction invisible on a TXV unit until the valve ran out of stroke. Sources disagree on the high-superheat + high-subcooling row; a starving TXV and an undersized piston look the same, so check the drier drop and the TXV bulb before condemning anything.

causes.name: Suction line or service valve restricted — valve not back-seated, crushed or kinked line, plugged strainer
causes.confirm: Suction at the compressor is lower than at a gauge on the evaporator side of the suspect point (more than 2–3 psi on medium-temp, about 1 psi on low-temp), or a cold or frosted spot at a service valve or kink. Common right after the system was opened.
causes.fix:
Open the suspect service valve fully (back-seat it, then crack it off the seat for the gauge port). Look for kinks
and crushed tubing, and clean or replace a suction strainer. If the pressure drop is across a drier or filter, replace it.

causes.name: TXV underfeeding — stuck closed, lost bulb charge, plugged inlet screen or ice in the valve
causes.confirm: High superheat and high subcooling with no drop across the drier, and the valve doesn't open when its bulb is warmed.
causes.fix:
Check the bulb is tight and in the right place first. Warm the bulb: no rise in suction means a dead power
head or a stuck valve. Pump down, check the inlet screen, and replace the power head or the valve (match the
refrigerant and capacity). If it works intermittently and the moisture indicator shows wet, moisture is
freezing at the port — replace the drier and evacuate deeply.
causes.safety: R-32, R-454B (A2L) and R-290/R-600a (A3) are flammable — no ignition sources, ventilate, use a rated recovery machine and leak detector, and follow the nameplate before brazing. Pressure-test with nitrogen through a regulator and never above the lowest test pressure on the nameplate; never use air or oxygen. Fill a recovery cylinder to 80 % by weight at most.

causes.name: TXV overfeeding — stuck open, bulb loose or uninsulated, oversized valve or superheat set too low
causes.confirm: Superheat near zero at the evaporator with a sweating or frosted compressor; check the bulb mounting before blaming the valve.
causes.fix:
Re-mount the bulb tight on a clean, straight run of suction line (4 or 8 o'clock on larger lines) and
insulate it. If superheat is still low, turn the adjusting stem clockwise (in) a quarter turn at a time to
raise superheat, waiting 15 minutes between turns; on an EEV, change the controller's superheat setpoint
instead. A valve that won't throttle when the bulb is iced is stuck open — replace it. Liquid floodback
kills compressors, so don't leave it running flooded.

causes.name: Metering orifice too large or piston missing
causes.confirm: Superheat stays low at a correct charge; the piston size stamped on it is larger than the outdoor unit's documentation calls for (common after a coil or condensing unit was swapped).
causes.fix:
Recover, pull the piston and compare the size with the condensing unit's literature (the outdoor unit
decides it). Install the correct piston with a new O-ring/seal, replace the drier, evacuate and weigh in the
nameplate charge plus the manufacturer's line-set adjustment, then trim to the superheat target.
causes.safety: R-32, R-454B (A2L) and R-290/R-600a (A3) are flammable — no ignition sources, ventilate, use a rated recovery machine and leak detector, and follow the nameplate before brazing. Pressure-test with nitrogen through a regulator and never above the lowest test pressure on the nameplate; never use air or oxygen. Fill a recovery cylinder to 80 % by weight at most.

causes.name: Metering device too small or partly plugged (piston or cap tube)
causes.confirm: High superheat and high subcooling with no drier drop; frost right after the metering device; the piston size doesn't match the literature, or the cap tube is kinked or plugged (wax, debris, moisture).
causes.fix:
For a piston: recover, inspect and clean or replace with the correct size. For a cap tube: look for kinks;
a plugged cap tube is replaced (with the drier) or cleared with a cap-tube cleaner by a shop with the right
tool. Evacuate deeply and weigh in the nameplate charge plus the manufacturer's line-set adjustment, then trim
a piston system to the superheat target — cap-tube systems are critically charged, so don't trim them by
gauge readings.
causes.safety: R-32, R-454B (A2L) and R-290/R-600a (A3) are flammable — no ignition sources, ventilate, use a rated recovery machine and leak detector, and follow the nameplate before brazing. Pressure-test with nitrogen through a regulator and never above the lowest test pressure on the nameplate; never use air or oxygen. Fill a recovery cylinder to 80 % by weight at most.

causes.name: Moisture in the system
causes.confirm: Moisture indicator reads wet after the system has run a while; feed comes and goes as ice forms and melts at the metering device.
causes.fix:
Recover the charge, replace the filter-drier (oversize it or add a suction-line drier if acid is
suspected — test the oil), evacuate to 500 microns or lower with a decay test, and recharge with the nameplate
charge plus the manufacturer's line-set adjustment, then trim to the subcooling (TXV) or superheat (piston)
target.
causes.safety: R-32, R-454B (A2L) and R-290/R-600a (A3) are flammable — no ignition sources, ventilate, use a rated recovery machine and leak detector, and follow the nameplate before brazing. Pressure-test with nitrogen through a regulator and never above the lowest test pressure on the nameplate; never use air or oxygen. Fill a recovery cylinder to 80 % by weight at most.

causes.name: Dirty or clogged air filter
causes.confirm: Filter visibly loaded; temperature split high; suction low.
causes.fix:
Replace the filter (and thaw the coil first if it's iced — run the fan only, or heat). Check that the
filter size and MERV rating suit the blower; a too-restrictive filter acts like a dirty one.

causes.name: Dirty evaporator coil
causes.confirm: Matted face on the air-entering side of the coil; high split; low suction.
causes.fix:
Power off. Clean the coil with a coil cleaner and low-pressure water from the leaving-air side (keep water off
the blower motor and control board), straighten fins, and check the drain afterward. Find out why it got
dirty (filter missing, bypass around the filter).

causes.name: Evaporator fan or blower running slow or weak (capacitor, speed tap, dirty wheel, slipping belt, failing ECM)
causes.confirm: Fan turns but moves little air; blower amps low, wheel loaded with dirt, capacitor low, belt slipping or the wrong speed tap selected.
causes.fix:
Test the blower capacitor, clean the wheel, set the right speed tap (or ECM airflow setting), and tension or
replace the belt. Check motor amps against nameplate and the bearings for drag.
causes.safety: Lock out before reaching into a fan or testing a capacitor; discharge the capacitor through a resistor, not a screwdriver.

causes.name: Evaporator fan or blower not running (motor, capacitor, relay, control board or fan delay)
causes.confirm: Fan not turning with a call present. Check voltage at the motor — present means the motor or its capacitor; absent means the relay, board or fan control.
causes.fix:
With voltage at the motor and nothing turning: check the capacitor, spin the shaft for seized bearings,
ohm the windings (and the thermal protector). Without voltage: check the fan relay, board output, door
switch, and fan-delay controls. Thaw the coil before testing the refrigeration side.
causes.safety: Lock out before reaching into a fan or testing a capacitor; discharge the capacitor through a resistor, not a screwdriver.

causes.name: Duct restriction — closed registers or dampers, crushed or undersized duct
causes.confirm: High external static with a clean filter and coil; closed or crushed runs.
causes.fix: Open dampers and registers, repair crushed flex, and add return capacity if the return is undersized.

causes.name: Duct leak or disconnect (return pulling in hot attic or outdoor air, supply dumping into a void)
causes.confirm: Return air at the unit much warmer than the room; a disconnected or torn duct.
causes.fix: Reconnect and seal (mastic or listed tape), and insulate ducts in unconditioned spaces.

causes.name: Heat load more than the unit can handle (very hot or humid day, undersized, extra equipment)
causes.confirm: Pressures high on both sides but in proportion, charge and airflow correct, unit runs nonstop.
causes.fix:
Confirm charge and airflow are right first. Then the fix is load or capacity: shade, seal, cut internal
loads, or a larger unit. On refrigeration, check for warm product loading, door use and failed door heaters
or gaskets.

causes.name: Dirty or blocked condenser coil
causes.confirm: Head pressure high for the outdoor temperature with the fan running, and a matted or dirty coil.
causes.fix:
Power off. Clean from the inside out with coil cleaner and low-pressure water (or brush and vacuum on
fragile fins), comb the fins, and clear debris from around the unit. Re-check head pressure afterwards.

causes.name: Condenser air blocked or recirculating (snow, walls, stacked units, wind)
causes.confirm: The air going into the condenser is warmer than the outdoor air, or the coil is boxed in or drifted over.
causes.fix: Clear snow and debris, open the space around the unit, add baffles or relocate so discharge air can't loop back into the inlet.

causes.name: Condenser fan not running (motor, capacitor, contactor or fan control)
causes.confirm: Compressor running, fan still. Voltage at the fan motor — present means motor or capacitor; absent means the contactor, relay or fan-cycling control.
causes.fix:
Shut the compressor off before head pressure trips it repeatedly. Test the fan capacitor, spin the blade
(seized bearings), ohm the windings, and check voltage at the motor. Replace with matching HP, RPM,
rotation and frame. Check the fan-cycling or head-pressure control if voltage never reaches the motor.
causes.safety: Lock out before reaching into a fan or testing a capacitor; discharge the capacitor through a resistor, not a screwdriver.

causes.name: Condenser fan weak or slow (capacitor, bearings, wrong blade or rotation)
causes.confirm: Fan turns slower than its siblings or than nameplate RPM, wobbles, or blows the wrong way.
causes.fix: Test and replace a weak capacitor, check bearings and blade pitch, correct rotation, and confirm the blade is the right one for the motor.
causes.safety: Lock out before reaching into a fan or testing a capacitor; discharge the capacitor through a resistor, not a screwdriver.

causes.name: Running in cold outdoor air without low-ambient control
causes.confirm: Head pressure low because the outdoor air is cold; the coil ices and suction falls.
causes.fix:
Add or repair a low-ambient kit (fan cycling or fan-speed head pressure control, crankcase heater, low-ambient
thermostat or a hard-start/time-delay as the maker specifies). For year-round cooling loads (server rooms),
use equipment rated for low ambient or an economizer.

causes.name: Compressor not pumping — worn or leaking valves, worn scroll, internal bypass
causes.confirm: Suction high and head low together with low amps; the compressor can't pump down — or, on a non-bleed TXV with the liquid valve closed, pressures equalize within a minute or two after shutdown (a piston, cap tube or bleed-port TXV equalizes by itself, so that proves nothing there).
causes.fix:
Confirm with a pump-down or compressor efficiency test before condemning it, and rule out an open internal
relief valve after a high-pressure event and (on heat pumps) a reversing valve leaking through. On a
three-phase scroll, prove the phase rotation first — a reversed scroll looks exactly like a worn one.
Replace the compressor, the drier (suction drier if it burned), and test the oil for acid.

causes.name: Compressor run capacitor failed (or the HERM side of a dual capacitor)
causes.confirm: Capacitor reads low or open (or is bulged) and the compressor hums and trips on overload — or, when the capacitor is only weak, the compressor starts, runs hot with high amps and trips on its overload.
causes.fix:
Discharge the capacitor through a resistor and replace it with the same µF and equal or higher voltage
rating. If the compressor still won't start on a good capacitor, try a hard-start kit (single-phase only, two
start attempts at most); if that fails, the compressor is locked or a winding is bad.
causes.safety: Lock out before reaching into a fan or testing a capacitor; discharge the capacitor through a resistor, not a screwdriver.

causes.name: Condenser fan capacitor failed (or the FAN side of a dual capacitor)
causes.confirm: Fan hums but doesn't spin (or starts only when pushed); the FAN–C side tests low.
causes.fix: Replace with matching µF and voltage. If the fan was running hot for a while, check the motor bearings too.
causes.safety: Lock out before reaching into a fan or testing a capacitor; discharge the capacitor through a resistor, not a screwdriver.

causes.name: Contactor failed — open coil or burnt contacts
causes.confirm: 24 V on the coil but it won't pull in (open coil); or pulled in with voltage lost across the contacts. A contactor welded closed is its own cause (the unit runs with no call).
causes.fix:
Replace the contactor (match coil voltage, poles and amp rating). Look for why it burned: loose terminals,
a hard-starting compressor, or chattering from low control voltage. Ants and dirt in the contacts are a
classic cause on outdoor units.

causes.name: Contactor welded closed — unit runs with no call
causes.confirm: The compressor and fans run with the call off; the contactor stays in with no 24 V on its coil.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Replace the contactor (match coil voltage, poles and amp rating) and find why it welded: a hard-starting
compressor, loose terminals, low control voltage that made it chatter. Check for an iced coil after a long run.
causes.safety: Lock out; a welded contactor means the unit can start at any moment.

causes.name: A safety in the control circuit is open (pressure switch, float switch, overload pilot, freeze stat)
causes.confirm: The call reaches the unit but the 24 V stops at a safety. Meter across each switch in the circuit — the open one shows 24 V across it.
causes.fix:
Don't just jumper it: a tripped safety is a messenger. High pressure → condenser, fan, charge, air in the
system. Low pressure → charge, restriction, airflow, iced coil. Float switch → clogged drain. Fix the cause,
then reset. Replace a switch only if it's open at normal pressures or levels.

causes.name: Compressor locked or hard to start (mechanical, or pressures not equalized)
causes.confirm: Good capacitor, good windings, good voltage — it still hums at locked-rotor amps and trips.
causes.fix:
Let pressures equalize (TXV systems without a bleed need minutes). Single-phase only: then try a hard-start
kit (start capacitor and relay) sized for the compressor, and limit yourself to two start attempts — each
locked-rotor start heats the winding. On a three-phase compressor check all three legs, the fuses and each
contactor pole first; no hard-start kit exists for it. If it still won't start, replace the compressor — and
find why it failed (floodback, overheating, low oil).

causes.name: Compressor windings open, shorted or grounded
causes.confirm: Ohm readings don't add up (R–S ≠ C–R + C–S), a winding reads open after the compressor has cooled for an hour, or any terminal reads to ground.
causes.fix:
Replace the compressor. A burnout means acid: test the oil, install a suction-line filter-drier (acid
core) and a new liquid drier, flush or clean as needed, evacuate deeply. Check the contactor and capacitor
before starting the new one.
causes.safety: A grounded compressor can blow its terminals out — never energize it to test.

causes.name: Three-phase compressor single-phased — one leg lost (blown fuse, burnt contactor pole, loose lug, utility)
causes.confirm: One pair of legs reads far below the other two, or a leg drops across a contactor pole; a compressor that was running draws high amps on the two good legs and trips its overload.
causes.fix:
Lock out. Work back from the compressor: voltage in and out of each contactor pole, the fuses in the disconnect
(one blown fuse is the classic), lugs and terminals for heat, then the supply. Replace the whole fuse set and any
burnt contactor or lug. Before restarting, meter the windings (T1–T2, T2–T3 and T1–T3 equal, none to ground).
Don't keep re-trying a humming compressor — every locked-rotor start heats the windings.
causes.safety: Lock out; a lost leg can still leave the other two live. Verify dead with a tested meter.

causes.name: Scroll compressor running backwards — phase sequence reversed after power, generator or wiring work
causes.confirm: A phase-sequence tester reads reversed, or the compressor is loud and pumps nothing right after power or wiring work (suction doesn't fall, head doesn't rise).
causes.fix:
Shut it down — a reversed scroll overheats, trips its protector and can fail if left running. Lock out and swap
any two line leads: at the compressor's contactor (load side) if only the compressor is wrong, or at the
disconnect if the fans are backwards too; then check the rotation of every three-phase motor. Confirm with a
rotation meter; suction should fall and head should rise within seconds.
Do not condemn the compressor on this signature until rotation is proven.
causes.safety: Lock out; verify dead before swapping leads.

causes.name: Start capacitor, relay or PTC failed — single-phase compressor hums and won't start
causes.confirm: Run capacitor and windings test good, but the start capacitor is open or low, the relay coil reads open or its contacts are pitted or stuck, or the PTC is open.
causes.fix:
Lock out and discharge the capacitors. Replace the start capacitor, relay or PTC with the exact manufacturer's
part — relay pick-up and drop-out are matched to the compressor, and a wrong relay burns the start winding.
Replace an old run capacitor at the same time. If it still won't start, the compressor is stuck or a winding is bad.
causes.safety: Lock out; discharge capacitors through a resistor before touching them.

causes.name: Compressor overheating and cycling on its internal overload
causes.confirm: The compressor is too hot to touch and its internal overload opens (C–R and C–S open, R–S fine) until it cools.
causes.fix:
It's a symptom — find why it's hot: low charge (high return-gas superheat), high head (dirty condenser,
fan), low voltage, a weak run capacitor, or short cycling. Lock out, then let it cool on its own (the
internal overload resets in 30–60 minutes); a fan on the shell is fine. Fix the root cause before
restarting.
causes.safety: Never spray water on a compressor or its terminal box.

causes.name: Condensate drain clogged (pan full, float switch tripped, water leaking)
causes.confirm: Water standing in the pan or the float switch open; drain line holds water.
causes.fix:
Clear the line (wet-vac from the outside end, or flush), clean the trap and pan, add a pan treatment tablet,
and confirm the float switch resets and actually cuts the unit. Check the trap is primed and the line slopes.

causes.name: Short cycling from controls (thermostat placement or differential, oversized unit)
causes.confirm: Pressures normal and no safety trips; the control satisfies within minutes (stat in a supply-air path, sun, near a door; controller differential too tight), or the unit is oversized.
causes.fix: Move or shield the sensor, widen the differential or set minimum on/off times, add an anti-short-cycle delay. An oversized unit needs staging or a smaller unit.
